Played the first Portal of course! Great game and storyline. Thought I'm very late on Portal 2. It's been out for a long time now and I waited for a good time to buy. Purchsed it on sale for a good deal. (Even better then the Summer Sale price)
I was very pleased with the puzzles and gameplay in the first one so I did not watch any trailers or youtube any game play for Portal 2 because I knew I was going to enjoy the game no matter what. I'm very glad I finally made the purchse. Portal 2 was a short game like the first one but the storyline was truly awesome and I felt like my life was complete after seeing how it ended.
I did like the fact that the game play was changed around a bit as in the "Paint" aspect of it. Threw me off guard with some of the solving. Had to think a little deeper to progress forward. I think i raged maybe a total of three times? Took a break then came back.
I beat the game within 10 hours to be exact. Same exact hours it took for Portal 1.
To be fair and defend the shortness of Portal 2. I must say Valve added alot of goodies and extras to enjoy. Such as creating your own test chamers and making blue prints to upload to the community for others to play.
Portal 2 also has an online Coop. You and a friend to tackle the test chamers.

A concept that has potential for both good and ill. Fun, asymmetrical gameplay (you never know just what kind of bots will be on your/the enemy team) is hindered by what feels like dev inexperience (questionable balance choices) and a moderately steep learning curve, which you might not expect from what appears on the surface to be a rather simple game.
Progression in the game is achieved via four metrics:
1) Player level, which determines your max CPU, which is a constraint system that limits how many parts you can equip on your robot. Higher level = more CPU = you can equip more, higher level parts.
2) Tech points, which is a currency you earn by defeating (keyword; you must land a killing blow in order to rack up TP) which is spent in the 'tech tree' to unlock the ability to purchase more powerful parts.
3) Robo Points, which is a currency you earn by basically doing anything during a match and is used in the shop to purchase parts you've unlocked in the tech tree.
4) Your 'tier', which is influenced by the sum of all 'rating' stats on every part your robot is made of. Tiers go from 1-10 and serve as a means of keeping matches fair (you only compete against bots that are in your tier) and also determines what tech tokens you earn in matches. (I.e. in order to unlock tier 3 parts, you need tier 3 tech points, which are earned from competing in tier 3 matches)
The aforementioned learning curve rears its head in a few ways. None of what I described above is taught to you by the game. It also does nothing to teach you how to build a good bot, or even let you experiment with parts before buying them; you have to spend your resources to unlock and buy parts, and ~then~ figure out how they fit (For example, higher level guns are physically larger than lower level guns) and function after the fact.
Nor does it teach you gameplay mechanics such as how to 'spot' enemies, how radar jammers work, how bots are destroyed, etc.
tl;dr: It's a fun game, but the learning curve may frustrate newer players, and the questionable balance may frustrate players who stick with it. But they're adding new stuff to the game fairly regularly and it's quite possible everything I wrote here will be outdated by the time you read this.

Portal 2's biggest flaw is that it is not made for people who played the first game. In fact, Portal 2 is even easier than Portal. I finished Portal multiple times and completed all of the advanced chambers (though not all of the challenges) and I wanted to play a game that is made for someone like me.
The game is easier than Portal for mainly the following two reasons: the places where you can put portals on are much more limited here. And secondly, there are no reflexes needed to solve any of the puzzles. This not only takes the reflexive skills out of the game, it also reduces the complexity of the puzzles.
In Portal you always have to take into account that you might need to shoot two portals in a very short time frame. In Portal 2 you realize pretty soon that the game never expects something like that from you and therefor you never have to think about possible solutions to puzzles that involve reflexes.
All of the new mechanics are a welcome addition and fit very well. Overall everything about this game is well done. Good controls, nice graphics and sound, interesting puzzles. It's clear that these developers are very talented.
What is sad to see is that Valve seems to be going the Nintendo way: they make games for everyone. Portal 2 is not a game made for people who loved Portal and wanted a more complex, difficult game. It's a dumbed down sequel with some nice new elements that can't hide that fact.
The humour, one of the strengths of Portal, is still here, but feels forced sometimes. Another small problem are the loading times. After every cleared chamber you have to wait a couple seconds before you can continue playing, which can get annoying.

This game made me appreciate what video games are supposed to be, what they once were.  A good challenge. Most games nowadays are made to be beaten easily, so you will want more, but this game stretched my imagination to unimaginable lengths. It made me think, not to mention the amazingly well thought out story that kept me entertained throughout the whole game, as well as making me want more. Portal 2 was a truly amazing experience that made me love it characters and all their well thought out depth, and made me think in ways that, in our day and age, are not possible.
This is the BEST game ever made and it is what all video game developers should judge their games off of, as it is what all video games should be.

What else can be said that hasn't been already? Challenging puzzles, charming humor, and an engaging story make this a great game for anyone's collection. I reccommend playing Portal 1 first to get the most from the story.

this is the greatest game that is free to play in existance, in my oppinion. and to think its in beta. i was able to build a tie fighter and a star destroyer. this game has caused me to even start a youtube series on it. it is free top play, and free to win. they had minor problems with eac but it accomplished its purpose. i have been with this game for longer than it has been on steam and i have seen so many improvements and i bet this game will continue to improve.
the only thing you can buy with your real money is some pree-made bots, garage slots, and cosmetic parts, making it not free to play. the pree-made bots may save time, but they do not garentee a win, they are only ok bots, you can probably build an easier one yourself. if you do spend money on this game, i have spent about 10$, you will find that it goes a long way because there is not a lot you can do. paying money may help you progress faster, but you can play the game forever and never pay a dollar.
this game is going to be a very popular game as soon as the public release comes out, as it is seeing simalar people playing the beta as minecraft PE did. this game may be early acess but it plays like a fully developed game. it is very impressive that this game was made by such a small group of devolpers, i think 12 right now but they started out with just 6 people.
robocraft takes feedback from the players, and that is sometimes the only downside of the game. they take the feedback, and sometimes nerf things that shoudn't be nerfed.
cheaters used to be problem but eac solved that problem and now it is very rare and very hard to hack robocraft at all.
now for the only downsides.
the comunity. i am sory, but as this game gets popular it gets a lot of bad people on the community. however, there are always peacekeepers like me who will try and keep the kiddy's from crying to hard.
also, the gamemakers seem to have devolped this, assumption, that if you are a t-10 player, than you are a good one, which is not at all. i am probably a better player and for sure a more creative one than probably 70% of the playerbase, but i am at teir 5 because i am always building robots, which drains resorces. robocraft even had the nerf to make colored chat only available at t-6
there were few things that the old version of this game had perfect, and those were the low teir parts. this game used to have low teir electroplates, wings, rails, everything. but the devs removed them to try and force people up in teirs
now to wrap this guide up i will take you through a brief history of robocraft
in march of 2013 the first downloadable demo came out. you could build robots from a set of limited types of parts and than drive it around. no multiplayer or other bots. no weapons
than in april they came out with more types of weels
soon after they came out with the cube depot
then in may, they came out with ai bots, which was big for the game and made it so you weren't quite so lonley
and then something bigger came, lazars, so you could fight the ai bots. it added a enitre new aspect to the game. those are the smgs that we have now.
then they added new thrusters
they then remade the mars map and added a day/night cycle, which they don't have today
then they made it so the ai bots fought back, which added some competition to the game, kind of
soon, they added enemy radars and, the rp colector, which was removed eventually. also the tech tree was added
then, the most amazing thing for the game yet happened, multiplayer gaes. it was a lot different from today, they had only a certain amount of battles each day with a countdown on the top. also, battles were deathmatches
they then added a daily bonus of 1000rp
at this point there were 2 major problem with the game, guns couldn't point up, and there were no limits on bot size.
they fixed both of these by adding the robot ranking system to limit lag bots and then they made it so you could look up
this was the first time player levels were used for something
then they added the premium galaxy cash and redid the robot teir system
then the next big thing was here, the garage. you could now build more than one bot. you had 3 garage slots and you could buy more for gc
then they added another mars map and hoverblades, which added even more types of movement
then they made higher teir weapons have more armor   (armor blocks still didn't exist)
they changed from deathmatch to the made we have now, 2 bases. this was to try and make people use teamplay
then they added the s types with are now the in between levels of items
back in those days there were 5 levels of weapons, with the stypes in between the levles
then they added the ability to sell your cubes
they then added in game chat and premium accounts, which granded 50% more moen yand early access to new features
next armor was added, and then buffed many times
next the ice plannet was added, only 1 map though. also, you now had register for robocraft and have your account activated. there was a limit on how many could be registered per day so the servers could still handel it
next they added platoons
they were testing mega bots at this time
next plasma cannons were added to add some weapon diversety
in a little while robocraft was on steam, after being greenlit in 5 days
they got a new dev added to their team as well
now the minimap was added now is is april 2014, game has already existed over a year
they added another devolper and rail cannons, except they had infinse range and were muuch different from today
they made the tech tree the hex one it is today and they added areofoils
they added a new ice map and redid the repair system so it auto repaired, but it took time and didn't cost you money. this was eventually removed
they added a lot soon after, including electroplates, and a new map
they then reached 1 million users
robocraft  then added spotting and the robo-shop
then, robocraft was made available on mac and linux
now wre recent new. robocraft came out with rise of the walkers and added both the walker legs and nano guns
then robosheild came up, caused a lot of probems but most are fixed right now
then most recently they came out with wolf fest adding overwold support
that is the history of robocraft until today, it has improved so much and will keep improving i highly recomend this game as it will most certainly be the next big thing

UPDATE:
Almost Solstice 2014 and still playing..  still a great game.
I don't know if others feel the same but...    the lower tiers, say through T-4 robots, provided some of the funniest moments I've ever had in gaming...
then around T-5 things begin to switch, become a little more serious..   still a blast, but a different kind of enjoyment.
Now that I've maxxed out my tech tree, I've been going back to mid and low levels exploring other ideas on bot construction.   Sometimes I'm seriously trying to come up with something kick♥♥♥♥♥.    and others..  well, I'm just being playful, going with whatever random idea comes to mind.
Two reccomendations for new players...  One: go slow-ish, focus on having fun more than winning.    Two: Buy a bot with a high CPU value (it'll bump up your cpu permanently, do this early if you're thinking about it)...  it's a great way to support the devs and it'll help you out w/o being a play-to-win kinda bs.    (If you have more money to burn, I'd go with "premium" over buying higher components.)
I can't wait to see what the devs bring as they flesh things out.

Portal was innovative for its time. Escape Aperture Laboratories by solving puzzles with a gun that shoots interdimensional rifts in space-time. Portal 2 is just like that, except with more plot development.

A great game; I absolutely loved the graphics, soundtrack, storyline, and the two new features: Co-op and Community test chambers! Portal was cool, but the sequel is something else altogether.
: I strongly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys puzzles, first-person shooters, plot-twists, and witty humor.
Edit: It's been 5 years since this sequel came out, and in that time, its fanbase has created some of the most amazing, inspiring, heartwrenching, and innovative fanart, test chambers, mods, and fanfiction surrounding a game that I have ever seen (i.e. Blue Sky, Portal Stories: Mel). Robocraft is a video game.  It is a video game you play with your hands and your eyes...and possibly other body parts, although I'm not exactly sure.  This game is available on Steam.  It is free to download and play as you please, but you can choose to pay for it if you want to.  You build the robots with blocks.  Robots start off on wheels, but can gain the ability to fly over time.  You use them to fight other robots, which will give you points to buy more blocks. Buying more blocks allows you to improve your robot so you can fight other robots to buy more blocks.  Buying more blocks allows you to rise up on tiers.  Tiers permit you to fight stronger robots so you can buy better blocks.  The higher your tier, the more challenging the game becomes.  You can also pay for blocks with real money, but this doesn't provide you with any particular advantage because you have to unlock stronger blocks by fighting more robots.  There are only 2 types of levels: desert and ice. Apparently these are the safest places for robots to fight each other because there are no humans to be potentially hurt by the damages of robot fighting, which is interesting considering you are a human piloting the robot and when you are killed, you seem to be okay and your robot automatically repairs itself.  You can make friends playing this game and form platoons.  Platoons are groups of friends that build robots and fight together.  Being on different tiers does not even out gameplay, and joining a platoon with people on higher tiers will put you in fights with other high-tiered robots and you will die easily.  You can also build multiple robots and sell them.  You can buy completed robots for real money, but this would take the fun out of a game that encourages you to build your own robots.  This game is still in beta stage and continues to improve with time.  It also has an anti-cheat system that some players find invasive.  Some people find this game entertaining.  Some do not.

Great game when it works. The only problem with this game is that it doesn't work half of the time. The game randomly decides to kick you from the match and you are removed from the match. The game shows that all the enemies are frozen in place.  You can still move all around the map and shoot stuff but has no effect on the real game. Funny thing is that you can still chat with your team while you wait for the match to be done.
I think this has to do with the lack of rubberbanding mechanic. The server basically tells all the players where all allies and enemies are at all times regardless of fog of war. This gives people plenty of opportunity to cheat. Robocraft decided to remedy this problem via a 3rd party anticheat software that kicks you from the game if your game is not totally in sync with the server. The side effect this is that you get kicked for even small ping spikes on your internet connection.

It's really two games. One is a sequel to Portal, and it's a funny, if short, plot-driven adventure. It's as superbly written as ever, though perhaps with a broader approach to comedy than its darker, more laser-guided predecessor. It's satisfying as a puzzle game, though I don't think it goes as far with its new mechanics as it should do. The second game is a masterful linear co-op puzzle experience, with some of the most devious, brain-wracking, death-defying challenges in a videogame. What would be endlessly frustrating in singleplayer becomes a light, fun, only occasionally murderous fun-with-friend time. Two brains are better than one, after all. Well. Sometimes.
Sadly, I can't really recommend Portal 2 unless you can play the co-op sections with a friend who hasn't already played it. The singleplayer is cool, but it's ultimately the less fulfilling of the two campaigns. The game's mod scene, mind, may well make up for it, as a post-release user level editor is easy-to-use and has resulted in a bevy of player-created test chambers that should, if nothing else, keep you occupied for a long time.
It's Portal except a longer and more fleshed out single-player experience, an online co-op mode with many player created levels as well as new mechanics. It's a lot of fun!

For example, I made a small frame, then filled it with helium tanks and mortars, then proceded to bomb the crap out of everyone without them knowing I was even there. But then came an update. The real issue with this game is how boring it starts out. You start with basic bricks, some basic wheels, and some basic laser guns. Now, on paper, this would be really fun, but everything has so much weight to it that if you try to deviate even a little bit outside of a set of designs that actually work, you're going to send a lot of games upside down completely unable to play for the entire battle.
I know that there is helium and hoverblades later in the game, but slogging through all those boring matches just to unlock the ability to not flip over every game is maddening.
Speaking of which, as much as this game acts like it's a creative build and battle, it really isn't. Along with the issues above, very few designs will do next to anything in battle. I sat there for hours trying to build some new creative effective thing, and it never worked. Each and every game, easily destroyed by one of the 'meta' designs.

Okay, so I think 61 hours on this game is enough to judge it, it's pretty well executed and reasonably polished for an indie game, the gameplay is pretty good, and the rewards definitely feel worth it, however, it should be noted that there's always a chance you'll be dropped into a game with terrible people. The kind that use high powered weapons on small, weak vehicles, this allows them to join lower level games with hideously overpowered weapons. They usually also play with helium that allows them to reach otherwise unreachable parts of the map, sniping you from afar while the game's 'meh' draw distance leaves it impossible to hit them regardless of skill. Oh and you'll likely die from one shot when this happens.
So basically, the game is entertaining and all, lots of fun when you're in a good game, but the balancing is pretty awful, and plasma bombers are probably the most overpowered invention since the Dirty Bomb. Flying vehicles are everywhere, 80% of the time piloted by those that are prone to sniping on COD, you know, annoying children that are so desperate to be different (by flying) that they all end up doing it making the game extremely unbalanced and sometimes infuriating.
But all in all, this game is great, especially good for an Alpha game, ranking up and making your robot bigger is a very rewarding experience, but how you rate this game all depends on the people you end up playing with.

I was curious about this game, but also sceptical, because I've always been that action shooting and killing guy so I didn't have high hopes for this game. So I tried this game at a friends house and that got me really curious. It cost below 4 euro and I thought hell, let's do it. I fell in love instantly.
I can't specifically describe what I liked the most, maybe because I liked it all, but the thing I felt first time ever in my life for a video game, was the love and dedication the creators have put into it. I could FEEL the seriousness with which the game was created with. I have been playing games since very young and this was practically the first time i felt like this playing a game. It isn't this factory stuff like COD, thats being pumped out every year just for the sake of it. The closest I've got was with Starcraft 2. It's like handycraft vs some plastic junk that has little value.
The voiceacting is out of this world. The converasations feel alive and colourful, even if the player ever says any lines. It has been made so belivable, you get lost in the  emotions and jokes and everything. 10/10 the voiceacting.
The graphics are top notch. While being a little under COD standards graphic wise, a good game is a game in which the player looses himself into the game and forgets about all this technical crap. Besides, the player can tell the level details are extreme. From epic constructions to little offices, everything has huge amounts of detail in it that its astonishing.
Story is interesting and the characters feel hugely alive, even the robots are made feel alive. There is a good balance between humor and seriousness. And the epic voice acting only boosts the experience. I feel a little though that the story was a bit short, but I think its in an excellent balance in the storytelling and gameplay. I maybe even wish there was a bit more cutscenes, other than the beginning and the ending, because Valve is so good at those.
The soundtrack was well-fit within the levels, there was quality music, loved the ending song. Especially liked when the music changed when doing different things, like jumping, running on the speed-boosting orange gel etc.
The puzzles were increasingly hard, but not hard enough for me to cheat with some webpage. They were nicely fit into the story and environment, I didn't once had a feeling something was forced into the scene.
With this game I looked more into the story and environment of the game. I enjoyed the scenery this game had to offer and the amazing voiceacting and soundtrack it had. I also enjoyed the puzzle solving and I think it ended just nicely and it didn't get repetitive. And I haven't even looked at the workshop contributions yet, so the fun doesn't end here. This also fixes the problem, when for somebody there wasn't enough puzzle stages.
I think Portal 2 is a must-play game for a proper gamer, even when he doesn't really like these kind of games. I recommend this game for the passion Valve has shown in developing it. It's like an artistic masterpiece everybody should know about.

Portal 2 is a great game. There really is a lot to love here.
-- User generated content makes for a very attractive extra. If you don't care about it, then no harm done. If you want more puzzles after the story mode, however, then you are covered.
-- Coop is there as its own entity, meaning if you are a solo-gamer like me, then it won't affect your experience. It's also a nice extra that adds something without taking away from anything
-- Gameplay is fresh and the portal mechanic is really fun. No other game really uses this mechanic as a core component of gameplay.
-- Music is fantastic. Music is something i typically don't notice. Portal, however, is an exception, Every track is memorable and enjoyable. Even the ambiance noise is nice to listen too.
-- Great characters (for what few there are). GLaDOS and Weatley are very memorable characters.
There are a lot of reasons to pick up this game. The game was made by Valve, and shows a level of polish and quality we rarely see today; even years after it's been out, it's still a great game. This game has so few flaws, it's hard to think of anything aside from nitpicking. This game is one of my favorite games, as it is for so many others. Give it a bash: it's cheap, habitually on sale, and inclusive for gamers of any gender or age (within reason. If they can beat a stage in Super Mario, then can probably play this).
Has to be the third or fourth time that I have completed this game, and I will be back for more again. Heartily recommended

A great improvement to Portal 1. Which means this game is really good, because Portal 1 was still very fun.
Portal 1 was mainly fun because it introduced (at least, I haven't heard of any earlier games with this) the concept of shooting two portals to complete levels. You shoot two portals, walk through one, come out the other. It's a fairly simple concept, but it opens all kinds of new puzzles. However, a downside of Portal 1 was that the average gamer would pretty much be done playing it after finishing the campaign, because there wasn't much more to offer. And the campaign wasn't very long.
This is where Portal 2 shines. The main new feature is the level editor, where you can create your own test chambers. And if you aren't very creative with creating test chambers, Steam Workshop has thousands of test chambers created by other users. So you'll probably never run out of puzzles. Also, the campaign is longer, so that is good as well.
In summary, if you enjoyed Portal 1, get this. If you haven't played Portal 1, you should still try it out; maybe get it at a Steam sale since it goes on sale often. You'll probably like Portal 2 no matter what genres you enjoy. 4/5 stars.

I played this game for a while, reached T10 and made a donation. A few weeks ago the problem of cheaters became the top priority. It was hardly a match without one. Reporting them didn't change much, there were detailed instructions on the net allowing any elementary kid to cheat.
At first dev's implemented server-side protection, which caused lots of issues when players could not actually play. Insted of working on the fixes, they do what? They implement a very doubtful 'solution' called EAC, causing even more players to not able to play.
For me it says "EAC is not able to run in windows Test mode"
I have Win x64 and have some modded audio drivers and some unsigned drivers for a legacy WiFi chip allowing it to run as virtaul AP. Disabling the test mode is currently not an option for me. Never ever I had a problem with this from, say, VAC or any other anti-cheat engine.
So what? I go to their forum and find out that not only they are aware of the problem, they doesn't plan on fixing it at all! Their argument is: "There are not that many people who need this, ok, we might block some legit players, but it's not a problem. They better buy themselves some new hardware. Or new version of windows. Or something. We don't care".
This somehow resembles an approach of executing innocent people along with the criminals without proper investigation - what's the problem? They won't be able to complain anyways. It's that kind of logic.
Create a VM or another boot record allowing you play this game you say? I might do that one day, because I like the game itself. I might even try to spoof EAC check for test mode. But a whole situation when a legit player have to hack anticheat to actually play _without_ cheats is wrong on soooo many levels.
Not only that, reading ito this EAC reveals it's invasive and pivacy violating nature.
Read the ToS.
The notorious "False Positive" alert from some of the AV vendors is not that much false as you can think. The EAC posess keylogging functionality and according to ToS you allow them to gather unspecified private data form you. Great, what's next? Charge my bank accounts directly for false cheating accusations?
Unfortunatelly, early access games combined with Free-to-play game model have one major drawback. There is no way a player can influence the changes devs make or have their money back EVEN if the game becomes broken beyond repair.
I really regret I have to put a negative mark for this game, but I find it the only way to let devs know I don't approve of their way of dealing with loyal player base. Sincirely hope the Dev's drop this horrible EAC stuff ASAP and forget it like a nightmare.
PS: Tech support finally sent me a reply (after 5 days) saying something like "We're working to fix this." Hope this is something more than a canned response.
PPS: Ended up with the dual boot to play. Never added any eclusions for my AV on this and would never do.

Firstly, yes, don't listen to what others say, this is pay to win in the late game when things start to really unlock, and they use a lot of clear tactics to get you to use micro trasnactions.
The game enough is fun, but many of the games progession aspects and gameplay aspects are centred around getting you  to pay to win with micro transactions, at at a certain point in the game it almost requires you to pay real money for some in game currrency to continue. There is a major lack of balance in how you are awarded with progression, because whenever you die you are considered to have lost, wether your team wins or not, and you are severly punished in points awarded when you do, and most pople dont end up surviving in the game on either side. It all feels like an even bigger ploy to get you to use mircrotransactions, as they are the only way to make up for the punishment and to keep up with the people paying to win. On top of that you are now forced to use your in game awarded currency to repair your vehicle, which you are severley hemoraged on when you die, and by the time your in level 7 or 8 every game in which you die you will need to auto spend more point than you get, forcing you at some point to literally need to pay to continue, as stated above. All of this games actions feel like tricks to try and get you to pay continuous money, like giving you a small amount of the pay to get currency when you start to get you hooked, EXACTLY like a drug dealer giving the first taste for free, because you need to come back (and I have a strong feeling that exactly what they thought about when implementing it)
The game quickly losses its fun in later teirs when everythings finally starting to unlock, and you just sit angry unless you drop 15 bucks very often (also as you get into later tiers it requires MORE real money to do what you did before, meaning you neeed to pay a climbing rate at the same frequncey)
Do not buy this, if it was something you just bought and was a normal game this would be great, but this whole game is a set up for micro trasnactions and pay to win, don't give sharks like this your support.

This game is not finished yet, it got some bugs, and there are some features I would love too see in this game. But is a game allready worth playing.
Lets build a tank and start to shoot others, its that simple,... or is it? Loose a wheel, get stuck with all wheels from the floor, or flip over, shoot and get shot/killed. Then improve your vehicle, and bounce back in the fight too take your vengance out on people again. And that is in a nutshell what for me the game is all about.
But only wheels and guns? Nope, 4 types of weapons that will all look/feel different and so something else. And wheels? you also got, legs, hoverblades, lighter then air blocks, and jet engines all at your disposal eventually.
The good:
- Its free to play and not pay to win, and even though there is a shop inside, there is nothing in the shop that is stronger than what you can get/build yourself eventually.
- There is a way to speed up your progres (with stuff in the shop or premium) but out of experience I can say that you DO NOT NEED any of this to get too the highest tier and/or get stuff done in any tier.
- Its amusing, its simple, got some depth, and is enjoyable.
- You start with only limited building blocks, and with the tiers your unlock all other stuff.
The bad:
- Graphics are, not top notch.
- Bugs and glitches do occur. (though I only notices a few)
- Hackers, though with easyanticheat, it should be less.
- It can be a bit repetitive...
Not good/not bad things in the game.
- People who buy a big vehicle in the store, like the t7 scorp, will get a headstart in experience, this can be considered pay to win, but anyone getting into the high lvls will eventually get to that point.
- Its possible to get in low tier fights with relatively high tier guns, for lol and giggles, though this is not allways fun for a beginning player.
So for anyone who read this far, try the game, its free. It should not dissapoint, and if so,.. you only wasted some time, and a few mouse clicks.

I have to confess to being behind the times when it comes to computer games. I haven’t played PC games for a long time, and my consoles are behind a generation or two. So when I finally got to play
, I had to admit to being excited. I’d played parts of both
games on a friend’s computer, but had never gotten to play it all the way through.
However, the experience was worth it.
combines the usually violent paradigm of first person shooters with puzzle-based gameplay, and adds a story that, while not particularly complex, is nonetheless entertaining, with a massive streak of dark humour that manages to make you laugh far more than it makes you cringe. There are even a few small twists and turns here and there. The small voice cast is used effectively, with Ellen McLain as the acerbic GlaDOS, Stephen Merchant as the endearing, if idiotic, Wheatley, and JK Simmons as the enthusiastically sociopathic Cave Johnson acting out their bizarre and unusual roles with aplomb.
It may seem boring and trite to praise a game that has had almost universal praise and more than a little hype, but it’s one of those games that deserves virtually total acclaim. I can’t say that the portal-based gameply is completely innovative, given that it was its immediate predecessor (as well as
) that broke first ground, but it still feels fresh amongst a panoply of FPSes. The gels add a new dimension to the game as well, forcing people to start thinking with gels as much as they were forced to start thinking with portals.
The puzzles can be frustrating at times, but it’s the good kind of frustrating, the frustration that leads to ‘
’ (as Ben ‘Yahtzee’ Croshaw of
once put it) once you overcome the obstacles. The graphics are beautiful, even when they’re showing the grottier parts of Aperture, and the sound effects and music all contribute to the whole atmosphere.
If I have to make a complaint, it’d be that the game is too short. Funnily enough, the story just goes on long enough, managing to not overstay its welcome, but I feel mildly let down by a game that seemed to have a bit more potential to go on. Maybe it’s because I won’t be doing the co-op mode or the Perpetual Testing Initiative, at least not for some time, that I feel slightly let down. But this is a relatively minor quibble for a game that is entertaining, enjoyable, and very darkly funny.
In short,
is certainly on the must-have list for any PC gamer. This has doubtless been said before, but it’s a point that nonetheless can be reiterated.
: ****½

Robocraft? Yes I played and yes, I recommend it, almost to the point of a hidden gem. I also say it has no Pay-To-Win. Why? Read on…
The game as a whole is very well done, well balanced, but might need some tweaking. You see, in here you make robots (they have a pilot but anyways…) , make the best one out of the blocks you have available and test it out against other players. The game’s physics engine allows for a large variety of robots. And you’re rarely pulled back by a pre-built part of your robot. Have a normal tank with a crapton of frontal armor, a guy with spider legs and wings, a bomber, a flying fortress and a landship. The choice is yours, block by block.
You have a limited amount of blocks to place (CPU) so you’re force to optimize the most you can, and in later Tiers, more blocks become available to you to further customize your creation.
One setback is that people often don’t realize what is the goal of designing a bot is to have the best possible fighter and not the best possible stick on wheels that snaps with a single bullet, making people rage quit and calling stuff OP. I personally tried playing in all three offensive classes (SMG/Sniper/Launcher(Not the actual real name but I used these here for better understanding.)) . As far as I know, none of them kicks the other out like cannon fodder as each one has weaknesses and strengths.
Imagine, your robot always gets destroyed in a single situation. Like a sniper, manages to always shred a wheel off or a launcher wrecks the whole front armor.  What you do? You build with those players in mind and with some luck and inspiration; you will withstand twice as many hits in battle.
The game is about building the best possible robot that works the best with your way of playing. And you also have to work with your team against the other enemy team to either wipe them out or capture the point. The reward system is well balanced, with giving a cut if you get in action; assists are valued similarly to kills. Even if you don’t kill anything, doing damage alone or helping capture the point will earn you techpoints and RP(The game’s currency).
Now the currency: RP, is what you use to buy stuff, useful stuff only. Blocks, guns, anything that has some role in the bot goes, even the headlights, which can be used to blind snipers at you. Techpoints, the game’s tech currency which you use to research stuff to get to higher tiers (will get to that in a moment.) . Techpoints are based on tiers, so if you’re a T2, you will get T2 techpoints and research some T3 stuff and all of T2, but not T1. Galaxy cash, the game’s premium currency, can be used to buy almost everything; you can buy every block, cosmetics, Premium (more on dat later), and Uber techpoints which can be used for every Tier(The research is a tree so you still need to unlock lower tier stuff before the high tier.), you can only make those if you have normal T1,T2,T3,etc. to turn, as you can’t make them out of thin air, it also puts leftover techpoints from old tiers to use. Galaxy cash can also be used to buy extra garage slots (3 are available for free), and Pre-Built robots.
So where’s the Pay-To-Win? Nope, there isn’t much of that there. Money simply speeds up your progression. it doesn’t make you abnormally stronger to the normal guy. Premium simply put adds another “private team” slot and doubles your techpoint and RP earnings each fight.
The stronger your robot gets (more blocks, more powerful weapons, better gadgets). Will automatically be matched to robots of similar strength, aka Tiers, represented by a bar on the bottom of the garage screen. I personally never met a higher Tier In a normal match, and if I had, there would be a handicap bonus to make up for it. The goal is to get to T10 and get the hottest merchandise available. From T8 forward you get access to the second of the two game’s modes. Boss fight, you play solo against 15 more or less lower Tiers. According to RNG, you as a lower Tier T2-T6 will be paired against one or more robots if you choose the normal match, this is random and fairly uncommon. If there are multiple bosses, the Tiers of players will automatically rise to balance it out.
The game also has 5? maps that are fairly well designed and stimulate a lot of different tactics to win, benefiting all types of robots in some way.
Heard the good? Now for the bad stuff…
The game even though has 5? Maps, there are only two themes, making the look always the same, snow and desert. More themes would alleviate this issue.
The game can be harsh for beginners as I mentioned before. I had to read multiple guides to figure out why my robot was failing so badly. And if you don’t have a decent imagination or be bad at making bots, you will lose, badly. The physics engine is also , kinda glitchy. Noticeably in lower tiers, where you would jump sky high from a tiny bump, and when flipped, not even the whole team could flip you back on your wheels like if you weighted the same as an aircraft carrier.
The game is an alpha, aka, glitches, bugs, bugs and more bugs. They range from connection issues, to missing blocks and worse.
In higher Tiers, getting RP and techpoints becomes a grind. A block costs a small fortune and guns an arm and a leg. Fortunately, after T8, the Boss fight game mode is there alleviate this issue, if successful, you’ll rack up insane amounts of RP and Techpoints… Which is all used up in buying a single gun. If you can afford, it would be a decent idea to get a premium to ease the grind.
Overtiering(T4 guns in a T2 match) is a thing, however this is debatable, as the robots are mostly glass cannons, like a buggy with a friggin huge cannon that it’s bigger than it.
Glitchy collision meshes in blocks, terrain and other things.
The music isn’t legend, but it isn’t bad either.
The matchmaker glitches up on occasion, leaving single Tiers with 500 players waiting for a game. Usually lasts for ten minutes or so.
Only 2 game modes can sometimes make it a little boring, even though they’re good, there are just two and one of them you get randomly if you’re under a T7 or with a 10 hour cool down with T8 and above.
With that said, I conclude my encyclopedia of the game in review form. If you like making stuff and shredding it in battle, or making chirurgic strikes in the enemy robots or team. Then this is the game for you. With no Pay-To-Win, and it’s possible to get to T10 for free.

Portal 2 is an UNMATCHABLE game. One of my own personal favorites.
Pros:
+ Various game elements
+ Exciting and intriguing story, even if you are new to games in general its easy to get into the plot and its also hilarious.
+ Proper difficulty that rises as you go further into the story
+ Content that lasts for a couple of hours, even more if you have a friend to play COOP-with.
+ Surpport steam workshop wich adds tons of more maps and puzzles.
+ It's portal
Cons:
- What else do you want ?!
Though it is redundant to write a review for such a famous game, I just cannot surppress my passion for it.
Portal2, similar to its precedent, is a first-person physics-based puzzle game. The player need to solve different puzzles in chambers, by using a special gun, a "portal gun" and interacting with various game elements. Compared with Portal 1, Portal 2's world is bigger, story thicker, and the character development more surprising and fun. The jokes and sarcasms from two robots, GLaDOS and Wheatley, make this interesting game a really intresting one, Besides, what surprised me is that the single-player mode is only the game's first half, and the multi-players mode provides players a even more interesting and challenging experience. Also, surpporting Steam Workshop greatly increases Portal2's re-playability.
But the advantages above are still insufficient to make Portal 2 a masterpeice. As a puzzle game, what disdinguishs Portal 2 from others is its ABILITY TO COMBINE. Firstly, there is a common drawback among other puzzle games: fragmented story. It is very hard to write a continuous story when puzzle-types are the same, for the repetition greatly weakens the reality. To solve it, most puzzle game choose to write a fragmented but poetic story. Therefore, players need to create the whole story by themselves from bits and pieces. Portal2 not only has a continuous story, but also connects every puzzle logically.  Portal 2 combines an element of action with puzzles. During the game, player will experience escape, exploration and even more stuff (dont want to add any major spoilers) Although its topic is puzzles-solving, players can still enjoy an exciting adventure. Thus, due to its continunous story and action element, actually I prefer classifying Portal 2 as a action-adventure game to a puzzle game. Even though you could say that the COOP-part adds more of a puzzle-challenge.
In conclusion, Portal2 is a unmatchable game which will be remembered forever. It is concise, it is intriguing, it is a instant classic. And you should play this game right now if you havent already.

This is what happens when world of tanks and minecraft are put together. You get a game that you can literally create whatever you want, be it a tank or a flying fortress.
Imagine this: you are new to this game, and you don't know what to build. You start out with tier one, and come up with something to build. You flip over 5 seconds in the game because you made it to narrow or wide. You see a guy in a giant mortar platform, or an X-wing, and you get killed. You go back and you start thinking smart, improving your design. You try it and it works somewhat, but you still flip over or burn out in the middle of the game and get killed by the same guy. And finally, you build something that works, and you start getting better. You get to higher tiers and you start putting shields and mech legs on your creation. You fight the same guy you fought before with the improved X-wing, and 3/4 of your creation is gone, but you win against him. You win the match with only one weapon, a few wheels or hoverblades, 3/4 of your vehicle gone and you go the enemy base and win the match. You go back you your mothership and you look at your masterpiece. Your creation. Your weapon of mass destruction/healing. You think 'I built this', and it WORKS. This creation is MINE. MY tank/hovercraft/hovertank/blimp/mech/jet/fortress/gunbed/minecraft pig/etc. without paying a dime.
There are so many things that are good about this game.
First, the damage. The damage is really realistic. Instead of having a healthbar like a lot of other games, it has the amount of blocks you have left. For instance: if you have a dune buggy that, lets say, has a large amount of weaponry attached to the front, but the front is only attached by a few blocks. If those few blocks get destroyed, congratulations. You are now cannon fodder for the rest of the game. if your wheels get shot, you are now a turret. If your helium tanks get vaporized, you are also cannon fodder. And finally, if you have everything but your pilot seat destroyed and if you win the game, you are counted as extremely lucky.
Next, the creation. Like I said, you can create ANYTHING you would like in this game. You can make tanks, blimps, gunbeds, jets, mechs, hover tanks, buggys, the pig from minecraft, and even freaking dinosaurs if you have the resources.
Next, is the progression. It's like a lot of other games in this, with the 'kill more enemies to level up' thing. But there is another mechanic, known as tiers. Basically, the more stuff you have, the higher of a tier you are. This is linked to the creation system, in which whatever you come up with will have a certain tier level which will determine who you will be up against.
The physics are funny as crap sometimes, too. If just one thing goes wrong, like if your tank or gunbed flips over, you are stuck there for the rest of the game, meaning you are either an upside down turret or you are cannon fodder. The only thing I complain about the physics is the ice physics. You literally drift across the ice like you are floating and you don't stop until you hit some land.
Overall, the game is just awesome to play. Although there is only one gamemode (only capture the enemy base) the positives outweigh the negatives. Btw, this is NOT A PTP/W.

Robocraft is a game crossed with Minecraft and World of Tanks. You can build your own Robot with one of 4 Different weapons, Nano-Disrupter which is your classical Medic. Plasma Launcher is your Shotgun weapon that can do large amounts of damage but has to reload. Railgun which is your everyday Sniper, doing large damage but takes time to reload and SMG, the all-round weapon, doing low damage but it's rate of fire makes up for it and can be a fierce opponent to fight against. There are many strategies and different kins of robots you can build. You can create a Plane, a Tank or even a Scorpion that can walk upside down! Although yes you will have to do a fair bit of grinding to get better gear etc this game is completely Free to Play and the only Pay thing in it is cosmetic badges that are for decoration or to get more RP (Money). There are very few hackers and glitches on it now thanks to the 10 developers at Freejam. All in all this is a great Free to Play game that i recommend to everyone!

Think one-part LEGO, one-part Twisted Metal, shake in a pinch of PvP, and you get Robocraft. Awesome gameplay, and it is definitely NOT pay to win. You can literally create any Robo that comes to mind with your blocks, and some creations from other players while in battle are hilarious. Understanding how your pFlops and your tier level works is tricky without any guidance, but you will get the gist of it after a few battles. Game works well with low end systems as well, as I am currently on my backup machine, a Mobile Core2Duo @ 2.2 Ghz + Radeon Mobile 3450 and get 20-40 FPS depending on how many players are in the arena at once. This game is AWESOME, despite still being in alpha stage.

The sequal to the original Portal, Portal 2 is an enganging and fun puzzle game that improved (in my opinion) on many aspects of the original Portal. In the beginning of the game, you meet a small little robot named Wheatley who is your companion throughout the game. With a personality of his own and a cool accent (I like it), Wheatley was a good addition to the game. Your goal is the same as the previous game; escape the test chambers alive. Although many gameplay mechanics and the story are the same, I feel that Portal 2 improved on a few things.
First of all, graphics. Of course, since it had a few years to evolve into a game that could support better graphics, the graphics are going to be better automatically, but I feel the jungle-like atmosphere really impressed me. Also, the additions of the Lens-Cube (as I call it) and a few other items really improved my expirience. The gameplay was longer and more interesting. All in all, I think that Portal 2 is a fantastic sequal that improved on Portal.
The one thing I have to say is that the original Portal's creepy atmosphere and the fact that you were alone are the biggest things that I feel Portal did better on. Of course, some people like to have more characters, and I agree with that, but Portal somehow manipulated my mind in a way that Portal 2 never could.
I was really impressed by this game and the amount of configurations it offers. Keep it up, Freejam!

A few things bother me greatly about this game. Some of it pertains to technical/installation quirks while the rest of it is in game related.
To start with, if you install this game (As of writing this), you will be forced to download some shovel-ware anti cheat system called 'easy anticheat'. Right off the bat, the fact that they need a separate system seems to be weird, and honestly it put me off. That aside, it seems easy enough to remove.
Now for the in game part, the most crucial part of this mess. For starts, the tutorial is not really helpful. It just throws you into everything without much concern and expects you to understand the mechanics and motions of the game. You will find that you are in control of a simple, bland ground robot craft that will most likely be flipped over, unable to move. That is, unless you know the hotkey to flip back, which is F. The game never stats things like this at all, and I found it aggravating each time I was flipped over and killed because of this simple problem.
The other glaring issue is the afore mentioned hacking that is involved. First game I played, there was an enemy player, ground based craft, under the ground, firing up at people. So much for the "easy anticheat" system they have in place, which at that point is just a waste of memory. The other issue is, again, the steep learning curve of the game. You have tech trees and items, but what do you do with them? Again, the game throws these things at you with no clear indication of how to get them, and how to make them all work in conjuction with eachother, it's more of a "Trial and Error" approach to figuring things out. For starting players who join their first match, they don't even realize they are on a team deathmatch battle, and shoot at eachother, only to frustrate others when the team loses because of this. Again, there is no real indicator of the match being a "TEAM DEATHMATCH", and you have to learn it through trial and error.
Now the game holds a lot of promise, we see it in the videos of awesome designs and creativity, but that doesn't really matter if your player base do not even grasp the basic foundation of the game which will cause them to leave.
Seeing as the game is F2P, expect a little bit of a cash shop, as I saw you can "Purchase" vehicles with currency. I don't think these vehicles will really give a competitive edge, but like I stated: Played the game for a few matches before I quit from loss after loss, frustration at the lack of info, Hacking players when there is a supposed "SYSTEM" installed against it.  However, the game is F2P, and if you are curious enough, you can easily install it and play a few rounds to see what the game has to offer you. You can always easily remove the anticheat system executables and the game afterwards, so there really is not much of excuse not to try it yourself.
I am only recommending this game because of the following:
1. It's "Free" .
2. It can be very fun and addicting to play, especially after you get through the steep learning curve.
3. It's got customizable robots and strategy (Imagine war thunder, but customizable vehicles.)
4. You can ALWAYS uninstall the game after the fact, as well as the other BS system.

If you want to play a game where minecraft meets tank battles then this is the one you should choose!
Having spent over 3000 hours playing this game, I can say for sure that this is one of the best, most addictive games I have ever played.
With all the negative reviews lately though I felt like I should make something clear. This game didn't become worse than it used to be in anyway, only better. The only people who have a problem with the current version of this game are old players who used to play the easy to farm/seal clubbing version of robocraft where you could reach the money cap in less than 2 months if you wanted to.
The current version of RC is MUCH easier for all types of players, no matter how good they are (easier building, easy to use weapons) and there is a lot of counterplay. Even though I said that, skilled players always have the advantage. The developers made it this way to increase player retention since a lot of players found the older version of RC really difficult and quitted early.
The subject of hate nowadays is the crates so let me explain this to you. Before the crates, after a battle you would earn ingame currency which you could use to buy everything you needed to build a bot except cosmetic items which required real money to buy. You could also use the ingame currency to buy bots from other players (which were really expensive).
When the crates arrived, after every battle you get one low-high level crate, depending on your performance, with random items inside including all cosmetic items! (higher level crates have better items). This means that from 1 battle you can get a rare and expensive item which you would have to farm for hours to buy before.  You can also buy bots from other players with the ingame currency but this time, if you already have the items used in this bot you can buy it for free!
This was a nice change but there is a problem with the crates, the random drops in rare crates are bad which caused the community to dislike them. The developers knew that this wasn't gonna be an easy change and the crates will need a lot of tweaking over time to make them perfect so this is where we are now. There have been a few updates to improve crates already and I can already see the difference since rare crates give much better items now!
Another thing the community dislikes are the low recycling rates (you can recycle an item to ingame currency and buy another one). The only reason these rates are low is to encourage players to buy crate packs with real money if they want to progress faster and as a result the developers will earn some money and keep the game free2win.
The only things you can actually buy with real money are Premium time, which will give you some nice features and make progression easier (esspecially if you are a new player) and packs of crates (which you can earn from battles anyways). This means that there is absolutely nothing in this game to make it P2W. There is always a number of players who complaing about paying features because they want everything for free which would be a highly unrealistic business plan for the developers.
Keeping a game Free2Win by finding other ways to make money and still keep the community happy is an extremely difficult task. I believe the robocraft developers found a good balance and seeing how they developed the game so far I am sure things will be even better in the future.
Finally. the developers always address the community's concerns and fix any issues with the game ASAP. They also make sure they improve the game by adding new items, features and improve visuals which vastly improves the experience of this game.
So far I only have 1 problem with the game, there is no reconnect feature. This can be really annoying for players who disconnect or crash a lot.  I am sure they will add it in the future but I feel like it should have been one of the first things to add in this game.
TL/DR I recommend this game and I am sure you will love it if you are a new player!

Great fun deathmatch game (with minor capture-the-base elements) where you build your robot out of bricks and enter it into randomly assigned team games.
There are two levelling systems:  Tier and player level.
Tier is how strong your robot is, you're put into games with other players of the same tier. You can build a robot purposly fitted to enter a specific tier, or just slap on everything you can afford and play at your highest tier.
Player level increases as you kill/repair other robots and with each level your 'bot gains CPU, which is one of two limiting factors on how much fun stuff you can stick on the 'bot. You can only have one type of weapon installed, so roles are generally pretty well defined.
You earn RoboPoints depending on how well you and your team does, and those are used to buy new parts, from blocks to wheels, radar, wings, hover-craft parts, weapons and shields.
At the moment there are only two biomes and four (I think?) maps and every online game is capture the base mode, but it's well worth a go! Despite being free but with an in-game cash shop this game isn't pay-to-win. A week of casual play has gotten me to Tier 6 and still able to break heads, and with the freedom to build almost anything I can see a lot more fun to come.

This is a good game no doubt, but it has developers who don't and won't always make the best decisions when it comes to updating the game. It has been like 8 or 9 months since they started and it's still in alpha, so expect this to go on for years unless they wisen up or if there's been a change in management.
A few days ago, an update came and prevented some 15% of us from playing. These days, that would easily translate to thousands of us, which is unfortunate. That said, I'd still recommend this game for its well-executed concept, even if the developers can't seem to carry it through all the time with equally decent updates.
EDIT (2015): The most recent update has taken away everything that Robocraft stood for. Creativity, diversity and flexibility is all but gone. The developer has a very long streak of making bad updates, and this is the worse of them all.
And this is coming from a very loyal player who sunk $40-$50 dollars and over 700 hours of time. Let's just say I may not do that again, until this has been resolved.
EDIT 2 (2017): Alas, here I am again, and it's Robocraft's 4th birthday. It has reached Beta. Freejam has improved the way they do things, the way they execute their updates, but it's been a rough road and they are still making really questionable decisions.
Right now, the worst thing that's really eating me up is their energy system, which gives small bots an even bigger energy pool and proportionally increased energy regeneration, ostracizing bigger bots. This is another example of Freejam's philosophy of whaling at the problem and shooting flies down with cannons. As a result, small gadgets have 2 huge advantages against bigger bots while bigger bots have only their generally better durability as an advantage.
I can never understand what the people behind these changes are thinking sometimes.
Despite all this, Robocraft is still fun... more often than not. I've decided that, after 2-3 years, I should amend my 'not recommended' review to 'recommended'.

Would love to give this game a positive review, but the recent addition of EAC (3rd Party anti cheat software) has made players on Non-windows machines unable to play, as well as people who use programs such as MSI Afterburner and related programs and anyone using unsigned drivers on Win7+. You want to open the Steam overlay? Yup, that has been known to be flagged by EAC. This program can scan your hard drive and active memory. They claim it only looks at Robocraft; that might be the case, but the EULA is so vague that while it DOESN'T do it, it has permission to do it. And from what I gather from forums, most of the hacks haven't even been stopped because they are caused by packet manipulation.
I have since uninstalled Robocraft, which is a shame because they have an incredibly fun game with good prospects. They have shot themselves in the foot with EasyAntiCheat. If EAC is removed and they stop trusting their client (ie server-side validation) then I will happily come back.

Okay, in all seriousness, this game is great. In fact, it's so great, that it deserves a multi-category review where I judge it on gameplay, story, graphics, and sound, each with a rating of "great", "good", "subpar", and "terrible", with a final rating in the end.
So, gameplay. Gameplay varies across all types of game, and shows you how they play; whether it's a 2D platformer, a top-down RPG, a first person shooter, and more. However, this game is very unique, as it is actually a first person puzzle game. I know this might sound complicated at first, but hear me out, it works beautifully. To sum it up, you have an Aperture Science Handheld Portal Device (AKA the "portal gun") With this, you can create two portals, and walking through one leads you to another. Sounds like an easy game, right? Not exactly. Different obstacles come across your path, such as...
-"un-portalable" walls
-doors that can only be opened by placing cubes on buttons, pressing buttons, and shining lasers at things.
-TURRETS.
-letting your companion cube go *sniffles*
-and just simply challenging levels!
The new game mechanics are also wonderful as well. As mentioned earlier, lasers are in the game, along with "hard-light bridges", excursion funnels, a gel that makes you go fast, a gel that makes you bounce, and more.
Another key part of Portal 2's gameplay is it's challenge. Portal 2 is one of those games that start off very simple and easy, and become increasingly challenging as you go on- and I mean VERY challenging. However, no challenge is large in comparison to the amazing feeling you get when you beat a level. If I were to kind of describe it, I'd just say doing the most challenging thing you've ever done that you knew you could do and was very possible but still took you a while and shouting out "HECK YEAH, I JUST DID THAT!"
In terms of content, the game has tons. To start off, it has a very extensive campaign of 8 chapters, each with a bunch of levels in them, some of which have multiple "test chambers" as the game puts it. It also have a 6-chaptered co-op campaign, which is also VERY challenging, and each chapter has 8 levels. However, going even further, the game have workshop support, meaning people can upload their own levels and play levels other people have made in the level editor! Oh yeah, I forgot to mention that. The game has a level editor. Anyway, there are THOUSANDS of levels already on the workshop, and people are making more as you read this very review.
So basically, I give gameplay a "Great". It's really solid, and tons of fun as well.
The story of the game is just amazing. Basically, it leaves off a long time after the first game ends, but nothing really happened  inbetween then and now. Basically, Aperture Science was a sciency-research center thingy, that made lots of stuff- like shower curtains. Anyway, one of their creations was GLaDOS, or the Genetic Lifeform and Disk Operating System. One thing led to another, GLaDOS is pretty much crazy, and she kills all of the employees with a deadly neurotoxin, and tests on some of the surviviors. Chell (your character) is one of the survivors, and it's GLaDOS's time to test on her. [MAJOR SPOILERS FOR THE FIRST GAME AHEAD] Anyway, you get through the 19 chambers hoping to be greeted with a cake she's bee teasing you with, but instead she tries to kill you, so you go rouge, find her, destroy her, and escape. However, you get dragged back in to the facility and put into stasis until Portal 2 begins. (I probably got some parts of that wrong, but oh well.) [SPOILERS END HERE]. Anyway, Portal 2 begins with you in stasis, and you've been in for quite a while. However, you're greeted by this ball-thing named Wheatley, who is one of Aperture Science's personality cores. He tries to break yout out of the facility, but adventure leads to mishaps, and a certain someone is rebooted. The certain someone does tests on you again, while Wheatley tries to break you out once more. It may not sound interesting so far, but there are some HUGE relevations and plot twists that make this story amazing. Unfortunatley, they're EXTREME spoilers, so I can't share them. You'll just have to play the game for yourself.
In terms of personality and dialogue, this game is action packed! The certain someone has a very sarcatic personality, cracking jokes at your faliures and mishaps all the time. It may sound annoying, but believe me, it's hilarious. The monotone voice she has increases the humor by at least 50%. Wheatley is pretty much an idiot. The game states it. His lines are amazing though, for his ignorance and stupidity lead to some of the best quotes in the game. Then you have Aperture Science founder Cave Johnson, who rambles on about the most odd, yet funny things. Although he doesn't have many lines in the campaign, he greets you with a message every time you play a community level. When pretty much any of the characters converse, it's utter hilarity, but don't think the game can't take itself seriously, as it also has it's fair share of serious and dark moments as well.
The co-op campaign is pretty starightforward though. You play as two robots, Atlas and P-Body, doing tests with the someone I have mentioned numerous times in order to prepare for finding a crud ton of humans preserved somewhere in aperture- to test on of course. While the co-op mode isn't story heavy, most of the dialouge is still as funny as the single player campaign, with even more laugh-out-loud lines.
Overall, I give the story a "Great". It's the perfect blend of humor, darkness, seriousness, and solidity that makes the story so amazing.
The graphics in Portal 2 are awesome. While it doesn't have such a varied color scheme (walls mostly consisting of black and white panels), the story and overall feel of the game mae it work REALLY well. It kind of gives you that gloomy, "you're trapped" feeling which goes perfectly with the game. Also, since it's been quite a while since the first game, and there's not exactly any "cleaning crew" in Aperture Science, there vergetation and broken panels ALL over the place for quite a while, also adding to the feel of the game. However, the graphics quality is AMAZING in my opinion. When this game does shading and lighting efects, it does it perfectly. Not to mention, the deterioration everywhere really shows you how much has changed since the first game, and it really is amazing
Overall, I give the graphics a "Great". They really make the game work, and I can't imagine a Portal 2 without the graphics it has right now.
As for sound, it's also wonderful. The intense, slightly creepy music just gives you the feeling that you're just absolutley trapped in Aperture Science, and no matter how hard you try, there's no way out. The music and graphics definetley work together to form the the overall feel of the game so perfectly. In fact, you can find the entire soundtrack for free on Portal 2's website
. It's in "media + downloads") in case you want to listen to it.
I give the soundtrack a "Great".
Overall, Portal 2 is one of the best games I've ever played. I give it a "Great".

What a wonderful little game this is. If Minecraft and World of Tanks had a baby, this would be it.
In this game you build your vehicle and ride it into batle against players online. Pretty simple it seems, right?
You are wrong.
This is one of the most complex free-to-play games I have ever seen.
Like in Minecraft, you get to build your own vehicle using different blocks, but unlike Minecraft, there are different shapes of blocks you can build with. An like World of Tanks, the online battling is well-planned and a very simple format. The unloocking of different blocks and items is very similar to WoT and another FTP game War Thunder.
So...what's different.
There are many different vehicles you can build. And each vehicle has a different purpose or 'role'. Although there are no exact roles you can build, there is always a major theme in each type of vehicle.
For example: A tank used for defense would usually be slow but have good armor and powerful guns. A small vehicle used for capturing a base would be weak but would be very fast and swift.
A full 'role' list can be found here
There also a multitude of guns you can unlock to, like fast firing SMG's to powerful and accurate Rail Cannons.
All and all, This is one of the best FTP games out there on Steam right now.

NOTE 2: It should also be very well noted that as this games popularity has grown Freejam hasn't done ANYTHING to makeup for the server space needed. This game has literally spent the last two weeks that I personally know of going day to day as to whether or not the servers are working. It is inevitable that at some point in a day they will be down. Honestly Freejam seems like  a bunch of lazy gamers who had an idea, s-h-i-t it out and barely pay attention to it now that it makes them money. Servers are not that damn expensive. There is an entire secondary market for used network equipment these idiots need to find and quickly. Don't blame Yahoo, it's the idiots paying yahoo for s-h-i-t service that you should blame.
Note 3: Exactly how long is a game supposed to be "Early Access" because this game is over 2 years old. If you dont have a finished product you just outright suck. Also it should be noted that the community of players for the most part is HORRIBLE. It's largely kids with absolutely no concept this is a team game. Add that to the lack of communication and you have a game that offers you a good matchup 1 out of every 10 matches. Pathetic ratio.
This game has a ton of potential. It's too bad the developers are making mistake ater mistake to really be able to capitalize on said potential. Instead of adding new maps (the game has a whopping 4) ( or improving gameplay (ice is RIDICULOUS, not even real ice is that slippery), they keep adding crap we don't need. Walker Legs, tank treads, etc. While these adds are definitely cool and do spice up the game play and building possibilities they really should be later adds. Initially they charged you Robopoints to repair your robot which essentially made advancing and gaining new equipment a painstakingly slow process. This was in no doubt there to "inspire" people to pay for Premium. Robopoints are also how you buy better equipment so if you spend them repairing then you can't really upgrade. It doesn't even matter if you get destroyed, just taking damage costed RP. Thankfully they no longer charge RP to repair bots after each match.
However paying for premium notably seems to be the only way to truly survive and advance through the upper tiers of the game without first being slaughtered over and over and over. They dont charge for repairs now but tiering up is still ridiculously slow. By that I mean getting enough next tier equipment to build a bot. The constant restriction on CPU load ( how big and how much gear your bot can have) is essentially completely against the point of the game. The idea is to build big fun robots and battle it out. That's what every ad for the game shows you and tries to sell you. The reality is it should show you tier 1-4 bots because that's pretty much where the first month of playing will be.
When you can barely have armor AND guns, the idea of a big fun bot is more of a dream. The armor to damage ratio when it comes to Plasma cannons and Rail guns is just pathetic. It's a joke. You basically buy armor just so you can survive the first shot. Added to the above detractors is the fact that it is a team based game with TEXT communication only. This is pretty ridiculous considering. So it's a team based game with realistically no communication because if you try to type chances are you will get railed or plasma'd . Huge detractor right there.
Then the matchmaking system makes DOTA look like a godsend. Skill has absolutely nothing to do with reaching higher tiers. It's a function of repetition and you'll reach them regardless. This makes higher tier battles which in theory should be the best battles in the game no better overall then Tier 1 battles. The same idiots plague all tiers. I'm sure that each game has its own nuances but in this one a major downfall is the fact that a large amount of the players A. aren't old enough to drive and as such can't drive AT ALL even in a game or B. They are just terrible drivers period. When getting out of your own base is basically like bumper cars you know you are in trouble.
Because of the lack of communication there is a HUGE gap in the ability to strategize in this game again robbing it of one of what should be it's core pieces. Instead it's a team based free for all.  The difference is that your teammates don't kill you directly they just dont do anything while you die. Unless you happen to get one of the exceedingly RARE good teams. This problem has been mediated to some degree by the addition of medic units. idea.

Despite all this the game is free to play and after having many of Steams offerings it is sad to say that the only reason to play this game is because it's not as s--h--i--t--t--y as most of Steams offerings. Sad thats what gaming has come to. Playing the games that suck the least.
