This is a good game that gets some unfair negative reviews and hate. I am going to address some unfair attacks at this game.
The BIG thing about these negative steam reviews is that anybody can write them thus many Loser players with idiot tank designs come here to take out their anger on the game’s store page. This is partly thanks to the chat window in the games main lobby where countless 9 year-olds tell the whole server why they lost because SMG’s are cheap and not because they rushed in alone with their no-armor hovercraft in between 5 enemy tanks. When other normal players lose to an SMG tank they see the chat and believe the exaggerated comments and join them, then they start venting their anger too. The other slightly more fair reviews I’ve seen are from the old-time players who say the game devs ruined the game. I’m a little newer at this than them and I’ve played almost 40 hours of gameplay in these "dark times," made it to T5 and had fun all the way, and there’s no signs of the fun stopping any time soon. The people who are having fun (and there’s a lot of us) don’t bother to write reviews, just the people who want to vent their anger do.
The first thing people say is that this game is pay2win but that just isn’t true. First of all, paying users and free users get all the same parts to work with and second, in this game your robot has a stat for ranking. When you add a part to your robot it raises the rank stat and if you reach a certain point it will go up in tier. There are 10 tiers of robots and you just about always get put against robots in your tier so paying 2-win is impossible. The only thing paying does for you is give you faster progression through the tiers. Some people say its pay to progress but I’m on top of T5 and I haven’t had that problem yet although I think during a certain update it was bad but they have already fixed that by now. Progression isn’t super important anyway because by T5 every TYPE of part is unlocked, just not the bigger stronger versions (which are in there own tier). Unlike World of tanks and other F2Ps you can still make cool stuff at lower tiers and there’s none of that “premium ammo” crud that I hate.
Now for the second big thing to talk about, op (over powered) weapons and parts. Every type of weapon gets called “op” 90 times in the same day because of that venting 9 year-old thing I told you about before. One big thing to keep in mind is that this game is in alpha so balance is subject to change. I hate when people say “plasma has ruined this game forever” because even if plasma was cheap the devs would rebalance it ASAP. There are only 3 different types of weapons in the game (for now) and they all have their intended functions. I’m not saying the game has always had perfect balance (and it still doesn’t) but it’s still a lot of fun to play. The last thing about balance is that a lot of players are new to this game and don’t know what they can do. An example would be that hovercrafts can dodge plasma shells vertically but I don’t see many players do this. Those players could go on to say that plasma is cheap or that hovercrafts are underpowered but the real problem is that the players don’t try new tactics.
People whine a little about other things like lag, warping and glitches but I have never had those problems, those things are just more problems that people unfairly vent out during their rants.
Overall I just wanted to tell you that this is a really fun game that can make you think and adapt, and also that the devs aren’t evil (I think), they gave us free stuff as makeup for a server crash they had. If the game gets big and devs finish this right then this could be a really great and solid game. Thanks for reading, PEACE OUT!

Robocraft is a solid custom-vehicle combat game. You start with a simple tank and a few parts to choose from, and as you play and improve your vehicles, more parts become available, giving you more options to strategically build and play with. Building happens block by block however, so it's best to plan your craft out early, because there's no options to split a craft and add somethig in the middle etc.
Combat is fun, taking down other players with a fresh upgrade or new weapon type feels great.
However, there is no respawning within a match, so if you're destroyed, you can only spectate the rest of the round or go back to the hangar.
As of this review the game is still being worked on, and a new weapon and movement type have been added. Balancing and rebalancing is an ongoing process.

I have mixed feelings about this one. On one hand it is a solid piece of engineering and those ten hours I spent with it were fun, if annoying at times. Yet remembering how revolutionary the first Portal was, it’s hard not to blame Portal 2 for its lost potential. A bigger budget and a bigger team, but the result is an uninspired sequel riding on the popularity of the original.
The story in the first Portal , and the progression of environments made sense. First you where a test subject, then you escaped and made your own way around the facility to finally fight GLaDOS. Hints that something was off with Aperture were subtle and built tension. The length was just right, you could complete it in one breathtaking sitting.
In Portal 2 you simply “follow the rail” as the helpful robot with an awful British accent (and forced humor) tells you. References to the original are in-your-face, everything lacks subtlety or any kind of suspense. At least puzzles rise up in difficulty nicely, if a bit slowly. It’s hard to get used to hand-holding popups and NPCs suggestions though. It’s a puzzle game, I want to figure this stuff out, OK?
Sure, the visuals are nicer, but that doesn’t really add anything to the game play. Unfortunately from the technology point of view Portal 2 has a major flaw: the loading screens. Loading between levels takes longer than in the original and there are now immersion-destroying separate loading screens. Both chase sequences in the game are also broken up with the loading screens. The funny thing is: elevators are still here. Yep, Portal 2 has both an elevator and a loading screen between levels.
Ultimately it’s just more of the same. Portal 2 doesn’t push any boundaries, it’s a high fidelity bonus pack to Portal. Sadly it’s nowhere near as important as the first Portal. You can go to
to explore interesting environments or to
for some real challenge.
Funny thing is that I’ve seen this before. It’s the same kind of thing that happened to BioShock. It was supposed to be a worthy successor to System Shock 2. Developers of both Portal 2 and BioShock made the game accessible to a wide audience. Both games achieved the same level of “critical acclaim” (top spot on metacritic in their year of release). Yet both lost the soul of its predecessor.
If you’re looking for a spiritual successor then it’s clearly somewhere else.

You build your own vehicle (LEGO/Minecraft style) and upgrade/customize it along the way. Best part of the game is that shooting at a certain part of the enemy vehicle, pieces start coming off. Robocraft is a solid custom-vehicle combat game. You start with a simple tank and a few parts to choose from, and as you play and improve your vehicles, more parts become available, giving you more options to strategically build and play with. Building happens block by block however, so it's best to plan your craft out early, because there's no options to split a craft and add somethig in the middle etc.
Combat is fun, taking down other players with a fresh upgrade or new weapon type feels great.
However, there is no respawning within a match, so if you're destroyed, you can only spectate the rest of the round or go back to the hangar.
As of this review the game is still being worked on, and a new weapon and movement type have been added. Balancing and rebalancing is an ongoing process.

*NOTE: THIS IS AN OLD REVIEW. Tiers aren't a thing anymore, but for all effective purposes, the game still handles well in that regard*
I totally reccommend this game to anyone and everyone.
Generic statement aside, the concept of building and fighting your own personalised robots is not only an amazing idea, but Freejam executed it in a very nice way. You build with the base armor blocks a frame for your robot, and then deck it out with weapons, movement, electroplate (shields) and various other tech. The variety of different things you can build is endless, even now with the game still in development, and there exists a Tier system that sorts robots based on their 'rank' (higher level blocks add more rank) so that, as a newbie you're not getting thrashed by the elites running around with Tier 10 death machines.
To me, the only downside is that Robocraft is a little pay-to-win. You can buy GC with real money, which you can use to buy parts at huge discounts, or to get premium, which boosts the amount of Tech Points and Robo Points you earn from battles. It's really, really enticing. Trust me, I have a bunch of Premium. However, this problem gets solved pretty nicely by the Tier system. All you do with premium is advance Tiers more quickly; the way the game is designed prevents premiums from being able to completely destroy non-premiums. So, aside from a little jealousy from the guys you leave behind in the lower Tiers, it really doesn't affect gameplay in any way.
ADDITION - 29/10/2015
So the first parts of my review are a year old now. Robocraft has seen a LOT of internal changes in that time. That sums up what Robocraft was and still is - an early access game. As a result, I've gone between playing and not playing over the course of the past year, as new changes turn me away from the game but I inevitably come back and learn to love them. Every new update, there are hordes of angry players - 'RIP Robocraft, wtf you doing Freejam I'm never playing this again'. And if you play too, you'll likely feel this way for a few days, but then after that it doesn't really matter. The game is still fun at its core and that's what matters.
Overall, I give Robocraft a 9/10

I got this game, found it amazing. Told my friends about this game, they found it amazing. This game is amazing, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise. I mean, you shove blocks together until you get something that looks painful (or is a fairly efficient cube!), add some lasers, then fight. AMAZING! This is so funny, and fun, and you can do so much stuff! Get it. Now. Trust me. Ignore the negative reviews, they are misled. Try it out for yourself and make your own mind up. After all, it is free, so why not? Download this game, you will not regret it. Unless your some naive gullible 9-year-old. In which case, get it anyway. Just cus.
EDIT: So I just took a look at the negative reviews, think "how on earth can there be any?" and it turns out that they are all complaining about the Easy Anti Cheat software, saying either A) it stops them logging in, or B) it invades their privacy. Well, for the first of these concerns, I have never experienced any trouble, and the people who did probably did not do much to try and fix it. EAC is supposed to stop you logging in if your client does not match their client. Verifying the integrity of the game cache should make sure that it does. With the second problem, this is just people being paranoid. I mean, grow up. Do you have anything to hide? It's not like they are hacking your bank account or anything. If you are paranoid and want to make sure you are safe, while the game is open, just play the game. Close it before going on to do anything else. That way, EAC will only be able to 'see' you playing the game, which, frankly, nobody cares about.
So yeah, get the game. It is a good game. It is constanly being updated to add more stuff, and with the upcoming new gamemodes it looks like this game will be a riot!

I would much rather pay $40 maybe even as high as $60 bucks once and be totally reliant on in game money to build, research, and repair my bots. I do put money into WOT because I knew I would enjoy the game enough to justify the costs.
I don't get this feeling with this game especially on reading other reviews with high repair bills and other in game economic issues I can't say I am moved to put money into this game to make worth the pay to play system.
My last issue of my first playthrough and is something that maybe a fixed in the furture is no clear cut way of increasing your CPU power which in this context is how many and what quality of parts you can put on your bot. There are no research trees that seem to address this and not even a "Buy more CPU power with cash" button. Maybe I missed something but the premise of the game is to build robots and fight, but otherwise if I can't build my Juggernaught of a bot then there goes a lot of willingness to play the game.
Again this is a first impression of the game since it was free on steam as of this review but I just don't think I will play this game much more than a handful of times and even then it will likely be "Just to peek in and see what's changed" type play throughs.

Ok. This is a mixed review. Yes I recommend this game but with reservations. I don't think I need to describe what the game is about. There is plenty of writeups that tell you about that so here's my opinions and advice about the game.
The game is still under development. It is by no means a finished product. This means tons of bugs and often times when you simply can't get into a battle. When things work ok, which is more often than not, it is a blast. Build - test - fight - destroy - rebuild - test - fight and on and on. It is highly addictive. The fact that the game is not nearly fully developed yet has not prevented the developer from charging for their in-game currency, Galaxy Cash, which is used to buy parts, buy premium account status, cosmetic items and to accelerate the rate at which you unlock new equipment. I would advice that you don't throw a load of cash into this game too soon. You may pay for a month premium time but chances are that your premium time will tick away while you wait for bugfixes, patches and server outages. I know they say your cash helps them develop the game but you are the consumer and should not be expected to bear the financial burden of their product development.
Do install and play the game though. It is a great game. The community is, for the most part, helpful and understanding.

I had seen this game about 2 months ago and decided to skip it do to all the negative reviews about it being pay2win. Then after seeing a friend playing this game for around 2-3 hours everyday for 2 weeks i decided why not give it a try, and i instantley hate myself for skipping it.
After running the game and creating an account i was greeted with a blocky looking tank, so the first thing i did was go into the games practice mode. The controls were pretty smooth and i proceeded to blow up the AI until i felt like i understood the game enough. I decided that i could create a great tank and made a blocky square with wheels and as many guns that could fit on it. I press the battle button and am launched into the field. I instantly run up the nearest hill to discover a horrible flaw, my ship loved to flip. A squad of the enemy team passed my upside down tank and proceeded to blow the blocks off one at a time and left me stranded as my squad was murdered infront of me. After losing the battle within 2 minutes i fix the robot and double check its stability. Confident i re-enter the field to seek my revenge. I am then shot to death by a 2x3 block wide chair with guns. This is where the guides come to play.
I spend the next hour reading through multiple guides on how to build proper death machines and return the the garage, ready for my masterpiece. Halfway through building it i discover a block limit. After much hassle i create a tank that guards both my wheels and chair. Entering the battlefield i end up killing 4 enemies and lose 1 of my guns. As i spin around frantically i look for these "pay to win" players. The only premium members i saw where the ones stuck in a trench being shot to death by 5 of my teamates. We win the battle and i am greeted with a nice amount of rp. Only upon looking at my clock did i realize 8 hours had passed and it was 3 am in the morning. Overall great game so far and I definately recommend that you at least try it once.

Robocraft is, overall, a well made and well thought out game, however, there are many MANY major issues. Many within control of the Developers, and a few that arn't.
First off, Robocraft has no guide. Nothing tells you how to play the game, or what to do. Its a matter of learning by doing, and if you do something wrong, it's because the game didn't explain.
Secondly, many things in the game are ludicrously over/underpowered. Take in the most recent update for example. Teir 7 Walker legs have a robot rating of over 12,000, where Teir 7 wheels only have just over 4,000... There is almost no reason to use walker legs in this respect, as they have a very small amount more of armour, and thus just eat a lot of your teir rating in one go for something that's... not much better.
Weapons are a huge problem in the game too. Snipers are far to overpowered ingame, with one hit kills if shot correctly. Plasma Cannons (grenade launcher things), are also too underpowered for their type and cost, only destroying maybe a gun and few bricks if you're lucky.
Lastly, players. Though not in control of the Developers, players are a huge issue in Robocraft. In my experience, once you've lost your guns and wheels... you're useless, theres no point really wasting your time killing that person when you're being shot to bits, BUT, no-one sees this. I've been killed multiple times by an enemy who was being targeted by 3 of my allies, but when NOT being targeted by myself... attacks me. What reason is there for this? None. It's much more efficient to kill, or at least disable, the enemy that IS attacking you.
Overall, Robocraft is good, however, is missing some many MAJOR features and balancing. It also doesn't seem to update all that often, and with barely any content, so don't hold your breath on this being a good game fast.

It is important to stress that Portal 2 is nothing like Portal, where static rooms and lifeless objects turned into an awesome storytelling experience by your own mind.
Portal 2 has a narrative line, has characters, has dialogue and is very different from its predecessor. I enjoyed the experience thoroughly (although there were game sequences better than others), the puzzles were rather good and the new effects (e.g the gels) very satisfying. My personal favourites must be the lasers, due to their sound. The audio in general in this game is very good - from the backtrack, sounds to voice-overs.
The best feature has to be the co-op mode. I have played it with several friends and it provides immense levels of fun, nothing like any experience I've had before.
My heart still belongs to the original Portal and its companion cube that I unsparingly threw into the furnace - that type of dark humour was heavily contrasted by the sterile world in the first game. Portal 2 has a rich, juicy world that supports the still sinister remarks, but overall felt lighter and with little probability of additional playthroughs for me (not counting the co-op, I could play that a dozen times more).
Overall, highly recommended!

You can obtain everything on your own for free or pay for premium to get it twice as fast. Everything can be obtained by farming RP and TP in the game. However you can pay real money instead of using RP and pay to have tech points of a different tier upgraded to uber points. Uber points can then be used to unlock anything early.
The game is divided into 10 tiers, 10 being rediculous cattleships and walkers with rail guns mounted to the top and 1 being a bug with a machine gun. You move up the tiers by placed better gear on your robot. Every piece of equipment has a tier rating and raise the tier bar until you have reached the next tier. Tier's can move up or down freely, depending whats equiped on you robot.
The downsides I have seen have been the platoon (party) matchmaking and the premium membership. Matchmaking is fairly quick and efficient when your alone queuing. When you create a platoon of friends, it is a mess or error's that has to be overcome be backing out of que and re-entering until the whole platoon gets in que right.  The premium membership is great when it actually gives it to you. when you buy a premium membership it usually only about 50% of the time gives you the bonus. The other half of the time it sometimes randomly gives it to my friends in my platooon, people on the enemy team, or just disappears entirely.
Overall this is a great game that allows you to be creative and have fun with good gameplay mechanics. Enjoy!

It is important to stress that Portal 2 is nothing like Portal, where static rooms and lifeless objects turned into an awesome storytelling experience by your own mind.
Portal 2 has a narrative line, has characters, has dialogue and is very different from its predecessor. I enjoyed the experience thoroughly (although there were game sequences better than others), the puzzles were rather good and the new effects (e.g the gels) very satisfying. My personal favourites must be the lasers, due to their sound. The audio in general in this game is very good - from the backtrack, sounds to voice-overs.
The best feature has to be the co-op mode. I have played it with several friends and it provides immense levels of fun, nothing like any experience I've had before.
My heart still belongs to the original Portal and its companion cube that I unsparingly threw into the furnace - that type of dark humour was heavily contrasted by the sterile world in the first game. Portal 2 has a rich, juicy world that supports the still sinister remarks, but overall felt lighter and with little probability of additional playthroughs for me (not counting the co-op, I could play that a dozen times more).
Overall, highly recommended!

Is Robocraft a fun game to play? Yes it is a fun game to use blocks of a few shapes to model your craft. The type of weapons you can pick from are nice. Also you can be on the ground, float, or hit from the air. You can try to make something look very nice or make a huge block with tons of weapons.
Is Robocraft easy to play? Well...yes and no. See I want you to think of this game as a Tradeing Card Game or a Fighting Video Game. There are players out there that will have more powerful weapons and armor even at Tier 1. They can even make hover crafts to attack from the air. The robots might not look very cool and might just be squares or huge box tanks but they can still deal out damage. The reason I mention TCG and Street Fighter players is that some will know exactly what to do, some know more than what you know, and others have unlocked more of the options for their Crafts.
Also lets mention something real quick. Each part takes up points in a sort of CPU limit. They also add to a Tier list. Better parts will boost your Craft into being in a much higher Tier. So you need to make your suit with the correct parts and correct shape.
Damage for the most part is fair. What ever you hit is what you will damage and slowly destory so by aimming at wheels and weapons you can handycap a Craft. However this brings out a slight flaw...and something that might need to be talked about. You can outright lose all your guns and even your wheels. This makes a gamer feel more like they lost because of the game rather than someone shooting them off. Its like think of any First Person Shooter and if you get shot in the legs arms or even gun you move slower, aim less effective, and lose your gun. Swat type of games are close to this feeling and damage. Also your own guns will not pass your own Craft or ally Crafts, so you have to build very carefuly. HOWEVER! There is a flaw...if the two blocks under your driver piece [which you NEED] get destoryed then your Craft gets destoryed. You should ALWAYS put the heavyist more durable blocks around these two blocks and as those two blocks.
Hows the driveing? Well you must be able to understand how driveing works. You can find your self stuck due to getting flipped over by bad driveing or uneven maps [this is mostly the fault of a driver but sometimes the maps makeing some stuck forever areas if you fall. Also you can add a flip device to bounce your Craft back side up.] Also driveing on ice with level 1 wheels outright NES style sucks. Hardly any track on the floor its self and youll slide about. Of course this could be that Im useing the wrong wheels. There are driveing wheels and turning wells. Lucky for you there is a training map with non-attacking AI Crafts.
So hows the respawn time? Hahaha, there is none. When your craft dies your out of the game, you can go back to the mother ship in advance after your destoryed and I don't think you lose anything. However it's the thought that theres no Human character to control, theres no Sentry Gun at base to control and theres no second chance. So forth and on when you die your forever out. Which gamers of today might dislike.
This game is for free, it allows you to buy credits to buy parts faster but you have to win or destory other Crafts to level up and earn some Technical Points to unlock the options to be able to buy new parts. So its free style is kind of fair.
Bottom line its a very small file size game and it works quite well. BUT...its very diffrent and some gamers might argue about things. One of the top reviews is based on July. This is October. As a Early Access Game this is a fun game. As a game that might ever cost money it might be worth around 5-10. Any higher with the lack of major things this game needs like basic molds, and idea blueprints and able to save allys or enemy suits to use for your own will make this game un-buyable by a few.
Games like 3D Dot Game Heroes and Magic Pengel The Quest For Color allowed you to create your own Pixle character and 3D Warrior. If player's can not fully grasp how the create process works then the character can suffer or this choice suffers. The Gummi Ship Creator in Kingdom Hearts I & II was kind of easyer than RoboCraft. Let's hope you have the time to build your ship correctly and perhaps have the ability to make it look cool.
RoboCraft currently gets a 6/10. Create your own Weapon/Warrior games could always suffer from this problem. If the method of createing is poor or complex then its hard to make anything that looks cool. [Like the Kirby Enemys in the pictures previews.] 6/10 is always a stander review but I boost it from 5 because it is a fun game. It does not get a 7 because it has problems. Being able to copy and paste part of your Craft would be nice. The ability to keep blueprints of your suit would also be great. Finally a second chance method would be wounderful. Takeing blueprints copys from others would be nice. Im sure that the players can think of more and better ideas.
To the game creators keep an eye out for it. I also wish you good luck with this.

Robocraft is an interesting game. It's central idea is enjoyable, it is only partially free-to-play and yet keeps the payed content neither utterly away from you, nor gives extreme advantage to those who do pay. It's matches are reasonably fair, and there are enough players that wait times are not excessively high.
Except, through all of this, the game is not exactly well-documented, and is nearly entirely a grind for more in-game money, XP, and tech-points. Further, it is not only a grind, but a very monotonous one: there is one gamemode, with two goals: kill all the enemy team, or capture their base faster than they are capturing yours.  This combined with the large map-size makes for a not very satisfying game. No matter how many times you play, there will never be a great match to finish with. There is simply the occasional game where your team actually acts like a team, and sets up something remotely resembling a killzone.
After a hundred minutes (or so steam tells me, I didn't time it myself), I had no further desire to keep playing. There are plenty of great things about this game, but the way they combine is wholly unsatisfying to me.
Your milage may vary, and the developers might be able to correct some of these issues in the future. In my eyes it is not good value for its size at this time (October, 2014).

So much potential, but a few fatal flaws kill it for me. Basic concept: take various parts (cubes, prisms, wheels, wings, thrusters, hover engines, shields, assorted weapons, and all kinds of other cool stuff) and build a 'bot to duke it out 12 vs 12. The first couple "non-fun" things I encountered were just personal issues for me, namely the irritation of having to shoot at small flying bots, and avoiding instant death from weapons with high alpha and long reload. But these shouldn't go away, as they're important for the variety they bring.
The game has 10 tiers to keep things relatively fair for players, but this is where the real problems start. At each tier, you get Tech Points that you use to unlock new parts. When you're playing a tier 1 'bot, you get tier 1 TP, which you can only use on parts that can be unlocked with tier 1TP, and so on. (Spending real money lets you convert any TP to 'uber TP, which can be used on any parts.) Typically you're unlocking parts that match the tier you're in, some that are a tier higher, and very occasionally two tiers higher.
Each part has an ascociated 'roborating', and the total roborating of all the parts in your 'bot is what determines the tier it's in. And this is where the problem lies: it's entirely possible to use parts from say tier 4 (which require tier 3 TP to unlock), but build a minimalist bot and keep your overall rating down at tier 1. This ends up being vastly overpowered, because 1-3 weapons several tiers higher are always considerably better than 10 weapons of the appropriate tier. Particularly because, when you use parts this way (known as 'up-tiering'), you also use basic building blocks of higher tiers which come with vastly better armor and are much harder to destroy, but also because the overall size of your 'bot ends up far smaller, making it much more difficult for enemies to hit it at all.
The end result is generally a 'bot that is physically a quarter the size of appropriate-tier 'bots, about twice as tough, and has the firepower to destroy any proper 'bot in one volley or (in the case of high-ROF weapons) in a matter of about 3-5 seconds.
If they were to address this glaring issue, I'd give it a solid 8/10 score. As it is, I can't give it better than 5/10. I don't see this game retaining many new players in its current state.

Please note that the Robocraft is currently in early access and still being developed, please look at the date of this review to determine whether it is still reflecting the game.
Robocraft is a free 2 play, online shooter.
In Robocraft you build your own unique robot and use it to win 10 versus 10 multiplayer matches.
Between flying and driving, sniping, healing and spraying the only thing that limit the way of your robot is your fantasy.
All Robots are separated into different Tiers, when you level up into the next Tier you unlock more powerful weapons and tools to strengthen your power and fight better. Additionally the Tiers separate the player base, while considering strength, so that you don't need to fight people that are stronger than you.
For example in Tier 2 you unlock the ability to build a flying robot and in Tier 4 you unlock sniping weapons (plasma gun).
The process of your robots creation reminds of Lego, as long as you have matching blocks you can build everything you want, even though your teammates won't like your Pacifistic "no-gun" robot that much :)
As you level up your player level you can use a higher amount of parts for each robot, allowing you to stack more power and more fun on a single Robot.
Currently the game only features one play mode.
In game you will play 10 versus 10 matches, that are all about controlling the enemies capture point, while defending your own.
Currently there are around 5 maps available which are all around the same size. They are designed very nicely and though full. They allow you to execute strategies such as flanking, camping, rushing or kiting.
In case your strategy fails and you die, instead of forcing you to spectate your teammates on the battlefield, you are free to leave the game and hit up for the next one, without getting any punishments or disadvantages.
The ability to start the next game, leads to less wasted time spend on "being death" and gives short and action packed rounds of  2-7 Minutes, just depending on how long you can survive.
Since you can play together with your friends, the only reason you might want to wait, is watching your 2 friends (3+ if you buy premium) how they win the game. Playing with friends is highly suggested, it allows you to execute even better tactics than before.
Additionally to normal rounds, there are "boss games". In this special games you will face a single player who is tier 7 or higher, with many low Tier players. Boss games are a great variances to the normal gameplay, that gives you a feeling on which guns you might want to unlock in the coming Tiers.
The great gameplay of Robocraft is shadowed by the developers interest in payments.
The game allows you on any player levels to buy high Tier weapons and mount them on a low Tier robot.
Every player can use this tactic, the problem is that new players are animated to use real money  in order to unlock new technologys faster, which is not only hurting the gameplay but, is bad for the player, too. It is only a short term advantage, until the player gets into the Tier that they already unlocked with money.
Even considering that flaw, I highly suggest you testing out Robocraft yourself, it is a very fun game and revolutes the way we think about death in multiplayer shooters.

Robocraft, the best thing since Lego!  I kid you not, I've not spent so much time in a game since Minecraft.  You build your vehicle with blocks you unlock from battle, some of the designs I've seen are insane.  From apartment buildings armed to the teeth - to X-Wing's and everything in-between...  Your imagination is truly the limitation when it comes to your designs.
There's a lot of good things about this game, and there's a lot that leaves much to be desired.  Since the good is too numerous to list, (seriously just play the game), I'll go with the much fewer bad points:
1) Flippers.  These things are the bane of my existance.  Yes, they'll flip you around ONLY if you'r vehicle is COMPLETELY still.  This means, if you're stuck on your back and SLOWLY sliding downhill, you can't flip yourself around leaving your soft, meaty belly open to attack.  Flippers seem to work on movement alone, not which side your vehicle is.  I really hope they do something about this as flippers as they stand are useless.
2) Sattellites.  Also known as "floating campers".  Like campers, these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s rely on sitting perfectly still to get a kill.  Sometimes these crafts are nothing more than three blocks: A helium block, a seat, and of course the weapon.  If you're not using an SMG or Rail gun, they're virtually impossible to take out.
3) Custom settings.  This annoys me almost as much as the flippers do.  I know my computer best, and what it can and cannot do.  So please, let ME decide which settings to use instead of some set "low-medium-high" choices preventing me from tailoring the game to my computers capabilities.
4) Connection errors.  Lately I've joined a game only to be disconnected.  Thankfully this doesn't happen much, but when it does it ruins my mood to play.
5) Block detection.  You can tell this is an early version of the game.  Sometimes you'll delete blocks behind the actual block you wanted to delete when you're building, or updating your vehicle.  Also, some blocks have issues detecting where other blocks are.  That in itself isn't a big issue, just annoying.
That's it for now.  I realize the game is still in its infancy, so please remember that as you look over my review.  I'm sure the majority, if not all of these issues will one day be addressed.  In the mean time, the game is more than playable.  It's extremely fun, and addicting!  So before you decide to download it, make sure to evaluate your time as this game will make hours seem like minutes!

Update Dec 2017
This game can be fun, but is often not.
The Developers have failed to address longstanding balance problems with this game.
In most games, there is a balance between fast and agile vehicles/characters, and slow and tanky characters. There is a balance with high mobility and low mobility: High Mobility = Squishy Low Mobility = Very Durable. That balance is lacking in Robocraft.
This game allows aircraft to be much faster than ground bots, yet have the same durability and damage output. Obviously, this leads to aircraft dominating matches. They have many, many pros and very few cons - if any at all.
There is also a balance in the skill it takes to play a character and the skill it takes to defeat that character/vehicle. Typically, spamming keys can be easily defeated with better game play. That is not so in Robocraft. Oftentimes, simply holding the W key allows you to wildly evade being hit, because of low fire rates and low projectile speeds. Other times, all it takes is randomly spamming directional keys to evage shots from the only weapon capable of taking these things down from the ground: The Railgun. Unfortunately, the Railgun is a weapon that has a very limited number of shots that can be fired before it needs to be recharged. The most powerful one can only fire twice every 8 seconds. This does not work when facing aircraft that can bombard with AoE damage from the sky. They do not have to actually hit you to deal damage, and on the ground, you are a much larger and slower moving target.
The game has rarely ever been balanced through various major changes - the decisive advanage always going to aircraft. The developers often take a very long time to address even the most absurd imbalance in favor of aircraft.
The game, when it is fair, is fun to play. Unfortunately, its a coin toss as to whether or not it will be a fair match with 'normal' bots that do not exploit terrible balance mechanics. One game is fun and engaging with both teams having fun, and the next may be a tedious game of peekaboo damage wallops from players that you have little to no chance of retaliating against.
Imagine if you will, a grenadier that is allowed to fly and move very fast to access high locations that your character cannot. That grenadier can strafe out from behind something waaaaay up high, toss a handful of grenades down in the blink of an eye, and immediately disappear back behind cover in an elevated position. The grenades, when exploding, are very difficult to see through due to particle effects - making you play half to fully blinded.
All that you can do is look up and wait for it to pop out again - but even as a sniper, you cannot headshot this grenadier to kill him. He will be hurt, but will not die. Instead, he will hide behind that elevated position again for a few seconds, heal, and begin the process all over again. Every capture point you must take is surrounded by elevated positions that he can use to peek out of and lob grenades at you. You are also highlighted on his screen with a name and health bar - as is he for you. However, if he manages to hit you with AoE explosions from that elevated position, and you fail to hit him with a single projectile from the ground, his name bar will disappear - but yours will stay. Congratulations, now you cant even see when and where he will pop out from, but he can see exactly where you are - through the walls.
If that does not sound like fun to you, do not play this game.

Fun game for a few hours. Afterwards it becomes a grind. The fact that experienced players can explot the levelling system by using advanced weapons in early tier matches takes some fun away of the game and you will need to spend many hours to get out of this uneven situation. Furthermore the scoring system is inadequate. Reviews are about how a game is now and not what it's potential is. In it's current state I therefor don't recommend it.
Pros:
-The ability to design and adjust vehicles and put them against other players is great. The strangest cars and hovercraft can be seen on the battlefield. A lot of the game dynamics are worked out adequately. The physics for example are basic but adequate, so top heavy vehicles will topple.
Cons:
-The levelling system is based on a certain amount of points for vehicle parts. After your vehicle has enough advanced parts/points, it advances a tier. With research points you can unlock specific parts every tier.
Downside of this system is that people who have played the game for many hours, already can use unlocked higher tier weapons in lower tier games, as long as they keep their vehicle basic. This means early on you will encounter small vehicles with little more than for example a single plasma cannon (which you can't get for a long time to come), which is enough to one shot kill you. This is an exploit used by those players to get a lot of credits by killing new players, often without much of a challenge. At the end of a game where all but one of a team is destroyed, you often see for example that the last player is someone hanging high over a base-area, sniping vehicles far below. Levelling up is frustrating this way. Even after 8 hours getting out of this uneven situation is still many more hours away.
-Even if you were the one who carried your team to victory, if you get killed before the match is over you don't get any bonus. This is a bad game mechanic since it's unfair and since it promotes passive gameplay.

After the outlandish setting, ingenious gameplay, and hilarious dialogue had all run their course, Portal left you with some pretty big unknowns. Chief among them were, "What happens now?" and "How did that whole weird situation come to pass?" Portal 2 sets out to answer these questions, and in doing so travels both forward and backward from the conclusion of Portal. The result is a sequel that doesn't try to replicate the successful formula of its predecessor. Rather, it expands upon that original experience, creating something that feels initially familiar. Yet as you progress through the enthralling single-player journey and tangle with the clever cooperative campaign, any worries that things might be too familiar are swept away by the scope of your adventure and the characters you meet along the way. Once again, you are caught up in the fantastic world of Aperture Science, where hilarious and endearing dialogue is delivered by disembodied voices and artificial intelligences, and where inventive gameplay mechanics and a smooth difficulty curve make the sublime satisfaction of puzzle solving accessible to all.

username: Don't let your dreams be dreams
text:
In a way this game want to teach you something...the cruelty of the humans? the corruption of the power? the importance of the cooperation? the devastating effects due to the abuse of the experimentation? And so on...play to find your point of view about it....
But back to business!
This game is really really really cool! Based on interactive puzzles this game will make your hours flying away like an airplane directed to the other side of the planet.
As the name suggest you have to use portals to move yourself from a point to another, or redirect laser beams, or to move objects...or to throw them....or even to throw yourself!
The gameplay is fun, but it will easily put a sad face on you in some parts...and vice versa. The co-op mode is indeed the best one I've ever seen. In this game the co-op mode is FINALLY a true co-op mode (and I will say "co-op mode" another time just because I like to say "co-op mode" today). If you don't talk with your partner, if you don't plan to do stuff at the right time, if you go ahead alone....forget this game...is not for you; if you don't cooperate you will be unable to pass the first co-op level.
The fact that this game is even multiplatform compatible means that you can even play it with friend that have this game on PS3. This is a very interesting and good thing.
The graphic is indeed good, mostly based on HL2 engine (well...is a Valve game...lol) and the sounds are pretty nice too (funny the music based/created on the laser beams or in other puzzles you have to solve); and the support of the contoller will put a smile on the console's enthusiast.
The story is related to the first portal and as I said in the beginning the single player mode is more deeper than a simple game; a very good observer and listener will easy understand what this game wants to tell you...probably in its own way but still it is a message.
Overall:
Graphics 8/10
Sounds 8/10
Gameplay 9/10
Co-Op Gameplay 10/10
Longevity 9/10

I've loved this game for a long time because it's unique creative ability. When the repair cost system was added, I could no longer make things for the fun of it. The game quickly became a P2W grinding game, with the community becomming ever more immature and rude to people who complained about the updates. As time went on further I truely realised how long it would take me to make anything I'd like. I remember being a T4 tank with good armor, and an assortment of SMGs, everytime I would be taken out by someone who decided a box with some plasma cannons and 4 wheels would beat all. Turns out it did, and constantly the insta-death ran up my repair cost totals. Not being able to purchase more than a block
every round and only being able to build up to a very low-roof "CPU" system, plus repair costs. I couldn't stand it any longer, so I can say honestly I've quit. And once this review is written I will uninstall Robocraft and search for something else more promising, and hope they don't make the same mistakes.

This game is brilliant. Played it before it came on steam and loved every moment. If you have a robocraft account already, and are worried you will lose your robots, dont worry. The steam version will still use your existing account. The game is a very nice 3rd person shooter in which you build robots and fight in teams to capture the other team's base. There are many types of robot: walkers, fliers, hovercrafts and cars/tanks/trucks. If you die, you will NOT respawn, so bear that in mind, or you will rage a LOT. Robocraft is a type of game where you will start out bad, and work your way up to pro. The game will not throw you in with pros instantly. It will match you with equal tiered players. There are 3 types of weapons: SMGs, plasma cannons and rail guns. SMGs are the most basic, plasma cannons are for ground artillery/flying bombers and rail guns are for snipers. SMGs are for anyone, while plasmas and rail guns are for advanced players. Overall, I give this game a 9/10, as this is still in early alpha, so things aren't finished yet and lots of things are constantly changing, but the game feels like a finished MMO. Just remember: Nobody likes OP gunbeds. Have fun!

Looking at this game, I can't help but compare it to World of Tanks, which also puts vehicles onto a battleground where victory is obtained by either destroying all enemy vehicles or capturing the opponent's base. In WoT, the pace is much slower, and combat is much more careful, as well as trying to create an environment for WWII-Korean War era tanks.
Robocraft is much more fantastic and sci-fi in nature, trading tanks and European/Asian warfronts for two different planets, and this is the game's biggest problem so far: there's only 2 planets and 6 maps. Granted, it's still Early Access, and things are being introduced, like the recent (as of this writing) Walker parts and Boss Battles.
The name of the game is customization, giving you a good variety of parts to build your Robot (an odd name, since it requries a pilot). You have cube blocks, triangular blocks, tetra blocks, and windows for the base. Then you get into gear with wheels, guns, radar, radar jammers, and if you're up to it, hoverlifts and thrusters, allowing you to fly, but physics are in play, and you need to balance it properly, otherwise you're flopping all over the place. You unlock parts by earning stars you win in battle and spending them at the tech tree. In order to win stars in a particular tier, you have to use that tier-level robot. You increase your robot's tier by using higher-level parts. However, you can also create a small robot that's Tier 1, but uses a Tier 4 weapon.
Combat is much faster paced than in WoT. The robots move faster, and combat is more active than taking shots and hiding behind buildings and rocks. You can use different weapons, from your regular blasters to sniper rifles (railguns, which have a charge time) to artillery (plasma launchers, which also have a charge time, but it's also odd that an energy weapon arcs). Also, be aware of your gun placement, if you put one gun in front of the other, the one in the back won't fire.
Also like WoT, this game is "Freemium", free-to-play, but there's also a Premium mode you pay for for extra experience and credits. You can also use the GC you buy with actual money to purchase parts, and convert Tier stars to Uber Stars, which can be spent on any Tier in the Tech Tree.
Overall, this is a fun game with good amount of customization, but still lacks in map variety, but this is still Early Access, so I'll cut them slack on that. Also, you can rename your robots. Apparently people are failing to notice this, and I see way too many "Robo1"s around.

Starting with the Single-player campaign (no spoilers): I played it first on the PS3 when my brother got it. Back then I was enraptured in the whole story, much of which kept me on my toes (or should I say spring-boots?). Character development, continuing the story arc, and psychological hurdles are all present, as you would expect, given the first Portal game. I must say it was every bit exilharating playing through it on the PC the second time as it was on the PS3.
DLC: (kindof spoilerish) Secondly, the Portal 2 Testing Initiative for the PC version of the game is one of the greatest inventions of modern gaming. Countless thousands of intricate, confounding puzzles that you can download and play through - all created by users like you - are available in the 'Community' section for the game on the Steam platform. The tool is so in-depth that many of the unique puzzles I have played through have had traps that caught me completely off-guard, which subsequently left me fearing for my life even though real me wasn't in any real danger - and I loved it.
Multiplayer: This aspect of the game is, in my opinion, less fulfilling. There is not a story, really, you have to work with your friend to solve the puzzles. There's not much more to it than that. That's not to say the multiplayer is not fun, though! My brother and I spent hours playing together solving them as a team, hitting each other and whatnot as siblings do. It's a whole new experience in multiplayer, just as fun as the campaign.
A must-play on your gaming to-do list, and thoroughly exciting, all across the board, 11/10.

- Plasma (rocket launcher) feels OP early game, because there are few aircrafts. It's an anti-ground weapon
- Railguns (sniper) are NOT for close quarter combat. If you have a railgun, you are VERY vulnerable. Good Anti-air weapon
- SMG (assault rifle) are okay for everything, but require a bit of aiming. Good for heavy fights. Good overall weapon.
EDIT++: Most of the cons are gone now, PLAY THIS GAME

Use minecraft blocks, along with guns and other vehicle parts to build battle-bots. An efficient matchmaking system then drops you in a red vs. blue, capture-the-point engagement. The parts you use are constrained by the variables CPU, whose limit you raise through experience, and ranking which is used by the matchmaker to segregate robots into tiers. Parts also are priced in an in-game currency which is earned by destroying enemies in the battles. The resulting gameplay is a unique mix of design and somewhat class-based, though balanced, action.
The F2P model only requires real money for decorative parts. It also can multiply your in-game money prizes. Therefore it's not really pay-to-win so far but only pay-for-speed and pay-for-fashion. Account creation and all meaningful gameplay are free.
Huge potential.  I do hope they expand the number of maps and variety of parts, though.

I bought it a couple of days ago because I wasn't convinced that the game was actually worth 20€. And you know what, it isn't, at least to me. Yes, the single-player campaign is roughly 3 times longer than the original, but that's still only 6 hours of content. That's why I waited for a sale that gave me enough of a discount, and 5€ is much more justifiable for this game, but only because I have absolutely no interest whatsoever in the co-op part of this game. If I did, I'd say 10€ or 15€ would've been ok, but I won't touch that mode at all because I like to play with myself, so I'm left with another comparably short single-player campaign.
But on to the meat of the game. It seemed to me that the first part was really slow, possibly to accommodate new players who haven't played the original and even later on many of the puzzles were very obvious. I really only got stuck on one puzzle and that was because I missed a small surface that you could actually put a portal on and thus had to consult a walkthrough, but the rest were fairly easy. Still, the mechanics they've added definitely expand on the possibilities of the basic gameplay. I liked manipulating the gels, but again, the placement of tubes basically made the solution extremely obvious and the challenge wasn't so much figuring out what to do, but in what order, which basically involved trial and error. This is the problem with a puzzle game that has one and precisely one solution and which absolutely has to be in first-person. But I really liked the boss fight at the end, it's a really good demonstration of using all of the available elements and all the skills the player has acquired over the course of the game and designing the battle around that, similarly to what the original did. It should be an example to designers around the world, that a boss isn't just a regular enemy that has more health, but a final exam on what we've learned up to that point.
The environment design is pretty damn well executed. I especially liked the shift to the older abandoned tracts of the facility with the 50's and 70's inspired looks. In fact, the whole visual design is really pretty to look at, although the draw-distance is pretty damn horrible with all that fog they introduce in the broken and open sections of the facility. And I felt that the game underutilized the whole background of the chambers and maintenance areas to flesh out the world a bit. The original basically had the same layered concept the Half-Life games have, where you can either experience a very simplistic story on the surface, or you can investigate further and find a lot of hints which build the world, and this seemed absent in Portal 2. Still, there is a bit of world-building, though mostly through the audio logs of Cave Johnson and some of the dialogue form GLaDOS and Wheatley, though I felt that the ending, similarly to the original left me with little closure overall. I actually read this right now and saw that they changed the ending of the original from merely lying outside the facility to actually being dragged away again, which explains why Chell is back inside the Aperture Laboratories. But again, the ending in Portal 2 is a bit lacking.
Speaking of the characters, they're all very well realized. It's a lot of fun listening to these guys with their quirks. I especially enjoyed Cave Johnson's way of expression and his inflection during the various audio-logs. Though all of the voice-acting was top-notch.
One thing that did irk me greatly were the loading times. Seriously this game loads after every single room and it really breaks the flow at times. And if you die, the reloading of the level also takes ages. I assumed Valve would finally learn something but the loading times were even worse than in Half-Life 2.
Overall I'm very pleased with this game. I wish it were a bit longer and introduced more new ideas, but then again, drawing it out too much just leads to repetition.

This game started out pretty cool. But after it hit a certain update it quickly became a pay wall.
You have blocks to build your vehicles. Each block has a certain amount of points it provides. Hit a certain level of points and  your vehicle is considered a higher level. More powerful blocks give more points per block, and because each block as a 'flop' count, (a limiting factor on how many blocks you can place on your vehicle) you have to get more powerful blocks to get better vehicles.
The problem comes in that in order to /get/ those more powerful blocks, you have to be earning different tier  stars to unlock the blocks (that just unlocks the ability to /buy/ them one at a time, with points you earn from playing). To get a level 2 star, you have to have a higher level vehicle. I don't remember the exact level, but after 2-3 battles a day for a few weeks (which you can see isn't much time, Pro: the battles are short)  I had barely earned any tier 2 unlocks.
And the worst part? The cool stuff you see in the trailers: the flying vehicles, the engines for them, the bigger guns - those are all tier 5 or 6 or higher.
before Release there were tier 1 flight blocks. Then there werent when release came about.
I don't consider this 'Pay to Win' - and I hate those people who throw that term around everytime something is much easier to pay your way to victory than to play it. You certainly /can/ earn your way through everything you can buy with real money.  There is nothing other than decals that can be bought with real money that you can't earn by playing. It's not Pay2Win.
But it is very much so a slogfest that is absolutely no fun if you aren't paying.
Disclaimer: I haven't played this game for a good month. Maybe its changed, and hey, its free to play right? Very nice method of making free-to-play.  Instead of forcing people to wait if they didn't pay, you are forced to play to earn more credits to buy parts.  And if you pay, then you just get credits that you would have earned by paying.  Also, your ship is tiered against other ships made of a similar total credit (CPU) value.  So you're not going to have any trouble starting up as a newbie with no cash against someone that has the best parts.
The one exception to this is helium blocks, they don't take much CPU, but they are mid-level tech so usually people with Tier-1 ships that have helium blocks (floating satelites with a chair and a gun) are people that paid for those blocks but still need to unlock parts by just playing the game.  However, it's pretty easy taking out satelites if you just look in the sky, personally I hunt them down.  But people keep making satellite ships because not everyone looks in the sky, so they are effective for now.  However it isn't unbalanced, you see a laser shot from the sky, just take that guy out.
The very best part of this game, is the creativity that people show in unique ships.  It's just great going against a somewhat unlimited amount of possible configurations.  There are patterns like the stairs, satellites, edged boxes, but there are continuously cool designs and hybrids that I see in most rounds.
And it's really fun grinding points to new levels, because you are still playing the game.  I find myself playing a match, adjusting 2 or three blocks, and repeating for hours.  I've hardly ever played with the exact same ship in two consecutive rounds.  I'm always iterating on my design refining it.

In fact, the whole visual design is really pretty to look at, although the draw-distance is pretty damn horrible with all that fog they introduce in the broken and open sections of the facility. And I felt that the game underutilized the whole background of the chambers and maintenance areas to flesh out the world a bit. The original basically had the same layered concept the Half-Life games have, where you can either experience a very simplistic story on the surface, or you can investigate further and find a lot of hints which build the world, and this seemed absent in Portal 2. Still, there is a bit of world-building, though mostly through the audio logs of Cave Johnson and some of the dialogue form GLaDOS and Wheatley, though I felt that the ending, similarly to the original left me with little closure overall. I actually read this right now and saw that they changed the ending of the original from merely lying outside the facility to actually being dragged away again, which explains why Chell is back inside the Aperture Laboratories. But again, the ending in Portal 2 is a bit lacking.
Speaking of the characters, they're all very well realized. It's a lot of fun listening to these guys with their quirks. I especially enjoyed Cave Johnson's way of expression and his inflection during the various audio-logs. Though all of the voice-acting was top-notch.
One thing that did irk me greatly were the loading times. Seriously this game loads after every single room and it really breaks the flow at times. And if you die, the reloading of the level also takes ages. I assumed Valve would finally learn something but the loading times were even worse than in Half-Life 2.
Overall I'm very pleased with this game. I wish it were a bit longer and introduced more new ideas, but then again, drawing it out too much just leads to repetition.

This is an amazingly fun F2P game that has ZERO pay-2-win elements for the first 20-30 hours of gameplay. That's the first thing I judge F2P on.
There are 10 tiers. Each robot you build starts out in Tier 1. As you add blocks and weapons, the meter moves it closer to Tier 2. When you're in Tier 2, you fight Tier 2 robots. After each fight, you earn money and tech points. Tech points is what allows you to unlock better blocks/weapons, while money is how you purchase more blocks/weapons.
You have the option of spending your money in your propulsion, weaponry, or armor. Realistically, you can't have mega-good armor and mega-good weapons in any tier of combat you're playing in. That way, if you have T3 weapons, you can possibly play in T1 rank if you have zero armor. Or you can go for a TON of Tier 1 weapons and armor to play with in Tier 1, making your craft much more durable.
It's only when you get into tier 6-10 does the P2W elements appear, as grinding out the "cash" to purchase the ingame items truly seems baffling. I haven't gotten there, and frankly I enjoy T2 and T3 combat so much that I wouldn't mind if I never do.
The wait times between matches in this game are very, very short. Usually 10 seconds or so. Each match can go for a maximum length of 6 minutes, but usually ends after 2. This allows for many fast pace battles over a day, unlike 1 40-50 minute game of Dota or League.
I recommend this game to anybody who's feeling a litlte bored but doens't want to sink their time into a game that's going to require a weekend to beat.

The tiering system works well, with every block having a 'tier point' value.  You can bring high-tech equipment into a low-tier match, but only if you make real sacrifices to do so.
Combine this with spotting mechanics a-la Battlefield, and it's an amazing emergent teamplay experience.

This game scratches an itch I have always had: competitive creativity.  Whatever you imagine, try it out.  It might suck (I created a ship that looked like a Beholder - horrible manueverability) or can make you the guy who trounces everyone on the other team who is making the same standard tank.  On top of that, strategy, timing, aim, and manuevering all are critical to success.  You can make a tank that sacrifices handling in favor armor or power, or get a tank that can flip over to shoot above if the situation requires.  I find the weapons very balanced (I don't care for the plasma or railguns) and the different modes of transportation are fun to incorporate in new ways.  Planning your tank in terms of, "How will this guy fight if he takes a hit... here?" leaves me staring at the build screen for 10 minutes without placing a single block.
I also regularly laugh out loud when I am ghosting and watching the dumbest tank build helplessly flail about the battlefield.  It is equally enjoyable to see a well-made tank with a certain piece destroyed spin in circles while trying to make use of his last turret.
Haven't spent a penny and probably never will.  The matchmaking is lightning fast and very fair.  If you don't contribute to a fight, you'll only get enough resources to repair your tank.  You're never left in a situation where you can't immediately play again.
Tip - don't disregard lower-tier components.  They can perform just as well (though take less damage) and allow you to compete in the lower leagues.  Nice as backups, or if you want to have 5 hovercraft fans that you might not miss as much as 3 higher-tier hovercraft fans that leave you useless once one is lost.

Not a bad game, it is ruined by a few core failures:
- There is no point winning or losing the base capping game (the only format) for a reward, the only objective is to stay alive (this is due both to the cost of repairing your bot and you get no reward if you're dead and you're team wins).
- It is hacked frequently and the majority of games will have at least 1 aim-bot.

- The end game is really bad, the final tiers are about becoming massive, which is a both a grind and ruins the fun aspect of designing bot, just make it with as many expensive blocks as you can.

I'm not going to pain things pretty. While I do recommend the game, there are a couple of things I want to make clear:
1. Any reviews you read about the game being pay-to-win and unbalanced matchmaking and all that good stuff is absolutely, 100%, unbiased truth. I've seen it with my own eyes and makes me practically throw my computer across the room some days simply because I lose repeatedly, especially to damn high-fliers (planes) that you can't hit and perform full-frontal penetration to the face of your vehicle. I also can personally say that I've reached Tier 5 weaponry and have a Tier 2 vehicle (it just barely rests on the edge of Tier 2 and 3) that is loaded with Tier 2 heavy armor, 8 standard wheels, and 3 Tier 4 railguns. I am practically untouchable and win numerous games by one-shotting. Railguns can definitely be incredibly OP.
2. With that being said, there is still an element about this game that is fun in building. Sure, you go through repetitive gameplay to get to higher Tiers to get more money, but it's fun to go back and make cool designs and try out ideas when RP is no longer a problem in earning and you have more experience with the game.
3. This game is Early Access. There will be physics problems and that is always a given with games like this. It is still indev, so don't go all rage mode when your teammate runs into you causing you to take a flip and sit around for the remainder of the match. Same goes for ice physics.
Now here's the personal part. I have 31 hours on record at time of writing this. I always have my ups and downs in all multiplayer games. In the end, despite the terrible matchmaking (practically all multiplayer games screw this up and you can almost never perfect this), OP weapons, and very pay-to-win sort of system, the room for creativity this game gives is still worth it. The matchmaking is fast, so you don't have to worry about sitting in a queue for a couple of minutes after dying. You're almsot instantaneously right back in the game. Overall, i would still recommend giving it a go and trying it for yourself.
P.S: Another problem that I've personally seen is that prices for weapons and other materials getting into higher tiers can get a little frustrating. Going from a Tier 4 to a Tier 5 Plasma Bomber means an increase in RP from 4000 in 4 to 9000 in 5. To put in terms of the game, in those tiers, you earn anywhere around 1500-2000 (assuming you win, which almost never happens) RP AFTER repairs. Not to mention the fact that even though the prices double as your tier increases, your pay usually only increases by about 200-500 RP. This causes materials to become increasingly unrechable and hard to get for every tier you move up into (which causes people to start moving to the route of pay-to-win to stay ahead) to the point where I've all but given up on upgrading my tier 5 "Breadwinner." Instead, I'm using my untouchable Tier 2 rail sniper to gather tiny increments that still outweigh the frequency of earnings from my Tier 5. This is a problem I haven't seen addressed anywhere else and I think is worth noting.

(Skip to OPINION and/or ULTIMATUM if you don't care for in-depth description, and would like to see if this game is for you)
Within the first hour of playing this game, I realized two things: this definitely had a 'World of Tanks' vibe to it... that is, rushing head-first into the enemy will ultimately get you killed, no matter what vehicle you're playing.
The second thing that came to mind? This isn't Minecraft... this is more like the gummi ships from Kingdom Hearts, only more land-based! (Personal opinion states I loved that portion of the game, but should've had a game of its own. Moving on.)
That said, the game is (currently) brutal. There are three endings for you in a fight: Victory, Defeat, or Destroyed. Getting in-game money and tech is based on several factors such as spotting, dealing damage, and base capture... but mostly from kills, helping get kills, and reducing the times you see 'destroyed' at the end. New weapons and gear is researched by participating in respective tiers or, for those willing to pay, upgrading tech points into uber tech, and your vehicles are ranked by the parts that are given to them during construction in a garage. You CAN and WILL encounter people who abuse this fact by building vehicles to be placed in lower tiers with high-end weapons and the hated plasma launcher just to either earn RP or convert their tech points with real money, but if you're lucky, you'll spot them first and easily demolish their lightweights, rapidly netting you points. Also, as you get hit, your vehicle will lose blocks, resulting in a loss of mass and vital components such as weapons or even wheels/thrusters/whatever your mode of travel, making it hard or even impossible to move/steer. Expect to be reduced to nothing but your chair if you take too many shots.
There's a few problems about this game at this stage, such as my earlier example of people abusing the tier system or even how punishing the game is to earn your way forward, but my only true gripe about this game is sometimes how flaky it feels the breakaway mechanics work when you have a bulky vehicle, where it feels like you're losing whole sections even when they're all interlocked. This, again, can mainly be attributed to the earlier tiers, where almost any well-placed hit will destroy blocks, but can especially happen if you get hit with a railgun.
OPINION: Fun, but game mechanics and the 'no victory on death' rule make for an interesting, if not sometimes frustrating, challenge. For being labeled "Early Access," I recommend it only on condition that they continue work on the game and do not grant the paying players a combat advantage.
**ULTIMATUM**: Breakaway system often leads to being unable to help team in some situations, no such thing as 'victory' when actually destroyed, and sometimes have to deal with 'smurf' mechs with high-end gear. When you do score multiple victories, it can be moderately paced to advance to higher tiers even as a free player (almost 26 hours in and currently piloting a tier 5 plane.) Being an Alpha, progression/availability subject to change. ALL THESE POINTS CAN BE SEEN AS A POSITIVE/NEGATIVE.

If you enjoyed Portal, or a puzzle game of any kind, you should get this game. The creators have made challenging puzzles that are fun to solve, and improve on the puzzles in Portal in almost every way. Just as in the original, they designed the puzzles excellently with a natural progression in difficulty. The co-op is also a great addition; working with a partner to solve more intricate puzzles is very fun.
More than just game design, though, is the fun tone of the game. While the atmosphere doesn't feel quite as creepy/oppressive as the original, they improve on the humor and story of the game.
For all the people who loved Portal, you'll find just as much (and more) to love in Portal 2.

A brilliant game. Firstly, I'll reassure that while it is still in development, it is already very much playable, and has delivered me hours upon hours of entertainment. In this game, you build vehicles (not actually robots, they are piloted by you >.>) with wheels, wings, thrusters, rudders and/or hoverblades, mount them with either smg turrets, plasma cannons (ballistic weapons of doom) or gauss rifles (snipers, really) and go into 4-6 minute unforgiving team deathmatches.
The big nopes:
- The grind is a bit cruel, as your profit from each match is a direct result of the damage you deal and receive. Otherwise helping your team to victory is worth zilch to your wallet, and if you get one-shot at the start, that's a match wasted.
- Not all the physics are in place yet. Collision damage doesn't exist. Also, you're very much at the mercy of the randoms you get matched with.
The big yays:
- It's perfectly F2P and certainly not Pay-to-Win. Compare to Hearthstone, but being able to choose the cards you earn rather than getting random ones.
- Graphics don't feel bad at all, it's pleasant.
- Mass and momentum physics are wonderful. Whatever you build, you can really feel the results of your engineering.
- SO MUCH CREATIVITY AND ENGINEERING.
- Dem short games of a few minutes.
- Absolutely delightful for multiplayer with one or two friends. (Bringing three friends is only possible if you sub.)

Robocraft is a team deathmatch, vehicle building game, using a block grid style of construction. The games strong point is its concept, and the ability to be creative in your robot. However several major and minor problems i had were magnified with each tier i progressed.
This game mentions its not pay to win, which is true, you can grind everything in the game without paying a cent, but very quickly you see how similar the monetary system is to World of Tanks.
After the first few tiers where people are really creative and games are fun, the gameplay quickly degenerates with, less creativity (people start making boxes with guns on top) more people with access to weapons and armor above the tier they are in, which essentially results in a one shot death followed by a loss in the ingame currency then renders your robot useless unless you sell parts of it, or make an entirely new bot and play a few games to grind back some money so you can continue.
If you enjoy the prospect of small rewards and disproportionatly larger punishements (average winnings = 3000, average loss = 2900, items cost 20000+) for trying to progress, an unbalanced team matchmaking system ect. i can only recommend this game for the first 4-5 Tiers, after that i would not recommend playing any further unless you are willing to sink minimum $10 into it.

Portal 2 is an intensely cinematic game, with witty and meaningful dialogue throughout, a very clever storyline, and an incredibly well designed learning curve. The puzzles are all just challenging enough to be both fun and rewarding. The game is much longer than the original. The level design is visually amazing and functionally genius. The game is littered with easter eggs, and places that challenge the player to try to break the game or get outside the map, only to discover that the developers knew you would do this, and planned some clever surprise waiting there for you. Robocraft is the most addicting game I've played in years. It's fun to build your robot and tweak things like weight, armor, speed, handle-ability (robots control completely different depending on center of gravity, weight, wheel placement, etc). Once you get fighting its addicting to try and earn lots of money and dominate your tier. Always something to keep you going too. Technology unlocks, new levels (which equals more CPU power to load out your robot) and the slight changes in gameplay as you change tiers all keep you wanting to progress. Eventually you have to start dealing with plasma guns, then railguns and flying robots. I love the quick 5 to 10 minute battles. Simple gameplay but strategy and tactics are deep. Using charged up weapons peaking out from walls as defense, picking and choosing targets you're robot is particularily strong against, balancing weapons vs armor and shields or speed.... I love the strategy. I heard about the game from a friend who said it was the best game he played this year. I can go even further than that and say its the best game I've played in the last few years. I like the free to play model too. Sure you can advance faster by paying but you don't exactly gain anything. You just get through the game faster. Every tier of the game is enjoyable so its not painful to have to play at the free to play pace. If you do well, you can still progress quite fast for free. I've been playing for 4 days and already have 35 hours into the game. I can't remember the last time I've been this much into a game. The building part of the game reminds me of playing with Lego as a kid. The combat reminds me of the multiplayer fun I used to have as a kid playing Mario Kart. I told a friend about the game a couple days ago and he has also spent 20 hours playing it in the last two days. Playing it with a friend on skype makes it even more fun. I hope the game does well I can only see it improving as the tech tree gets bigger and we get more types of weapons, etc, to broaden the tactics and strategies. It is pretty sufficient as is though. I think I'll be playing this game for a long time.
