Great idea, fun game, bad business model.
This game has lots to offer in terms of gameplay. You get to build your own machine and fight in it with other players. You can unlock better parts and techs as you play. This really would have been a nice game, had it not been for the horrible business model.
Basically, you have to spent points on both buying new techs and parts for your machine and also on repairs after a match. The more the robot is damaged the more the repair costs. But here is the thing: Your only way to get points is by playing the game and being good at it, so if you go through a rough patch you can literally bankrupt yourself by having to spend points on repairs. But that is ok, because you can use your real world money to buy more points!
Even the paid for subscription doesn't spare you from having to pay for repairs. It just makes you earn points faster. So even if you are actually a paying customer, you can still see all your money be lost on repairs. In addition, you can also just outright buy all the parts you want for your robot, thus making sure that people who have more money than common sense will always have the better machines.
I'm sorry, but I am not dumb enough with my money to spend it on a game that has this kind of a business model. If you could pay a small subscription fee that would allow you to get repairs for free that would have been another story, but there is no such option.
I won't be too harsh on this game because the only thing that really prevents me from wanting to play it right now is the unfair business model. If it is changed, then I might alter this review. But in the meantime: no deal.
EDIT: Having played the game more, I find that having to repair your machine every now and then is not as costly as it might appear at first. This I feel that the overall game is good enough to change my rating to a good one. HOWEVER I still think this model isn't very good and that it should be changed.

So hello. Robocraft is a Free to play- game, and one of the best of them! Build/customize your vehicle, add weapons and go to fight online! There is limited amount of "cubes" you can place into your bay(Where your vehicle is). Each cube takes different amount of CPU, and CPU defines how much space is used/unused. However, most of the "armor cubes" have the same CPU value, so you can replace cubes without fearng about CPU. So, how do I get better parts? Answer is easy. Build a vehicle, add weapons and go to fight online! You will get RP(RoboPoints) by damaging enemy vehicles. But, only RP doesn't matter when buying better armor cubes/weapons/movement cubes(e.g hover blades)/other parts. You also need to get you tier up! If you are in Tier 1(where you always start), you can't get upper tier parts(And as Tier 2 player, you can't get tier 3 parts, etc). You need to get Tier points(You will get them when the game is over, just like RP). With Tier poits, you can buy things from the Tech Tree. After you have purchased some item, it will be avaible in the Cube Depot, where you can buy that cube with RP. But how do I get tier up? This requires more playing. You have to make your vehicle bigger, and add new things into it! You will see Tier meter going forward at the bottom of your screen. When it reaches new level, you can buy that tier parts with Tier points! Oh, I don't have CPU anymore! Should I delete my vehicle? Nope. you can always get more CPU when getting player level up. And player level comes just from playing(a lot, LOT of playing).
This was my first guide/review, but I hope you guys enjoy it!

Portal probably needs little introduction, as a pretty major hit upon release, although it was more of a proof-of-concept that got by on its gimmick of, well, portals and the disturbingly charming (if it can be called that) game atmosphere. Portal 2, then, can be considered the realization of Portal as a full-fledged game, giving Aperture Science and its inhabitants more characterization and exploration (Wheatley is awesome!), as well as introducing an array of new gameplay mechanics, including
,
,
, and
.
In this specific sense, Portal 2 is more of what the original Portal promised and delivered on. If that interests you, I would say that you can probably stop reading this now, and that that alone probably merits a purchase; the game is relatively cheap now, especially during the myriad sales that show up. Co-op (which is a separate mode, not a retreading of single player) also exists this time around, and makes for some interesting puzzles with a friend (though probably not quite as hard as single player, if challenge is what you seek).
Still, while it is Portal at heart, I will note one particular regression. While there are definitely many nicely designed levels, there are also quite a few poorly designed ones. Specifically, there are many puzzles where the challenge comes from nothing other than finding the obscure, hidden portal-supporting surface, from which the solution tends to fall into place immediately afterwards. This gets particularly annoying during the
testing chambers, where these kinds of puzzles crop up
testing chambers and effectively waste unnecessary time.
And, like many puzzle games, Portal 2 doesn't really have much replay value; sure, you can attempt speedruns or other challenges, but those are universal and not particularly applicable to Portal 2. While DLC and user-created content theoretically helps get around this, I haven't really seen much interest in those (and I haven't tried them myself), and you should probably interpret the high critical score as "Portal 2 was executed very well" rather than "Portal 2 will always be remembered as a landmark video game".
In short, Portal 2 is more Portal goodness, and that is almost certainly a very good thing. But there can always be too much of a good thing (well, except money).

When I first found this on the Steam Green Light page I wasn't impressed with it's write up, I couldn't really picture the true goal as described and so passed this title up and didn't vote.  I am really really glad there were enough supporters out there to get this title lit.
Robocraft is a game in the vain of Battlebots, an American TV show focused around teams creating robots and pitting them against other teams in an octagon of battle, there were numerious terrain hazards including a spinning buzzsaw on the battle field along with other nefarious pitfalls.  This game falls right in line with this iconoclast genre (with a minecraft bent) allowing you to create virtually any block style bot your mind can fashion and pit it in epic (mortal?) combat against other genious creations.
Robocraft is a fantastically addicting title with battles typically lasting only 10 minutes (usually less) and only take seconds to join.  There is no difference between a premium account and a regular free play account with the majority of real-cash payments being used to level faster rather than win.  Team making is exceptionally good, honestly leagues better than some major competitive titles and weapon/movement balance is really spot on; no single combination of guns and wheels/hoverblades/jet engines seems to be patently better than anything else.
All in, I'm glad I reveisted this title and decided to try it out. Thanks to the Steam community for voting for this title and thanks to the developers for bringing an awesome game to market, I definitely recommend trying this title!

However seeing how much more is to come I would definitely recommend this game, plus it's free so it's hard to complain.

Portal probably needs little introduction, as a pretty major hit upon release, although it was more of a proof-of-concept that got by on its gimmick of, well, portals and the disturbingly charming (if it can be called that) game atmosphere. Portal 2, then, can be considered the realization of Portal as a full-fledged game, giving Aperture Science and its inhabitants more characterization and exploration (Wheatley is awesome!), as well as introducing an array of new gameplay mechanics, including
,
,
, and
.
In this specific sense, Portal 2 is more of what the original Portal promised and delivered on. If that interests you, I would say that you can probably stop reading this now, and that that alone probably merits a purchase; the game is relatively cheap now, especially during the myriad sales that show up. Co-op (which is a separate mode, not a retreading of single player) also exists this time around, and makes for some interesting puzzles with a friend (though probably not quite as hard as single player, if challenge is what you seek).
Still, while it is Portal at heart, I will note one particular regression. While there are definitely many nicely designed levels, there are also quite a few poorly designed ones. Specifically, there are many puzzles where the challenge comes from nothing other than finding the obscure, hidden portal-supporting surface, from which the solution tends to fall into place immediately afterwards. This gets particularly annoying during the
testing chambers, where these kinds of puzzles crop up
testing chambers and effectively waste unnecessary time.
And, like many puzzle games, Portal 2 doesn't really have much replay value; sure, you can attempt speedruns or other challenges, but those are universal and not particularly applicable to Portal 2. While DLC and user-created content theoretically helps get around this, I haven't really seen much interest in those (and I haven't tried them myself), and you should probably interpret the high critical score as "Portal 2 was executed very well" rather than "Portal 2 will always be remembered as a landmark video game".
In short, Portal 2 is more Portal goodness, and that is almost certainly a very good thing. But there can always be too much of a good thing (well, except money).

An interesting game with solid potential, but unfortunately gets progressively more "Grind2Win". The RP awards for battles seem to be increasingly smaller relative to upgrade costs as the Tier increases - for instance, a typical RP reward for a decent T4 performance might be 500 RP. Nice, but a single T4 SMG is going to take 6 of those to buy. One of those same battles will buy you an amazing TWO cubes of T4 armor. Now contemplate the RP invested in any of the craft seen in the trailer.
At first, I thought maybe this would get better - but looking at the "Robocraft Bonus Engine" page on the game's site we find this, under "goals of this system":
"To reduce the frequency of receiving a net loss in T5-10 i.e. when RP total is less than robot repair cost"
So apparently I've got THAT to look forward to in T5+ - actually LOSING RP when I get one-shotted by a skybox camper.
SPEAKING OF WHICH...
The single most game-breaking annoyance is SKYBOX CAMPERS. They seem to be more prevalent in the lower tiers - "vehicles" that consist of a T3/T4 weapon, a pilot seat, and a couple helium blocks. They float all the way up to the absolute top of the skybox, and usually can't even move.
Not that they need to, given what a T3 plasma cannon does to T1 armor and the difficulty of hitting a 2px wide target with SMGs.
There's a simple solution to this: make touching the top of the skybox for more than a brief moment destroy the vehicle, perhaps with a snarky death-message like "[player_name] floated away". Mobile flying platforms shouldn't have a problem, but gunchairs will only be useful for the first twenty seconds until they float away.
The "Fair Play Expectations" claim that doing this is asking for a ban, but I'd say 80% of the T1 and T2 matches I've played have featured at least one person doing this on each side. Supremely annoying when you've destroyed every opposing tank except for the gunchair, who then systematically massacres everyone who tries to cap.

Robocraft is a game where you build robots, then smash up other people's robot's with your robot. Sounds cool, right?
It really is. Sort of.
As the trailer describes, it's essentialy Minecraft and Robot Wars combined. It's creative (I've seen people with♥♥♥♥♥♥shaped robots that spunk out lasers. Yeah.) and it's certaintly a fun thing, but my issues lie with the gameplay itself.
The tier system is
. Depending on what's on your robot, you level up. Level up enough and you go up a tier.
This system allows for people with very good weapons to be in the same tier as those  with the basic lasers still. Same for people with better armer, movement, etc. This renders this game as not-newbie friendly. (VIDEO GAME SIN #1)
Microtransactions. Sadly, FreeJam have gone down the 2 currencies route, which really is dissapointing. (VIDEO GAME SIN #2) Can't afford to buy that special armour block? You can play the game, and be put against people who will demolish you in a multitude of violent ways, or pay for the alternate currency (with real cash), buy that block (in-game cash), and then be one of the people who exacts the violent executions. In other words, this is pay-to-win. (VIDEO GAME SIN #3)
To upgrade, you earn Tier Tech Points from the grindingly dull gameplay (which of course can be purchased from the second currency. Duh. Oh, and I guess that's another sin. VIDEO GAME SIN #4) so you can start buying better guns, armour, wheels, whatever. FreeJam claims that you get these from simply playing, and you get more for destroying enemies and capturing the base (Because that's the only gamemode. Capture the base. No variation. VIDEO GAME SIN #5), but only one is true. You could have killed every damn enemy on the field if you wanted, and you'd only walk away with about 3. Help or complete the base capture, however, and you get an influx of TTPs. So the developers are liars. (VIDEO GAME SIN #6)
Always Online DRM. Yeah, I get it's an online game, but heck, should I HAVE to be online just to build my robot? DRM can suck my DIK. (VIDEO GAME SIN #7)
And that's it. I shouldn't have to say any more.
The Good: Concept
The Bad: Microtransactions, DRM, dull gameplay, and an overall unpleasant experience.
Verdict: This game had so much oppurtunity. I guess FreeJam'll have fun brainwashing those who ae suppressed by the 2-currencies trick into topping up their cash swimming pool.
2/10.
(And that's a total of 7 video game sins.)

Now, before you go ahead and count this as a positive review, allow me to tell you that it is neither positive nor negative.
When i first started playing the game, i thought it was terrible, however, i later determined that Robocraft has a play style of its own and can't really be compared to any other multiplayer game like it. The level designs are great for the team play available and suits all types of robots that you can build. The weapons in the game function perfectly depending on your imagination; you want to fire down on everyone on the opposing team? Then you add guns to the bottom of your robot and add thrusters and hover blades to it. The possibilities are only limited to your own imagination.
However, this is not to say that Robocraft is absolutely flawless, the primary issue which i, and i only guess everyone else faces, is the teamwork. The people that you're paired with are always within your tier, however, this cannot be said for skill level. The other issue in regards to the team play of Robocraft isn't of the developers fault, but rather the players. When you're playing the game it doesn't feel like you're part of a team, it feels like everyone is out for themselves and is more like a free for all except you can only kill certain people. Futhermore, the vast majority of the people dont seem to be able to communicate with you when you need help, they just ignore you.
So, if you're looking for a game where you can drive whatever your mind can think of, Robocraft is for you, just keep in mind that you shouldn't expect too much out of your team, they may as well just be the distraction for you to move in and do your business.

After playing this game for over 30 hours and progressing through 4 (almost 5) tiers, I think I'm qualified to write a good, informed review. The concept of this game is to build a functioning robot (it isn't really a robot due to the fact that you have a pilot seat, but that's beside the point) out of the parts they give you, then take this robot into battles. The more you fight with your robot, the more currency you earn (represented by RP) along with Tech Points, which are used to unlock new parts, which are then bought with RP. You must also use RP to repair your bot if it is damaged in battle, and the repair costs varry depending on just how damaged your bot was. Currently, there is only one gamemode in which you must capture the opponent's base before they capture yours. So, if you're a fan of varrying gamemodes I can't really recommend this to you...yet.
One major thing that I feel like I should address is that this game does include microtransactions. BUT, before you hear that word and automatically deny the existance of the game, the game is not pay to win in the way that you would be able to notice it while playing a match, and arguably not pay to win at all. The reason for this is that the game works by matching up your bot with other bots which fit in your tier (I saw one of the reviews not recommending the game complaining that they are constantly matched with players in tiers higher then themselves, but I have never had that experience in over 30 hours of gameplay). Due to this system, someone who buys the best parts in the game is going to be automatically moved into the highest tier in the game, where they will still not gain an advantage over other players. If anything, those who pay for parts would have a disadvantage due to the fact that they are not as experienced in building their robots or fighting with them. Building off of my last sentence, the way you build your robot is very important. Someone with the lowest avaliable items in a tier with a well designed bot could still defeat someone with the highest weapons in the tier with a badly-designed bot.
Another major aspect of this game is progression through levels. The only time this game gives me the feeling of grinding is after I've maxed out my robot for the tier I'm in but I don't quite want to step up to the next tier yet, which is really only a limit I put on myself. There is rarely a time (in the first 4 tiers anyway, I haven't progressed to the tiers above so I can't speak for those yet) when you get back from a battle and can't afford to upgrade your robot in a at least a minor way, such as upgrading a few sheets of armor. Due to this constant ability to upgrade at least something, I never really feel like I'm grinding away at the next level, but rather slowly progressing through the level towards the next one, something I really enjoy.
All in all, Robocraft is a game with a great premise, currently limited gameplay elements (in terms of gamemodes) and a few glitches, but those are to be expected in early access games. I would recommend it to anyone who has ever wanted to be able to build and use the vehicle you take into battle and don't mind the fact that there is curently only one gamemode. To those who are turned away by that fact, there are still 3 maps which provide areas for using different strategies with different robots, adding some sort of variety into the gamemodes. Even if that still doesn't seem like enough of a redeeming factor, just try it anyway, as the worst that can happen if you end up absolutely hating it is that it took up some space on your computer and some of your time.

After playing this game for over 30 hours and progressing through 4 (almost 5) tiers, I think I'm qualified to write a good, informed review. The concept of this game is to build a functioning robot (it isn't really a robot due to the fact that you have a pilot seat, but that's beside the point) out of the parts they give you, then take this robot into battles. The more you fight with your robot, the more currency you earn (represented by RP) along with Tech Points, which are used to unlock new parts, which are then bought with RP. You must also use RP to repair your bot if it is damaged in battle, and the repair costs varry depending on just how damaged your bot was. Currently, there is only one gamemode in which you must capture the opponent's base before they capture yours. So, if you're a fan of varrying gamemodes I can't really recommend this to you...yet.
One major thing that I feel like I should address is that this game does include microtransactions. BUT, before you hear that word and automatically deny the existance of the game, the game is not pay to win in the way that you would be able to notice it while playing a match, and arguably not pay to win at all. The reason for this is that the game works by matching up your bot with other bots which fit in your tier (I saw one of the reviews not recommending the game complaining that they are constantly matched with players in tiers higher then themselves, but I have never had that experience in over 30 hours of gameplay). Due to this system, someone who buys the best parts in the game is going to be automatically moved into the highest tier in the game, where they will still not gain an advantage over other players. If anything, those who pay for parts would have a disadvantage due to the fact that they are not as experienced in building their robots or fighting with them. Building off of my last sentence, the way you build your robot is very important. Someone with the lowest avaliable items in a tier with a well designed bot could still defeat someone with the highest weapons in the tier with a badly-designed bot.
Another major aspect of this game is progression through levels. The only time this game gives me the feeling of grinding is after I've maxed out my robot for the tier I'm in but I don't quite want to step up to the next tier yet, which is really only a limit I put on myself. There is rarely a time (in the first 4 tiers anyway, I haven't progressed to the tiers above so I can't speak for those yet) when you get back from a battle and can't afford to upgrade your robot in a at least a minor way, such as upgrading a few sheets of armor. Due to this constant ability to upgrade at least something, I never really feel like I'm grinding away at the next level, but rather slowly progressing through the level towards the next one, something I really enjoy.
All in all, Robocraft is a game with a great premise, currently limited gameplay elements (in terms of gamemodes) and a few glitches, but those are to be expected in early access games. I would recommend it to anyone who has ever wanted to be able to build and use the vehicle you take into battle and don't mind the fact that there is curently only one gamemode. To those who are turned away by that fact, there are still 3 maps which provide areas for using different strategies with different robots, adding some sort of variety into the gamemodes. Even if that still doesn't seem like enough of a redeeming factor, just try it anyway, as the worst that can happen if you end up absolutely hating it is that it took up some space on your computer and some of your time.

This game is amazing, it's a crossover between a World of Tanks type game and Minecraft. That results in a sandbox-ish type version of World of Tanks and it really will consume your time!
Every tank is different, some aren't even tanks they're flying hoverpods flying through the Sky with lasers.
The concept is amazing and they really pulled this off.
With all the upgrades and increased building size makes the game expand for a long time until you're bored of it, and since it's early access it's being updated all the time so there's always new stuff! This isn't just blocks put into a game, you can actually make something that's yours and unique.
The matchmaking uses tiers which is determined by high end the stuff it on the vehicle, it's usually incredibly effective and you get into games with people who're just as good as you. It's also very quick for a free-to-play I usually get into a game 2 seconds after clicking search.
Another amazing thing about this game is that you can team up with friends! Friends make any game more fun and this game is no exception you can show off your amazing / awful creations to your friends and either race around the map shooting people or just flip over at the start.
You can run it on a toaster! Not literally but you can run this on pretty low end hardware. I have a few friends running awful spec laptops and they can run this game on medium and still  run silky smooth.
This game is designed for anyone to play, kids or gamers it's a fun game, everything is yours and unique  and you never know if your design will be the best.
Even though the game doesn't have an anti-cheat as far as I know I've come across no hackers which is suprising for a popular free-to-play maybe it's just because I'm in the lower half of the tiers but still.
I'd recommend this game to everyone I can, it's fun you get to do your own stuff and be unique and share it with your friends and then battle to the death. 9/10

This game is pretty simple. You build your own vehicles from the ground up using a wide selection of cubes and other shape blocks. What sets it apart from similar games is the level of freedom in creation. By winning matches, you'll earn points to buy new building materials, hardware, and modes of transportation. The addicting factor lies in the excitement of unlocking new parts and materials so you can build bigger, better, and cooler robots! That being said, the game is not perfect yet. There are issues with paying money to increase experience gained from matches. The physics engine is a little wonky as well. It would be really neat if they added more combat scenarios in the future such as protecting a convoy from the other team, game types with multiple capture points and multiple respawns, and some online co-op missions. For a free to play game, it is worth downloading and checking out.

It reminds me a little bit of banjo and kazooi nuts and bolts( let me state i only liked that game cause i didnt look at it like a BaK game and more like a building game). Yes it can be annoying to flip upside down, but this can be fixed with the flip tech which will flip you back over if you do become an upsidedown turtle. I personally find the only annoyances in this game from some of the straegys the other players use(like floating at the top of the map with a rail gun and killing everyone in there base). But none the less, it is a fair way to play since they are not glitching the game or modding it. The people floating at the top can easliy be taken care of if you have smg's equiped. Everything in this game is balanced. Air craft truely are fragile in this game and must be used carefully or you will end up spinning out of control due to the loss of an engine or two from a few shots. Nothing is overpowered, they just have their distinct advantages and are mostly used with their advantages.
So in short I due recomend this game if you enjoy the block building system along with playing to unlock new tech and items. A very rewarding system I say. There is no dull point in which you get impatient from not geting new items like other games have these days.

This review was written on September 15th, 2014.
I just started playing this game a week ago and I have been having a blast with it. There are a lot of negative reviews but I would not reccomend you take them seriously, as they can be disregarded for a number of reasons which I shall explain. Please don't let them dissuage you from at least trying the game.
So, what is Robocraft? The game description is fairly accurate: it's basically a cross between World of Tanks and Minecraft, but it's much deeper than that. There is a ridiculous amount of hidden depth in the game and it gives it a really high skill cap which can take a very long time to master, as far as I can tell.
First of all, there are really separate games, sort of like a CCG. First there is the part where you design your vehicle. I sometimes spend more time doing this than I do actually fighting. You can basically build anything under the sun: a standard tank with a cannon, a hoverbike with machineguns, a heavily armored static defense turret, a high speed fighter jet, a long range bomber, a lighter-than-air dirigible, or whatever. You could even build something that isn't very "standard" but is just fun to drive or look at, and still potential an effective fighting vehicle. I have seen some really creative designs (like one that looked like a giant steam train, for example).
At first a lot of designs are similar, but as you progress through the game you unlock different components you can use, ranging from weapons to energy shields, thrusters and radar jammers, and more. I should note that after you reach rank 5 (out of 10) you don't really unlock anything new, but just better versions of the old stuff (I will go into more detail about that later). Also as you progress through the game you get a better understanding of how the game mechanics and damage mechanics work, and this will additionally add a lot of variety to your vehicle. For example, there is a very clever method of re-distributing damage taken in one section to another, less-essential part of your vehicle using triangles called "triforce armor" which you can Google search if you want to learn more about.
The second part of the game is the actual fighting part, which is a lot like World of Tanks in that you lump 2 groups of players in tank-like vehicles on opposite sides of the map and they fight to the death or capture the enemy's base. It's fairly self explanatory, but unless you get instantly destroyed (which is a possible, but somewhat rare occurence) every game plays differently because as your vehicle takes damage, part of it are literally blown off. If a couple guns are blown off, no big deal, you probably have more. But what if you are in a lighter-than-air vehicle and your floaty bits are blown off? Or what if you are in a tank and your "steering wheels" get blown off? After getting out of a close fight with half your thrusters missing, it is a fun challenge to try and figure out how to get your vehicle to go where you want it even though it isn't in the same shape that you designed it in. And if your vehicle is alive and out of harms way, but damaged to the point where it has no fighting capability (for example, all your guns were destroyed) you can always self destruct (after 10 seconds of taking no damage) and be back in a new match within 30-45 seconds. Don't give up hope- I've gotten plenty of kills where all that was left of me was the pilot seat, a couple blocks, and a single gun. A 95% destroyed vehicle lying on the ground helpless should not be underestimated!
About general graphics and whatnot. Graphics are nothing spectular but they are good enough to look current. The game is fairly well polished even though it doesn't look like a AAA title. The soundtrack is pretty good, I will say, not everyone will agree but I think it's solid. I am usually fine leaving the music on rather than listening to my music library in the background. Controls are pretty well set-up, everything tends to work how you intend it to, which rare exception.
Now to address some concerns people may have about the game:
For those worried about insta-kills, I will say this- it is certainly possible, but only with both a poorly designed vehicle and a well aimed shot. A well designed vehicle should never be insta-killed no matter what the circumstances.
For people worried about the fact that you can take higher tier weapons into lower tier games, you will have to sacrifice a lot to do so. For example, you might be able to bring a tier 5 gun into a tier 2 game, but to fit into that tier you will basically need to build a tricycle with a single gun strapped to the front of it. Sure you can kill people quickly, but they can kill you pretty quick as well if you aren't careful. I have been on both sides of this and it is balanced.
Every game will be different, and if you are getting destroyed a lot, you generally get good feedback about how you got destroyed and it's fun to start from scratch with new ideas in mind. I never really let it "get me down" because there isn't much penalty to having a streak of bad games and I can always try to new things. It's not like in World of Tanks when you are stuck grinding with one tank. As an example, I made this really long and thin tank loaded with plasma cannons but I wasn't really doing too well with it, so I took off the wheels, moved the guns from the top to the bottom, strapped on a whole bunch of helium tanks and thrusters, and suddenly my tank had become something more akin to a zeppelin, and I ended up doing a lot better with it.
Nothing is overpowered, the game is surprisingly well balanced. I would think it's an impossible task but the developers pulled it off and everything has it's counter. A standard SMG tank will usually get killed by a plasma tank- however plasma tanks are extremely vulnerable to anything that's flying and will generally get wrecked. Slow moving flying vehicle, no matter how small, stand no chance against railgun tanks, and the larger flying vehicles tend to get picked apart by SMG tanks if they aren't careful. There is the random chance that you get a game where nobody on the enemy team happens to have a good counter to you, and you can get a lot of kills without fear of effective retaliation. These games are fun if you get put in that position but pretty rare so not a big deal overall.
About pay2win. Remember where I said I would talk more about how you don't unlock anything new past rank 5? Well here's the deal: past rank 5, the game can get a tad pay2win. The blocks are very expensive, you lose money if you die without dealing a bit of damage, and the balance between different archetypes is skewed (for example, using a rank 10 railgun in a rank 10 match is much less effective than using a rank 4 railgun in a rank 4 match). HOWEVER the fun part is that there is really no reason to play past rank 5. You can get up to rank 5, unlock everything up to that point very easily without paying a dime, and then have fun trying to get the best possible vehicle for tiers 1-5. You don't have to go to tier 6. The queue times at lower levels are shorter and you can get access to all the same stuff, mostly. For the most part rank 5 gets you access to all the game has to offer. So that's basically my reasoning for why you can discount most of the negatives about pay2win and balance.
Another reason why most of the negative reviews can be discounted is because they are out of date. My only experience is with the game in it's current form (August 15 2014) so I have an unbiased opinion that does not take into account the previous state of the game. The developers seem to have a good attitude and have a lot of content in development for the future. They did an AMA on Reddit recently which you can check out if interested.
I hope you choose to give the game a shot after reading my review so you can decide for yourself whether it's worth your time or not.

I started playing this game about two weeks ago. It is alot of fun to tweak and tinker with bot designs and pit them against others. I thoroughly enjoyed the game....at first (heck, i spent almost a full day working with a hover bot design trying to get the balance right). But, after i hit tech tier 3, i began to notice something. Getting Tech Points (which are used to unlock better parts for upgrading your designs) quickly became a hellish nightmare just to acquire even one.
After taking a look at the opponents who kept beating me, i realised why. The game seems to be set up so that how you equip your bot determines what tier matches you can join. That said, i was seeing in nearly every match that people were using parts that were listed as tier 5, 6, 7, even up to 10 (which is the max). These players were one hit killing entire teams. Some matches barely lasted 2 minutes.
Each part has a point value that builds up your bot's tier level. This would be a good idea, if not for how easily such a system can be exploited. Removing most of your high tech gear and leaving your high powered weapons, allows you to join low tier matches with high tier weapons that can pretty much one shot everyone on the map. For a new player, those who exploit this system cause progress to be agonizing slow before your even in the middle tiers. Matches become horribly one sided, and whether or not your able to gain any Tech points at all from each match is just a matter of pure chance (odds being that...no, you will gain nothing because of someone on the enemies team that rips through everyone that gets near him).
It is because of this that i currently find Robocraft to be very much broken and in serious need of a rebalancing. Maybe increase the points on higher tier gear making it harder to use them in lower tier matches, or set it so that as long as you have....say...a tier 6 weapon equiped, youll only be allowed into a tier 6 or higher game. As it stands, newcomers to the game will likely find progression to be a futile, oppressively time consuming grind. I do however see potential in this game, and hope to see improvements on it in the future. Robocraft has alot to offer once it irons out the exploitation issues.

World of Tanks for those that like fun as he focus, not so much simulation.
Build your 'tank' (robot) minecraft style, unlocking new parts and blocks as you go, and blast some bots!
Then, come back with money and research earned, upgrade/redesign/refine your bot and have at it again.
A very innovative approach to the teir system. The more you add, the higher your vehicle is rated untill you enter T2, T3 etc. Research is for teir-specific equiptment and blocks, so to get T3 guns and armour you need to earn T3 experience with a T3 rated bot.
Nothing is stopping you bringing T5 guns to a T1 fight, but you wont be bringing much armour or redundant systems, since those guns would be pushing the T1 limit. This clever system is always there, ensuring a fair fight.
Its free to play, and i'm up to T4 as of writing with no need to drop any money for progression at this point.
In fact, this brings me to the complaints.
1: There is not enough bling for me to waste my money on.
2. Weapon variety is a little small, with only 3 escillating types.
3. Flying vehicles are a novelty, and are still not practical as of T4. The power armour helps, but I think they will come into their own in T5 with the better power-plates
4. LAZOR GUNBEDS
5. Give me a zoom option for my lasers, dammit
6. Why have a sniper bot when lasers are perfectly accurate when fired conservatively?
But otherwise its a very neat little competitive game that I think anyone can have a bit of fun with. Also it has very good social elements, but I dont have any friends

This game is great.  Obviously, it's in alpha, so there are some tweaks to work out, but the patches are fairly often (every 2-3 weeks) so things get changed up.
The one thing I dont like is how in lower tiers, people can come in with a tiny robot with a giant gun and just sit there and one shot you.  If they fixed that, it would be more enjoyable.  But as you get to higher tiers, the problem disappears (I'm at Tier 8 now).
The repair costs are fine, you will *always* make more money then you lose in a match.  *Always* until tier 5 or 6.  That's when you may lose money if you get destroyed early.
This is where people start complaining, because if you buy premium, you continue to never lose money in a match.  People whine that it's "pay to play", but I've spent many hours in this game, it took at least 20 to get to Tier 5.  With some of the features they are adding to the game, they've said that Tier 1-5 is "Practice" and Tier 6+ is when the real game starts.  I think its perfectly reasonable to have to buy premium (I gave them 10$, bought premium for a month, and still have lots of in game cash leftover) to keep the game easy and not lose money on repairs.
Support the developers!  This game isn't perfect yet, but it has massive potential and I'm excited to see it evolve.

A really fun game, and a beast concept, ruined by a terrible multiplayer experience.
-Matchmaking is based on a point system which all blocks have. This would work great, except for the fact that you can bring a big gun, place it in a cube, add some wheels and you can go farm Low-level newbees by insta-killing everything (i know this because i do this since on the "mid-tier" matches everything is unbalanced and matchmaking is done on robot potential rather player skill)
-Platoon system is stupid, why would you bring a Tier 1 Robot to a Tier 5 fight?
-Weapons are terribly unbalanced. A well placed railgun will insta-kill your pilot. Air Plasma Bombers are the bane of everything and can't be stopped unles you SMG their weapons, provided they don't kill you first.
-the Tech system encourages a Pay-to-win and an "abuse the lower levels" mode. Just get lots of tech points by farming on low tiers with a big weapon, and then convert them all to Uber Tech points on a 1:1 rate, paying with buyable currency.
It's a great concept, but the multiplayer is so flawed it's outrageous. And you know what's worse? You can't stop playing it. No matter what, you'll still go back, win some games, get some stuff, move a tier upwars, and the cycle will repeat. You go back to this game no matter what. I don't recommend this level of pseudo-addiction.

Do you like strategy games? Do you like action games? Do you like games that have extremely hard to follow plot points and that ultimately wind up making you physically disfigured?
Well Portal accomodates 2.5 of what's written above, because the plot is actually easy to follow.

The characters in it are immediately likable and you won't be dissappointed for the next seven years after finishing it by waiting for a third installment, wait... Yeah, you probably will.
The best part is it's designed to be playable on no matter how good your rig is.
Plenty of easter eggs and funny little additions to the game make it lovable in a special way.
Plus the community behind it is amazing, it's like minecraft... except better. And with portals... lot's of portals.
So if you haven't yet buy the game and be enveloped by it as you rage in hard to finish puzzles for the duration of the game.
So I have been ranting on about how it's good so now I'll try to come up with some negative reasons to not buy it:
1. You need to have played Portal 1 to get the whole storyline (or maybe not, I can't relate to it)
2. You need money to by the game (bummer, am I right?)
3. You do need some form of puzzle solving abilities (the levels are designed to develop cognitive reasoning though)
4. You need to be able to understand pommy British accents (it'll annoy you so much)
5. People complain that it is too short (I don't think so though)
Anyway, do buy this game it is so worth it and while your at it get TF2 and some other Valve games.

A lot of people seem to be complaining about how the game is "pay-to-win" now.  I'm having a hard time sympathizing with them; I'm doing quite alright without having paid a dime.
Granted, it's not a great game.  It's in Early Access, though; this is to be expected.
The Good:
- It's addicting.  You keep telling yourself "alright, just one more match" over and over again.  Even with the sheer lack of environmental variety (more on that later), there's enough room for variety in "robot" (more on *that* later) designs that it's hard to be tired of tweaking and tuning your creations to be the best they can be.
- Definitely *not* a pay-to-win.  Some long-timers complain that it now costs money to repair your "robots", but I think that's perfectly reasonable; it adds a bit of challenge and rewards those who actually *survive* battles.  Meanwhile, all the parts (other than the cosmetic ones, which don't do anything beyond looking pretty) can be obtained through hard work and diligence - and not really that much of it, either.  Basically, I think they're just whining.
- The Tier system is pretty well thought-out, though it does need some polish (like weighting powerful weapons a bit heavier to keep railgunners out of Tier 1).
The Bad:
- Multi-tier battles need to be either removed or reworked.  By "reworked", I mean drastically unbalancing the number of low-tier players relative to high-tier ones in such a match.  Multi-tier battles would be *way* more fun if they were implemented as hordes of low-tier "robots" against one or two higher-tier death machines.
- Speaking of different battle types: there should be more battle types.  The simple "capture the base" mode is alright, but it's getting a tad old.  How about some capture-the-flag?  Deathmatches (fighting to the last bot standing)?  The "weak horde against strong behemoth" like I mentioned above?  Some new maps would go a long way, too.
- Receiving the results of someone else's radar shouldn't require a separate part, especially one at such a high tier requirement.  What's the point of "scouting" if you're not even sure that the team you're scouting for is able to reap those benefits?
- On the above note, more variety in what the "robot" can do would be nice.  There's some discussion on the forums about a "repair" weapon that fixes teammates; that would be a good start.  Some close-range "melee" weaponry would be fun, too; rather disappointing that ramming one's adversary doesn't actually do damage.
The Ugly:
- They're not actually "robots" you're building; rather, they're vehicles *controlled by* a little humanoid robot (you, presumably).
- Some of the parts like the hoverblades, wings, thrusters, etc. reference non-existent parts in their descriptions (i.e. a Tier 3 hoverblade mentioning that it's better than some nonexistent "L1 hoverblade" or somesuch), which is a bit jarring.
- Mars' sky is green on two of the maps (basically, the two that aren't the crater one from the practice mode).  Since when did Mars have a green sky?  It's red, dangit.
Verdict:
Would recommend regardless of its faults.  It's an "Early Alpha"; I'm curious as to how it evolves going into beta and eventual release.  Even as an alpha, it's still pretty fun.

- Mars' sky is green on two of the maps (basically, the two that aren't the crater one from the practice mode).  Since when did Mars have a green sky?  It's red, dangit.
Verdict:
Would recommend regardless of its faults.  It's an "Early Alpha"; I'm curious as to how it evolves going into beta and eventual release.  Even as an alpha, it's still pretty fun.

I was very fortunate to been over at my friends house when I learned of this game. He was a space enthusist and had spent countless hours on KSP and I had seen him play World of Tanks. I always joke at his intrests but this game stood out. I had pictured it being very mathamatical or slow paced like KSP or World Of Tanks respectivly but surprising, it has neither of these elements. How does this outlander of the space frontier stand? It's a long story.
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay almost mirrors World of Tanks. The players start on oppisite sides of a map and fight each other. In this game, you fight to either eliminate the others or take control of their base. While your space tank attack dogs are what you start out with, it's not long til you're left with a plane or hovercraft. It's miraculous to see the change from a small rover with a gun to a fully fledged jet, bombing tanks that are nothing to sneeze at and flying away into the sky. The control are tight for the most part, everything does feel like you did it, but depending on your arrangment and your choice of parts, the vessel might capsize quite often and you can find yourself helpless upside down, (hilarious to watch, miserable to have happen to you.) Getting stuck to some outlandish term is frusterating to say the least and to have to watch people pass you, helplessly, is depressing. The players are divided into tiers and while people are very tough, you usually feel you can take anyone depending on your approach and desigh, (unless it's a god forsaken rail gun.)
GRAPHICS: The graphics are very good. The metal shines and the textures, despite low quality when stuck to the wall, are inmpressive from a distance. The bases and block designs are clean and well designed. The lasors each have a different type of visual effect, letting you know what gun you may be facing ahead. While the selection is decent, the maps are repetative and limit themselves as of now to Mars and an Icy tundra. A couple new maps in future updates would help.
SOUND: There is no music but the sounds fit, as they are space-like and contain the typical sounds you'd expect from a future space shooter....a lot of "pews" and "zaps"...not a lot to say here.
QUANTITY: The game is very well paced in the fact that whatever you add to your tank and whatever armor you have determines your tier and each stronger peice adds a little bit to your next tier. Since parts are expensive, you must battle in your current state to get cash to buy weapons. You do have to pay to fix a broken tank/plane but the benefit of a fight always outweights the cost so you always get a gain of some sort. There are numerous types of armor, wheels, guns, thrusters, hover panels, etc. to have you playing for a long time.

I was very fortunate to been over at my friends house when I learned of this game. He was a space enthusist and had spent countless hours on KSP and I had seen him play World of Tanks. I always joke at his intrests but this game stood out. I had pictured it being very mathamatical or slow paced like KSP or World Of Tanks respectivly but surprising, it has neither of these elements. How does this outlander of the space frontier stand? It's a long story.
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay almost mirrors World of Tanks. The players start on oppisite sides of a map and fight each other. In this game, you fight to either eliminate the others or take control of their base. While your space tank attack dogs are what you start out with, it's not long til you're left with a plane or hovercraft. It's miraculous to see the change from a small rover with a gun to a fully fledged jet, bombing tanks that are nothing to sneeze at and flying away into the sky. The control are tight for the most part, everything does feel like you did it, but depending on your arrangment and your choice of parts, the vessel might capsize quite often and you can find yourself helpless upside down, (hilarious to watch, miserable to have happen to you.) Getting stuck to some outlandish term is frusterating to say the least and to have to watch people pass you, helplessly, is depressing. The players are divided into tiers and while people are very tough, you usually feel you can take anyone depending on your approach and desigh, (unless it's a god forsaken rail gun.)
GRAPHICS: The graphics are very good. The metal shines and the textures, despite low quality when stuck to the wall, are inmpressive from a distance. The bases and block designs are clean and well designed. The lasors each have a different type of visual effect, letting you know what gun you may be facing ahead. While the selection is decent, the maps are repetative and limit themselves as of now to Mars and an Icy tundra. A couple new maps in future updates would help.
SOUND: There is no music but the sounds fit, as they are space-like and contain the typical sounds you'd expect from a future space shooter....a lot of "pews" and "zaps"...not a lot to say here.
QUANTITY: The game is very well paced in the fact that whatever you add to your tank and whatever armor you have determines your tier and each stronger peice adds a little bit to your next tier. Since parts are expensive, you must battle in your current state to get cash to buy weapons. You do have to pay to fix a broken tank/plane but the benefit of a fight always outweights the cost so you always get a gain of some sort. There are numerous types of armor, wheels, guns, thrusters, hover panels, etc. to have you playing for a long time.
Conclusion: 8/10. It's a great time to be had. If you've never gotten into Minecraft or World of Tanks, don't let that discourage you to not check this out. It's free for the most part and you can have a lot of fun. The fun combat, the cool sounds and graphics, and the overall feel and quantity are praises while the sometimes repetative fighting, maps, and the occational problem like flipping over, (seriously, the game gives you an item to flip you back over and even that barely works,) are minor annoyances compared to the action and struggle to craft your own weapon and be the best.

Alright, may as well throw my 2 cents in, show that there are people who haven't played the old version that likes it.  Where to begin, Robocraft is really fun to play, really, really fun, my only complaint is that it IS sorta unbalanced, especially when people bring in tier 6 and tier 7 weaponry into tier 2 and 3 fights, that's just asking to wreck players who can't use better.  That definitely needs to be changed, like, say, tier one equipment can be used in any, but tier 2 equipment can be used in tier 3, 2, and 1.  It should be more balanced that way, I think it would really, really benefit the game, like World of Tanks, which this takes inspiration from, tier 3 tanks can face tier 2 and tier 4 opponents, but not tier 1, one tier above or below would definitely help the balancing issue, so again, people can't bring in the railgun, like someone called a "point and kill" gun, whcih it is, it's a sniper rifle, that's to be expected.  Anyway, railguns are tier 6 if I'm not mistaken, maybe tier 5, either way they're not fair for lower-tier players (like myself who is tier 3).
Another issue I should point out is that until you reach tier 5, your creativity IS limited.  Tier 5 is when you unlock balloons (satellites, as they're called by players), and planes, and you can use everything (Tier 1 only has wheels).  So you're limited until you actually spend a lot of hours in the game grinding up to tier 5 research.  That isn't made easier by the fact you can't convert research points you don't need, to higher tiers, without paying money. Even at a loss it would work, like, say, 3 tier 1 tech points make a tier 2, 3 tier 2s make a tier 3, etc.  The game is early alpha so this is subject to change.
performance wise, the game performs well, I've had no connection issues MOST of the time, and have experienced no latency or game lag.  Handling is a little rough, and it does take time getting a robot balanced right so it works (too many times has my tank decided to spin in circles, or my hovercraft wanted to flip.), So that does need a little work.  collision effects for vehicles would be cool too, so you could help teammates that were flipped without a flipper thingy (angular rectifier i think is what it's called),
Overall, I do recommend this game, but be warned, it IS ALPHA, so there are some balancing issues and stuff that needs reworking, however killing a vehicle that brings in an OP weapon is so satisfying.

This is a game that separates three types of people:  bad players, good players, and good Payers.  You can read about how this game is Pay to win but it’s simply not.  I have played enough to know that, unlike pay to win games, if you don’t suck at this game, you’re not going to notice the true difference until the much higher tiers of the game.  Let’s break it down:
1.  You need be smart enough to design your own vehicle and place your weapons well enough to use them from multiple angles, not as easy as you would think.
2.  You need to choose which tech upgrades you want if you want to move fast through the tiers.  Otherwise they are all up for grabs if you are willing to do the grinding.
3.  Like any other game, there are times when others will have an advantage.  If you practice, learn how to use the maps, and customize and perfect your vehicle and weapons, the advantage will be minimized to non-existent most of the time.
4.  It’s free, they have to make a little money somewhere!

I really like this game, and unlike a lot of people who have reviewed (Recommended, whatever) this game gave it Not Recommended because it has become "Pay to Win". It has got an option to go premium, but this is un-intrusive and doesn't completely throw things out of balance. You can also use real money to buy "Galaxy Cash". You can spend Galaxy Cash to buy cubes (What you use to build your robot), instead of the normal currency, which isn't TOO bad, but still not great. The worst this "Pay to Play" aspect ever gets (In my opinion) is that you can use GC to convert normal Tech Points into Uber Tech Points. The normal TP are tiered, so you can not get Tier 7 TP on your first battle, and better armor, weapons, utilities and wheels/hoverblades are on a higher tier. Anyway, I can use GC to convert my Tier 2/3/etc. TP into Uber TP. Uber TP can be used for ANY upgrade, but you only have access to any below you or one above you. This means that someone with what is essentially a rocket launcher can go against other people you don't have rocket launchers. The thing is, though, is that hardly anyone gets premium or buys GC. Which means that everything I just said isn't really a problem. The actual game is very addictive, and lots of fun. All in all, I think that unless you reckon that "It's the thought that counts" when it comes to using real money in games, this game is worth the $0 it costs, and I would still buy it for $10 or even $15. This is a good game that gets some unfair negative reviews and hate.  I am going to address some unfair attacks at this game.
The BIG thing about these negative steam reviews is that anybody can write them thus many Loser players with idiot tank designs come here to take out their anger on the game’s store page.  This is partly thanks to the chat window in the games main lobby where countless 9 year-olds tell the whole server why they lost because SMG’s are cheap and not because they rushed in alone with their no-armor hovercraft in between 5 enemy tanks.  When other normal players lose to an SMG tank they see the chat and believe the exaggerated comments and join them, then they start venting their anger too. The other slightly more fair reviews I’ve seen are from the old-time players who say the game devs ruined the game. I’m a little newer at this than them and I’ve played almost 40 hours of gameplay in these "dark times," made it to T5 and had fun all the way, and there’s no signs of the fun stopping any time soon. The people who are having fun (and there’s a lot of us) don’t bother to write reviews, just the people who want to vent their anger do.
The first thing people say is that this game is pay2win but that just isn’t true. First of all, paying users and free users get all the same parts to work with and second, in this game your robot has a stat for ranking. When you add a part to your robot it raises the rank stat and if you reach a certain point it will go up in tier. There are 10 tiers of robots and you just about always get put against robots in your tier so paying 2-win is impossible. The only thing paying does for you is give you faster progression through the tiers. Some people say its pay to progress but I’m on top of T5 and I haven’t had that problem yet although I think during a certain update it was bad but they have already fixed that by now. Progression isn’t super important anyway because by T5 every TYPE of part is unlocked, just not the bigger stronger versions (which are in there own tier). Unlike World of tanks and other F2Ps you can still make cool stuff at lower tiers and there’s none of that “premium ammo” crud that I hate.
Now for the second big thing to talk about, op (over powered) weapons and parts. Every type of weapon gets called “op” 90 times in the same day because of that venting 9 year-old thing I told you about before. One big thing to keep in mind is that this game is in alpha so balance is subject to change. I hate when people say “plasma has ruined this game forever” because even if plasma was cheap the devs would rebalance it ASAP. There are only 3 different types of weapons in the game (for now) and they all have their intended functions. I’m not saying the game has always had perfect balance (and it still doesn’t) but it’s still a lot of fun to play. The last thing about balance is that a lot of players are new to this game and don’t know what they can do. An example would be that hovercrafts can dodge plasma shells vertically but I don’t see many players do this. Those players could go on to say that plasma is cheap or that hovercrafts are underpowered but the real problem is that the players don’t try new tactics.
People whine a little about other things like lag, warping and glitches but I have never had those problems, those things are just more problems that people unfairly vent out during their rants.
Overall I just wanted to tell you that this is a really fun game that can make you think and adapt, and also that the devs aren’t evil (I think), they gave us free stuff as makeup for a server crash they had. If the game gets big and devs finish this right then this could be a really great and solid game. Thanks for reading, PEACE OUT!

There's been a lot of bad reviews floating around, and most of the complaints are either non-existent, or a bit petty to be perfectly honest! This game is in early access, it's not going to be perfect - but that said, it's near enough to it, and the devs keep adding new stuff in to make it even better. The premise is simple, build a robot, fight, win/lose, invest points into upgrades and buying new blocks/weapons/armour/forms of movement. Yes, it could be a bit repetitive to some people, but it's so quick to jump in and out of games and great fun testing out new designs that if it ever feels even slightly stale, just rebuild your robot from scratch and try something else!
There are a lot of people moaning about the rate at which you earn the in-game currency for buying stuff, but if they really expected it to be easy then everyone would max out in minutes. Yes, if you get destroyed, repairing costs about 60/70% of what you earned on a loss. But you earn more than enough to keep going on wins, and the devs are kind enough at the moment give regular promo codes out for bonus premium days and other bits and pieces.
Downoad this, you won't be disappointed. It's great fun, casual, easy to pick up, hard to master, occasionally even laugh-out-loud funny and best of all, totally free!

This game is quite addictive and has a lot of promise, but:
Physics is very unrealistic. All sorts of vehicles don't work how you expect them to. Even for very conventional designs, the handling is barely believeable, if you go for something strange, you get something impossible to control. If your car loses a few wheels it behaves very different from a real car in the same situation. Proper air friction & gravity? Forget it.
There are only, like, 5 maps, and a single objective. The game gets boring very quickly.
Sometimes you can get stuck in invisible scenery, having to drive around big obstacle you can't see.
Many weapons are overpowered, surviving them is a matter of luck (and cowardice). Some weapons can literally one-shot you from huge distance, and you don't respawn after that and have to wait till the end of battle and then pay for repair.
Creating complex constructions is nearly pointless, because the main construction blocks are too weak to withstand a single shot from almost any weapon. You only have to rely on armor of active modules, such as guns/wheels/etc and try to get them into smallest possible volume.

LIKE
-Not very p2w, since it's easy to get money anyways.
-Very nice building
-Can create different types of vehicles, planes, tanks, etc.
-Looks about as good as you'd expect it.
DISLIKE
-Tiering system is a bit off. It works with how many blocks you have on your robot, so a small robot with t4 equipment can fight a t1.

If you want to skip a few tiers and get some extra gear, you can pay for it, but it's not that hard to unlock it all yourself. Unless you expect to be in tier 10 within your first couple of days, you wont have to pay for anything. It's a brilliant game, sure the battles get a bit repetitive, but you can always try out a different sort of vehicle.
Also, it's not fair to complain about the prices. It's an indie game remember, and it's free, so it's fair for them to price some things so that they can make the game better than it already is. You might as well give it a try, and buy something if you want to support the game and it's developers. It may not be for everyone, but it's free and you might as well give it a try. As I said you'll have to work a bit to get to the higher tiers, but what do you expect?
And don't forget, it's in early acces which means there will be a lot of updates before the full game. (Which will come quicker if you buy some stuff.)

This is great for a game what is still in alpha. The money system is pretty good, but if you dont play good, you can start to loose money in T6. If you want you can also buy premium what gives you 50% more income in tokens and credits. Because the game is still in alpha it has only 5 maps, 1 gamemode and not so many customisations. You have 3 guns (railgun, plasma cannon and SMG) and 4 different vehicle types (ground, hovercraft, planes and satellites).  This game is fun but it can become frustrating and boring because there are players who dont give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about teamplay and playing alone is just boring. But you have the ability to   make 3 player platoons (4 player if you are premium).  Matches are maximum like 7 min long but they are usually 2-3 minutes. IMO its good because not all players have time to play like 15+ minute long matches.
There are a lot of bugs in the game and some combinations like plasma+plane could be a little OP, but if you have a SMG or railgun planes are very easy to take down. Sometimes the MM also screws you by placing you +1 tier matches (usually in tier 6+ because many players unlock big tier guns and then just go sealclubbing in T1-4 or some play in T5 and T6. Also the physics aren't the best atm. And there are some laggs in the network so sometimes vehicles teleport and that can tip you upside down, but there are things that help you get back on your wheels.
Many people say it is Pay 2 win, but there actually aren't any possibilitys that with using cash can make your vehicle better. You will only save yourself some time.

Believe me when I say that I absolutely love puzzle games. They provide interesting challenges and can really make you think. This sequel defies the cliche that sequels are terrible, and is arguably better then its previous entry in the Portal series. Adding new features to solve puzzles with and new characters to love, you won't find a better puzzle game out there.
Starting with the story, you would think a puzzle game like Portal 2 wouldn't havee all that great a story, but you couldn't be more wrong. In fact, this game shines in its story. Involving various plot twists and introducing the best character Cave Johnson, this game is to be taken seriously.
Moving along the lines of the first game, you are soon taken out of the bounds of the testing chambers and into the depths of Aperture Science. However, unlike the first game they are not holding your hand most of the way (mostly). Instead you are left to wander around the huge areas to make your way back into the testing areas to thwart the villain. And avoiding spoilers, let's just say at the end the villain gets whats coming to him/her/it.

World of Tanks, meet Space Engineers. This is really interesting game. It sparks creativity, just like Kerbal Space Program and Space Engineers, but allows for quick, evolving action. There is no manual - you have to learn all the tricks all by yourself. Gameplay is well balanced, with three paper-rock-scisissors type weapon classes (without mixing!), and diferrentiation between light hit and run vechicle and tank lying only in builder's imagination.
Of course it has tendencies - out of every 10 tiers of vechicles, there are pulls for particular build types on each tier range, but every battle you can see something really creative. It's mostly - it aint't stupid if it works. Battles are not long, and usually fun, until you get emotional about loosing - it will happen, there is always someone better, or who will get lucky shot - and it's team sport. Also over higher tiers they tend to shift from capture the base to team deathmatch.
I like, that it's not pay-to-win game - you can still dump much money into the game, and get fair amount of equipment in return, but you still have to use your imagination and experinece to build something - and if you don't have skill (pretty good aim and orientation), you won't get far.
Reward system limits ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to manageable minimum, only problem is with highly-skilled players roaming around lower tiers. It shows good replay value, but it poses a problem for beginners. I'm Tier 6-7 now, and I just for fun built T1 vechicle, and got 7 kills straight in the first battle. Defenitely it wasn't fun for other players...
Technical aspects are pretty good - if game servers are ok, matchmaking is fast, and there are no drops. Even crappy internet with high ping is handled by Robocraft well. Graphics wise, Any mid-shelf GPU will allow comfortable play, and if you're on integrated (Sandy Bridge-Haswell, no clue about AMD), lower to 1400x900 or below - 1920x1080 is too much - and you will be fine.
Game has potential to get many loyal players, but it needs to evolve, especially new game modes will need to be added, and social part of the game needs overhaul, but even for quick fun, game si very good.

Portal 2 is the puzzle game for FPS lovers.
No seriously.  The game is structured as an FPS, but is instead a brilliantly-designed puzzle game.  The idea is simple - get from point A at the start to point B at the end.  You have your basic tools - running, jumping, crouching, crouch-walking, picking up and dropping objects, but most of the time these are not sufficient on their own to get to the goal.
The gimmick here, and where this game shines, is the Portal Gun.  On it's face, it's simple; you have two portals, which attach to any white, portal-able surface.  Stuff goes in one, comes out the other, and vice versa.  They're fired from a gun that has unlimited range (and I do mean unlimited) - if you can see it and it's portalable, you can place a portal on it, and you can reposition them more-or-less freely.  Just fire the portal at a different target to move it.
This is all stuff that should be old-hat to veterans of the first game, but where Portal 2 shines is that it takes you out of the sterile, predesigned environments of the first game and throws you into the depths of Aperture, where the crumbling and decaying test chambers of days gone by have produced new and interesting obstacles to navigate with your portals.  Portal 2 feels less like a series of unconnected test chambers, and more like a seamless whole, with your character naturally progressing from one area to another.  It also introduces new mechanics and substances to be manipulated with the Portal Gun, which I don't want to spoil... completely.  Ever wanted to bounce off walls, run like The Flash, soar through the air without even a momentum-launch, or place portals nearly anywhere, even on surfaces that normally won't accept them?  Well... Portal 2 will give you the opportunity to explore those things.
This is not to say that Portal 2 is newbie-unfriendly.  Not by a long shot.  The game's pacing is incredible, easing you into the use of your personal movement abilities and the use of the Portal Gun, then slowly ramping it up, introducing new concepts and obstacles steadily until you've mastered them all.  Few things feel quite as good as overcoming a stumper of a puzzle through persistence and logic.
If you enjoy a more cerebral challenge from time-to-time, you could do a lot worse than Portal 2.

When jumping into Portal 2 it is very important to remember one thing...it's a sequel. With that knowledge in mind, we can answer a few key questions:
1. Will it achieve the same level of originality as the first?
2. Will it strike the player as equally as intriguing as the first?
3. Will it offer a story as witty and wonderfully constructed as the first?
4. Will it be as good as the first?
In my humble opinion the answer to these questions is as follows:
1. It'll try.
2. Yes-ish
3. Sort of.
4. Definitely not.
The fact is, Portal is the greatest video game ever created. There are simply too many wonderful things to say about the original game, and hardly anything negative to add. However, the sequel has made the mistake of giving plenty of negative things to mention. Too often does the player find themselves in a room of empty space. Grand, yes, and very open, sure. A wonderful showing-off of the Aperture Science labs, but lacking in motivation. It's not much fun to just walk around looking for the one place on the wall that's lit up and able to hold a portal. The game consists of too much, "Where next?" and not enough "How do I get to there?"
There is the added element of the gels, and this is a wonderful new feature that adds a whole new dimension to the gameplay. That being said; I found them to be a bit underused, not even being introduced until somewhere between half-way and three-quarters of the way through the game.
The story is great, don't get me wrong. Of course, it's pretty hard to mess up the perfection of the story the first game presented. I really enjoyed how, though the game was a sequel, the player was taken through history in order to answer the questions that led up to the events of the first game. In this way the sequel acts more like a prequel, and that's something that I think should be praised. Certainly the new cast of characters (specifically Wheatley) is worth mentioning, and they add a wonderful new level to the game as well.
Ultimately however, I feel like the first game was a happy accident. A side project that ended up being the greatest thing Valve has done. Whereas, with the sequel, they knew exactly what they were getting into. They knew that, no matter what, their creation would be met with great admiration and excitement. Quite frankly, there was no way Portal 2 could fail. Through a combination of (dare I say) over funding and over ambition, coupled with the knowledge that failure would not be a possibility, Portal 2 attempted to take Portal 1 to new heights....but instead falls a little short.
Still, this is a Portal game, and that's enough for me.

there are probably plenty of other/better things they could do, but i can't think of any.
otherwise though it's an awesome game, especially for a free to play that's still early access.  The fact that it's so good so early on in it's development is very promising.

There is a lot I have to say about this game, so prepare for a long♥♥♥♥♥review.
The Idea for this game is simple, yet brilliant and if worked on carefully, it can be a great game. However there are just so many factors that this game has that I would sooner buy SimCity from origin than tell my friends to play this.
The basic idea is easy to get across. Build something with guns, send it to battle, try to win the battle with your creation. However executing this is a great pain. If you want to build something big you have to play the game for a week before your level allows you to place enough blocks to create it, regardless of your rank (will get into that later) and don't even bother being creative/imaginative because they don't work and no-one will give you any sympathy. The game therefore, consists of the exact same design everywhere, which tends to be big blocks builds which take forever to take down. The building of "robots" can also incur more challenges. If you wish to get further into the game you need to spend ages grinding away to get "RP" (money) and Tech Points, the latter of which is much harder to obtain. You earn more RP from the people you damage, the game shines in this aspect. The game takes into account how much you damage someone more than how many you kill, meaning you can still profit from somebody running in at the last second and finishing the guy off, but varies massively and is completely unbalanced. You gain tech tokens easier if you go for the CP (Capture Point), which is one of two ways to win.. oh yeah.. that's the only gamemode... CTP, however you can still earn TP from being good at the game. The idea of the game is obviously to win, except it isn't. Living and losing is better than dying. After a battle you have 3 things to be concerned with. Your winnings, double points and repair. It's all just broken in a way. It varies with massive differences and differes even more the higher your tier is. You get 50% more for PTW (Pay-To-Win) and 1 double points match per day if you win (and also lived).
The PTW aspect was in the most recent update but it breaks the game heavily. PTW literally allows you to grind tier 1 and use it to unlock every items in the game and pay for it with next to no limits other than running out of pFlops (the amount of things you can place). Thanks to it's broken ranking system, It makes you unstoppable and a game-killer if you don't want to support the glorious con that Robocraft's PTW is. As SOON as you hit tier 2 you start getting rammed by things you cannot obtain until a week of non-stop grinding.
TL,DR: DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME UNLESS YOU ARE A RICH 4 YEAR OLD.
