Portal 2 is the puzzle game for FPS lovers.
No seriously.  The game is structured as an FPS, but is instead a brilliantly-designed puzzle game.  The idea is simple - get from point A at the start to point B at the end.  You have your basic tools - running, jumping, crouching, crouch-walking, picking up and dropping objects, but most of the time these are not sufficient on their own to get to the goal.
The gimmick here, and where this game shines, is the Portal Gun.  On it's face, it's simple; you have two portals, which attach to any white, portal-able surface.  Stuff goes in one, comes out the other, and vice versa.  They're fired from a gun that has unlimited range (and I do mean unlimited) - if you can see it and it's portalable, you can place a portal on it, and you can reposition them more-or-less freely.  Just fire the portal at a different target to move it.
This is all stuff that should be old-hat to veterans of the first game, but where Portal 2 shines is that it takes you out of the sterile, predesigned environments of the first game and throws you into the depths of Aperture, where the crumbling and decaying test chambers of days gone by have produced new and interesting obstacles to navigate with your portals.  Portal 2 feels less like a series of unconnected test chambers, and more like a seamless whole, with your character naturally progressing from one area to another.  It also introduces new mechanics and substances to be manipulated with the Portal Gun, which I don't want to spoil... completely.  Ever wanted to bounce off walls, run like The Flash, soar through the air without even a momentum-launch, or place portals nearly anywhere, even on surfaces that normally won't accept them?  Well... Portal 2 will give you the opportunity to explore those things.
This is not to say that Portal 2 is newbie-unfriendly.  Not by a long shot.  The game's pacing is incredible, easing you into the use of your personal movement abilities and the use of the Portal Gun, then slowly ramping it up, introducing new concepts and obstacles steadily until you've mastered them all.  Few things feel quite as good as overcoming a stumper of a puzzle through persistence and logic.
If you enjoy a more cerebral challenge from time-to-time, you could do a lot worse than Portal 2.

Game is fun, but you soon figure out the major balance issues. People unlock tier 5-7 weapons and just throw them on lightly armored vehicles to keep their tier down. Then they just 1 shot everybody in that tier. You could do it as well, but it takes a REALLY long time to unlock tier 5''s and up. You'll be level 24 before you can afford anything worthwhile to do the same. I got frustrated today and threw on 3 tier 5 blasters against tier 3's... ended up with 5 kills and winning the game. I crippled everybody I hit with the first shot. The second shot was only for a pilot kill. I 1 hit 3 of those kills. This is robocraft in a nutshell.
If using tier 4 blocks, guns, boosters, etc... put you into tier 4 automatically it would be a really good game. The way it works now is people just throw on a tier 4 weapon on a flat platform with wheels and end up 1 shotting everything they come across. It gets worse as the tiers go up. You will be in tier 4 up against tier 7 weapons and tier 5 everything else. If you build compact it lets you punish lower tiered players. If you build big it just gives a bigger target for the blast cannons.
Your first run into a tier 3 game will more than likely be you getting 1 shot by a sniper on helium blocks and a tier 5 rail gun. Tier 4 will most likely be a bomber (flying craft with wings and boosters)  with tier 5 assortment and some tier 6 guns. Building compact is the way to go, so any creative design you come up with just puts you at a bigger risk. The cannons have a blast radius and if they hit you they deal a rather large burst of damage which can often cripple your vehicle. It also just makes it easier for snipers to hit you.
All those cool commical looking designs in the screen shots don't mean squat because you're just going to get smashed, never gain any xp or RP, so upgrading will take ages and you will spend most of your RP on repairs.

Really guys? you ruined a perfectly good game just by making it nearly impossible to play withouth paying to go the extra mile. I recomend if you are an EXTREMELY casual gamer and you dont mind a long grind. But for others that hate a grind. I recomend going elsewhere.

I do enjoy this game, but there is a glaring flaw that has to be addressed first and foremost: The tier system.
If a tier system is going to be used in the game, the rank point system needs to be removed and forever forgotten. A craft's tier should be determined by it's highest tier weapon or armor blocks. If you build your craft with a tier 3 weapon and level 6 armor blocks, then the craft should be in a tier 6 battle. If you build a craft with a tier 10 weapon and tier 1 armor, the craft should be a tier 10 craft. More often than not, players will be killed with a single shot (myself included) because another player will have a tier 6 gun in a tier 3 battle. This is frustrating beyond belief and often cuts battle time down to under a minute.
Another flaw is the repair system. It is designed so that if a player's vehicle is damaged in a battle, it costs points to have it repaired. I understand that, but the cost of repair shouldn't feel arbitrary. The cost of repair is not determined by the cost of the parts damaged, but by how much you earned in battle. If a game is going to have a repair system, the cost of repairing a block on your craft should be set: perhaps a quarter of what it was worth? Or do away with the repair system altogether and simply deduct possible points earned if you do not survive?
With that out of the way, I do think that this game has potential. When there is a fighting chance to win, it is fun. The Tech Tree mechanic is actually pretty well designed, though I would probably offer some of the tech options a tier sooner.
Overall, I would recommend this game, but it does need improvement in some key areas.

The game for people who want freely build a vehicle of different moving abilities like car, tank, hovercraft, plane, rocket and their hybrids. Additionally you can add armor and weapons and go to fight against other people so that you can observe the advantages and disadvantages of your design.
Game advantages:
-- crafting system is very easy and versatile,
-- the built vehicle could be tested in very hard conditions against opposite players,
-- controls of the vehicles are very well chosen, developers did good job,
-- paying players are not able to make better vehicles than you (only more profit from battles),
-- well weighted types of gun systems (three: SMG, plasma, railgun),
-- nice tactically rich maps.
Disadvantages:
-- max 3 (premium players 4) teammates in lobby with 6 and more players,
-- some not important graphics imperfections like recognizable skyboxes.
-- unclear properties of physics simulator,
-- missing undo button in the construction bay.
So I recommend this game if you are enought bold and creative.

IMMENSE penalty for failure in this game makes it virtually a pay-to-enjoy setup.  Unless you buy premium, you will barely earn enough credits to make your repairs, let alone buy new items.
It then becomes a long grind of earning enough points to unlock and buy new equipment so that you're actually viable in a tier, only to have those items cost more to repair.
Also, it doesn't matter if you killed all but one enemy on the opposing team yourself- if you are destroyed and your team still wins, you still get stripped of any bonuses you might have had for performance.  This discourages players from throwing themselves headlong into battles, which normally would create epic war arenas with lasers flying all over.
Instead, people camp behind corners or fly waaaaaay up in the sky an make pot-shots or snipe at those who haven't unlocked the gear to do so themselves.
The structure of the game is fundamentally flawed and wears out its enjoyability pretty quickly.
Free is good, pay to enjoy is not.
Don't waste your time on this grind.

Before I say anything else about the game, I want to address an issue regarding it. Most of the reviews for this game make it out to be a pay-to-win game, and say that it isn't worth playing because of this.
I started playing it after the patch that supposedly made it into a p2w game, and I've found that it isn't as much a pay to win, but a pay to progress game. I'm going to explain this a bit better later on, but for now I'll explain the basics of the game to you.
You start off with a basic inventory of parts. (a couple hundred basic blocks, wheels, guns, etc.) Enough to build your first robot. (although they're not technically robots, as they are operated by an astronaut in a pilot's seat) You have two limits for your robot, that is the number of parts you currently have in your inventory, and your hard drive space.
Your hard drive basically prevents you from adding too many blocks to your robot. Each block is worth a certain number of pflops. (the unit of storage of the hard drive) Some blocks are worth more than others (i.e. guns and wheels take up 8 or so and normal blocks take up 1) So for instance if you have a 300-pflop hard drive; you can't make a robot made up of over 300 basic cubes. I believe your hard drive space grows larger the more you level up, which you do through damaging and destroying other robots.
Now that you have a robot, you go into battle. Combat feels really smooth, and if you build your robot right, it should control like a dream. The objective of each match is to either destroy all the robots on the opposing team, or get to their base and capture it. There are 4 or so maps, all of them taking place on Mars, either on the dusty red plains or the snowy ice caps.
Once you win (or lose) a battle, you will be rewarded with both RP (the basic currency of the game) and Tech Points. Usually you gain a couple hundred RP, even if you lost. I believe it gives you more depending on how much damage you delt, seeing as how I usually get more if I focus on destroying enemies rather than capturing their base. If your robot got damaged or destroyed in the previous battle, you now have to spend either RP (usually from 50-400) or the game's pay-to-get currency, GC (of which you only have to pay 1 to repair any damage). GC is worth around $5 for 4500, and you start off with 100, so I usually use it for repairing.
In order to unlock new pieces (i.e. better weapons, armor blocks, hover blades) you spend tech points. Now's probably a good time to explain the tier system. As you add blocks to your robot, a little bar on the bottom of the screen will go up. If you add enough blocks that are slightly better than the ones you were previously using (i.e. T2 SMGs instead of T1s) then your robot will go from a Tier 1 bot into a Tier 2 bot. Now the game will match you against other T2 bots, and you will earn T2 Tech Points from winning. Using the T2 tech points, you can unlock even better blocks, until you can reach Tier 3 and start earning T3 points, so on until Tier 10 (the highest one) This is the game's primary balancing system, as you will always go up against bots of a similar technological level as yours, making it NOT a pay-to-win. Something to note is that after you unlock a part, you still have to buy them with either RP or GC before you can use them.
Now, about those GC points I was talking about earlier. You can use them to
-Repair your robot
-Buy parts cheaply
-Upgrade lower-tier Tech Points into Uber Tech Points, which act as any tier and can unlock any item
-Purchase pre-made robots
-Purchase premium (usually in day-based time periods)
Premium basically doubles the amount of RP and Tech Points you earn from battles, which I have heard used to be the normal amount you would get (without premium) This is why the game is pay-to-progress. I've spent 7 or so hours in the game without premium, and I have just reached the level of being able to build T3 robots. If you have premium, this process would happen MUCH faster, but the game is still enjoyable even if you can't build those cool airplanes you see in the trailers without either shelling out $50 (probably more, actually) or spending 20 hours in the game.
In summary, the game is well-polished, and balanced, although difficult to progress without paying money. Congrats if you got this far, but I have nothing to give you. Sorry. Anyway, I give this game a solid 8/10, with the recommendation to play it. It may take a while to get those cool wings and sniper rifles, but it's still an entertaining little game, that's worth at least a little bit of your time.

======================OLD REVIEW (13 Mar, 2016)======================
Came back to this game and a lot had changed, but those old pros and cons mostly still apply
Pros:
+ Straightforward gameplay
+ Robot construction is intuitive
+ Seal clubbing no longer an issue. The robot ranking system appears to be doing a decent job keeping people in their correct tiers.
+ Reasonable population
+ You can paint your robot
Cons:
- You still need premium to get any decent progression
- Creativity is hampered by cost of parts
- Mid-Late game parts are horrendously expensive.
- RP gain is really slow after the update even for premium users
- Uptiering is an long and arduous process due to poor RP gain and cost of parts
- Progress cost increases exponentially as you go (Exp needed to level up, cost of newer parts, etc)
- You only get access to the full paint set while premium is active. No option for a one off payment to get all the paints without limit.
- If the megabot on your team fails to load in, then you've pretty much lost from the get-go
Fun game for a while, but then the grindfest takes over.

Cool idea, poor execution. Didn't spend a cent on this to measure it's worth

Realistic, these are minor issues that you will encounter briefly from time to time in the lower levels. Level 5 and above is where the gameplay really starts to shine. Early Access ... Yeah, there are bugs and the devs are tweaking things to balance the game. This process is called iteration and will bubble up what is right and what is wrong equally. There are a few issues that may grind on you at first. Those are being worked out examples: inconsistent balancing for a battle, tiers vs. weapon levels, etc.
The product manager for the game has not gotten the right mix of the elements to purchase to generate revenue vs opening themselves up to critics with the old pay to win complaint. The recent update brought a robo store to purchase pre built vehicles at several different tiers. This let people skip the grid and jump to a higher tier ... some people were taken aback by this. But the real effect was null when it came to the battles. Sure someone had a sweet pre built vehicle that looked great but they jumped tiers too quickly without understanding the gameplay changes the higher in the ladder you go. So what happened? Purchaser had fun for a bit dealing average damage for a few moments until they got wrecked by someone who has competed in that tier for a period of time. So the purchaser had fun, paid the devs salary and server bill (a wee bit) and got inspired to grind build something better for that tier in other words ... Became more engaged in the game. The pay for premium to get extra resources and additional friend slot on a platoon is priced a little aggressively.

Qute interesting concept with totally horrible aplication.
Matchmaking is based on vehicle tier. Tier is determined by points given by blocks used on your vehicle.
Tech tree points are different for different tiers, so you can not research tier II weaponery with tier I robot.
This results in 2 main problems
1) you need to create an obsolete, useless vehicle with unreasonably high ammounts of useless blocks just to reach higher tier to have an opportunity to research better equipment
2) you will find many vehicles that are composed of 2 blocks, pilot and very high level weapon 1-shooting any opponent it encounters
Matchmaking itself is totally crappy... At least when i have score of 1 win in 10 games. commonly situation of opponent team got 2 deaths and i have 1 kill and 1 assist, rest of out team consists of 1 with the same score and 8 who did exactly nothing at all, i call it really, really bad matchmaking...
And there is YET ANOTHER problem... Game gives you double bonus for first victory... So yeah, you will go out, have your 3 kills and 2 assists, then killing 4th opponent you die horrible death from someone who himself is left immobile and 1 shot from death and your team wins... So you expect a decent 16 tech points (2points for kill 1 for assist and double for firstwin), yet you are awarded only with 8 because you have died! In conclusion, it is really possible to finish whole tech rank without being awarded double XP for first win (in fact it is quite possible to finish whole tech rank without even winning a game)
Weaponry is funny... You have SMG (standart, first weapon you can have, only weapon you can have until tier 4, but definitely not only weapon type you will see, because it is completely normal to see tier 4 weapon on tier 1 vehicle), railgun and plasma launcher (both have sort of AOE, rail killing anything in line, plasma have explosion radius. SMG cannot hit/destroy multiple blocks at once) As i didnt had enought time (and nerves) to go to higher tiers, here is how SMG works: You will put multiple guns on your vehicle, some might be destroyed by enemy fire, so you want to have few more. Or you just need to have unreasonably big vehicle with unreasonably high ammount of guns to put yourself in higher tier. Great... Highest possible cadency is with 4 SMGs... any more gun will provide NO ADDITIONAL FIREPOWER as you have about 1,5 shots or so per second no matter if you have 4 or 40 guns installed and you cannot shoot multiple SMGs at a same time. Also firing a gun makes another SHOT less accurate. And game really dont care about which gun put that next shot. So you cannot make your gun more accurate, or specifically dispersion after fire lower by putting more guns, so in fact if you care about your accuracy, optimal number of guns would be something like 2. If you care about your rate of fire, it would be 4. Higher than that you will loose efficiency by accuracy, reload time and most probably both and will make you unreasonably easy (big) target.
Really, game concept is awesome, but currently i cannot think of a worse application...

I have changed my review to "Recommend" because fo the improvements made. Nit-picking ahead.
Earlier on there were lots of balance issues with people manipulating game mechanics to have an unfair advantage. The devs have done a great job of mitigating these issues recently and have really made the game worth playing. There are some issues with gameplay, most of which can be eliminated by tweeks to the damage traits of weapons and armor ratings of certain parts. I believe that Freejam will be able to hone the game into a wonderful game thanks to the freedback they take from players.
Right now the issues that hold this game back are not game breaking but annoyances. One issue is the variety(or lack thereof) in player bots. Far too often you will enter a game where there are four or more flying bombers on the enemy team and the same number of healers on your team. This makes it so that your team is unable to fight back while the other team bombs you to oblivion from on high. A limit to what classes are matched to a game would rectify this. Doing so would be somewhat of a technical challenge and problematic in regards to matchmaking times but would improve gameplay when you actually were to get into a match. I don't expect such a matchmaking mechanic to be impemented, but it could be nice if done well.
It would be nice if players could swap robots in game to another class as is found in other class based competative games like Team Fortress 2. I don't expect that to be added simply because it would require player lives to be implemented to allow it. It would, however, provide a means to counter the excessive multiples of a class from making a round less than fun.
Legs were added recently and are great fun to use and design bots around. They are very low in defense and are large targets. This causes you to think a little more strategically than your wheeled counterparts who can almost charge into battle haphazardly. The armor of the legs was doubled since implementation, but they still feel too frail, especially with the widespread use of plasma bombers.
After the recent updates there are a lot less cheaty designs which are difficult to counter and simple to build. There are a lot more creative designs being built, especially with walkers. It is always enjoyable to see the oddball designs in the shape of household items or pixel art lumbering about(except in the case of a house I saw, THe owner must not have researched the property before buying a lot in the middle of an active war zone on Mars.). There are of course the immature designs that pop up from time to time. About an hour ago I was destroyed by a flying phallic bomber, that guy was a real♥♥♥♥♥♥
Overall if you are willing to forgive the issues inherent in an early release free to play game and have a creative edge, this game would be fun to you. Be prepared to grind or shell out the money to build the bot of your dreams.

This game is super fun, the problem is the greedy developers try to trap you the further into the game you reach, basically trying to force your hand into paying for microtransactions.
I will give an example of why its an issue:
There are 2 types of currency, RP and GC, GC is bought money, RP is earned money.
You use blocks to build your robot, each different type of block you unlock offers higher damage resistance.
The better your robot the higher the division your robot can enter into; Tier 1 is first, Tier 2, Tier 3, etc to Tier 10.
1 White block cost 0 RP and 0 GC.
1 Brown block cost 10 RP and 5 GC.
1 Green block cost 40 RP and 10 GC.
1 Blue block cost 105 RP and 15 GC.
1 Orange block cost 235 RP and 20 GC. and so on...
Each of these block offer more protection, as you can see the cost of an orange block is pretty high, I usually earn around 400-800 RP per game which is ok but if your robot is damaged or destroyed that can cost 400 RP to repair... so often you can only afford 1 block per game... if your lucky... basically it becomes SO unfeasible to try to earn the blocks that the cost in GC is just that more appealing.
So really this game stops at Tier 3-4 if you dont want to get wrapped up in the rediculous Pay to Win logistics of this game.

Begin with the game you woke up in a room which resembles an typical hotel room, then some banging on the door begins the great adventure of our heroine Chell. A sudden shake-off of the room which reveals the room is actually one container of 10 thousand people multi-complex. The show begins with an tremendous fashion. It appeals the player right away as if it is inviting them into the story.
And right away do you also feel the witty sarcasm which exists throughout the entire game. When the robot manager tell you: `This is art, stare at the art for 5 seconds.' and then plays classical music, it just makes me smile. The script writers are geniuses. The lines are comical but not too funny, and with a sense of dark humor. The robot themselves are always joking around with the death or termination of themselves, and sometimes to each other too. Almost childish but not overdone. Especially GLaDOS herself is a very charming character, I have to confess I fell in love with GLaDOS when she tried to talk Wheatley into a paradox, and mumbling "dont think about it dont think about it". It's just so cute.
The story and background setting are definitely deepened deliberately this time. When I played the first three chambers I was kind of worried they are just remaking Portal 1 - because I played 2 right after 1 so I could remember the puzzles as the same. Gladly they weren't! It's a fairly lengthy brand new game - about 8 hours - and every minute of it worths it. They put a lot of effort laying the background and showing the player how Aperture and the facility come to be. They laid huge architectural work for the game, I couldn't even imagine how big the facility is because it was so massive, there are so many rooms which you can't see the top end or the bottom end - which surprisingly reminds me of BioShock not at the time of playing but now. I've seen Valve done this large-world trick before in Half-Life 2, and I know they are getting good at it because this one is even better.
Music is great, not repetitive and well paced. Voice acting is tremendous, both Wheatley and GLaDOS.
The end game was also very good (and surprising!). I'm very happy that they didn't make the final boss very hard - after all, who would want to fight a difficult boss after solving all the puzzles? The tired player deserves a relaxed good show.
10/10, I haven't felt this kind of excitement for years, and Portal 2 brought it to me. It's a fine piece of work and I strongly recommended it.
Ps: I haven't played the multiplayer yet, but I heard it's very good too.

First I would like to start by saying this game has a amazing concept with more potential than most. I love its ideas which allow for silly accidents, in depth custimizing and fun combat.
Unfortunately I have to warn people away from this game as is. the upgrade  system is beyond broken. now to be clear this game is nowhere near pay to win in any single form, however its system favors players who are vets so much that you will NOT get to play any fair games at all.
The key upgrade system in this is called tech points. you get them in matches where you do well or win. they are used to unlock the ability to use parts that are more unique and powerful. problem is the parts you begin with are so bad they cannot fight any upgraded parts. the game splits the players up by ranking of their robot but it is possible to give your bot a insanely good gun then lower everything else to sneak into lower rank play. you will see robots that will kill you in one shot while you have to keep a steady barrage to do any harm.
the game does not tend to give you tech points if you lose so you will not upgrade your parts. the enemy will keep killing you and so you will take a age and a half to earn any tech points. then it gets worse. not only is every new part unlock expensive but as soon as you get a truly unique part that would even the playing field it says you need tech points lv2. turns out there are many types of tech point and you can only get the higher rank ones by winning higher rank matches which you cannot fight in because you do not have those parts.
it is beyond broken and means that the veteren players decide a match. a single vet player robot will destroy a whole team of new players easy. until they fix the broken tech point system this game is a horrible waste of your time.
If you liked the first game you will want to play this one.

I think it bears saying that, as this is an 'Early Access' title, many things may change.  As it stands, though, it doesn't appear that they will.
The main selling point I was hooked on with Robocraft was the idea that it was a game with multiple possibilities for designing your crafts.  You would design, go into a multiplayer arena, and then tweak from there.  And that's where the first problem comes in: yes, you can design; yes, you can tweak; yes, it takes a damn long time.
The primary design philosophy behind successful crafts is this: put a lot of guns on it, put a lot of armor on it, and avoid getting shot.  Don't feel like being a slow, hulking behemoth?  Then you can use 'prism' (literally just slopes), corner, and inner-corner blocks to build a craft with half the weight, just as much bulk, and twice the headache.
These two glaring gameplay issues are what keeps Robocraft from being remotely fun after you've breached Tier 2.  If you learned the hard way that your design doesn't work, you'll probably sell your robot: and then you'll need to make a bare-bones bot that's even worse off while you slog your way through twenty matches to try to build a bot that does work.
As for technical issues, it requires a bit of tweaking with your security softwares to get the game to run properly: that's just a matter of exceptions being required for the game to load its nested assets.  There are frustrating points, in-game, where the player will find one's wheels stuck in the ground -- this has an easy, 100 token fix in-game, though.
Put simply, Robocraft is yet another freemium game, but with a good idea.  It's not pay-to-win, hardly.  It's just 'pay-to-have-fun', as one player put it.
Don't get this game if:
- You expect your creativity to be rewarded.
- You don't want to slog through dozens of matches just to get to a point where you're effective.
Do get this game if:
- You enjoy grinding a lot.
- You just want to kill a couple of hours and don't care about 'winning' or 'losing.'

Were you ever the kind of kid who would take numerous amounts of Legos and build some awesome rover or hovercraft and then act like you and your friend's creation were fighting in some kind of lego turf war? If that answer is yes, then you'll love Robocraft where you can build any kind of vehicle you want to your heart's content, and then pit it with other people's vehicles.
Pros:
You can build anything you want given what is free and what you must pay for. Very well done currency system that compinsates you well for your work on the team by providing more the enough money back to repair your bot (even if you lose), and increases payment from your performance (do better, get more $). Different kinds of blocks to choose from so you can create a very UNIQUE (I want to stress that word) bot. Dfferent kinds of weapons to suit your play style. Nice community. And last, but not least, 3 free garages for you to build WHATEVER YOU WANT! Seriously, anything, as long as it has the pilots seat.
Cons:
Not much annoys me about games, but there is one thing that really irks me, and that is the lack of creativity in this game. I am going to say it again, YOU CAN BUILD ANYTHING YOU WANT! EVEN IF YOU LOSE OR ARE COMPLETELY DESTROYED, YOU MAKE A PROFIT! That being said, there is a disturbing amount of bots that simply are a few blocks and a railgun sitting at the spawn and the top of the skybox (they are called blimps by the community apperently, but I prefer to call them snipers because they're super accurate, you don't always see them before they see you, and they can kill you in one hit in most cases or that may just be my experience). These blimps are usually hard to spot if you don't have a radar, or if they have a radar jammer (which also in my experience most do) as they are just a few pixels when they are at the very top of the roof. Another noncreative bot I've seen a bit is what is called a gun bed (as its name suggests, is little more than a bunch of guns on a flat bot).
That is the most annoying part for me, some of you may prefer these bot types, and if so, I pity your noncreativity. Other thing that you may find annoying are a free player and premium player status. I'm not quite sure what all is intaled with a premium account such as compensation with premium money, but what is provided by being a premium player is double what you would recieve as a free player at the end of a battle, both in money and tech points (what you use for researching new upgrades). But you do not need to be a premium member to make good money in the game, it is simply a shortcut.
Summary:
This game is uber fun! You can build anything you want, even if some may choose not to, and make super cool designs.
It is the most fun PvP game I have played in a long time. I give it a 10/10.

Actually a good game with a cool concept but at the moment I wouldn't recommend it for several reasons:
1. Server stability. I know some people are not affected by this but for me (and others) it's unplayable at the moment. I don't know whether the servers are plainly too full or if it's something else but the fact of the matter is that out of 10 games I have 8 games with severe lag spikes (several seconds, sometimes up to 20-30) with 3-4 out of those ending in a disconnect and 2 games where everything works fine. That's plainly unacceptable. At first I thought it was my own fault but checking several other online games right after having severe issues in RC proved pretty conclusively that the problem is not coming from my side.
2. The monetisation concept is just one step short of a con. In the lower levels you still gain some in-game currency, even if you get destroyed (which will kick you out of the current game and bring you back to vehicle assembly where you have to repair the vehicle for in-game points) but I hear at higher levels you will pay more for the repair of your vehicle than you get as a reward for playing that round. Coupled with the current state of servers it's easy to get destroyed very often so at this point it's just unplayable for those affected.
3. This is an Early Access Game, so take this bullet point with a grain of salt. I'm not gonna get into the ethics of Early Access too much, I'll just say that I think it's not a good thing. Now that that's out of my system, I'll say that this game is extremely unbalanced in its current state, which is certainly to be expected but considering that they are already taking your money for testing their late Alpha/early Beta you would guess that they'd be a bit more eager to keep everything in check. You'll also encounter the occasional bug, which is, like I already said, to be expected and normally nothing to complain about in an Early Access game. I do think that a game that offers a completely functioning shop and basically runs on a pay to win (or pay to gain a considerable edge) model has to be held to different standards than your average run-of-the-mill Alpha/Beta version though.
So, like I already said in my opening sentence: Great concept spoiled by bad management decisions, lacking server infrastructure and too many (and too game breaking) bugs and balancing issues for a game that really really wants to get some of your tasty Euros, Dollars or whatever your local currency is.
At this point, definitely not recommended.

::ORIGINAL REVIEW::
This is a fun little game where you build a vehicle out of pieces and fight in team vs team battles against other vehicles.
So you charge into battle, get damaged; blocks are flying everywhere. Hopefully you kill an enemy or two in the process. At the end of the match or after you've died, you gain money (RP) and tech points (TP) based on how well you did in battle.
You use TP to unlock new technology in the tech tree, and RP to repair your vehicle and buy some new guns or armor for the next battle.
The game is in Early Access and has a lot of potential, but feels pretty "grindy" at the moment, which is where the real money shop comes in. You can pay to shorten the grind by getting bonus money per match. It's not pay2win, which is nice to see for a free to play game.
Overall a fun, free game to kill time on.

Strange as it may seem to start a five-star review on a note of concern, I worry about Valve. It's not that I think the developer has put a foot wrong so far, or that its latest release won't meet the impossibly high expectations of its audience. On the whole, the titles that Valve has produced have been critically lauded and have sold very respectably.
But if the history of art and entertainment has taught us one thing it is this: if you habitually make genius look easy, audiences and critics will round on you if you stumble, even more viciously than they would have done if your track record was of a mediocre quality. Valve's winning streak has to get snapped at some point, doesn't it? And if it does, the knives will be out in force.
Well, thankfully, Portal 2 isn't the game that's going to cause this, which is remarkable when you consider it's arguably the sequel of 2011 with the toughest act to follow. The first Portal, released in 2007 as part of the Orange Box, was a short, ingenious puzzler wrapped up in first-person-shooter mechanics, underpinned by a darkly comic story about scientific research taken to dangerous extremes. The game seemed like lightning in a bottle and a sequel sounded unnecessary. Still, Valve has managed to go one better than what its team created before, and then built on its impressive foundations.
Portal 2 kicks off with player waking up in the Aperture Laboratories, the human behaviour research facility from the first game, and finding out very quickly that things have gone haywire. Aperture is a wreck: without GlaDOS – Portal 1's female AI antagonist – to run things, the facility is in an advanced state of disrepair. Walls are crumbling, test chambers malfunction and every room the player moves through is riddled with smashed windows, natural overgrowth and broken machinery. In the opening stages of the game, players are introduced to Wheatly, a stammering, motor-mouthed droid voiced by Stephen Merchant, and reacquainted with the Portal Gun, which creates interconnecting portals capable of bending distances, and physics, in their environment.

They're also soon reunited with GlaDOS, who takes umbrage at their presence and decides that a new round of potentially lethal tests is in order.
While the set-up will sound incredibly familiar to Portal veterans, Portal 2 is hardly a retread of the first game. Yes, using the Portal Gun to navigate one's way through every new environment is the core premise of the game – and cubes, gun turrets, floating platforms and pressure pads all make a return. But Valve has added some mind-bending mechanics and tools to the mix.
As the player advances through the Apeture Labs they're introduced to new items that the research facility has created to exercise their grey matter and potentially kill them off. There are Hard Light Bridges, which can create walkways or block off the sensors of lasers and gun turrets. There are Aerial Faith Plates, which fling the player through the air. There's Propulsion Gel, which allows them to zoom across the floor, building momentum for jumps and portal leaps. Puddles of Repulsion Gel can create areas the player can bounce on– and the higher the ledge they drop from, the higher they'll fly through the air. White Gel can be sprayed on to surfaces to make them Portal Gun-friendly. Excursion funnels are blue tubes of anti-gravity, which gently transport the player from one end of the map to the other, and they too can be redirected and repositioned with the Portal Gun. Each new item is introduced gently, to let the player become familiar with its capabilities, and then Valve starts ramping up the difficulty.
The puzzle rooms are incredibly well designed in that there's no hard and fast rule with the game's difficulty curve. Once the tutorials are out of the way, it's down to every individual player's desire to break the code on each environment, which allows them to move from the entrance to the exit. Even if one player finds the solution to one particular room obvious, this doesn't mean that everyone else will, and some puzzles may take up to hour to solve. All the while GlaDOS pours scorn over the player's efforts, with a stream of insults that are petty, vindictive and immature – made more hilarious by her robotic, sing-song voice.
The humour in Portal 2 is another trump card in the game's well-paced, engrossing and unsettling story. Without giving too much of the game's plot away, the player will find Portal 2 funny throughout, but also faintly spinechilling. GlaDOS and Wheatly are by turns funny and monstrous and the Aperture Labs take on an increasingly oppressive atmosphere as the player ventures deeper into the facility, learning more about its origins. Meanwhile, the unseen character from the first Portal is still lurking behind the scenes, scrawling paranoid messages and horrific cartoons on the walls.
The game's main campaign is longer than in Portal 1, and arguably better too. Once that's over and done with, however, players can return to Aperture in the multiplayer. This mode is a standalone story starring two cute droids, Atlas and Peabody, who are sent testing by GlaDOS, and the series of puzzles they have to navigate depends on them working successfully as a team. While it may sound strange that a game offering such a successful solitary experience as Portal should include such a mode, it's actually delightful fun. Once again, the puzzles are well-balanced and brilliantly constructed and, GlaDOS has a new collection of insults.
Valve has created a masterpiece in Portal 2. The depth of content, the mind-bending mechanics and fantastic experience are almost certain to satisfy ardent fans of the first game; and to all newcomers to the series, it's as simple as this: prepare to have your mind blown. Over and over again.

This game is a lot of fun mechanically, however there are a lot of problems that prevent it from being fun from Tier 3 and on.
Entering a new tier makes you essentially useless. You're matched with people from the top of the Tier with better armor and weapons. You basically have to cower behind your teammates until you can afford to buy better parts (which takes FOREVER by the way, without premium. Yay for more free to play games that overprice benefits that make progression easy).
The explosive turrets are extremely overpowered. 80% of the people in this game just place as many as possible on their brick car and literally one shot anything within a few hundred meters. I don't blame them for doing so either as its very difficult to win a duel with laser turrets.
Speaking of which, hovercraft vs. your typical ground vehicle with cannons is pointless. You get one shot out of the sky. If there were lobbies that only allowed laser turrets, I'd be all over that.
Additionally there are parts that allow you to float to the top of the map and sit there and one shot snipe people. This also happens in a lot of lower tiers. I don't know how people find that fun, but its in most games.
This sounds like a rant, yes, because it kinda is. There are still a lot of balance issues with this, primarily with gauss and cannon turrets. They do far too much damage.
Want to hover around in an aircraft with laser turrets and have a futuristic pirate ship battle? Too bad. You'll explode instantly before that ever happens.

I definitely suggest this game.  Please read on to see what I like and to get a better understanding of the "issues" others seem to not like about the game.
I'm not sure it should still be considered Early Access to be honest, but they do update often so I'll leave that topic alone.  If you can get past that Early Access moniker, it's a fun and addictive game.  If you can't figure it out from the video, you're building tanks, hovercraft, and airborne ships with blocks in a Minecraft style.  Then you add guns, radar, group radar receivers, radar jammers, hoverblades, jet thrusters, wheels, and weapons of three different varieties to round out the build and make yours unique and effective.  Once yours is built, it's all about the arena battles where you test your mettle against other players creations.
This is a free to play game that is funded by player incentive micro-transactions.  It is in no way pay-to-win though you'll often hear that in chat, reviews, and forum posts.  There is nothing available in game that affects your performance that can't be earned with the in game currency.  The only thing purchasable that you can't get with in game money is what they refer to as their premium subscription which provides 50% more tech points and income which means it speeds development of your tank and character up.  That's nothing that you can't grind for free if you so choose.
There are three issues that people bring up that I would like to help a new player understand before they're totaly turned off to the game concepts by inexperienced players.
First, there's much complaining about railguns and their ability to "one shot" an enemy tank.  This is OVERLY exagerated.  It is possible to do this, no questions asked!  However, as an experienced rail gun tank and flier pilot, I can say with certainty that it's not easy, and usualy requires that the enemy tank be poorly armored and sheilded.  When the sniper (or any gun) hits a block, the damage needed to destroy that block is assigned, and then all remaining damage spreads to adjacent blocks.  SMG (sub-machine guns) never do enough damage to do this, since they're weak fire at rediculous fast intervals.  If the enemy tank has little armor or energy sheilding then that damage from a plasma canon or rail gun can hit and spread to the pilot's chair causing a one shot kill.  Lesson to be learned here is shield the pilots chair, not ruin a strategic and ballanced weapon.  The current damage and long reload times of the guns more than ballance any alpha damage they may do against a decent tank.  Moreover, their CPU cost (an in game ballancing concept) makes them only fit on tanks that are also in turn vulnerable to a quick high damage attack too.  Rush them from their flank or attack between their 15 second recharge times, and they have no chance.
Second, the ballance of the matches is constantly bashed.  This is because you'll often see a match with 2 different tiers togather once you get out of the first couple levels.  What you must take the time to notice and understand is that the game doesn't pair us by tiers at all.  It's a combination of your win/loss ratio (which can be summaraised as your player skill) and your tank's rank (which is a calculation of the rank of all the blocks that make up your tank).  The player skill is an invisible number for now, but you'll notice that as you play better you'll get placed with higher tiered tanks in matches, and as you loose a few in a row, you'll get placed with lower tiers.  The "imballance" that people complain about is the game taking the player skill into consideration.  It is actualy ballancing well!  Just tonight even I fought against a team (and we lost) with 4 T10 tanks, a few T9s, a T5, and  T4.  Seriously, that even seemed unballanced to me.  But at the end of the game I saw that the T5 and T4 both survived the match and even had kills.  They were ungodly good players who were well ballanced for my 2x T10 and all the rest T9 team.  Don't just look at the tiers (which I call rating for dummies) but watch to see how the high or low tier players play.  That high tier player is probably the weakest skilled pilot on your team, and the low tier player is probably one of the strongest.
Third, I continuously hear that the game is P2W (pay 2 win) as I discussed above.  Some try to justify this because of an update that upset many early-early access players.  That update introduced repair costs in battle.  Yep, they're upset that the tank doesn't fix itself for free.  Instead, like your car or (I don't know) a real tank it must be mended after damage to keep it's effectiveness.  This is completely doable with in game currency.  At levels 1 - 4 you'll never experience more cost to repair than earnings from battle.  Congrats guaranteed in game currency.  At level 5 you hit a tipping point where a player who contributed nothing to his team and died without any base capture points, kill points, or assist points can potentialy leave battle with less than it costs to repair the tank.  My advice here isn't to rage quit a game or complain endlessly.  Instead, learn from your mistakes, figure out a better strategy, and get back into the next battle.  If you at least kill one other player before you die, you'll do more than come out ahead of the repair costs.  Add in capture points or kill assists and it's easy money.  Even if not, hopefully with some minor budgeting you still had enough points to completely repair when those bad rounds do happen (and we all experience it sometime).  Where people turn this simple mechanic that rewards skilled and/or team minded players more than their overly ambitious or selfish teammates into P2W is with the Premium Membership concept I mentioned above.  If you earn 50% more per battle, you can technicaly be a much weaker teammate and still turn a profit.  This isn't truely pay to win though since it isn't giving them a tactical advantage.  At worst you can claim they leveled faster and built up into higher tiers easier, but it's nothing a good gamer can't do without the premium membership.  That's not pay to win, the worst you could say is it's pay to progress quickly (P2PQ just doesn't roll of the tounge as well though).
I heavily encourage you to try the game, enjoy it, and if you play for more than a week or two, reward the devs with a premium membership.  This shouldn't be a negative thing or something to be looked down on.  Getting the membership funds the game.  Funding the game is how it keeps running and getting better.  In the end, no one says, "I want to be a broke game developer who makes a kick butt game but can't afford the power and internet access to play it myself."  Nope, this is their job.  They deserve the money, and it helps encourage them to make more content and better ballance that content as the game develops further.  Everyone benefits and you can be the next one that the cheap ones are whining about because you moved on and left them in the newb tiers.

I really love this game!!! But there are a few things that bug me that people should probably be aware of before playing.
Servers can be temperamental and crash if your connection is even slightly slow, usually forcing the entire lobby back to their bays, but that's not a big issue. Occassionally you'll find players in very low tier matches with bots armed with some very overpowered weapons, i.e. the plasma cannons and rail guns. This is very irritating starting out because these two weapons will tear through your bot with minimal effort, the railgun usually killing in one hit if the owner is a good shot, the plasma cannon being for everyone that isn't or that don't feel like looking for a cockpit because of its AoE.
The membership is also pretty stupid, allowing people that sink money into the game to progress much faster than everybody else, practically becoming compulsory at a certain point as from what I've noticed and what others below have said, earning points gets exponentially harder the higher up you get. Meaning if you die a lot going into higher tier games with a freshly able bot, which you probably will, you'll earn fewer and fewer points to upgrade it. Obviously this can make matches very unbalanced.
Yet as rage inducing as the game can be, there is a lot of promise in this game and it can be really, REALLY addicting. If the way points are allocated or the tech tree rehashed to make non-paid play practical past tier 4 or rescale the membership benefits to make it less unfair, unlikey, I know, but I can hope, this could be a really amazing game. I recommend this game solely because it's (largely) free-to-play and you may really enjoy it while you can still make progress.
A small addition that could be made to the social menu is the ability to search or scroll through a list of recent players. Maybe to add them to your platoon, add as a friend, view their bot(s) and their tiers. Just something small like that, food for thought.

TL;DR: If you liked the Gummi Ships from Kingdom Hearts 1 and wished they would do more with the concept of building ships out of blocks than that... rail shooter.... thing in KH2, this game is for you. If you hate even thinking about Gummi Ships, you should probably avoid Robocraft.
I am quite fond of this game. I love being able to make my own vehicles with various propulsion systems and all sorts of weapons. The jets, the hover fans, the wheels, they all contribute to the physics of your vehicle, and when they get blown off in battle, the vehicle is crippled how you think it would be. It's a joy to blow someone away and be left with only two working wheels from the fire fight, and still manage to limp your way to the next encounter or to the opponents base. I'm having fun even when we're losing sometimes. Once, my team was down to the last couple people, and neither of them had a way of moving their robot. But they manage to blow off the wheels and weapons of the remaining opponents, and everyone was just kind of stuck. It was a hilarious moment!
Maybe that last paragraph drove you away; after all, I'm the one guy who absolutely loved the Gummi Ship stuff in Kingdom Hearts (1 and 2), and wished that they had expanded upon it with actual physics. Well, this game does just that! Except, it's mostly land combat instead of space flight, but it works nonetheless.
The downside, of course, is that it is indeed pay-to-win. Paying for premium access gets you 1.5 to 2 times the rewards that free-to-play-ers get from a battle, and it would indeed be nice if I didn't have to grind so much to get money to buy more blocks. But honestly, the money you get will get you more capital to buy blocks, and the tech tree will unlock faster, but the tech tree is still locked off at teirs (unless you convert the tech points or something I guess), and you still have to damage other people to gain levels (each level raises your block cap). So the whole pay to win aspect doesn't get in the way too much. And I just ignore the whole premium thing usually.
And honestly, I just love playing. I love tweaking my vehicle and testing it in battle to see how it works to my play style. I love the community (rather, when they talk, they're more often laughing at the hilarious situations than being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it probably helps that every battle starts with a reminder on the bottom to refrain from bad language or else). I would love it if they added more modes to play, as right now it's a 2 team capture-the-flag-them-up, with about 10 players per team usually. But it is early access, and it's pretty damn good fun right now as it stands.

Even if you contributed in no way, shape, or form it will give you enough RP to cover the cost of repair. If you don't get destroyed, and contribute in a major way you can end up earning 1500-2000 RP with a 0-minimal repair cost. Paying customers don't get any advantage over free customers, they can simply get to the top of a tier quicker, by buying parts. That's it. I'm glad my brother ignored these negative reviews and downloaded it anyway. One of the best F2P games on steam without a doubt.

Oh Portal 2, how I love thee. This is probably my favorite game by Valve, and considering what Valve has made, that is an amazing feat. The original game was already great by design. It was one of the funniest games when it came out, it had nice puzzles, it was innovative in its own right, and it introduced one of the greatest villains of video games in the form of GlaDos.
Portal 2 just takes everything about the original, and multiplies how awesome it is by about a thousand. That is what Portal 2 is, which makes this one of the best games around. In Portal 2, Aperture Science is dormant, GlaDos awakens and you have to go through a series of deviating puzzles again. Literally, EVERYTHING about Portal 2 shines. The story is a delight with extremely clever humor, Portal 2 is hammered with phenonmenal voice acting, and the gameplay is improved in everyway from the original.
Speaking of gameplay, Portal 2's improvements come in the form of the amazing puzzles. With the addition of different mechanisms such as gels and light bridges, the game instantly makes it better. The puzzles are fair too, so while you might be stuck on a puzzle at one point, it will be rewarding when you complete it. The most surprising part of Portal 2, in my opinion, is the multiplayer. The cooperative multiplayer is AWESOME, and really gets both you and your partner thinking, provided you haven't played the coop before. Some might complain the game is short, but additional custom maps by the community can help alleviate those problems, if you even have any.
Portal 2 is everything a sequel should be. It improves on the original, and easily pleases both fans of the series and newcomers alike. I highly recommend this game, and it is definitely one of the best games around. Well done Valve!

Foreword: Please disregard all reviews saying this game is p2w. It's really not, it's more a "pay-to-advance-faster", and even then you still need skill. Basically, what premium membership gives you is a 50% addative to your earnings from each battle. Oh, and it allows you to have one extra person in your squad, if you're leader.
Short Review: I blew up 3 enemies with my plasma-cannon-wielding tank made of over 200 blocks only to be sniped by a guy in a 5 block floating sniper chair. Out of 10, I'd give it a 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 because I can't even.
Long Review: Wait, you want to actually hear about the game too? Oh, okay. Well, Robocraft(Hereafter referenced as RC) is an extremely fun game, similar to World of Tanks. However, in no way would I say it's a copycat game: It's very far from what WWT is. RC allows you to build your tank/hovercraft/plane/whatever-the-heck-you-want ground up.
Something to note right off the bat, team work is essential in this game. If you're not with members of your team, you're going to die. If your entire team only goes down one lane of the map, you're going to die. If you or your team runs gun-ho into the middle of map, you're going to die. Cautious play, teamwork, and surviving are all the key elements to ever winning a match.
You're given 4 basic types of building blocks: the cube, ramp, prism, and crystal shapes. You have SMG turrets, plasma turrets(Similar to the wraith's gun in halo), and rail guns(snipers) for weapons, and these grow larger and more powerful(as most things do in this game) with each tier(We'll get to tiers later). Some special block types are radar, radar jammers, shield blocks, and the flipper(If your vehicle flips over, this allows you to flip it back).
For movement, you're given basic wheels, hoverfans, thrusters, airfoils, and rudders. Wheels are, well, wheels. Nothing much to say to that, though be wary of having only 4 wheels on your craft: You'll find it rather hard to control, especially once you lose a wheel. Hoverfans allow you to make hovercrafts(No duh), and are pretty awesome as they allow you to be a low flying drone. Thrusters, aw, thrusters. These babies will almost always be in your more rediculous designs, as well as your good ones. Want more speed? Stick a few thrusters on. Want to make a 6 block sniping chair that sits in the sky? Take some helium blocks, slap on some thrusters and guns, and all thats left is adding the pilot chair. Anyways, you'll find out more about those bad babies once you get to around tier 3-4(When they actually become viable to use). So, lastly, we have the airfoils and rudders. Airfoils function exactly like you think they would, and if you don't know what an airfoil is, google is your best friend(And stalker, but that's beside the point). Rudders are simply smaller airfoils with steer capabilities. Combine airfoils and rudders, a lot of testing to get the weight balance correct, and you have yourself a plane!
Well, I said I would talk about tiers earlier. It's pretty simple. There are 10 tiers in the game. Each block you place on your ship has a robot rating. Every tier is a range of robot ratings, and you'll fall into whatever tier your robot's total rating applies to.
All in all, I would recommend this game for anyone who just want's to have a bit of fun, try crazy♥♥♥♥♥stuff that shouldn't be physically possible, or to hardcore blow things up.

Original Review:
_________________________________________________________________
I don't know how to describe Robocraft. If I had to try, I would start by saying how Robocraft can be seen as a cake, picture it now, the most delicious cake you have ever eaten. Now take that cake, and place it inside the locked cage that is Robocraft's servers.
Now here you are, with your delicious cake, made from little cubes, locked inside a cage. "Robocraft server, may I have some cake?" You ask. "Sure buddy, let me find your key here." Says the Robocraft server, as it starts flicking through the sizable bunch of keys that is the login queue. "Joyous day my dear fellow!" You exclaim in delight as the Robocraft server finally allows you to receive your delicious cake. You admire this cake, your cake, your.. unique cake, and you gleefully hit 'B' to take your cake into battle, to see how it fares against the enemy cake. Several minutes pass while you wait for your cake to bake before you can use it. "Why is my cake taking so long to bake? The average baking time is only seven seconds!" You proclaim, feeling something amiss. But aha! Your cake bakes, and you take it to battle.
The oven door opens, the majestic battlefield revealed. "I think I've played this map before.." You think to yourself in the back of your mind, but you don't dwell on the thought, as there are other cakes to face, each challange different!
The countdown begins! 3! 2! 1! ?! declares the timer, hanging at a puzzling '?' mark.
"I hate it when this happens to my cake." You say to yourself as you start pushing all the buttons to control your cake, but no joy. The timer still reports '?'.
In dispair you bring up the task manager to end the cake process before restarting it. "Hello again!" Says the Robocraft server as it waves to you. "I'm sorry, but I'll have to find your key again." Declares the server sheepishly. You nod, knowing the cake is worth the wait.
Much time passes, and the server brings you the much awaited cake. "Hang on.." You say while giving your cake the once-over. "..My cake's broken!" The server does not respond, the only movement coming from the diminishing cake fund as the server spends your money fixing the broken cake.
You huff, feeling slightly saddend by this, but still, you must battle your cake!
The oven door lowers again, your cake ready. 3! 2! 1! Goes the countdown, the excitement building as you prepare to unleash your cake. Huzzah! Your cake is active, you jet around, proudly displaying your cake to the others.
..But, what's this? The other cakes, They arent moving!
You quirk an eyebrow before deciding to fire at an enemy cake. It hits! But no damage is done, and the enemy cake remains unscathed.
"Woops! Sorry!" Declares the server rudely as it pops up in front of you, the server clears it's throat before reading you a message. "Sorry, I've lost connection to the bakery, shall we head back to the oven?"
With little choice, you agree, finding yourself back in the oven, where your cake is once again damaged.
"All this trouble for cake, would it not be easier to simply go and find a different bakery?" You ponder, seeing many different bakeries available. "No!" You declare proudly. "None are as fun as the Robocraft bakery!" You stand proudly before entering another battle with your now-fixed cake.
You enter the battlefield once more, but alas! You have no team - and no enemies.
You glare at the server out of the corner of your eye before trundling off to capture the teamless base, the desolate martian landscape would, under usual circumstances, be harsh and unforgiving. But not today, because you have cake. You have your cake. The cake you made with your own blocks, and you shall forever be inseparable.
"Maybe one day.. one day. The cake battle will work." You think to yourself as you jet off, leaving only dust in your wake.

Yes

– The story
You are set in the future where a Robot called GLaDOS is presented as a sarcastic nemesis who just won’t leave you alone. You first are introduced to a seemingly friendly floating robot head Wheatley. He takes you through a bunch of tests which GLaDOS is presenting you with while he tries to take over the place. What happens next You have to find out for yourself.
– My thought’s
The game itself is a piece of Art. Everything about the game just screams yes. The game is about puzzles and thinking with portals. If you haven’t played the first portal that’s ok, I’ve played the first portal a long time ago and it didn’t impact the second game that much. Story mode of the game is done perfectly, voice acting as silly as it may in a robot game is done very well + animations are great. Maybe the only way it would be improved if you could play co-op with more people, other than that it’s perfect. I personally like the introductions of the Portal gun. Co-op was executed as good as you can possibly execute it, I was stunned to see how well the Multiplayer was made. A lot of games don’t have a good co-op system and/or multiplayer, but Portal 2 just took made it as easy as possible. If you wish to play co-op I suggest finishing singleplayer beforehand. Co-op doesn’t include a story, but rather multiple puzzles for you and your friend. I honestly can’t find anything bad to say about this game because it is just perfect, little to no bugs at all.
– The summary
The game is excellent for people who wan’t to challenge themselves and friends.
– The Pros
+ Story – The game has an excellent story mode for you to complete.
+ Co-op – This game includes a co-op mode for you and your friends to play, and can be set up in a matter seconds.
+ Smooth graphics – The graphics of the game are just stunning and perform well even for not so good computers.
+ Little to no Bugs – In my time of gameplay I didn’t experience any bug at all.
+ Community workshop – When I found out I could play other people’s creations I was just sucked even more into the game then before.
+ Level editor – Another option the game allows is a custom editor for you to make your own maps and creations and share with the world.
+ Independant game – What I mean by this is, even if you haven’t played the first portal game you don’t need to because the game’s story mode isn’t affected by the other game.
– The Cons
+ Short ending – To be honest this is the only thing I could put on this, it doesn’t even deserve a “The bad” section because it was so darn good.
+ Micro-Transactions – The only way to customize your character within the game is to spend a few bucks on a skin.
– The rating
+ I would rate the game a solid 9/10 just because of the performance and everything about it. Definitely suggest this game to your more puzzle-loving friends.

I am recommending this game because of the fun it gave me during a 3-day binge session at my brother's house. I am definitely coming back to this game if I can get my home internet and computer to cooperate, and I'm definitely playing it when I go see my brother again.
Overview:
The whole point of the game is to earn currency, called robo-points (RP), which you use to buy more blocks to add to your vehicle (think Legos), and tech points (TP) which you use to unlock better (higher tier) armor blocks and weapons. All of this you then use to build and rebuild your own fighting vehicle.
The type of vehicle you can build is not very restricted. At low levels, in fact, you see a lot of vehicles that just fall over right at the start, which is hilarious. You can build more than just a tank though, there are parts that make your vehicle hover above the ground, or even fly way up to the top of the map so that you can snipe what’s below. One limiting factor is the “CPU load” measured in “pFLOPS”. You have a limited number of pFLOPS to use to add blocks to your vehicle, but your limit increases as you gain more experience points, at a rate of 11 pFLOPS per level (may be subject to change). Basically, you can build a bigger vehicle as you level up, but the most limiting factor is the vehicle ranking system.
The better parts you use, or the more powerful weapons you attach, the more ranking points your vehicle gets. In an effort to create classes of vehicles, Robocraft uses 10 tiers of ranking point limits to better balance the multiplayer. This way, you will never see a tier 10 weapon in a tier 1 battle. It is however possible, for example, to use a tier 4 weapon in a tier 1 match if one built a vehicle that has very little armor. A tier 4 weapon, however, may not be easy to come by.
To unlock higher tiers of equipment and parts, you need to earn tech points. Each tier has its own TP, so for example, you have to use tier 1 TP to unlock tier 2 parts, but then to unlock the tier 3 parts, you have to use tier 2 TP. You earn the TP for whatever tier your vehicle is in. So it takes a bit of time to build up your vehicle to the higher tiers, at which point you can build a new vehicle for lower tiers that uses the powerful weapon. This may seem a bit overpowered, but then consider the fact that you would be fighting against a bunch of people using multiple low tier weapons, as opposed to you using only one high tier weapon (putting on more weapons would give you too many ranking points to stay in the low tier). It can be fun to play like that (sometimes called smurfing), but not very rewarding, because you will have already unlocked all of the lower-tier tech, and the amount of RP you get is lower in lower tiers.
Comparing this to World of Tanks, which I've also played, I find that benefits from the fact that it doesn't take itself too seriously, unlike the psuedo-historical theme present in WoT (which I really don’t prefer). The whole sci-fi style of the game to me is reminiscent of the Halo series, and I would say that in this respect WoT would be analogous to Call of Duty.
There is only one game mode currently, which is also similar to WoT, in which the win conditions are: blow up everyone on the opposing team, or capture the other team’s base. If you’ve played WoT, capping is not a very popular or useful strategy in that game, but in Robocraft, capping is very important. The strategy has to strike a balance between just rushing the other team’s base, or spreading out close to home so you can see what the other team is doing. If both teams just rush, it’s a matter of who gets there first, but if you can defend your base while sending a small party to capture theirs, victory will be ensured.
Responding to criticism:
After reading some of the reviews (possibly just some of the negative ones) I find that some common complaints are that the game is boring/repetitive, unbalanced, and pay-to-win. To these complaints, I will respond first by saying: this is a vehicle combat game, which, by the standard of WoT, can be a repetitive grind-fest if you don’t see the depth in the gameplay. The genre doesn’t lend itself well to emerging gameplay. I will admit, yes, there is a limited map selection, and yes, the games are relatively short, but to me that wasn’t a problem. Basically, it is a vehicle combat game, don’t expect it to do anything else.
Now, saying that Robocraft is unbalanced is not valid to me, because the idea that a sandbox-esque vehicle fighting game can be completely balanced really shows a lack of understanding of what the game is trying to do. Yes, the game can seem unbalanced if your vehicle is under-powered, but that’s not a permanent state. If you build your way up from the bottom of tier 1 to the top of tier 1, you’re going to be getting a decent number of kills most of the time. However, once your vehicle qualifies as tier 2, for example, you’re back to playing at the bottom again, which is very similar to the system in WoT. So again, it is unreasonable to expect wins every time if you’re at the bottom of a tier. Another thing you’ll find by playing this game is that sometimes battles can seem a bit like rock-paper-scissors. There are three main weapon types, and they all require different strategies, and they have their own weaknesses and strengths. This is, by-no-means, a sign of an unbalanced game. Each strategy has a weakness, and if you don’t like one strategy, you are always free to rebuild and try something new. Even the maps themselves give advantages to certain weapon types, like the sniper/rail cannon. The amount of variety still present in even tier 4 matches really indicates to me that there is no overpowered strategy or weapon, or at least one hasn’t been discovered yet. I see just as many complaints in chat saying that rail cannons are op as I do complaints that the lasers are op.
Finally, is the game pay-to-win? Not through tier 4, that I can guarantee, because I have not paid a cent and I destroy people all the time, and it’s awesome. If it is true that in tier 5 repair costs start going up, then I would maybe question that design choice, but really, the majority of players stick with tier 1 or 2 just for the fun of it. In conclusion I would say, don’t pay too much attention to the complaints because if you get bored you can always just quit playing until the next update, and if that’s not a message to the developers, I don’t know what is.

FULL DISCLOSURE: I have not spent an iota more than $0.00 on this game.
Now that that's out of the way, let me start by saying that I don't understand all these negative reviews I'm seeing at the top. And before you pass me off as being some rabid fanboy because of said reviews, just hear me out:
I found Robocraft a few months ago when it was on Greenlight and decided to check it out, dowloading it from the game's website. I'm VERY glad I did. It's pretty much every little boy's (and some little girls') dream at some point to build their own battlebot from scratch to fight other bots. This game gives you the opportunity to do just that and it does a great job to boot. Put plainly, it's just straight-up fun.
And it's not only fun; it's FAIR. I've never been killed and thought to myself, "What the hell?!? That wasn't my fault! That shouldn't have happened!" like I do so often in many supposedly "AAA" titles with HUGE amounts of funding. Every time I've gotten myself blown up, I've always felt like it was because of something I did or didn't do. Every. Single. Time. Seriously, bar none. That's really not an exaggeration. In addition to that, once you have an idea of where you want your bot to go design-wise, you get to finish each game (and especially the ones you lose) thinking, "Heh heh heh heh heh... Just wait 'til I buy that new upgraded part I just unlocked! I'll show them! I'll show them all!!!" And you probably rub your hands together or drum your fingers against each other and you feel like some variety of evil mastermind and it's GREAT.
Finally, I feel a colossal need to address Robocraft's "GC" and "Premium" systems so many people have been railing against in their reviews. First, and most obviously, Freejam has to make money somehow. Yeah, I know, you're probably readying those fingers to type out some form of scathing, vitriol-filled comment about how I'm a horrible person who's supporting the downfall of the gaming industy and all that, but that's not what I'm talking about here, and it's not what ANYONE should be talking about in reference to this game. Except to say that it's not a problem. Like I am. So stick THAT in your ear!
Let me explain the payment system in this game:
RP is the primary currency earned each match through normal play (there's also TP earned each match, but that's not important to this review). It can be used to buy everything except cosmetic items that only help you get killed anyway. GC is the secondary currency, obtained through real-world money (GASP! SHOCK AND HORROR!), with which you can buy everything (including those flashy cosmetics). Good so far, right? I mean, this seems to be the compromise I hear tons of people calling for in other games and I, for one, agree whole-heartedly with it. But there's also a "Premium" subscription you can buy for a fee which gives you a 50% bonus on whatever you earn from a fight.
I just have no clue why people hate this so much. What's the big deal with it? Are people really so childishly insistent that supporters of a game not get anything better than what they can get for paying nothing? And it's not even like it's an unfair advantage, either. If you rush yourself into the next Tier without having the necessary experience, you will get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you on a very shiny laser-filled platter. Repeatedly.
TL;DR: Please take the time to read the above. But if you really just can't afford to do that, at least give Robocraft a try. It's a fun, fair game that I honestly enjoy playing. And who knows? You just might enjoy it too.

-Members can climb the ranks much more easily than free players

The downsides:

2. There is a "pay-to-win" element, but it is minimized by a robot tiering system that controls how different robots are matched against each other. This means that the people who pay to make really high end robots quickly will get matched with other people within the same robot tier, not against new players who stand no chance against them. This is a game where you construct a ship, out of various edges and blocks, guns, radars, and many other things to build the ultimate drivable/flyable weapon. After building said vehicle or plane, you drive it into a battlefield on Mars or Hoth, (Yes I said Hoth.) and battle other players to an awesome death. The battles require strategy and teamwork, and depending on how well you did/how much you contributed for the team, you get money and tech points, which can be used to upgrade your weapons.
Key Points about the game:
-Your ship's design is fully up to you: You can build anything you want.
-Once you die, you die for the round: this adds more sense of belonging in your team when you defeat a teammate.
-No tutorial: Yes, it's difficult to start up, but once you begin, it's easier to continue.
Pro(s):
Good graphics
Good Minecraft-ish feel
Great Combat
Fluid Animations
Good gameplay/replayability
Con(s):
No Tutorial (Like i said, kinda hard to start)
