THIS IS A EARLY ACCESS REVIEW WRITTEN FROM THE GAME AS IT IS ON 20.08.2014.
I love this game, but right now I'm on the edge would I recommend it.
There are 3 main reasons why I'm doupting:
1. Just one gamemode "Capture the point and it can get quite tedious...
2. The minor reward from winning a round encourages players preparing to advance to next tier not to actually play the objective of the gamemode. Instead they play somekind of a farce of a Teamdeathmatch while the players new to the tier try to get the enemy point and when the one side have more of the other that the other side battles tend to be quite one sided. To open this problem a bit I think it's because, you get the main RP-currency used to buy unlocked parts by killing/damaging your opponents and repairing your robot after battle uses this same currency, while from winning the round you get just more TP that can be used to unlock new parts to buy and you get enough TP to research everything in your tier far before actually getting enought RPs to buy those parts so you can advance to next tier.
3. Constant quite major tweaks to weapon balance. This is also a good thing, but it makes it very fustrating as you never know when your playstyle becomes obsolite. For example day before yesterday I finally after ~20h of playing unlocked railgun (sniper) and bolted on my hoverboat thingy. This proved to suit my playstyle well and I enjoyed playing very much and felt that my hoverboat+sniper combo was quite balanced. Well waking up yesterday morning Robotcraft downloaded a patch before I got to playing and after few fustrating rounds of not hitting anyone with my railguns I realized that they had done a tweak how much your robot can move and still get the best accuracy. This rendered the hoverboat totally obsolite as sniper platform as it's never quite still and so cannot get the best accuracy... So I went back to SMG...
Despite constant patching Plasma feels quite OP. Nearly every match that I die in, the instrument of my demise seems to be Plasma. Thought I'm in full health I might get suddenly owned (or at least severly handicapped) by some stray plasma shot... At least Railgun gives away the shooters location with the laser sight before delivering it's one-shot deathray and takes ages to reload and cannot practically be mounted on anything without wheels or heliumballs to take it to the height limit...
Despite these huge complaints I generally enjoy this game. I enjoy the building mechanics of the robots and found the combat mechanics tought not 100% there yet on fairly solid foundations. Also I'm quite sure that they are going to adress my two main complaints about the gamemode and rewards for winning quite soon as these are quite big flaws and could hurt retention of the players quite seriously in the long run. The third one I'm also quite sure will be made more stable and you can more comfortably settle into playstyles more long term so allowing more team tactics. While I'm too part of the problem whining about nerfing of the railgun and plasma being OP the correct balance is found just with time and carefull metrics from whitch percentage of any guntype is used in any particular tier.
I will redo this review when there is bigger patch directly adressing flaws I talked about in this review or when the game comes out of Early access.

Game: Portal 2
Summary: Brilliant, funny continuation puzzle game
Rating (5/10 = failure): 9.5/10
Multiplayer: Yes
Completion: 12 hrs
Cards: Yes
Cloud: Yes
Cost: 3.125 USD bundled
Portal 2 brings our favorite protagonist and antagonist back together with some fun new backstory, circumstances, and enemies. Basic gameplay is the same - first person puzzle platformer, move blocks onto platforms, go through doors. Some new mechanics are introduced in the form of environmental gels. They help considerably to break up the monotony of gameplay.
Whereas Portal 1 was more about atmosphere, Portal 2 has a much more amusing script. Great humor throughout. The voice acting is top notch, as all the actors nailed their roles and then some. The nearly double-length journey was made more memorable and less lonely with the "companions" and sound logs that accompany you. There's a lot more backstory this time too.
The environments are great; there's considerably less of the drab, lifeless test facility backdrops (though it's still there!), and instead you get mostly cavernous, factory environments to play around in. I like the areas that look outdoors-ish, though it can be difficult to tell where to go in those areas.
The ending song isn't nearly as catchy, but the farewell of the sentries was a nice touch, and the final battle had a more satisfying conclusion.
Overall it's a great game. Hopefully we'll get to see if Valve learns how to count to three in the near future!

Old review:
I really like the concept and wanted to like the game.  And for awhile, it was a decent time.  Unfortunately, the annoyances I encountered early in the game... started to become MAJOR problems.  This game is Free to Play in the worse ways you can imagine.  It's grindy, power imbalance is the norm, and the power disparity between those who have paid to those that simply play is vast.
And the feel of the game is just insulting after a certain point.  You go forth and design a sensible battle bot with armor, lasers, and other bits in the right places.  You battle, fight some other people in a fair match... Then WHAM!  Either you've been completely one shot by a gimmicky, fragile bot overloaded with plasma launchers or someone with tier 5 equipment in a tier 3 match just ripped you into pieces.  There are balance problems EVERYWHERE.  And the sad part is that they could be fixed easily.  The trouble is that developer intent isn't there.  The developers WANT vast power differences to frustrate people into paying money.  It's that simple.  Why is higher tier equipment allowed in a lower tier matches?  To frustrate people in to paying money.  Why are the RP reward/repair values and tech points done in such a way to make it so grindy?  To get people to pay money.  Why is X weapon so overpowered to Y?  To get you willing to pay money to jump up the research path and get the good gear to bring back down to the lower tier.  Why aren't PFLOPs restricted for certain tier levels to keep the designs sensible for everyone in a match?  The same reason you can buy PFLOPs...  The power level disparity to frustrate people into paying money.
It's pay to win.  That's all it is.  The mechanics in the game don't lie.  They are all tweaked to make pay to win the best way to accomplish anything.  There are many, many easy way to slightly tweak and impose sensible limits to provide a level playing field for all the matches of all tiers...  But that's not what they want.  It's an early release game, that they are taking real money on.  They are making people pay to win in an ALPHA game.  They are strictly for the cash folks, they are only going to provide enough of a game to draw you in and hook those with loose wallets.
It's just depressing to see such a neat idea, squandered by a greedy bunch of hack developers.  It could have been done far better by more honorable and competent people.

+ Great concept that works well in practice
+ Designing and building is actually fun and intuitive
+ Gameplay is similar to that of World of Tanks, but is simpler and easier for the average player to pick up
+ Community is much less toxic than mose F2P titles that I've tried
+ Battles are fast-paced and short (typically ~5 minutes)
+ Unlike other reviews that I've read, I don't think the payment and premium system is broken, and I felt that, even without premium, I was making enough of an income to cover repair costs and buy better blocks and equipment at an agreeable pace; the devs need to see a return on their product, and I didn't feel cheated this time around
+ Crisp, responsive, visually pleasing, and refreshingly minimalist UI; the devs clearly went with "less is more" and it looks and feels great as a result
+ Finally, the game was simply fun as all get-out; I feel that this title has a lot of replay value and it has still more room to improve
- Weapons felt slightly imbalanced, namely rail-guns; players who load a cockpit on top of a few lighter-than-air blocks, fly to the map ceiling, and one-hit snipe people with alarming accuracy is not at all fun, and really took me out of the game on more than one occasion
- There were some problems with bugs, namely terrain and hit-detection, but nothing game-breaking; it's still better off than what I expected from an early-access title

The fact that you build virtually all of your robots from scratch using very simple components changes an otherwise ordinary tank shooter into an exciting creative sandbox. Portal 2 brings our favorite protagonist and antagonist back together with some fun new backstory, circumstances, and enemies. Basic gameplay is the same - first person puzzle platformer, move blocks onto platforms, go through doors. Some new mechanics are introduced in the form of environmental gels. They help considerably to break up the monotony of gameplay.
Whereas Portal 1 was more about atmosphere, Portal 2 has a much more amusing script. Great humor throughout. The voice acting is top notch, as all the actors nailed their roles and then some. The nearly double-length journey was made more memorable and less lonely with the "companions" and sound logs that accompany you. There's a lot more backstory this time too.
The environments are great; there's considerably less of the drab, lifeless test facility backdrops (though it's still there!), and instead you get mostly cavernous, factory environments to play around in. I like the areas that look outdoors-ish, though it can be difficult to tell where to go in those areas.
The ending song isn't nearly as catchy, but the farewell of the sentries was a nice touch, and the final battle had a more satisfying conclusion.
Overall it's a great game. Hopefully we'll get to see if Valve learns how to count to three in the near future!

Don't bother, it's pay to win garbage. You can pay money to unlock all progression from tier 1 and sneak late game superweapons into starting arenas.
What's a tier you ask? The game involves building robots, and the parts you build them out of come in tiers. Your robot is also rated on what tier it is by the net value of all parts attached to it. Matches also come in tiers, and your x tier robot will be placed in an x tier match.You have few options in the first few tiers, one of which is that you can't use anything but SMG weapons until tier 3, where you get a launcher, you can't use railgun or helium blocks until tier 4. And now you should have a slightly easier time reading the rest of this.
That's the first problem. Almost every match has at least one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who loads pilot seat+helium+railgun and becomes a nigh undetectable sniper 5 miles up in the sky. This is extremely annoying, on my 1080p monitor they show up as a few pixels they're so high up. Good luck getting them with your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ SMG weapons you're restricted to, too, that's not happening. The railgun and helium are not even available until Tier 4 but like I said, people get to sneak in late game bits and receive it way too early by paying the developers money.
Another problem is that the game incentivizes that you be a selfish♥♥♥♥♥♥ getting blown up will penalize you even harder than a team loss(making out with barely enough to repair your own bot vs intact bot and even higher winnings for losing), regardless of whether you win or not. I personally don't find it fun to be penalized this hard for dying because I helped my team. The result is a game that penalizes you for having fun and not just cowering like a ♥♥♥♥♥.
Those are the two major issues that I think need to be fixed the most. On top of that, physics are confusing, the game seems to roll a coin to decide, in a player-player collision, which player will be treated as a static object and which player will get pushed around. I've had players phase through me while I spaz-bolted 50m into the air and landed on my head unable to move more times than I can count.
The developers need to find a different way to get money out of players - Pay to Win is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Tier-locking needs to be done a lot better: prevent players from slapping high-tier weapons onto their T1-T2 bots, period. Not this system where they can still fudge it on there. Everyone who enters a tier should be on equal footing and equal opportunity with the rest of the tier.
Robocraft has potential, and it is addictive, but it has so many issues that I wouldn't recommend it to a friend. Mostly because Pay to Win leaves a bad taste in my mouth. Besides the physics problem, these problems aren't really the type caused by early development, so this unrecommendation goes until they fix P2W/Tier fudging, which I doubt they will.

Some of the negative reviews here aren't too detailed, so I'll try my best to change that.  I'd like to offer some valid reasons why I can't recommend this game. Of course they're my personal observations, and the issues won't affect everyone, but they could affect *you*.
Bugs in over 35% of the wretched puzzle rooms. Whether it was pixel hunting for the correct atom of usable wall to pop a portal on, or the game presenting busted mechanics you cannot work around as there is only one solution to everything. Sometimes repeating the same action five times would result in four failures and one success. Most of the time I had to reload an older save to start that area all over again, hoping that this time the puzzle would be functional. In a puzzle game, these bugs are not so much game-breaking as fun-breaking. I only realised something was amiss when I consulted a YouTube walkthrough, and found out I was doing the right thing but the game was bugged.
I'm now stuck on (what feels like) the nadir of the game. I'm in a glitched puzzle where Stephen Merchant keeps yammering at me in an attempt to be funny. This room (Wheatley puzzle 17 I think, blue tunnel of light going horizontally) has murdered the game for me. I just don't have the interest in it to bother completing this room. Tried the video walkthroughs, but guess what? The wall others can use, I can't!  To play a game where I can't tell when it's bugged or not is literally gaming torture.
Second smaller gripe: Stephen Merchant's voice acting. Holy flurking schnit, who thought this was a good idea?! I'm English, but this man's voice gets on my nerves, let alone his awful attempt at jokes and ad-libbing. With all the reloading I've had to do, I've heard his rotten material probably sixty times more than other players.
Multiplayer wasn't free of bugs either, and after trying it once I didn't return to it for a very good reason. Whether it was lag or bugs/glitches, bits of these puzzles didn't work either. Marvellous!
If you are intent on getting the game, I'd heartily recommend getting it discounted. Of course, you may not experience these bugs. My friends didn't - their run through was completely fine. Nor can I explain why over 50% of the game bugged out. The faulty turret puzzle was the first major issue that halted progress for days, as the only cure was reloading old saves before I had entered a 'bugged' area. Can you imagine how much of a pain that was, having to reload whole areas because one room's puzzle wouldn't let me through? There are no backdoors or workarounds, so when something goes wrong, it completely blocks your progress.
I really wanted to enjoy this game, as there are some really good elements. I loved controlling the liquid so I could make new portals. I didn't have a problem with this element at all, and it was lovely to experience it working properly. The super-bouncy areas were a lot of fun too. I also enjoyed seeing the roots of Aperture Science, and GLAdOS's history.
The bugs utterly ruined it for me. You can't afford to have bugs in a puzzle game that requires precision, timing, and thought from the player: It's like performing surgery with a carrot instead of a scalpel.

This is a "Minecraft style" Block builder game that very closely resembles early "World of Tanks". In essence, It's a beautiful game with lots of great mechanics at a very early stage compared to It's very light weight download weight. The game has great mechanics for building "RoboS" that are always unique and not forgiving if the design has flaws... Which is a good thing. The game is always giving you room for advancement and that extra breathing room to create a design which works, that you didn't have to look up on YouTube. As the tiers go higher, the game begins to become more intense, more design work, more team play, more strategy. Unlike in World of Tanks, I quite like the feel of the tier system in Robocraft, It's much more rewarding. Like many people i downloaded this "Free To Play" game when it first arrived on steam, as it looked like a pretty decent game. Upon starting the game i found three pre-made robots to unleash upon everybody else and to edit or re-make as i desired. At first i quite enjoyed it, though i could not for the life of me get along with the flying vehicles and the damn ice maps! And i was constantly getting destroyed in the first 30 seconds of most of the matches by various OPed weaponary or by being put into matches where i was pitted against robots of higher tiers than my own robot.
In fact i almost shouted out in joy when i actually won a match and earned some considerable RP and TP points to upgrade my robots, because upgrading my robots when i'm losing every match is practically impossible.
But anyway, i enjoyed this game long enough to re-design my flyer and to get my three robots up to tier two and one to tier three. And then i got rather fed up and bored with losing most of the time and not being able to upgrade my robots because i couldn't earn enough money by losing.
I just went on this game again for the first time in roughly a month or so only to find that half of the parts on my robots have been made obsolete (which makes this game rather obsolete) and that i have been reimbursed my RP and TB, which is great....i now have 500 level two tech points which i can spend on precisely nothing at all. The majority of the low level upgrades have vanished, so those lovely aerofoils i put on my plane to make it look like an actual plane......nope....gone, along with those electroplates i had to try and stop my robot from blowing up in my face every time i got hit by plasma cannons....also gone. I am lucky enough to have been able to keep my radar jammer though, but as for my radar reciever....nope.
I haven't even got the courage to check my third robot to see what has been removed from that one.
I fear for the poor newbies to this game who must be finding it quite difficult to get up there with the best, now that half the stuff has been removed. And it was difficult enough when it was all there.
So to sum it up, this game started off as relatively decent and sorta enjoyable if you had some time to kill and enjoy shooting at other peoples creations (and some of them are very impressive) But now it's just another one of "those" games that's been ruined. But it's "free" so get it and enjoy it for a bit, but it probably won't last very long.

Short disclaimer first: If you want to unlock all content, this game will involve quite a bit of grinding (or premium time), but you can have much fun without.
It is much fun to design and build your own bots and then test them versus other players. Bots and bot parts are categorized in 10 tiers, but bot and part tiers are not the same: Your player level (determined by play time/kills) increases your "CPU", which will allow you to use more (but not new kinds of) parts on your bots. Every part needs CPU and gives you robot ranking, and the total robot ranking determines your bot tier. The bot tier determines the quality of the other bots in your games, and the tier of the tech points you will earn. Tech points can then be used to unlock new kinds of parts.
This mechanic is the reason why you can encounter, e.g., tier 3 parts in a tier 1 match; bots wielding tier 3 parts at tier 1 have to live with many weaknesses because otherwise their bot would be rated tier 2 or higher.
You will earn in-game currency (RP) for kills and damage done, and after the match you might have to use some of it to repair your own bot, but up to tier 5 you will always at least win enough for all repairs, and on average you will earn quite a bit. However, the progress slows down; at tier 4, you have to win about ten matches to afford a new weapon. I don't think I will every play enough to reach tier 10, but the game is much fun anyway.
Regarding the reviews that are unhappy with weapon balance: It is annoying to get hit by a very lucky rail gun shot or a plasma salvo early in a match, but I feel the weapon balance is quite well (or maybe became so after the recent changes, this is still alpha, after all). You have to pay attention to your team and flanks. And no, rail guns do not have penetration power, the whole damage is done to the target and then propagates like SMG damage.
In conclusion, try this out for yourself and see if you like it, especially if you liked the ancient game Stratosphere. ^^

Some of the negative reviews here aren't too detailed, so I'll try my best to change that.  I'd like to offer some valid reasons why I can't recommend this game. Of course they're my personal observations, and the issues won't affect everyone, but they could affect *you*.
Bugs in over 35% of the wretched puzzle rooms. Whether it was pixel hunting for the correct atom of usable wall to pop a portal on, or the game presenting busted mechanics you cannot work around as there is only one solution to everything. Sometimes repeating the same action five times would result in four failures and one success. Most of the time I had to reload an older save to start that area all over again, hoping that this time the puzzle would be functional. In a puzzle game, these bugs are not so much game-breaking as fun-breaking. I only realised something was amiss when I consulted a YouTube walkthrough, and found out I was doing the right thing but the game was bugged.
I'm now stuck on (what feels like) the nadir of the game. I'm in a glitched puzzle where Stephen Merchant keeps yammering at me in an attempt to be funny. This room (Wheatley puzzle 17 I think, blue tunnel of light going horizontally) has murdered the game for me. I just don't have the interest in it to bother completing this room. Tried the video walkthroughs, but guess what? The wall others can use, I can't!  To play a game where I can't tell when it's bugged or not is literally gaming torture.
Second smaller gripe: Stephen Merchant's voice acting. Holy flurking schnit, who thought this was a good idea?! I'm English, but this man's voice gets on my nerves, let alone his awful attempt at jokes and ad-libbing. With all the reloading I've had to do, I've heard his rotten material probably sixty times more than other players.
Multiplayer wasn't free of bugs either, and after trying it once I didn't return to it for a very good reason. Whether it was lag or bugs/glitches, bits of these puzzles didn't work either. Marvellous!
If you are intent on getting the game, I'd heartily recommend getting it discounted. Of course, you may not experience these bugs. My friends didn't - their run through was completely fine. Nor can I explain why over 50% of the game bugged out. The faulty turret puzzle was the first major issue that halted progress for days, as the only cure was reloading old saves before I had entered a 'bugged' area. Can you imagine how much of a pain that was, having to reload whole areas because one room's puzzle wouldn't let me through? There are no backdoors or workarounds, so when something goes wrong, it completely blocks your progress.
I really wanted to enjoy this game, as there are some really good elements. I loved controlling the liquid so I could make new portals. I didn't have a problem with this element at all, and it was lovely to experience it working properly. The super-bouncy areas were a lot of fun too. I also enjoyed seeing the roots of Aperture Science, and GLAdOS's history.
The bugs utterly ruined it for me. You can't afford to have bugs in a puzzle game that requires precision, timing, and thought from the player: It's like performing surgery with a carrot instead of a scalpel.

This review was written August 18th, 2014.
So Robocraft has a lot of good things going for it. Very fast, strategic and has so many different situations that you won't be bored for hours. There is a progression system that takes some time but is rather quick as long as you keep surviving and getting kills.
This game would be really balanced except for one thing - People can modify their robots so they have high end weapons and be capable of playing low tier matches. Normally, this wouldn't be too much of an issue since you can have only one or two compared to the same tier's 5 or 6. But the problem lies in that these weapons have such an obvious increase in power in comparison to their lower models, plus the fact that new players are only allowed the SMG whereas veteran players can get launchers (mortars) or railguns (snipers) to be capable of one-shotting you. This effect is at all tiers of play until you get in the higher tiers (though this can still happen in a skill based manner) and is really unfun to play against since you won't be able to tell if someone can one-shot you until the bullet is in your face.
My advice to ANYONE when starting this game is three things: 1) Once you die, one-shot or not, return to mothership immediately. This will let you get in your next game much faster and really help with the stress. 2) Do your very best to not die, but still contribute. This means taking a few shots but if you are the only person left, try to keep away and let them take the game. Repair costs really limit your points per match. 3) Keep on playing. Unless you need to make some modifications to your robots, try to just keep on playing. You want to keep advancing and getting the best gear, gear has a steep curve upward in usefulness. Try to focus on buying really good guns first so you can keep going forward.

Thought it was good right until tier 3, where i quit for a day and came back to find a ridiculous update. Robocraft is a game that you build a robot go into battle, then get very little in game currency and tech points to "upgrade" your robot. Its all theory though. This game was a good idea with perfect potential that decided to abuse it's original support.
What's the problem, you may ask? Well to start, the game's servers are buggy as hell, with frequent crashes. I could say a number of times where I a) couldn't find any servers. or b) crashed after a match. When you manage to find a match, you drive or fly or whatever into the "heat" of battle, you stroll in to find yourself instantly dying to an over leveled "rail cannon" that's really just a sniper rifle, not sure why they call it something so stupid.
Also, you try matchmaking with friends to find that it is nigh impossible to get the platoons to work, because the game never starts looking for the match or someone bugs and can't join the platoon. And this is where the tier system becomes a problem, because if someone's in a different tier in your platoon, you can't find a match. It pretty much gets to a point where it's better just to talk and play your own matches instead of trying to find a match together. That's my experiences, at least.
Then there's the grinding. At the first two tiers its not a problem, because every thing's affordable because you get enough RP from a little match to test your adorable little robot that for some reason, has a pilot seat. However when you get to tier 3,  you find yourself using the same robot over and over and over again to grind for a little weapon.
This is where the devastating part comes. At about tier 6, the F2P part of it is given up, and most players spend thier money to get "premium" which gets them double the RP. Now I'm completely sure what has happened to F2P nowadays, but I think this looks like a pay to win.
People back this game, because it's "early access", but to me, and many, many, others, there is a consensus. DO NOT CHARGE IN A F2P EARLY ACCESS! I mean it. If you're charging for your game, in early access, the game must be fit for release, and purchases should only be accepted for the game itself, for support, or through a direct donation from one very nice person, to the developers.
You, the reader, might like this game, or how it looks, and that's fine by me, but there are better uses of your time, trust me.  Look at the other reviews that educate, acknowledge every one of them, negative or not. These are the facts. Listen to them, trust them, and when you decide, I hope you make the right choice.

Edit: 256 Hours into the game, 7-15-15
THIS FREE GAME IS NOT WORTH YOUR TIME!!!
I have been playing off and on since my last update just to check if the problems have been fixed. It is now worse than before. The "Average wait times" say that it takes approximately 1 min to 3 min to enter a game. However, I and 10 others clocked it at 15 minutes to enter classic and challenge, and now battle mode takes at least 3 minutes, but up to 5 minutes to enter. They have also began to change the way that the bots are classed. This could have been done in a way that improved the game, or at least kept the usefulness of lower end parts, but instead they have made getting to the final tiers of the game the only goal, while also making the parts you get along the way utterly useless once you get to that final tier.
If you want a game that you wait a minimum of 3 minutes to enter a terrible mode of play, to then play with a team, which at least 1 person will crash out of, sometimes as many as 3 per team, all the while, a several people on both sides will likely have a bot that just spins or can't move properly because they didn't test it (yes, that still happens on T10). If this kind of game excites the inner masochist in you, then remember that you only get to play it for about 4 minutes, 7 minutes if both teams are either really good/bad, or 2 minutes of gameplay if the teams get imbalanced due to above mentioned problems.
This will go down as one of the games that I loved!!! But another example of creators destroying a good concept by not listening to the players concerns. They refused to listened to the majority of players main requests of lowering the team requirements to ensure faster access to gameplay, and instead "fixed" problems that didn't exist by adding non useful stuff to purchase instead. Thisresulted in more people getting tired of waiting to play a game that still has some of the core issues I described in August of 2014, almost a full year ago. Which (sadly) resulted in a loss of many players that made the game fun.
Oh, and one more somewhat serious concern. They still only have the same 4 maps since my first review of the game. They have updated the look, but haven't spent the time to make any new ones. That too, is very disapointing.
________________________________________________________________
Edit: 220 hours into the game, 3-12-15
So the last patch destroyed the game. Wait times are now terrible, for 2 of the three modes. Classic, which use to be fast in and fast out, and Challenge, which is a team of big bots versus small bots, both of them now have 5-10 minute wait times. The only option is battle mode, and it's been the least fun addition to the game. Also, entering the program now takes (depending on your PC and connection) about 2-3 minutes.
That being said, it's been fun, but they overreached and it's caused a significant amount of players to leave the game.
________________________________________________________________
Edit: 202 hours into the game. 1/5/2015
Something of note, they have changed quite a bit since the beginning, such as adding tank treads, spider crawling, healing, and some other minor improvements. The game is stronger now than it was just the few months ago when I wrote the original review, and now they have eliminated the worst part of the game, the pay to repair. It’s still a little “grindy” at times, but overall, it’s a great game to play. Now if they could just work on the flying physics….
On the downside, the healer turns out to be one of the most damaging choices. I hope they fix that.
Something important to note about all games in the beta stage, they will have bugs. That being said, this game doesn't have many, but it does have some drawbacks, the time to enter the game has increased, and the wait times have gone up slightly, but not to an unreasonable amount of time.

So here is the three best parts about the game so far 8/17/2014
1. Huge selection of things that you can make, want a WW2 (ish) plane, to fight a Tie Fighter, make them and fight them.
2. Fast game interaction times. Average load time into a game is about 20 seconds, with a minute being max that I have ever waited. The rounds are usually less than 5 minutes, and that makes this a quick game! (This is no longer the case, as of 1-5-15)
3. The biggest bonus is this, the balance system. The way that it works is that it goes off of the gear you use to build your robot, the better gear you use, the higher tier you will be placed into, while still allowing a bit of farming from one to three tiers (anything more than that is pointless) below your current max build. Yes, this means that you will come across a sniper with a tier four weapon right out the gate against your noob gear, however, you will also be placed on teams with other people doing the same thing, and you progress through the first 4 tiers really fast.
So here is the three worst parts about the game so far
1. More often than I like, the game crashes/freezes, that being said, I've restarted the whole game and gotten into matches faster than I have gone from lobby into a match with some other games... So this one’s kind of a draw, but to some people, it's a deal breaker.
2. Flying and hovering machines are difficult to make work. For every 1 that flies correctly, you'll have tested 10 that just loop and/or spin uncontrollably.
3. The only true negative in my opinion, is the game physics... Always test your robot out before entering the game, because the physics are not kind to you. If you don't test it out, you'll likely spend the game upside down or flying off into the wall. They give you a flipping device (removed as of 1-5-15, you now press F to turn upright, which causes a bright blue orb to glow around you and YOU CAN BE SHOT AT AND DESTROYED IN THE PROCESS WHILE YOU ARE HELPLESS = terrible).
Also, I feel I must note this, this is not a pay to win game, anything that you can pay to acquire, you can play to acquire. This is instead a pay to speed up game, and I'm OK with that.

Portal 2 is a game that combines a deviously planned and dark plot with great puzzles in the single player. It also has a great co-op option that has an entirely different and equally enticing campaign. I'll start with the single player.
***NO SPOILERS FOLLOW***
Single Player:
In Portal 2s single player branch, the focus is mostly on the mysterious history of Aperture Science. Originally founded as a world reknown shower curtain company in the mid 1930's. When the 1940's came, they branched off to what they would continue to be, a company that broadened it's products to not just shower curtains, but all things science-related. They made the ground breaking development of the portal gun, or quantam tunneling device, which led them to begin mass-testing in which they created test chambers an used ens of thousands of "privately kept" test subjects. Over the years though,they began to decay. All of this and so many more shady details are uncovereed in the single player.
Co-op/Multiplayer:
The multiplayer stars the two blue and orange robots you keep seeing in the trailers. One is you, one is your partner, and I would only play multiplayer with a close friend who you communicate well with, otherwise the tests may pose a frustrating ordeal. The great thing about this co-op though, is that it has its own story, and countless levels.
New Mechanics:
The main new mechanic is gels, which change a surface's properties, such as increasing speed while running on them or making them portalable. These are introduced midway through the campaign and are used from then on frequently.
Other:
EASTER EGGS. There are so many, and each adds to the mystery of an already unfathomably awesome campaign. If you finish everything else, these should give you another good few hours of gameplay.
Summary:
It's almost like reading a great novel, except you are the main character.
10/10

I love this game, but there's a couple of major flaws.
For one, 2 blocks is what saves you from life and death. I know you've heard that from a lot of others, but it's honestly the truth. Not only that, since most robots tend to tip over, you're normally exposed on the bottom, which not only makes you immobile, but it makes you easier to kill as they just have to aim where they think your cockpit is and blow it up.
The second thing is the servers. On occasion you'll find that your time will go to 2:00 and you still haven't found a game, even though the average says it's 0:15 or 0:05; thus games are harder to get into.
The third thing would be the fact that all youtubers recorded before the Tier-changing update, giving false hopes to those who  joined to make a helicopter or airplane the moment they get the game with their starting RP. This leads to mass confusion and annoyance in said people, such as me for one.
The fourth and final thing is that there re people who have played the game for quite a while and got different types of guns- specifically the other 2 types you've seen in the videos, plasma guns and rail guns. The thing is, since new players can't get those, older players can just waltz into earlier tier games (T10 goes into T1 with a T5 railgun, which penetrates blocks until damage is fulfilled or it hits the terrain) and absolutely dominate and make a horrible situation for both people, as you get around 50 - 100 RP per T1 round, even with kills.
However, there's still hope. The thing they have to do is this:
- Restore the railgun from the last update and change it's qualities to reduce the damage output so that a T4 tech point railgun can take down a single T4 tech point electroplate (a armor plate, for those who don't know) without the current results: piercing through 10 other blocks afterwards. Yes, that's a thing.
- Reduce the blast radius of the Plasma cannon. You don't have to remove the damage output, as it IS a compact explosive capable of doing massive damage, but the fact the radius is approximately 3 blocks means a single T5 plasma cannon can possibly anihlate any T1 ship, reguardless of it's size. At the very least, they could nerf it in a way that allows fairness.
- SMG's should have some form of cooldown so that it can't just be spammed and seem like the best weapon in close range (which it is, but a bit TOO powerful.) as it can shred apart huge ships in massive numbers by just looking at the ship, and holding left click. at the very least it should have a cooldown after dealing X amount of damage.
For now, please stay away from this game until it's fully released, and even then you should look at some gameplay episodes first.

I love this game, but there's a couple of major flaws.
For one, 2 blocks is what saves you from life and death. I know you've heard that from a lot of others, but it's honestly the truth. Not only that, since most robots tend to tip over, you're normally exposed on the bottom, which not only makes you immobile, but it makes you easier to kill as they just have to aim where they think your cockpit is and blow it up.
The second thing is the servers. On occasion you'll find that your time will go to 2:00 and you still haven't found a game, even though the average says it's 0:15 or 0:05; thus games are harder to get into.
The third thing would be the fact that all youtubers recorded before the Tier-changing update, giving false hopes to those who  joined to make a helicopter or airplane the moment they get the game with their starting RP. This leads to mass confusion and annoyance in said people, such as me for one.
The fourth and final thing is that there re people who have played the game for quite a while and got different types of guns- specifically the other 2 types you've seen in the videos, plasma guns and rail guns. The thing is, since new players can't get those, older players can just waltz into earlier tier games (T10 goes into T1 with a T5 railgun, which penetrates blocks until damage is fulfilled or it hits the terrain) and absolutely dominate and make a horrible situation for both people, as you get around 50 - 100 RP per T1 round, even with kills.
However, there's still hope. The thing they have to do is this:
- Restore the railgun from the last update and change it's qualities to reduce the damage output so that a T4 tech point railgun can take down a single T4 tech point electroplate (a armor plate, for those who don't know) without the current results: piercing through 10 other blocks afterwards. Yes, that's a thing.
- Reduce the blast radius of the Plasma cannon. You don't have to remove the damage output, as it IS a compact explosive capable of doing massive damage, but the fact the radius is approximately 3 blocks means a single T5 plasma cannon can possibly anihlate any T1 ship, reguardless of it's size. At the very least, they could nerf it in a way that allows fairness.
- SMG's should have some form of cooldown so that it can't just be spammed and seem like the best weapon in close range (which it is, but a bit TOO powerful.) as it can shred apart huge ships in massive numbers by just looking at the ship, and holding left click. at the very least it should have a cooldown after dealing X amount of damage.
For now, please stay away from this game until it's fully released, and even then you should look at some gameplay episodes first.

This is one of the most stunning fps/platformer/puzzle games that has ever been created. If you played the original Portal you will definitely enjoy this title. The writing is just as witty and brilliant as ever, with Wheatley at the helm instead of Glados. I spent a lot of the game smiling and laughing at most of the dialogue, and finding myself wrapped in the games fictional world. I wanted to know more about what happened here after listening to J.K. Simmons doing the voice of Cave Johnson. He was absolutely spot on, such a brilliant actor, and definitely had some great dialogue throughout the game.
This game also includes amazing new elements that make the puzzles even more fun such as the goo. There is orange, blue, and white goo you will come across in the game that do different things and add even more brilliance to the puzzles. Theres nothing more satisfying than running top speed down a path thanks to some blue goo to pick up speed and blasting thru a portal to another area where theres orange goo on the wall, making you bounce to your next objective. The white goo comes into play later and allows you to create portals where you normally wouldnt be able to before. The designers also come up with air lifts, where you can place portals on the flow of these gravity elevators and access areas you couldnt get to before. The soundtrack is actually quite good, with bits and pieces picking up at certain points in the story adding to the dramatic flare of the level you are on or what you are doing. For example, you can rocket yourself into the air via portals or a spring loaded platform and the music will kick in at just the right time as your are ascending into the air, giving it a more breathtaking feeling.
The game now features something the original did not have: multiplayer. This is some of the most fun you can have in a multiplayer game out there. Controlling two Aperture Science Bots created to run test chambers over and over again, you have to use both of your critical thinking abilities to get thru some of these levels, as each robot has their own portal gun giving you the ability to have 4 portals on the level at once. I found that the only drawback to the multiplayer was sometimes playing with someone who already did this feature with someone else, they can push you along very quicky and solve the puzzles almost for you rather than have you both think it thru. It is still a lot of fun to go thru the game a second or even third time to see how people use their brain to figure out some of these very fun and often challenging puzzles. All this adds to a much deeper, immersive, critical thinking game that was hailed as one of the best if not THE best games of 2011. 10/10

TL;DR: This game is fun for a few hours then gets boring quick.
This game is recommended because it is free, and the first 3 tiers are blissful fun of building lego robots for robowars. However, the only thing you have to work towards apart from arbitarily more powerful gear is wings for flying aircraft at tier 5 (after that everything is the same).
After working towards this and playing 50 hours of the game, the flying mechanics are horribly disappointing because of how fragile the wings are, you are much better off with a hover tank possibly combo'd with wheels and thrusters.
Redundancy in movability leads to survivability, but it is difficult to get any design that is both functional and aesthetically pleasing.
As you tier up, the next tier gives you so many more points to build bigger and badder robots, but players from higher tiers deliberately drop down to use more powerful weapons. The only strategy is to let the dumb teammates go first, or move around the sides of the map and try to pick the enemy off. The only way to get more pflops to actually build bigger stuff if by getting kills and assists, meaning its better to camp your own base or the edges of the map than capture the enemies.
If you are not a full time student or a child, it is worth the time to buy a ship from the in game shop at Tier 5/7 simply so you can avoid wasting time grinding your way to disappointment. You'll get more hours of fun than seeing a movie in cinema, but it quickly wears off as there is nothing meaningful in this game to work towards.
Yes it is in alpha and still being developed, but everyone's mom's indie game is in alpha yet you can drop cash on them still.
I doubt it will get better than this, but enjoy the trend while it lasts.

This game is what happens when you take something good and tumblrfy it.
.The puzzles are dumbed down for a more casual audience - most of the time, you will be looking for the only spot you can shoot a portal on, especially towards the end. The aerial faith plates and lazers are just old gameplay elements given a new skin, momentum and energy pellets, respectively, and the other, more innovative gameplay elements, the gels, hard light bridge and excursion funnels, are never fully implemented before being tossed aside.
.The jokes have been reduced to three, constantly repeated categories: blunt insults, irony and shouty reactions. It's not an issue of sensitivity, but when the joke is just "You're fat" over and over again, it loses its value.
.Given a completely unnecessary backstory, from Caroline to every single one of Cave Johnson's messsages. Not only do they ruin the character of GLaDOS by giving her a sappy backstory that no one asked for, but they devalue the credibility and seriousness of Aperture Science through Cave Johnson's inconsistent, outlandish antics. It's no secret that they were just done for a cheap laugh, though.
The combination of the previous two points means that Portal 2 loses the subtlety of the original. What was once the humorous dark environment of the original game has been reduced to a so quirky exdee floating British accent and cheap insult after cheap insult with no sustenance, what was the eerie writings of an ecapee on the walls warning you about the madness to come should you keep following the voice guiding you has become the ramblings of a complete idiot that would never have had any kind of funding to begin with, and what was once a mysterious robot who you only knew as the thing out for your death became some petty love interest to the same man, creating a back story that no one wanted or asked for. Not only was this unnecessary, but poorly implemented. We're introduced to Caroline so late into the game, and she appears so rarely into the game that we're barely given any chance to grow attatched to her as a charcter. Caroline is only given one setting: slightly ditzy. We don't even hear any growth between Cave and Caroline, we're only given the information that Cave has feelings for her.  It's also just a bad backstory.
I am by no way suggesting that Portal 1 was some kind of modern gaming masterpiece with excellent storytelling and jokes, but it did what it did beautifully, and Portal 2 threw it all out of the window for a new, more casual audience.

Generally a great game. Lacks the violent action that some people may be looking for, but the problem-solving and story aspects are absolutely amazing. Character design is quite interesting, with the Personality Constructs (otherwise known as cores) being one of the most expressive robots I've ever seen.
As for the storyline, it's arguably best to have played the original Portal, if only to know why you're recognized by the Central Core. Otherwise you can easily figure out what happened previously based on what the AI tells you.
Portal 2 includes a co-op mode for two players, and is more focused on solving tests than following a story. Quite entertaining to try to complete. Along with that, Workshop integration is also available, allowing players to build tests from scratch. If the PeTI ends up being too limited for creators, they can try to use Hammer and other authoring tools.
The soundtrack can be downloaded for free, and is quite a good source of background music, at least for me.

Great concept, wonderfully polished for an Alpha game, and good execution on the concept. A bit more customization to the T1 would be a wonderful addition, so that the players can pick their style and roll with it from the beginning, rather than be stuck on some iteration of the starter vehicle for all of T1 and most of T2. All in all, I would highly recommend this game.
Edit: In a lot of the negative reviews, I'm seeing complaints about balance, economy, small map selection, and limited game mode being the main reasons for the negative review. I would like to remind people that the game isn't even in Beta yet, much less a released finished product. The purpose of the Alpha testing is to get feedback on mechanics and the system, then Beta to fully flesh out balance and add additional content. If you don't like the game, that's perfectly fine, but don't bash an Alpha game for no reason beyond having the content and balance of an Alpha game.

Generally a great game. Lacks the violent action that some people may be looking for, but the problem-solving and story aspects are absolutely amazing. Character design is quite interesting, with the Personality Constructs (otherwise known as cores) being one of the most expressive robots I've ever seen.

Portal 2 includes a co-op mode for two players, and is more focused on solving tests than following a story. Quite entertaining to try to complete. Along with that, Workshop integration is also available, allowing players to build tests from scratch. The soundtrack can be downloaded for free, and is quite a good source of background music, at least for me.

Best free to play game I've enjoyed over Steam. Imagine World of Tanks, except you get to build your own tanks. Robocraft is still early access and it shows but I've already spent many hours creating new robot designs and battling with friends. It's great fun at no price and a very small download.
(Please remember this is Early Access and being frequently updated by a small team. The following reflects the build of the game being played at the time the review was written, and may be outdated by the time it is read.)
As of 2/12/2015
I've got 200+ hours logged into Robocraft, and probably somewhere around $20-$30. I've reached Tier 10 (the highest current tier) and played everything from flying bombers to healing tanks. This is by far and above one of my favorite games of all time. There are few other experiences that allow you to feel the pride of destroying other players with your own creations. Even fewer that challenge you to innovate on those designs over time and constantly improve them.
The construction system is incredibly solid and versatile. Pilot Seats are attached to any block, which in turn will be attached to another block in a simple minecraft-esque fashion. They can be rotated with the scroll wheel and are positioned simply by placing the center-screen crosshair over the desired location. Provided they don't collide with other blocks of course. Wheels, Treads, Hoverdiscs, Aerofoils, and Jet Engines provide mobility. For weapons you can choose between fast-firing SMG lasers or the slow-to-reload Rail Cannon. Or if you prefer a balanced mix the arcing Plasma Launchers provide great burst damage. At the middle tiers you get access to a healing beam that also damages enemies, and eventually the mighty Tesla blades that slice apart anything they touch.
Matchmaking for the moment is very straightforward, involving a combination of twelve players fighting another team of twelve for control of an enemy capture point and total elimination of the enemy. It feels very World of Tanks in practice, except much more enjoyable and varied in the designs you fight against. The addition of a spotting system (Q) makes even a disarmed enemy useful as a scout and a minimap with a grid in the bottom right makes communicating targets easier.
The failings I've encountered are that the gameplay itself can actually get repetitive as there are precious few maps (I believe five as of this review revision). While there is an alternative gamemode called Boss Battles, it does little to mix the gameplay itself besides pitting a team of lower tier robots against one high tier robot.
Biggest problem? By far and above the party system. It allows a maximum of three (3) players to join up in a squad for matchmaking, or four (4) if you have a Premium Subscription. Premium Time is very cheap and also provides double the in-game rewards from matches, but this still can get annoying when you have a forth person wanting to play and nobody has premium time. However what's more annoying is that even with the premium sized parties of four, my own group frequently experienced the matchmaking times going to extreme lengths until we all restarted our games and remade the party. The server also often said that a player on the friends list was online when the player (and steam) said otherwise.
Overall those problems are actually fairly easy to overcome, and hopefully will be fixed in time like so many of the others have been. Robocraft is an incredible game and outlet for creativity, and it's the best price in the world. What have you got to lose?
Edit as of 6/24/2015
Today's "Team Orders" update has killed this game for me. Broken robots fill every game that doesn't kick me out from a server connection error. Robots fail to save properly in the build-garage. Every match at endgame is SMG-ladden bricks smashing into eachother. It's no longer fun. The end.

...Since writing the above recommendation, my opinion of the game has changed due to a whole bunch of annoyances that have built up to me deciding to stop playing this.
- You drop out regularly
- There's no indication that you've dropped except that everyone stops moving
- The growth of targetting system is the same regardless of weapons (I found that single shots with the default guns did the same, if not more, damage over time as a railgun because you couldn't see where it was coming from and you had a really small target radius.
- The hit and the graphics don't match (Fire long range down a map and the smoke cloud appears before the blast hit)
- There's no build guide for hover blades (though I'll admit it's hilarious watching a damaged hovercraft fly around)
Lastly, and most importantly for me, it takes too long to reach the fun techs. I wanted to build a goa'uld mothership, the power rangers skyship and zepplin or hot air balloon but the amount of grinding needed to reach the appropriate techs is so high that I've just lost interest. While it's what put me off, I realize that it's a free-to-play game and it's a way to incentivize microtransactions. Robocraft doesn't give me the impression that it would be more enjoyable if I bought the tech.
My reasons might seem unreasonable, with the "It's early access" defence coming out. But in my opinion, developers shouldn't be hiding behind that shield AND have the games microtransaction system in play at the same time.

Simply put, this game is beyond amazing.
I wasn't really into puzzle-genre games until I played Portal 2, it's so beautifully designed and rich in every detail.
Some of you might think: 'Well you're only going through test chambers completing one by one until it finishes right?' I had the same thought but the storyline is far from 'boring'.
Some of the levels gets you to think quite a lot, it's not always straightforward and requires a lot of thinking, so you better put your thinking caps on.
And when you fail so many times, trial and error becomes natural. It's okay to make mistakes and the best bit of it all, you learn from them and you get the feel of success. Thats what makes Portal 2 so unique.
As you explore the test chambers, you get uncover the dark secrets of the Aperture Science Lab, along with your companion Wheatly, who is very amusing and makes you forget about the whole testing thingy. It gets more and more intense the more you go through the story. Trust me, you'll love it.
Once you get the satisfaction of completing the storyline, you get a play Co-op!
The Co-op extends the gameplay so you're not just sitting there bored because you finished the campaign, you can team up with a friend or stranger if you don't have any friends (who have Portal 2). But Co-op isn't the same as single player, Co-op tests your ability to work well as pair to complete tests specially designed for teamwork.
And if you are still hungry for more tests, the online community offer their own creations of test levels for you to dig at.
Portal 2 is one of my favourite games at the moment, even for a game thats 3 years old, I still love it more than most games nowadays. A true classic.
Overall though, It's mad NOT to get this game, A lot of time and effort has been put into this (I think) and pretty sure you will enjoy is as mush I do.

You can play to at least tier 5 according to people, without having to pay.
Personally, I've played to tier 4, and I rather like it.
If you want to make stupid, strange and funny robots, then this isn't really for you. At least not right now.
You can make such robots, but they'd be quite useless in combat... and combat is the only thing there is.
If you want to build robots from various pieces (armor, wheels, wings, hoverpads, weapons, etc) then this could be for you.
I think there are 6 or 8 maps so far, so if you can accept that, then give this game a try... it's free, and you'll not have any problems until you hit tier 5 or 6, and that could still give you a lot of hours of play.
It seems plausible that after tier 5, if you die, you lose more in-game currency than you get (from dying).
This means you would have to subscribe to get 2x the money and continue to gain currency even while dying or being severely hurt from battle... or just use one of your other bots to play lower tiers to fill up on cash for repairs.
At the time I'm writing this, the rules are that winning/losing a battle will only affect the number of tech points you get, and of course your rating if it was a ranked match.
The money you get is not affected by winning or losing, only by the amount of damage you deal to your enemies.
That's a good thing, because I read another review where he complained that if you were to sacrifice yourself in combat to win, you would get much less for it. That's no longer true.
So, if you like short 5-minute competitive games, then give it try.

Let me start off by saying this: the game isn't bad.
This game is certainly a lot of fun. If you're just searching for a game in which to screw around with friends, this is a game you won't regret giving a try. I personally have had some good times with this game, especially in a rather small amount of time.
However, if one is to don the identity of a critic, there's a lot of interesting points to bring up, both good and bad.
As if we're in a cheesy 1970's action movie, we'll start off with the bad, and then work our way to the good.
THE BAD:
1.
This game has some of the weirdest (and no, I don't mean wacky/enjoyable) physics I have had the ultimate displeasure to lay my precious eyes on. Seriously.
In the FIRST game I joined (with, admittedly, a precariously built little WALL-E that obviously couldn't tell which of its sides was which) , I found myself flipped in the first thirty seconds. Helplessly, I tried comming in the chat for one of the other new WALL-E clones to try and flip me over. Thankfully, they obliged to give it their all, which in the end meant nothing because robot collisions are barely even a thing in this game. You can ram into a tiny little 3-block retardcycle at full speed, attempting to move him a centimeter, and he won't budge at all. However, as he does not budge, you go flying at the speed of a middle-aged mother attempting to buy the next installment of mommy porn.
And of course, you flip over at the smaleST GODADCNM THIBGN FCKUK EVRFY ♥♥♥♥IN TMEIE I DRIVE ROTBOT IT FLIP VOER YWUFVU VDD WEFIDFH.
Second on the list of the bad:
Balance is nonexistent. If you disagree, I challenge you to go find a railgun-user who doesn't at least admit that the railgun is incredibly overpowered. Plasma cannons are pretty close after the railguns as well, completely outclassing SMGs in the first 4-5 tiers of the game, especially after a certain update that shall go unnamed until later on.
Recently, the developers have made efforts to change this incredible gap in the risk-reward/skill-payoff differences between the weapons. It still hasn't been enough, it seems. I've taken a pretty big break from the game now, and I don't expect to be picking it up much sooner if the balance in SMGS/Rails/Plasmas doesn't drastically, and I mean goddamn DRASTICALLY change.
"oh but afx ur just urmad cuz ur gt rekt (xd) by ppl whu r butter than uuu!!!11"
Un-equip the railguns/plasma cannons, give yourself the equivalent of a new player's robot, and then survive more than 2 rails in a tier one game.
Third on the list:
Omfg. July 31st/August 1st, 2014. The days that made me want to kill people IRL. Before this update, railguns, plasma cannons, all the tools needed to customize an early robot, EVERYTHING was available to the new player after a couple matches and a few clicks in the Tech Tree.  While weapons were certainly overpowered, EVERYBODY could be overpowered with each other. However, the developers decided to cut that circlejerk in half. They removed the ability to acquire railguns, plasma cannons, aerofoils, and thrusters (as well as other things, I believe) before Tier 4~ish. This basically just ♥♥♥♥ed new players. It ♥♥♥♥ed 'em. Straight up gave them the hard Ron Jeremy, right in the♥♥♥♥♥ Anybody who played after/on August 1st could not unlock the same things other players had unlocked before. Anyone who had had the luck to install the game and get involved in it early on became a god. It was like WALL-E vs. Mega-♥♥♥♥ing-tron for days on end, as the new players, including myself, struggled to put a dent in the mechanical messiahs that were the more experienced players.
When I had seen the capability to build a goddamn airplane robot thingie, I was so excited. Sure, it could offer quite a challenge to make a design work as I intended it to, but I was hella ready to get on that♥♥♥♥♥♥ Now, after the update, I couldn't do that. No Starscream for me. Just normal old R2D2 with a water pistol against Mecha-Hitler with sniper rifle bazookas.
Fourth, and more of a nit-pick:
Finding a game can be buggy. Dunno. Kinda dumb.
THE GOOD:
The possibilities are kind of amazing. When I played with a friend, the very first thing I saw him in was a stick-figure on a platform with wheels. After seeing a bunch of power-ranger wannabe robots, this was pretty refreshing, ridiculous, and hilarious. Even disregarding the not-so-practical possibilities a robot design can have, there's a ton of room for creativity and imagination. If the interface for building were more streamlined, I daresay building the robots could take more of my time in the game than shooting other robots. This is one of the best things the game has working for it. The amount of things one needs to take into consideration while building a robot that can take and give damage is astounding. There's no real metagame of robot, no OMG MEGAZORD ROHBOT that you're expected to build to get the highest score or whatever. Your robot is only as good as you allow it to be.
Secondly, the gameplay itself:
Understandably clunky at times, the gameplay is still pretty charming. Getting kills is satisfying, the combat is easy to understand, and it can be skill-based depending on how you approach each situation. You never know what you're facing, and no two matches will have the same outcome. Not too much to say about it other than that it's pretty good.
Third, the potential:
This game has such a huge potential for growth. The developers, while not making the best choices at all times, show that they care for the game in the multitude of changes they continue to throw at the community. If the developers don't act on the potential in games (I'm looking at you, Stomping Land), there's only so far it can go. Thankfully, this game has shown that it can adapt, in good ways and bad, with the community around it. With the other things working in its favor, this game can certainly grow far beyond its beginnings and overcome the negatives that are sure to come with a rather new game.
tl:dr : bad physics, bad weapon balance, dumb dumb dumb retard updates, good gameplay, great possibilities, and fantastic potential.
For new players' sake, I won't recommend it now. But after this game has been turned around and flipped upside-down, changed to be the best it can be, I sure will be recommending it.

Even though this game was released in 2010, it is the most fun puzzle game I have ever played.
The single player storyline is great! The test chambers get much harder, but it is so much fun experimenting to see where that Portal is supposed to go. The one part of the single player story I just love, is the plot twist. Not going to say what it is. (You will have to see for yourself)
After completing the single player storyline, you can do co-op. You will probably need a friend, being that not many others do co-op these days. The co-op story features GlaDOS, who constantly reminds you in the tests they were originally supposed to be done by humans. The end of the co-op story though, has got to be the greatest ending for a co-op game ever.
After completing the co-op and single player, you may think you are basically done with the game. WRONG. The community continues to create tons of maps, and even mods, to expand even the Portal 2 story, or even just fun chambers you can do. The one thing I just love about this game is the community. The community keeps on creating, making Portal 2 a joy to play, and see what awesome chambers were created, and which peek your interest. I'm sure you will find great maps, even created in Hammer, not just the in game test chamber creator.
Overall, this game deserves a 10/10, for being a great puzzle game, and for having a great story, and huge community.

In lieu the top most reviews, which are mainly negative, I felt some positive feedback on a great concept is necessary, albeit its current poor execution. There are many, many faults in Robocraft, enough faults that I simply cannot recall every single one. But there are fair counter-arguments with most complaints players make. Instead of giving both pros and cons, I will focus only on pros. The con you can read in the other reviews.
This review will be categorized based on the two major things players complain about, gathered from the top reviews.
Pay-to-Win:
This seem to be the aspect complained about the most. From what I can gather, Robocraft had free repairs, the implementation of repair fees and premium membership had upset some people. And, most likely, the same group of people then without deeper thought, complained about Robocraft moving toward a pay-to-win path.
Now, before you instantly hit the unhelpful button, hear my reasons for believing otherwise. Pay-to-win is paying money to gain an unfair advantage over other players, usually in the form of having more power. For example, a giant rail cannon that  fires 300 beams/sec in a beginner match. That, is having advantages over players. Robocraft, on the other hand, employed pay-for-efficiency. Premium membership grants the buyer 50% increase in RP and TP gained, boosting the speed which you advance. That means, in no scenario will you be against a player that you cannot be at the same level of just by playing the game for free. The underwhelming power you feel, however, is due to the horrible matchmaking system, and how Robocraft's item ranking system works.
In regards to the repair fee. If you take no damage, there is no reason for you to repair. If you are destroyed, repair fees will then apply. Based on a bad performance, you will either earn no RP, or lose a bit of RP after mid Tier. Pair that up with the horrible matchmaking system, and you get angry people. This is nothing that cannot be fixed with an adjustment with the matchmaker. Until then, I will make no further comments about the repair fee.
Gameplay:
The shining holy grail of this game is the customization. I see way too many people playing this as World of Tanks. Why? They build tanks. You can quite literally build anything to your heart's desire (within physic's limitations), and use them to crush your enemies. I saw a guy make a hole, car, thing, I made a flying d*** that shot plasma bolts, you can see where this is going. It is a hellalot of ridiculousness. Yet part of being creative and making designs is failing at making designs, then improve the design so it performs better. If you get one shot by plasma cannon, maybe add a few shields, maybe add a pseudo roof so you can survive at least one shot, maybe redesign the entire vehicle so you can maneuver out of the way, maybe build a giant so one shot is simply not enough to destroy you. Build a monument of Chuck Norris so they risk being round-housed if they shoot you. Possibilities are endless.
Robocraft's damage system can be vastly improved, but as players, we work with what we have. And in Robocraft, we have very vulnerable, easily destroyed armor. Now would you employ that vulnerability as your strength? No, that's just plain stupid. Yet I see players believing themselves invincible, be shot down, then cry to the community and developers for making something they are not familiar with. Imagine if this were a first person shooter, something along the lines of perhaps Arma. Cover, terrain, and ambush is the way to go. Apply the same mentality with Robocraft. Pop out of cover, fire your volley of plasma, go back in cover. Or rush out of cover and use your SMGs to take advantage of plasma/rail's slow firing rate. Playing smart is the way to go. I see too many doing the opposite, and then complain about it.
Other things:
Teamwork - There is none. Players also drive like its China; there are no traffic rules, we make up our own.
Lag - There are delays in actions, and you will feel it. But, then again, it's present in every online game. A little bit more in this one.
Repetition - Very little maps, very little choice in weaponry, very little variety in every round. The first is because of early access, the second is also due to early access but some what elevated by the amount of potential customization, the third is because of the player mindset.
Dev Team - Listens to the community occasionally. We complained about railguns, they changed railguns.
Think before you make complaints.

This game is great! Let me first say, this is my second most played game on my steam library, first being Civilization of course...
At first, when you start, you aren't really sure what to really do...I only wish there was more detailed help at the beginning for new players, but most of the time the guides cover the controls and such nicely.
Basically a quick run down of the game is...you battle aganist players in the different arenas (a snow one, an iced up lake one, a mountainous one, and mars type of one) you try to get as much damage on the opponents as possible so you are able to then get RP(robo points) and purchase a wide variety of blocks and guns for your robot, which of course is up to you to make, and desgin! You also recieve TP(tech points) to reaserch, or rather just instantly unlock new armor types, guns, etc.
As you progress up tiers you face new challenges, like flying bots, and snipers, and plasma bombers which you wouldn't normally see in T1. Once you get a bit more advanced, I'ld say T4 you can create a working plane. By T5 or so, you can create an even better plance, bigger and more powerful.
My few recommendations to new players are...; make sure you have a high level, so farm and play lots of matches. With a higher level you can place more blocks on your ship (CPU or f-LOPS). Don't be afraid to put that new gun on to promote you to T3 or something, just because you think it'll be harder...but it will...but it's worth it...you get more RP! Make sure you find a suttable desgin you like, and if you see other good ones copy those. I copied a premium T5 plane and it works fantasticly! Other then that it should be fairly easy to figure out.
Lastly, as for a game suggestion, I would really enjoy a whole new tech line: NAVAL BATTLING!! Then there could be sea, air, and land battles...awesome to think about!

It's a good concept that was executed somewhat poorly. The game, overall, is enjoyable, but there are still quite a few downsides.
First off, the weapon balancing. Anyone that has bothered to play this game or read other reviews will notice the consistent trend of complaints of weapons being OP. I would agree, as most of said weapons are one shot, extremely accurate, and, if you survive, completely immobilize you. As a player, one of my goals (sadly) is to obtain these weapons because it is nearly impossible to fight back against higher level players.
Second, tech trees. As far as I understand, before this game was released on Steam, there was no such thing as a tech tree. Now, it is the only way to advance yourself. This is extremely difficult for newer players, partially because of what I stated about the weapons earlier.
In order to fully explain, I need to give a bit of background.
The game divides Bots into "tiers," similar to leagues or whatever in games such as Clash of Clans. This is how the game groups players for battles. In order to unlock new weapons and armor, you require stars of a certain tier. For example, tier 3 bots earn tier 3 stars, tier 4 earn tier 4 stars, and so on. But because the game allows you to own multiple bots, players use higher bots to unlock higher level equipment and use the said equipment on lower level bots, thus making them substantially more powerful than those who only have lower level bots and cannot purchase higher tier technology.
Finally, pay to win. As a tryhard mobile gamer, I have noticed countless games with microtransactions or subscription payments. Most players in the community look down upon developers making games into this form. As far as I understood, most companies have abandoned this model because of said hate from players. However, I was extremely dissapointed when I discovered this game pretty much force feeds its membership system down your throat.
I may be exagerating these problems a bit, as they are somewhat pet peeves of mine. I still enjoy playing this game, however, as the concept that was meant to portrayed is still partially there. If there was someway I could rate this game, 3.5/5 until devs change their current course from Pay 2 Win and buggy grouping.

What can I say? This game is legendary. A great sequel to Portal, which served as a small "Test" to show us what it was capable of. I've only played the Steam version once or twice, but the PS3 game was brilliant, the story for multiplayer with it's Sneek Preview DLC gave us many laughs, and was even better when we got some friends with sibling rivalry to have a go at it, killing each other all the way and taking half an hour on a small test chamber. A game where you don't have to play it to have fun (just watch everyone else!).
Although I haven't played the Steam version all that much, I do get an idea as to what extras have been put in. For instance, you can customise your own multiplayer robot with different DLC skins (I think the Ninja skin is awesome), and then show them off to friends or anyone worldwide when you go online!
The online features have gone a step further than the PS3 as well. On Steam, you can now create your own test chambers! It can be a bit tricky at the start but once you get used to it, you can start to span out and make more complicated chambers for everyone to enjoy!
Now, for the singleplayer I'm not going to make comparisons because they're completely the same! Brilliant plot twists, nice introductions to characters and the story along with the ending was as imaginative as it could get (I mean, the Moon!?)! Now I'm not the type of person to play first-person games, but this game was incredible, the only first-person i have ever bothered playing all the way through.
I'm glad I got to talk about this amazing game like this and I hope it can be of some use to everyone out there. I highly recommend this game to the world!
