'Free to play' is always a set of words I approach with caution.
Robocraft showed quite a bit of promise, however. It's possible to buy everything non-cosmetic in the game using the free currency. Progression isn't grindingly slow. The actual gameplay delivers wonderfully on 'build your own death machine."
Or... delivered, it would appear.
With the most recent patch, Robocraft has decided to remove massive portions of the gameplay, gating them behind a large timesink you can, you guessed it, skip with cash.
Where before, you could use any of three gun types (arcing artillery death, stunningly inaccurate machinegun, or penetrating sniper round), our wonderful developers have decided that you only get the stunningly inaccurate machinegun until you reach tiers three (arcing artillery) or five (railgun.) I will note that after 13 hours of gameplay,my robot is still only tier two.
It gets even better. You want something that hovers? Wait for tier two. Oh, you want to fly higher than a few feet above the ground? Well then, better wait until tier five when you can finally unlock wings.
In short, if you want to have any real fun anytime soon, Robocraft heartily suggests you open your wallet.

[ NO SPOILERS :)) ]
Portal 2 is continuation of a new-themed Valve Software game - Portal. First person shooter, logic, fun and action combination makes this game one of the best ever made, with a metascore 95 / 100. It contains single player and cooperation modes, both with Steam Workshop compability.
Story (no spoilers)
Since the begining of Valve Software games, they were realy making a very interesting and well-planed plots and stories, but in Portal 2, its more than great. It is possibly one of the best stories I have ever 'survived', and maybe even the best. The first Portal wasn't realy about plot itself at the begining. Only at the end 'something' happens [don't wanna spoil, ya' know], but durring the Portal 2, the story goes all the time and is getting more and more engaging, til the end. This game has a lot of easter eggs, not even about Portal, but also about other Valve games. GLaDOS and personality cores are more human (even if they are robots) than in Portal. Game is also very long, but interesting all the time, which makes you don't stop. Seriously, you, don't stop, never.
Gameplay
Portal 2 has a lot of difirent puzzles to solve using not only the Portal Gun, but also cubes, shooting turrets, momentum, lasers and more! Speaking of portal gun - what is this? With this magic thing you can create two portals - a blue and an orange. When you go through a blue one, you go out out of the orange one, and vice versa. The momentum gained before entering the first portal is not being loost in the second one. Controls in game are not very complicated. Left and right mouse button to shoot portals, and standard keys for movement and E for interaction. Back to puzzles.. you are going to be stuck there for more than 10 minutes, I promise. Puzzles in this game are not easy, realy. The singleplayer campaign is way easier than the cooperation one, cause during the coop, you both have to think and comunicate.
Sounds and music
The sound envitoment makes this game sound very realistic. The surround 3D sounds gives you the feeling as you were realy into this game. Also, voice acting is awesome. The characters give away their emotions and speak very clearly, giving sometimes a sense of humour by speaking something funny. Even at the begining of the game you can hear some funny quotes from Wheatley. And what now? Oh, music. How could I forget about this masterpiece? Seriously, music here is climatic, original and gives Portal 2 good atmosphere. You can even buy a full set of all music tracks from this game. Modern electronic sounds were placed into right game - Portal 2.
Level design
Unlike Portal 1, in Portal 2, the level design is very detailed, original and changing all the time. It isn't the same durring whole gameplay. Maps are big, the enviroment is well planed, What else can I say? Its just pure masterpiece.
Graphics
The Source Engine gives Portal 2 titre of the best looking game ever made. Color correction shaders, detailed particles, high resolution textures and perfect models gives Portal 2 adequate atmosphere. Also, light shaders, advanced animation system and modern GUI gives feeling that something is happening in a game all the time. You are never going to get bored. I promise.
So..
Portal 2, for me, is the best game ever made. I'm waiting for Valve to continue this awesome story - don't f*ck up guys.. you have created a pure masterpiece. And also something to you, my reader. If you are going to buy this game - click the godd*mn button right now and buy it. You are going to survive the best story of your life, and will never regret this decision. Play with a friend a cooperation mode. You are realy going to be suprised, how amazing this game is. I'm sorry I can't show how amazing is it by writing this review. You are definitely going to like it.

This game is everything that I could possibly want it to be. You can design your robot however you like and pit it against other robots in an objective-based team deathmatch. To win a game, you either eliminate all of the enemy robots or capture their main base, both of which are equally challenging.
One main screen that you will see almost all the time while out of combat is the hangar, where you can customize your creation, test it to your liking, and repair it after it's been damaged or destroyed in a previous battle. Here, you can also buy parts for your robot, level up your tech tree to unlock more parts, or create a platoon and play with friends (the party system is a bit buggy as of now, but surely the developers will work out the kinks in future patches).
Combat is the best part about this game, mostly because of all the different creations people come up with. Creativity runs wild on the handful of well-made maps that players do battle on. Blowing the hell out of enemies or whittling them down to almost nothing is very satisfying, but it's always a challenge when they shoot back.
Of course, it's always funny when the enemy is down to a pilot seat and a couple of wheels, rendering them totally helpless against the onslaught of projectiles. My friend and I refer to these poor souls as "Wheelchairs" (based on their appearance), which also makes this the most unintentionally hilarious game I've ever played on Steam. Nothing is better than watching an overconfident player charge into battle and quickly turn around and run once they've been reduced to almost nothing.
I would have to say that this is an incredible game, and so far I give it a 10/10 for its ingenuity and hilarity.

I'm going to try to be as unbiased as possible in this review, so hear me out. This a review of the game on July 31st, 2014 during its Alpha.
This game has potential to be great. While it is a very fun game, it still has its faults.
_________________________________
Here's a quick list of the pros and cons:
Pros:
- Great customization system.
- Plenty of variety in terms of robots.
- Designs either make or break your robot. Building a good design is essential to winning.
- Combat is fast paced and fun.
- The Ranking up/Tiering Up/Leveling Up/Match-Making system is perfect (IMO.)
- COMPLETELY FREE to play. There's really no need to go premium. The benefits of going premium only give you more platoon slots (Party slots. I'm sure this will change soon), more money per match, and a few minor things. They aren't essential (except for maybe the platoon slots). The "Early Access" system has been taken down as quickly as it was brought up, as the devs believed that it ruined the game for everyone.
- Very active dev team! They frequent the forums and listen to players.
- THE GUNS ARE BALANCED. Anyone who says otherwise is a noob and hasn't risen up the ranks/tiers to fully understand the game mechanics.
Cons:
- Sometimes it takes a while to queue up for a match.
- Punishing to REALLY bad players. And I mean REALLY bad players. Every time you get damaged or destroyed, you have to pay in-game currency to repair your robot. So if you're TERRIBLE, you won't make as much in-game money as the better players. The thing is, a lot of the playerbase is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrible. So you'll see them crying and whining about this. If they only designed a better robot, they probably wouldn't be whining.
- The platoon system is stupid.
- Only a few maps.
- Only ONE game mode.
- Rare glitches.
_________________________________
Obviously, the game is advertised as a cross between minecraft and a robot shooter, and this is where the game excels. The game allows us to customize robots (I'm still not sure why they call them robots, when we HAVE to put a pilot into them) in any way we like (to a degree, of course). This allows us to build very creative designs. I've seen players make an Octopus-like robot that uses Rail Cannons on each tentacle. I've seen robots akin to Satellites that fly into far into the sky, raining down bombs by using Plasma Launchers or sniping unsuspecting enemies with the Rail Cannons. I've seen players make ENORMOUS tanks with so much armor and shields, that they take forever to take down. I've even seen hovering diamonds covered in shields that speed across the map. This game is simply amazing when it comes to designing and building robots. The building system may still need some few tweaks here and there to make it easier and more comfortable to build, but so far, it has most of the essentials when it comes to building.
That said, designs either make or break your robot. If you're an awful designer, you're going to have a bad time playing this game. I've seen a bunch of players whine and cry over the forums because they've been "one-shot" so many times. But when I ask them for their designs, they don't reply. I wonder why...
Let me make this clear to anyone who's thinking about playing this game: You die because you're either: A) A bad player. Or B) A bad designer. Or maybe you're a both. In no way did I feel like any gun was overpowered (yea, Rail Cannons aren't OP, most players crying on the forums are just terrible) or underpowered.
The combat in this game is very satisfying. Outgunned? Shoot the enemy's guns off their robot. This turns them into useless robots (they can, however, capture points still.) Out-manuevered? Shoot their wheels/wings/jets/hoverblades. This causes most robots to become unbalanced and will prevent them from escaping or chasing you. Are you a sniper? Look for the enemy's sweet spot (by that, I mean the block underneath the cockpit), and blast it away. This is a one-hit kill, equivalent to headshots in ALL other FPS games (this is something that all of the noobs on the forums are complaining about. They don't understand that snipers in this game are JUST LIKE SNIPERS in other games). Higher-tier players know how to take advantage of the one-hit kill mechanic, so in the higher-tier games, you'll find better designs compared to the lower tiers.
The Ranking/Tier/Leveling/Matchmaking system is awesome. You can play in any tier you want as long as you put the proper ranking gear into your robot. Higher-ranking gear = higher-tier matchmaking. To get to higher tiers, you simply have to buy better gear and equip them. If you equip lower-ranking gear, you end up in the lower tiers of matchmaking. There IS a cutoff point due to your player level, but it is still great to see so much freedom given to players. Because of this, you'll find players trying to optimize designs for Tier 1 matchmaking, or Tier 2, etc. This adds a whole new level fo customization, and maybe, if this game gets huge, a whole new "league" of players when it comes to tournaments (for example, a Tier 1 league or Tier 4 league.)
The dev team is very active. They frequent the steam forums often, and reply QUICKLY.
Guns are balanced. Guns. Are. Balanced. Anyone who says otherwise are noobs. SMGs are fully-automatic and small (allowing you to place more on your robot and in more intricate ways), and are the weakest in terms of damage per shot. They excel in close range and sometimes even medium to long range if you use burst-fire. Plasma Launchers are semi-automatic, medium-sized, deal the most damage per shot, fire in an arc, cause Area-of-Effect damage, and are GREAT for planes as it allows them to drop bombs from the sky. The arcing mechanic allows Launcher-users to take advantage of the environment and shoot over hills. Rail Cannons deal the second most damage per shot, shoot in a straight line, pierce through armor (to a degree), are very accurate, allows use of a zoom-in scope, but have VERY LONG reload times. This very long reload time is the main con for Rail Cannons, and something that noobs don't understand and don't take advantage of.
The Cons:
Queue times are wonky. But now that there's thousands of players playing, this shouldn't be an issue soon.
This game is very punishing for noobs. This is a con simply because there are SO many terrible players. They really don't understand the mechanics of this game while continuing to cry for nerfs. I guess the REAL con of this game is the ignorance of players. I'm going to say it again, Rail Cannons are NOT OP. They can be countered by use of the environment, flanking, headlamps (to blind snipers), fighting in close-quarters, and waiting for Rail Cannon-users to reload. Simply put, some people just aren't very bright.
Currently (July 31st 2014, Alpha Version) the platoon system only allows up to 3 players to be in a party. Parties are used to queue up as a team into matchmaking. As of right now, you need to get premium (pay real-life money) to increase the amount of players in your platoon. This means groups of 4 or more friends will likely not be playing together. However, there's really no need for microstransactions other than this one small detail.
Also, as of today, there are VERY few maps and only one game mode. This make playing the game pretty stale after a while. The current list of maps, I believe, has only 5 maps in rotation. The current game mode is Capture the Point, in which 2 teams are fighting for their enemies' point. The first time to eliminate the other team, or to capture their point, wins the match.
There are also a few glitches, most of which have to do with the environment. By that, I mean players' robots get stuck pretty easily in certain parts of the map. Also, sometimes player collisions cause massive flips on your vehicle. This is so ANNOYING. But with the new Alignment Rectifier, this shouldn't be an issue.

This, along with its predecessor, is in my humble opinion one of the greatest games ever made. The storyline is brilliant and elegant. It both captures, you, as well as makes you laugh at times. The concept of hidden story, which this game thrives on, is beautifully done. You spend a great deal of time wondering what is going on, and what the world is like beyond where you are. Hints and glimpses provided you with increased stimulation.
The gameplay itself is simple yet extremely versatile. The puzzles include multiple ways for solving. They are all within reach, but are difficult enough to provide the player with the satisfaction of having completed them, without becoming frustrated and losing interest. Not a particularly long game, but the steam workshop means that there is the ability to sink hours upon hours into the game through user-made puzzles. The co-op campaign, which is multiplatform, is just as fun as the solo campaign, and stands as its own unique storyline. This is the only game that I ever bothered to seek after achievements, because it is interesting, stimulating, and fun. I cannot say enough about this game!

Apart from the rather misleading title description of "Minecraft fused with World of Tanks", the game is utterly wonderful. The only Minecraft inspired part is the ability to create your vehicles from the ground up through the usage of cubes and variations of said shape.
The game does borrow heavily from World of Tanks in terms of its general gameplay: two sides battling over a simmetric organic map with the goal of either killing all opponents or capturing the base. The controls and overall 3rd person arcadeish feel will also feel familiar to anyone used to either WoT or Warthunder.
The ability to fully make your own battle vehicle and then upgrade it via unlocking new parts is where the game shines, but in its current state the choice of gear and modules is rather limited, forcing the developers to use item ''levels'' with different statistics.
The game calculates the ''tier'' of the vehicle through giving every block and item its own ''weight''. This allows for a limited, but still overall unfair advantage for players, who have unlocked high-level blocks and can somehow squeeze them within a tier I vehicle.
The physics of the game is very arcadeish, but in a good manner. Depending on the vehicle you build it can end up behaving as a tank or as the Mako from Mass Effect.
While the game does allow a lot of freedom for shapes and there have been many screenshots with outright fantastic builds for vehicles, the actual gameplay forces the player to give up esthetic design for practicality and as one would expect from a game like this, at some point you start noticing patterns which most players have ended up dubbing as ''best'' for their tier.
In all, a very interesting game and concept, but still has more than enough shoulder room to fill in the expectations they have earned from the community.

This is an epic game. You build your own vehicle, land or air, and fight to the death (or, until someone caps the point) with the enemy team. It's basically a 3rd person lego shooter. Sounds awesome, right? Well, there's a catch. Actually quite a few of them.
There are 2 in-game currencies, RP (Robo-Points) and GC (Galaxy Cash). RP is earned evey game, and you get more for killing enemies, winning the game, or just damaging enemies. However, if you take any damage at all, you have to spend RP or GC to repair it. Most of the time you barely have a net gain in RP though. GC is purchaseable with real money, and quite a bit of it. GC can also be used in place of RP for buying parts, and repairing your vehicle.
You want a premium account? Well the best priced option is 6 months for $20, but the benefits aren't even that good. Normal accounts can just get by repairing their ships constantly. In addition to this, after every game you are taunted with how much RP you would have gotten if you had a premium account.
Alright, enough about the currencies. Let's move on to gameplay. Each match is between two teams attempting to kill all of the enemies, or capture the enemy's base. This in itself seems like a simple and balanced setup, but it definitely isn't. SMG lasers are free to use, but almost irrelevant because of the other weapons' ability to one-shot you in almost any scenario. The plasma cannons are my personal favorite. They shoots plasma bolts that do a lot of damage individually, but have an arc and long travel time. You can load up your vehicle with these canons, and become a long range shotgun. The only thing stopping you is your own aim, since each bolt can destroy multiple blocks. Next up is the railgun. The railgun is your standard sniper rifle, with a recharge on it. Like the other weapons you can have multiple, but your vehicle may get in the way of itself since it only fires one beam at a time, and you must fire all beams before the long recharge starts on it. This would balance the weapon well, if only it couldn't one-shot you from across the map. See, railguns pierce blocks, so they just aim at where your pilot is and BAM! you're dead. That brings me to the next topic, which is damage. You can't see your own vehicle's health until you take damage. Also, if your pilot block (2 blocks), or the block it's sitting on is destroyed, you die instantly. This is what gives the railgun so much power, and it's completely absurd. Aircraft are much more susceptible to this, because they have to be much smaller.
Finally, I'll talk about the vehicles themselves. You buy blocks, and build them into whatever your heart desires. However, they are INSANELY overpriced for what a regular account can get, or even a premium one. This almost forces you to buy GC, and even then it's not worth it. The tech tree seems like a great idea, but once again there's a catch. If you go willy-nilly and level up as you get XP, you'll find that there are different tiers of XP. Your XP level is determined by how many blocks are in your vehicle, and you need certain tiers later on to get things like airplane wings. This encourages high-skill players to drop down to tier 1 and crush noobs until they're able to fly high in the sky. But, put all that aside and it's actually a pretty sweet building system.
In conclusion, this is a fun game. HOWEVER it IS pay-to-win, no matter what anyone says. Sure, you can get everything for free, but you can get it practically instantly for a ton of money. The premium system isn't worth it, and the blocks are overpriced. You can barely get by just to play the game, and the combat system is extremely unbalanced.
Don't get me wrong, this is an amazing game. I just hope that it doesn't remain pay-to-win, and becomes more like TF2, in the sense of aesthetical propety being awesome and paid for, and weapons have to be earned by skill.

Steam needs a "It's okay" rating, instead of just "Recommend" and "Not Recommend".
Once upon a time, one of these creative games rise upon all other generic team-based "kill each other for fun" games, but sadly, this is not one of the greatest I've seen. Probably because it's unfinished as hell. But hey, I did play it on Early Access, and I was expecting it to be dissapointing. How dissapointed I was?
Actually, not as dissapointed as I expected!  Don't get me wrong, the game could have been WAY better (since it's not even finished, it would be more acurate to say that I expect it to be WAY better), it's quite fun. The main problem of it, is that the fun doesn't last as long, as the Devs expect it to last.
When you first join, you have a weird-looking machine infront of you, and you're tasked to either ♥♥♥♥-it to pieces and rebuild it as your own abomination, or to just use that one. There's a big problem, though: The game doesn't even bother to tell you how things work. It is easy to understand, but while to try to experiment and see how things work, you're CONSTANTLY HEARING THE POP-UP SOUNDS OF USELESS TIPS YOU ALREADY KNOW, BECAUSE OF HOW BASIC THEY ARE. Getting your first minutes out of the way, how is the gameplay?
Your first matches will be dull, boring, and painful to watch. Your machine will end up flipping all over the place, you'll die really fast without a chance to be of any use to your team, and in the end, you will feel cheated. This, is the main problem of the game: The matchmaking sucks balls so hard, it created a Black-hole on them. Now I can't ejaculate for♥♥♥♥♥♥
Whenever you join a game alone, or with a friend, 8 of the 10 times you do it, there won't be a full list of players in the same Tiers, but a random number of people of tier 1, 2, 3 and so on. And now think; Is there a way to make people of Tier 1 useful vs people of Tier 3? HELL NO. If you're Tier 1 vs Tier 3, you will feel cheated, and probably will get the urge of just not playing it again. Then, when you're Tier 3, you'll usually have to face some Tier 1 players, and you will even feel bad for annihilating them, because you where once one of them.
Another big problem with this game, is that even if the kind of machines you can build is large, and there's a lot of room for experimentation, the number of actual guns you can use is as small as it gets: generic "SMG-Like" turrets that will probably hit the first bullet and then the recoil will make them useless (unless you "tap-shoot", like if this was CS:GO or something), some sort of "Plasma-Grenade-Launcher" that can be devastating in close range, but takes a while to reload, and the generic "Over-the-top-Sniper-weapon", that even if it takes like 20 seconds to reload, it's as cheap as it can get. Only 3 types of weapons, you can either pick an unreliable SMG that feels like trying to snipe people with a shotgun, a good grenade-launcher-like weapon that loads so slow, you might as well retreat and camp, and a weapon that forces people to hide on the skies aiming their rail-guns uppon your♥♥♥♥♥
Now, here's the thing: People with SMG's will be easily killed by any weapons, and are only good at close range. People with the plasma-thingy are only good at close combat because of the limited range. Thus, the only way to kill one of those camping dumbasses, is to be a camping dumbass yourself. Great. And don't tell me to "tap-shoot" with SMG's, they still miss because of how far they are, and while you try and do minor damage, they can insta-kill you with one well-placed shoot.
Of course, I bet the game will get better and better with time. I did had fun with it, after all! But the problem is, as it is right now, you will get more fustrated than playing Dark Souls in PC, most of the time. The only reason I recommend it, it's because it's free, and it's NOT pay-2-win, like most other F2P♥♥♥♥♥♥games you'll see on steam. By paying, you just get points faster, and INCASE THEY EVER DO IT, you'll get access to the new guns a bit faster.
Oh and, I saw the Devs say that there are almost no bugs on the game. I broke the shop-system MULTIPLE times. ON MY FIRST MINUTES OF GAMEPLAY. The hell, man?

Firstly, they have a 'pay to win' type system, where if you pay, you get tokens that can buy the more expensive equipment instead of battling to earn money and buy your things. Second, the electroplates were just a horrible idea in my opinion since they are now being over used. The guns are not balanced well enough, my favorite being the Railgun that takes too long to load, while the SMGs don't do enough damage and Plasma blasters fire faster and do mjust as much damage to me as a railgun would. Lastly they allow cheating, just today I was in a battle with my robot at full HP, I was shooting at an enemy WITH NO SHIELDS and was doing no damage to him with all 6 guns, I was then slaughtered by 4+ enemies all toting plasma launchers. The point system for battles is seriously flawed, the game is suppose to be capture the base, but you get no points for capturing it, just a multiplier to the damage points you get for killing and damaging enemies. It should instead me Mass Kill, with the option of capturing the base. The players vary, but I have noticed your team is never there to back you up, many times I could have lasted much longer had my team not hidden to avoid getting shot at to avoid high repair costs. Over all I think it could be a good game if they would fix some of the things like Hacking.

As of the time that I have written this review, I've played it for 80 hours. Now, let's get into the pros and cons:
PROS:
-Large variety of robots that you can make and fight, nearly unlimited
-Fighting your robot is very fun
-Robots are physics based, meaning that your robot can have different levels of handling than other robots, and it is possible to tip them over if you don't have a good design
-You can play different roles in combat than just "damage dealer"
-Easy to recognize enemies from allies, as all enemy robots are tinted black and red
-If you have patience, you can play the game completely free of charge, with the exception of some cosmetic items that don't effect combat
CONS:
-Without paying,  it can take some time to level up, though again, it can still be done
-As of the time this was written, there are only two modes, boss fight (in which a high tier player fights lower tiered players) and TDM
In conclusion, I would definitely recommend this game, assuming you have the time to put into it.

Robocraft is quite a nice Game. You can build your very own Robots and fight with them, or if you aren't that creative, theres a Community Shop, where you can buy robots from anyone providing these. This game has still it bugs and other flaws, but also has great things.
Pros:
- "Endless" Creativity
You can build anything you want with the provided items. Planes, Helicopters, Tanks and so on. You may are limited to blocky design, but there are rounded Blocks to spice things up, also some nice cosmetic parts, like Masks.
- Different Gamemodes
You have 6 different Gamemode to choose from. A.I. TDM, in which you fight against A.I Bots, that use random Bots from other Players provided in the CRF. Normal TDM against other Players. Battle Arena, in which 2 Teams capture 3 Towers and try to destroy the Enemy base. This gamemode has a League version, League Arena, where you fight for Ranks. Then there is a classic Deathmatch called "The Pit". Lastly the classic gamemode of Robocraft, Elimination. In which a Team wins, when the Enemy base is either caputured, or all players of a Team is destroyed.
- Different Weapons.
You have a quite large amount of weapons to choose from. From the Classic SMG's (Lasers) and Plasma Launchers ( high explosiv grenade launcher) to Railguns, Shotguns, Missles and more. There are different Tiers of Weapons (and also other Items have different Tiers) ranging from Uncommon (Green) to Legendary (Orange).
- Community Shop
There is a Community Shop in this game, where you can buy Robots (or just single Items to help other People out with the ingame currency "Robits") from other Players. There are thousands of creation to choose from. You can also upload your own Robots, which cost nothing at all.
Cons:
-Bugs/Glitches
Ofcourse any game has this, but yet there are some annoying Bugs/Glitches that need to get fixed ASAP. One is being desynced players. These players can do damage to other Players and the Towers/Bases in Elimination/Battle Arena. This allows these players to do the objective without taking any damage. Sadly, this happens quite alot and really makes the match unfair. Secondly, you get randomly disconnected from the Chat server, or you'll get a black screen while loading a match. This can't always be on my Side, since friends of my also get these. Also, mirror mode has glitches, in which cases Blocks are not Mirrore'd, or placed wrong in the Mirror Mode ( As an example the Rhino Tank Tracks for me)
- Getting Robits
Robits are the ingame Currency used to forge items or buy bots in the Community Shop. These are obtained by selling Item you don't need or by selling Robots in the Comunity Shop. However, in each cases you only get 25% of what the actual Item is worth. By getting Premium, selling items gives you 75% of the original price. This leads to a really long grinding and makes it less fun to get new items.
- Premium Colours
While this game is about being Creative, players that do not have Premium are only provided with 4 Colours, which are White, Grey, Light Blue, and Orange. Premium users get a lot more colours to choose from. In my honest opinion, all current colours should be available for all players atleast, and make a whole RGB system for Premium Users, to make advanced colouring, if the Devs really want colours being a Premium thing.
These are the Pros and Cons i have for this game. I still recommend it despite the fact of the endless grinding, but after all its a Free 2 Play game, and the Devs need to earn money.

WARNING: STRANGE POSITIVE REVIEW
Robocraft is very intresting game, but calling it a mash up of Minecraft and World of Tanks is an INCORRECT statement. I already played a game back when it came out in 2008 on the XBOX 360 that played just like Robocraft, note for note. It's name however is dreaded and feared by all, even by Jontron himself.. It's name is..
--BANJO-KAZOOIE; NUTS & BOLTS--
Yes, Robocraft and Banjo-Kazooie; Nuts & Bolts are one in the same, if anything, Robocraft is a "Spirtual Successor" to Banjo-Kazooie; Nuts & Bolts. The main reason why Nuts & Bolts failed was cause it was made as a Banjo-Kazooie game, a sequel to Banjo-Tooie. Was Nuts & Bolts a "bad game"? No, it was a misunderstood game and a game that could have had great potential-oh wait, IT DID. I spent hours, days, & months making vehicles of all kinds in Nuts & Bolts, ignoring the fact it was a Banjo-Kazooie game. Robocraft is exactly the same. How vehicles are made, all parts being made of blocks, when parts are heavly damaged they will fly off, being able to build anything you wish. All of it is here, except a Bear & Bird and an easy to use menu to build stuff. I could spend the same about of time as I did playing Nuts & Bolts with Robocraft. The possibilities are endless of what could be built and without said Bear & Bird, it has nothing to weigh it down.
Robocraft is not perfected yet at this time. I can live without the "Minecraft" first-person cam and functions when building things, it being only a MMO PvP game without escalation horde mode, the long tedious method of unlocking stuff, and the password sign-in issues that prevent playing the game all-together. The main question is if this game worth trying? Answer; ABSOLUTELY YES. I'm sure when alot of the issues are fixed, this game will flourish beyond what it is now.

Awesome game with some minor roughness around the edges. Essentially Lego where you build vehicles and enter short matches where you must eliminate the entire enemy team or capture their base. Every part of your vehicle can be individually damaged or blown off by weapons. As you gain player levels you can attach more and more stuff to your vehicle, and the more stuff you attach to your vehicle the more money you get from matches to buy more blocks. Playing matches also gets you tech  points to unlock other kinds of blocks and weapons.
Gameplay itself is simplistic but the matches are nice and short (~5 mins) so it's easy to pick up and play, and in the higher tier matches people have absurd vehicle designs. One of the few F2P games on steam that isn't constantly trying to pick your pocket.

-You will love Robocraft.  I've always loved building machines with Legos, but always used to wish there was a game that let me try out my creations.
I have since stopped wishing for that, because ROBOCRAFT IS THAT GAME.  It was built with all of my favorite parts of all the things listed above, and none of the shortfalls.  For example, say you like World of Tanks.  You have your primary tank, the love of your life.  It falls in battle, and you are forced to wait until a match ends to get it back.  Well, remember that bit where I said "none of the shortfalls"?  In Robocraft, you do something wrong and get 'sploded, you get shunted back to your garage where you can immediately repair, refine your design, and vault back into a different battle in under a minute.
Now imagine the other stuff I mentioned above, and mentally subtract all the downfalls from those things, and you have an idea of what this is.
As a testament to it's quality: It is still in beta, yet I installed it yesterday and have 34 hours of gametime.  It's scary amounts of fun.

I've been playing Robocraft since it first appeared on Greenlight, and now find myself playing with a Robot of Tier 10, the highest in this game. I believe I can give a thorough andcomplete impression of the game as I have played through every Tier, tried every weapon, every means of transportation and even the Premium functionality.
Robocraft is a team-based arena battle game, where you construct your own machines of war from a set of components, namely armor cubes, weapons, transportation, special components like radar and the newly added Electroplate, which is like a second layer of rechargable armor. Once finished and ready to battle, your robot will be grouped up with other people's robots and thrown on one of four maps to either destroy the other team, or capture the opponents base.
To begin with, The game may appear extremely unbalanced and the repairing (after a match, all damage done to your robot must be repaired, at the cost of in-game currency called RP, which is also gained through play) may not make sense. I can tell you, this is not true.
The three weapons may be used in slightly unfair ways, like snipers hiding on the map, waiting to reload, but really, this stuff hapens in *every* game with snipers, not just Robocraft.
The repair system may cause you to gain less RP, but you'll never actually lose RP, unless you have performed so bad one should question your ability to play games in general. Just make a better Robot or just play better (don't go out on your own, but stick with the group is one way to do this).
The premium is also quite well-balanced. Sure, they gain 50% more stuff for every battle, and can purchase components with the other in-game currency, GC, which can be purchased with real money. But really, they should be compensated in some way for paying for the game, just be grateful you don't have to pay a single penny to actually play the game at all. That, as well as the fact that however you can buy components this way, even premium members are limited by their level which can only be increased through regular play, as well as their tech progression. Tech points cannot be bought with GC, though you can convert tier-specific tech points to universally usable tech points, but even so the progress to very expensive and is generally not worth it.
I would really recommend this game if you like building either serious death machines, whacky structures or even Touhou characters and mutilate other people's creatons with them.

Some people like driving a tank or flying an aircraft. Some people like building things. Others... like both of these. If you're looking for a game that allows you to create an absolute train-wreck of a tank (or aircraft), and then send that tank (or aircraft) into battle against other similar train-wrecks, then this game is definitely for you. The building aspect is straightforward, the unlocking of new building blocks and gizmos is pretty quick once you get going, but slows down as you hit higher tiers (the highest of which is 10), and the combat is basically as smooth or as clunky as you make your vehicle. Overall, it's a fun way to kill some time, but I get the feeling that the game may end up looking more like World of Tanks as one progresses through the tiers. The difference here is that you can't buy a tier 8 tank with real money, or fancy ammunition. Everyone gets everything, it's just how you use it that counts.
Note: I'm only tier 2 right now. So... take this review with the knowledge that I don't know everything.

I'm going to make my review quick and to the point for each of you.  At the start, you will have 3 basic vehicles.  One vehicle is about high damage and speed, another is about survival and anti-air, and the last is air.  This gives you a solid start to know what guns and type of vehicle you want to make yourself.  You will create vehicles and fail, but you will get a good laugh. Some vehicles players put a great deal of time and effort into, and when I hit that point, I can tell from the little time in I have that it will make it all worth it.  Understand that there is no pay to win, and it is more like world of tanks with premium time (really cheap however) and icons.  I'm going to put a good deal more time into this game to give a better review and even add a video to help more of you see what the game is about.
Scaling from 1 to 10
Graphics - 7 - Nothing fancy, but nothing terrible.  It is just right for what the game is, and the game is free.
Gameplay - 8 - I am a world of tanks player, and this game brings me to world of tanks except now I make my own vehicles. When you work hard on making a vehicle, and finally get it to where you want, it really gives you a great feeling.  Highly recommend this to any world of tanks player to at least try.  Only thing the game needs is a little better physics (like when a tank flips over, other tanks should be able to help get them upright again)
Community - 8 - Have not dealt with much trash talk or toxic players yet, but this one can change at any point.  If you are a toxic player, this game is not for you since most players don't read the chat anyway.  A good example of the community as it stands now is my tank was flipped and a flying bot and 2 ground vehicles helped get me on my tracks.  Only issue is the games physics are a bit off, so they couldn't do it and I had to tell them to carry on without me.
Combat - 8 - You are making a vehicle to destroy other vehicles players made.  Some people are starting to copy other players, but as of right now most vehicles are different.  Still, you will find some guns are severly underpowered and sometimes when you climb a tier you might get overwhelmed.  I highly recommend farming tier one for a bit to save up RP.
Customization - 10 - The game is your imaginary vehicle vs another persons imaginary vehicle.  Don't have an imagination? Then make a Tie fighter or something from a movie.
This review is subject to change per update, and I did try to keep it short.  Next time I update this I will add a video.

EDIT: This review is quite a bit out of date now, but I am looking into reinstalling and trying the new additions, which including the walker legs and tank treads that I said were missing before.
I think Robocraft is best described as a cross between World of Tanks and you, being eight years old, on your floor, playing with your Space Lego and wishing they could actually fire at each other.
It is "Early Access" and it shows in the features available. For example, there are no huge Tonka truck wheels and actuating scorpion arms, like the vehicle on the front cover has. The balance of the weapons also appears to need some work. However, I have not had issues with entering games, latency or performance, which is good news so far.
In terms of gameplay, there currently consists of a few maps of an standard "Base Capture" mode, identical to the default battle type of World of Tanks, where you must capture the enemy base or destroy all enemy vehicles. The system also lacks respawns, so get destroyed and you're out for the match. The damage of a vehicle is counted by actual pieces of it flying off depending on the hit taken, so your vehicle can actually fall apart well before its destruction.
Vehicles are built, by the player, using a block-based method, similar to a Lego vehicle except most blocks are currently perfect cubes, with more detail on the weapons, method of movements, and some optional bits such as headlights. Current weaponry consists of rapid fire SMG lasers, moderately overpowered AOE Plasma Cannons, and Sniper Railguns. You can make a wheeled vehicle, hovercraft (small rotors, not air cushion like real life) and light aircraft. There are currently no tank treads or walkers available, but I'm sure they are on the list for the future.
Now, down to my opinion...I say play the crap out of it. The game is fast-paced and fun on the battlefield and challenging in the design stage, as you try to resolve something that will fall apart in just the right way to keep fighting as long as possible. Or go crazy with weird, impractical designs too. I have also never had as much fun getting my face blown off, or watch other people try to get around missing four of six wheels or all the hoverblades on one side, causing them to spin around like a drug-addled hummingbird. I also find it very fun to see what neat designs other folks have some up with. I have seen UFOs, tractor-trailers loaded with guns, rolling walls, almost period-accurate WWII tank destroyers and WWI biplanes, and some incredibile failure designs too.
The vehicles need more options for neat stuff, including moving or activatable parts (booster rockets, missiles, melee weapons etc) and the design stage needs a few quality of life tweaks, like the ability to shift the entire design up or down levels without having to rebuild, or a revert button, but otherwise this is looking really promising. For those worried about freemium, it seems 100% no hassle to afford enough RP to repair and buy some new blocks to pimp your sweet ride, but I haven't progressed very far as of yet.
Hope this was helpful to you. See you around!

You can build robots that either move on ground or air, with default items, and items unlocked through the aforementioned system, then buying them ( with a seperate currancy) . How you will play and how well you will do all depends on how you build your robots. For example, railguns are great for sniping, but take up a lot of CPU ( this limits how much you can build your robot). You can put alot of them on (up to six) , but expect to have a frail robot. Due to the removal of some of the weapons, and equipment from the lower tiers tiers 1 through 3 tend to be pretty repetitive and it won't really seem like much interesting progress is happening. This change was implemented in order to make it easier for players to absorb the game as they progress and give them something to look forward to as they move up the tiers.
That's all fine and good but looking at these early tiers now they are rather boring shootouts with everyone having the same means of movement and weaponry.
I still think the game is worth it to stick out but it will be a little less interesting to get to the fun stuff.
There are a lot of complaints that the game is trending towards "play to win" but it remains that there is nothing that can be purchased with real money that you can't get with in game currency earned through playing.
The only real thing that I feel is wrong with this game is that at the upper tiers you can lose more currency through repairs than you gain through playing. It is unlikely but possible that you can get into a position where you are "repair locked" and can't use that vehicle. It's recommended that you have a lower tier vehicle in another garage to build up some extra currency to repair the higher tier vehicle if that happens. This should not be necessary though and is a bit of a hit on the game in my opinion.
Alpha status continues and things are still being balanced out so be prepared for that as well.

If you like building things that look awesome, and also love blowing stuff up, this is the game for you. Create your own vehicle from blocks and other shapes on a grid, in a very Minecraft-like manner, then take to the battlefield and use it to destroy other people's vehicles in explosive battles. At the time of this review, the game is early access in the Open Alpha stage, and it is very, very alpha. There are currently only three weapons to choose from and four methods of movement, and also has a few bugs, only one mode of play, and four maps, but despite that, is still pretty fun. Plus, it is not at all Pay-to-Win, as you can only purchase cosmetic features, which happen also to take up space and resources so you can look cool. You can also accelerate the levelling up and tech unlocking processes, as well as unlock more storage space for vehicles, but that still doesn't unbalance gameplay. Designing new vehicles is also fun, as it often blows up in your face if done incorrectly, and balancingflying vehicles is tough, but luckily there is a practice mode for testing everything, and doesn't make you pay repair costs if you take damage during Practice, either. In the end, the game will entertain you for a good while, but you'll want more from it, which we'll probably get later on as development continues. Certainly a good download, though.

Rating: 4/10
This game has great potential. There's limited content, but that's okay since it's not a finished game. I would expect to see much more content once this game is done building!
There are many ways to build and fight with the amount of parts. Once you finish building, you get to go out and see how it goes against other vehicles. I like that aspect.
Now why it's a 4/10? For one, multiplayer is EXTREMELY LAGGY. Slow, glitchy, and takes an entire minute to respond at the worst, and if I'm lucky, it responds in 5 seconds, but that's still outrageous. Next thing you know you get shot down before even reacting, because of the lag. Balancing is also terrible. I got placed in a team full of tier 1s against tier 4s. Tier 4+ platoons are also completely empty.
Weapons are also anoying: railguns shooting down planes with no problems, launchers hitting people across the map, and SMGs somehow shooting down people when it clearly missed. Now the railguns are extremely annoying and the launchers are god damn long-ranged (literally can hit all the way across the map). But still, seriously? Railguns shooting down planes? Railguns are buitl against heavily armored vehicles so they can cut down on the armor, launchers break apart weak-armored units, SMGs hit against fragile targets, such as planes. However, players take the complete opposite of this.
Also, I would expect players to create amazing vehicles, built out of creativity and all, but no. You know what I saw? I saw a person make a giantic floating♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Oh wow, a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ great job. So much creativity there. Also, people don't CARE about looks. They literally glue every single weapon to every single possible spot to maximize damage, and guess what? It works, but it kills EVERYTHING in its path and gets irritating.
"Cubes", the name they use for parts, are god damn expensive. The cubes to build the structure and all is a decent price, but once you start getting higher tier weapons, the prices becomes ridiculous. Thing is that when I self destruct, I get 88 cubes/credits (whatever the currency is) and it costs 40 to repair. That round, I got stuck and lost half of my vehicle from launchers. HOWEVER, I got four kills one round and lost a wing. After that round, I earned 500 cubes/credits and paid 400 for repair. What the hell, the repair funds aren't fair whatsoever. It's based upon how much you earn and makes it HARD to earn in-game currency to buy more parts.
The chat rooms are also terrible. The rules state "No offensive language" but all I see is racist comments, extreme profanity, and spamming. I'm very sure there are no moderators or admins monitoring the chat at all. So the chat is something I just completely ignore...
Lastly, RoboCRAFT? Craft? Really? Couldn't come up with a better suffix than -craft? Seems very unoriginal.
I do understand that there may be a huge load of people from Steam you didn't expect, but still, I can't say I enjoyed the multiplayer experience. Expand your servers, balance the weapons, balance the tiers, fix the repair funds, and maybe I'll change my rating. Honestly, if you deal with the problems I stated, this game is a straight up 9/10.
I enjoyed it at first, but the more I play it, the more I find that there are things to rant about. I know that this game isn't finished, but that state that it's in, it's a downvote.

Take a game with a good concept and throw in every con known to mankind, and you have RoboCraft, the game you want to love but want to strangle to death at any given time. Robocraft wants to be a good game that can allow players from around the world make their own tanks/planes/mechs/flying pinwheels and pit them against everyone else's, except that it fails on every part on what a good multiplayer experience should have and soon becomes boring, repetitive, and rage inducing.
In Robocraft, you can make just about anything you want to a degree (but more on that later). You have many options of movement from wheels that let you tread around the terrain to hoverblades that let you cushion some air between you and the hard ground. Advanced players can arm themselves with wings and take to the skies or mix everything together into some monstrosity that were not meant for the eyes of mere mortals. From the start, you get 3 robots to work with and 3 garages for each one. Each also demonstrates the unique weapons of the game: the sub machine gun, the plasma cannon, and the railgun.
Let's talk about the weapons: the sub machine gun is you standard 'SMG'; high fire rate, decent accuracy, and good effective range. They are the only weapon (at this time) to have two varieties: front mounted and top mounted, with front mounted being able to lay on the face of a cube and top mounted being best for being on top of a cube. The plasma cannon is an arcing explosion-on-hit weapon that requires some skill to use, but once mastered, it can easily be one of the better weapons in the game. It is only trumped by the railgun, which might as well be the 'point and kill' weapon. The SMG and plasma gun do not have block penetrating damage (though the plasma has splash damage), whereas the railgun does. While it's balancing factor is that it takes 20 seconds to reload, this creates a problem because of how the game determines 'death.'
In your design of a mech (robot, mech, at this point, the game doesn't really seem to define what on earth you are building), you have a pilot seat, which is where your pilot sits. For a game called 'Robocraft', this seems out of place, and in gameplay, it is. It is a 'block' that consists of 2 blocks outwards and 3 blocks in height. It must rest on two blocks underneath and those two blocks are your only lifeline. Let me repeat: TWO BLOCKS DEFINE IF YOU ARE ALIVE OR DEAD. Remember the railgun's penetration ability? It didn't get the nickname 'point and kill' sitting around drinking on a summer beach (the plasma cannon is no better). Your dream robot better have a huge underbelly because that is your only way to survive, but even then that only gives you a slightly better chance at not dying.
So let's talk about gameplay. At the moment, there is only one game mode: Capture the point. A team wins by sitting on their enemy's base until the timer gods are satisfied with your demonstration of doing nothing or you can kill the enemy team in your quest for showing off your mad Plasma cannon skills. This is all assuming you survive the first 5 seconds of the match. The game's physics engine is your first real enemy: assuming there is at least one impatient person on your team (pro tip: there always will be one), you may run into the situation that just a gentle bump will send your Robotic death machine into a flying whirl that can only be achieved in a cartoon. If you land right side up, proceed to call that teammate a moron and move on. If you don't, congratulations: you are now target practice for the enemy railgunners and plasma cannon users until either they kill you (and your two blocks too), or the match ends. You can quit the game at this point with the penalty of taking 25% damage (more on that later).
Assuming you survive the onslaught called 'Lack of Teamwork', the network engine will come out to play. 'Warping', or when an entity moves from place to place due to network latency, is common and the same happens with their bullets. This can make SMGs get magical penetrating powers and make enemies appear to attempt a re-run at flipping you over like the impatient teammate whose mech looked like a fried egg. This doesn't have a lot but when it does happen, you can join the therapy party for everyone else who died from the same reason, and that party is at least a third of the player base.
So about damage in the game. The game's definition of 'damage' is the total health of your mech, which is mostly attributed by what blocks you used, since each one's armor value is different depending on which ones you do use. If a set of blocks becomes disconnected, that is considered to be doing a massive amount of damage and your health will plummet like most of your hopes and dreams of what could be achieved in the game. Any damage you receive at the end of a match (including if one of the two blocks providing your pilot leg room gets destroyed) must be repaired at the cost of either the in-game currency or actual money. Remember that 25% that you lose if you quit the game early? That also falls under your bill and if you get flipped over after taking damage, the 25% is only tacked on to what you have. This makes any earnings you received from the game get minimized even further. The game has a 'bonus engine', but the rules for that are to laugh at any player trying to actually achieve it: you must not die and your team must win. This means if your team wins but you were sacrificed to ensure victory, congratulations: you haven't appeased the Robocraftian gods enough for a pay raise. Will that be cash or cash?
Surely there has to be a way to keep the game balanced, and the game's attempt at it is laughable at best. There are 10 tiers, with each tier under the assumption that the weapons and armor of that tier is better. Unfortunately, this isn't the real world situation. You can be shoved into a higher tier due to using more blocks for your beach ball of doom or because of the weapon's lethality. On top of that, assuming you have evenly matched lethality and good looks, the matchmaking will often pit you against tiers 1 to 2 above your own. Suddenly those pair of sunglasses you added aren't looking so hot and floorless pilot is you with the enemy team's highest tier mech mowing your fellow team's tier mechs for target practice.
The icing on the cake is the map selection, and unlike the flavor selection at your Dairy Queen, you have only 4 to choose from, two being ice and the other being on Mars. If you have the misfortune to be rocking out with tires on the ice area, have fun on the ice river that each ice map offers, as it has a physical property where you will glide forever in one direction despite how much you try to turn and reverse the other way. You will grow thankful for how other games interprets ice physics after experiencing Robocraft's interpretation. Mars doesn't really have much going for it and the blandness will make you wish for another map, all of which are chosen randomly while matchmaking, which is the only option you have (no picking a match, no choosing an enemy platoon to face).
In closing, Robocraft is the game that wants to be unique and enjoyable, but falls flat on its face on its own ice physics only shortly after tripping over its own flaws. I haven't even covered its 'premium membership' and other obvious ploys to earn money quickly and with as little effort as possible, but those would only add insult to injury. Give Robocraft a try for an hour, but turn away and don't come back afterwards. At least until they get their act together and actually try listening to what little of a community they have.

Take a game with a good concept and throw in every con known to mankind, and you have RoboCraft, the game you want to love but want to strangle to death at any given time. Robocraft wants to be a good game that can allow players from around the world make their own tanks/planes/mechs/flying pinwheels and pit them against everyone else's, except that it fails on every part on what a good multiplayer experience should have and soon becomes boring, repetitive, and rage inducing.
In Robocraft, you can make just about anything you want to a degree (but more on that later). You have many options of movement from wheels that let you tread around the terrain to hoverblades that let you cushion some air between you and the hard ground. Advanced players can arm themselves with wings and take to the skies or mix everything together into some monstrosity that were not meant for the eyes of mere mortals. From the start, you get 3 robots to work with and 3 garages for each one. Each also demonstrates the unique weapons of the game: the sub machine gun, the plasma cannon, and the railgun.
Let's talk about the weapons: the sub machine gun is you standard 'SMG'; high fire rate, decent accuracy, and good effective range. They are the only weapon (at this time) to have two varieties: front mounted and top mounted, with front mounted being able to lay on the face of a cube and top mounted being best for being on top of a cube. The plasma cannon is an arcing explosion-on-hit weapon that requires some skill to use, but once mastered, it can easily be one of the better weapons in the game. It is only trumped by the railgun, which might as well be the 'point and kill' weapon. The SMG and plasma gun do not have block penetrating damage (though the plasma has splash damage), whereas the railgun does. While it's balancing factor is that it takes 20 seconds to reload, this creates a problem because of how the game determines 'death.'
In your design of a mech (robot, mech, at this point, the game doesn't really seem to define what on earth you are building), you have a pilot seat, which is where your pilot sits. For a game called 'Robocraft', this seems out of place, and in gameplay, it is. It is a 'block' that consists of 2 blocks outwards and 3 blocks in height. It must rest on two blocks underneath and those two blocks are your only lifeline. Let me repeat: TWO BLOCKS DEFINE IF YOU ARE ALIVE OR DEAD. Remember the railgun's penetration ability? It didn't get the nickname 'point and kill' sitting around drinking on a summer beach (the plasma cannon is no better). Your dream robot better have a huge underbelly because that is your only way to survive, but even then that only gives you a slightly better chance at not dying.
So let's talk about gameplay. At the moment, there is only one game mode: Capture the point. A team wins by sitting on their enemy's base until the timer gods are satisfied with your demonstration of doing nothing or you can kill the enemy team in your quest for showing off your mad Plasma cannon skills. This is all assuming you survive the first 5 seconds of the match. The game's physics engine is your first real enemy: assuming there is at least one impatient person on your team (pro tip: there always will be one), you may run into the situation that just a gentle bump will send your Robotic death machine into a flying whirl that can only be achieved in a cartoon. If you land right side up, proceed to call that teammate a moron and move on. If you don't, congratulations: you are now target practice for the enemy railgunners and plasma cannon users until either they kill you (and your two blocks too), or the match ends. You can quit the game at this point with the penalty of taking 25% damage (more on that later).
Assuming you survive the onslaught called 'Lack of Teamwork', the network engine will come out to play. 'Warping', or when an entity moves from place to place due to network latency, is common and the same happens with their bullets. This can make SMGs get magical penetrating powers and make enemies appear to attempt a re-run at flipping you over like the impatient teammate whose mech looked like a fried egg. This doesn't have a lot but when it does happen, you can join the therapy party for everyone else who died from the same reason, and that party is at least a third of the player base.
So about damage in the game. The game's definition of 'damage' is the total health of your mech, which is mostly attributed by what blocks you used, since each one's armor value is different depending on which ones you do use. If a set of blocks becomes disconnected, that is considered to be doing a massive amount of damage and your health will plummet like most of your hopes and dreams of what could be achieved in the game. Been loving my time with this game so far. Built an epic artillery pickup, a glass cannon laser hovercraft, and am now tinkering with a tiny little hovercraft sniper. I guess a flier should be next, then maybe update my pickup into a tank worthy of tier 4.
The buiding mode took a moment to get used to, but it soon became intuitive and easy to piece together anything my imagination could come up with. Little buggy hidden inside a tank, no problem. A flier/hovercraft that can flip on will, no problem.
The creative aspect is part of the beauty of this game. Seeing what other players have designed is awesome. Marvel at perfect biplane reproductions, maybe a 40k rhino rolls past you, perhaps even a macross bot. And some of them just crack you up. A crazy tall tripod bot, with no chance of standing up if a leg is taken out, and little chance of staying upright anyway. An owl rolled past me yesterday, resplete with glowing laser eyes.
The combat itself is pretty simple, but fast and fun despite that - perhaps because of that. Standard rock/paper/scissors affair, with plasma (artillery), laser (machine gun), and railgun (sniper). Battles usually take less than 10 minutes, and can be sneaky tactical affairs, or full on blitzkrieg madness. It helps to work with your team.
Getting out of a bad situation, maybe with just a chair on 2 wheels, is as hilarious as it is satisfying.
Best part, it's all for free.
On the negative side, the sudden growth of interest in the game has forced the developers to move servers. The move caused several issues with lag and connections dropping. Hopefully the will be sorted out soon.
It's free, it's small, it's fun - give it a try.

As summer rolled by and the clutches of boredom eventually wound around my sould, I decided that this would be the summer that I finally returned to gaming.
Upon my return, I ultimately wanted to try something new for a change. I have always been a sandbox or FPS player, and I was looking for something that would scratch my itch without being overly trite for me, and after hours of searching online, I had stumbled upon this game on steam. Little did I know that I have sold my soul to the devil upon playing it.
I do not know how many hours I have clocked on this game already, but let me warn you, you will waste your life playing it. It will be blissful during the times that you do, but seriously, if you have a dissertation to work on DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME.
Now here's the actually review:
This game boasts itself to be a cross of World of Tanks and Minecraft; I have played Minecraft a bit and I respectfully disagree. While I may not have played WoT before, I can tell you for a fact that the only similarity to Minecraft is the block-based 3D construction involved in creating robots that you fight with.
Now, each block has a certain physical aspect to it, altering the way your bot handles in the end. Meaning, you dont have to make tanks. You can make blimps, planes, cars, and a flipping tyrannosaur if you wanted to (youtube it, I sh*t you not.) And that being said, while I have never played WoT, I doubt that they are the same.
Now this mixture of action and sandbox is incredibly synergetic, and creates a game with nearly infinite replayability. Players spend hours on end trying to craft up the perfect robot that will dominate the battlefield. Of course, this never happens, and the game mechanics makes sure of that (or else everyone would be using the same build of robot)
However, there are also cons to this game that I do have to mention, but they can become pro's if you want them to be.
The game operates on a tier system when sending you out to battle, using a hidden algorithm. You battle tier is determined by the level of blocks that you use and the quantity of blocks that you use. That being said, you can create the crappiest motorcycle in the entire world, plop a Tier 5 cannon on it, then run around 1-hit killing everything in Tier 1 battlefields.
Of course, since you're a crappy motorcycle, ♥♥♥♥ up once (get flipped over, get a wheel knocked out) and you're ♥♥♥♥ed as well. (Which is rare. Typically this strategy is a surefire way to win.) This tactic can also be applied at higher tiers as well.
The only time where the game is truly balanced is at tier 10, where everyone is OP as f*ck.
Blocks also need to unlocked in this game, and the scaling at which one receives these blocks is also pretty bad, but nothing gamebreaking. Although I am biased on this point since I shoved cheddar at this game the moment I played it, because it's just that good.
So my final verdict is that this game is incredibly great, it's complete (even in Early Access), and even though there are some balancing issues, the Devs are highly active in fixing them. (They've wiped out the entire hackerbase in a single update! But of course, they'll just return like in every game.)

I don't know why you wouldn't buy this game if you loved the original Portal as much as I did. Even if you're new to the series, or puzzle games in general, Portal 2 would be a good place to start. The story builds off of the first game, but that doesn't mean you have to play it inorder to understand what's happening. All in all, this is my favorite puzzle game of all time, and one of my favorite games in general. I can't reccomend it enough!

I do particularly like this game a bit, but there ARE a few problems.
First, the tutorial's not really much of a tutorial per se, but more like, "Good luck and go shoot everything."
Second, the building mechanics for a vehicle, whether it be air or land, is tedious. When you got a vehicle you think might work, it usually doesn't, with aircraft spazzing and shooting off randomly when you try to move and shoot things and land vehicles busting apart after a few well-aimed shots and flipping over, making you a huge target to attacks. I personally feel that the physics are way too strong in this game.
Third, the displays. For the in-game online battles, the Domination theme is somewhat understandable, but at first I didn't understand when the blue goes up, the RED is capturing your side, and vice versa. It just feels so odd for this game to do that.
Fourth and finally, the community. I understand that you have to be 13+ and everything, and that you can't say or do many offensive things, but the COMMUNITY... There are some REALLY profane things people name their ships and what they model their ship after, which I won't point out. I know that the game is made for an older audience but still acceptable for younger kids, but COME ON. This NEEDS to be checked.

The game isn't horrible, but it has some very clear design flaws. The biggest change needed would be to change how parts scale from being 50-100% more powerful per tier to something closer to 10-25% (or any small range really). Otherwise you get a case of going into battles either completely underpowered or overpowered. If you want an even match where gameplay and design determine the outcome, you are in the wrong game. Regardless, let's cover the other parts of the game:
The building mechanic is nice and fairly simple, but a quick access bar while building would make life much easier. For example when building a robot and I need to place a different type of block you would expect a quick action bar like Minecraft, Space Engineers, or any modern block placing game. Instead, you have to open the menu, click the submenu and then click the part you want EVERY time you switch blocks you want to place. It isn't a huge issue, but its really a simple mechanic that would make the building a better experience.
Let's cover building itself. The game is laid out so their are multiple tiers of every part. This means your overall designs from the start of the game won't change significantly as you progress but from trial and error you will learn what things work and which designs to avoid.
Let's cover upgrades now. For each upgrade you have to play at a certain rank to unlock 'all' the nodes at the current tier, your tier is mostly determined by the quality of the parts you place and to a lesser extend the number of parts you place on your robot. Each tier is about 50-100% more powerful as the previous which means upgrades are very important. In fact upgrades are the only real important part because if someone has armor that is 3 times stronger than you but all else equal (which is rare) they will be either in the same tier or one tier higher.
Let's cover battling now. Each game is very short and sweet, it isn't often you live very long if you get up close and personal with other people. It usually leads to people prefering flying robots with rail guns to snip you from a long distance. Considering you only have one life, we all know how thrilling that can be. However, it is worse when you learn matchmaking will put you in battles with people upto 2 tiers above you or below you. It means some games you dominate and other games you get completely slaughtered. Neither of which are really fun after a while (dominating is fun at first, but gets boring). The real issue with this is because upgrades are 50-100% more powerful as the last tier your design actually becomes fairly meaningless. A guy two tiers above you will almost always win even if they do something really stupid because they have guns which will destroy your armor and guns in seconds and you will have to shoot them for almost half a minute to break their armor.
The grind in the game is pretty noticable once you get your bearings. It isn't a bad thing, but when you switch between hard enemies and easy enemies, like a person with a bipolar disorder, the game just seems to make any 'skill' factor less important. It is a pretty fun game, but getting evenly balanced matches is very hard once you get to higher tiers as you end up in battles completely underpowered or overpowered...

This is a very interesting game, but to sum it up I would have to compare it to banjo kazooie nuts and bolts. You make a ship out of blocks and all the blocks have different stats, functions, etc. What makes it interesting is that there are actual lightweight physics in the game. You aren't just stacking parts on for stat bonuses but are actually designing a vehicle.
A better example of this would be design flaws. Most people who use ground vehicles will do something stupid like trying to ramp up and jump over a cliff, only to wind up upside down at the bottom of a canyon and become unable to flip themselves back over.
But you can fix that.
I added a couple of jet engines to the back of my truck and used them to flip it back over if it ever gets flipped. This is where the actual designs can come in.
Now truth be told, it's not all rainbows and plasma fire. There are two major things that are hindering the game at this time. The first is that some people blatently abuse the tier ranking mechanics.
Since tiers are based on part level and part count, some people artifitially put OP vehicles into lower tiers. They usually do this by making a small robot with high level armor blocks and a decent gun. What ends up happening is you end up facing a target the size of a fly with armor and weapons that would make the death star happy.
The second issue involves the lack of diversity, and will probably be fixed in the near future.
The game revolves around a single game mode with perma death, meaning that when you get killed you are done. This might not seem bad, but it basically means people have to leave the game to play again. While this isn't a problem when the server is up, it means excruciating wait times for slower connections.
If the game developers create a new game mode that allows people to respawn then it would become much more fun for everyone involved.
All in all, I like this game. It's easy to have fun, and you can mess around with whatever crazy contraption you like. But if you play this game to level up and pwn noobs, then I would recommend something else.

An EXCELLENT game ! Looking forward to watching this one develop ! No "pay to win" frustration as those who SPEND $$$ for better / faster access to advanced tech are unlikely to have the SKILLS required to use it effectively ... and the games reward system is sufficient to keep you advancing as rapidly as the extent of your enthusiasm for PLAYING.
My only complaint is ... the game needs a stupid filter. There are a LOT of players on the field who obviously don't have a clue about what works and what doesn't, can't drive or fly the monstosities they create, and are likely to screw you up if you don't watch out for them. This situation improves some as you advance to the higher levels.
Right now, game play is based on the old "capture the flag" scenario, which is fun and challenging with a fair number of reasonably complex maps that alternate every round. More maps (?) in rotation should keep this mode fresh. I expect that the developers will expand the action into some kind of campaign scenario and I do look forward to that.
The BEST tip I can give you is to TEST the robots you design. There's an arena for doing that. Test a design, determine the problem, try and fix it, repeat the process until you get it right. Stability can be just as important as how many railguns you can cram onto your robot. Unless you just like  being upside down and spinning a lot.
Eventually someone will create a tutorial that will help get you started, but for now it's learn by doing, which works ok ... here's one hint it took me a while to catch onto, >>> use the RIGHT mouse button to get a zoomed gunsight <<< it helps a lot.
If you enjoy fast paced action, HUMAN opponents, The challange of building your own "Dream Machine" and proveing  it worthy ... You will LOVE this game. I do ...

Used to be fun and innovative in the beginning but now every update is taking increasingly big steps towards a bad pay-to-win scenario.
Under these conditions I can't recommend it any more.
I played Robocraft since the very early alpha version in april - quite some time before it came to steam and followed the developement process ever since.
Even though you can get the same stuff by buying it or unlocking it only by playing, several updates made it more and more tedious to unlock parts and grind for credits to buy them.
In contrast by paying real money, you can have them instantly.
Since this does give you a significant advantage and matches are not only fought within the same tiers this is one of many possible ways, pay2win can manifest.
If it was just a quicker unlock I would not even mind too much - that's how it was from the very beginning but the change that ruined it for me the most is that robots now have to get repaired after every fight with ingame or bought credits. You can run bankrupt and end up having to choose between starting all over on a low tier, selling all your parts for 1/3rd of the original price, spending a lot of time designing a new robot from scratch and grinding for credits or just buying the credits for cash.
