2 years later, this game is still garbage. Not that it was ever that good.
1. They removed the Tier System, the best aspect of the game. They also removed pilot seats so people could make ridiculously unrealistic robot designs with no strategic placing whatsover. The game now places you against superior oppenents with ridiculously overpowered robot designs.
2. Matchmaking is terrible. Wait times are generally over two and a half minutes, and you will get placed with the same people that you played with before (even if there are >4000 people online)
3. New mech types are absolutely unrealistic. Walkers can run as fast as a tank with 4 wheels and a thruster on the back of it. One helicopter blade can support an entire robot if it is on the back of it.
4. Microtransactions everywhere. Pay for premium, cosmetics, robot designs, building materials, you name it. The game is a living advertisement of its own microtransactions. The queue window features robot designs that you can buy with premium currency. It even has a little note that states how much the ingame currency amount is equivelant to in USD, so all the little 10 year olds that buy these stupid and uneeded items can tell their mommies exactly how much money they are wasting on this game.
The only positives about this game is the originality of the concept of the game. However, its 2 years old now, and I think the hype has died down. The updates they made to the game don't make it fun anymore. I wouldn't waste your time.

Robocraft is an interesting game. You build robots, then battle them. For an early access game, it's pretty polished. I occasionally find myself complaining about something small, then have to remind myself that it's still in Alpha testing.
Basically, the gameplay is as simple as it sounds. Build a robot; fight other robots. Where this game shines is the ability to build pretty much any robot you can think of. You are only limited by your CPU consumption, which you get more of each time you level. The robots are broken into ten tiers for some semblence of fair matches, although this system needs some work, as the games are often imbalanced.

There are plenty of good reasons to play this game, and no bad reasons, really!
You can build your own tank, or blimp, or hovercraft, or plane, or buggy, car, quadbike, you name it (though motorbikes are a bit tricky with the currently available wheels).  The only limits to what you make are what blocks you have available (they come in squares and various types of triangle) and your own imagination.
Then you choose from 1 of 3 weapon types.  Machine guns for up-close rapid damage, plasma cannons for mid-range mortaring, or railguns for long-range sniping.  Each weapon has it's own pros and cons, such as recharge times or accuracy, just play about with them till you find a playstyle that best suits you.  All guns operate as mounted turrets (except machine gun nose turrets :P), able to rotate 180 degrees left and right, and 90 degrees up and down, enabling you to hit enemy vehicles no matter where they are around you (provided your gun is not obstructed by your own vehicle)
Once you have your tank/plane/blimp/whatever and it's fitted with guns, you can test it out against the A.I to make sure it all works ok (defenitely something you need to do when making flying vehicles), and then jump right into the game and start blowing people up!!!
Combat is a lot of fun, landing a hit on an enemy causes overall HP damage and can also damage or even destroy a block of their vehicle, or multiple blocks, heck, you can leave them with just a pilot seat and maybe a wheel with a well aimed shot!  You can also blow off wheels to screw up their steering and movement, or destroy their guns to prevent them fighting back.
Matches take place on a nice variety of maps.  Each match pits a certain number of players (around 8-10 usually) against another team of the same or equivalent size.  The objective is either, 1: Destroy all enemies or 2: capture the enemy base, which you do by sitting on their base point until the capture bar fills up.
After each match you're awarded RP (In-game currency) and tech stars (for your tech tree) based on your performance, and then you can use your RP to buy new guns, blocks, support pieces, wheels, wings, thrusters, lots of stuff!  Your tech stars you spend in your tech tree to unlock new tiers of items, such as more armoured blocks, better wheels, advanced weaponry etc.  The more you play, and the better you get at it, the more awesome your creation can become.
The great thing is it isn't pay-to-win, all items in the game can be obtained using tech stars and RP, the only items that are limited to paying players are cosmetic.
You also gain levels are you play, increasing the amount of things you can fit to your vehicle.  Also as you fit more things to your creation it's tier bar fills up, and once it reaches a certain threshold it'll move on to the next tier.  Tiers determine the kinds of players you'll be up against, higher tiers means tougher armour and more powerful weapons.  Nice thing about this is if you feel you aren't ready for the next tier yet or you want to save up a little more RP to add an extra gun or two, or swap out your armour blocks for better ones, you can remove some stuff from your vehicle to drop it to a lower tier and keep playing on a more fair playing field until you're ready to jump to the next level, so you aren't forced to fight tougher people just 'cos you're getting good at the game.
What more can I say?  The graphics is nice, the sound and music is well suited for the atmosphere, the creativity it gives the player is above anything else I've played, it's user friendly, easy to get into, and it's great for both long playing periods or even short bursts here and there (matches only last a maximum of 6 minutes so it's great if you just need to kill a small amount of time)
Give it a shot, fun guaranteed!

Portal 2 is a triumph. There's no getting around it, the game is simply exceptional. The writing, voice acting, humor, atmosphere, puzzle design, physics, and even graphics (in areas) are stellar. The game returns with a significantly longer but also more complex and more developed campaign, which sees Chell waking up within Aperture labs several hundred years after the events of portal. The atmosphere of decay really permeates the entire game.
The puzzles are surprisingly innovative. Valve has expertly integrated more small project ideas (like the gel) into portal, expanding the possibilities and factors present in test chambers. While it can seem overwhelmingly complex at first, you get used to it, and the feeling of accomplishment you get after completing some of the harder tests simply can't be beat. They've really done a lot by adding more and more elements to the tests, although it does make me wonder how many more new tests can really be created without being Repeats. I guess we'll see in the free DLC for coop.
Speaking of coop, while the coop campaign doesn't have much of a narrative, it's a blast to play. You really have to not only work together, but to think together as well in order to solve some of the harder tests. It's really fun to play with a friend over skype.
Overall though, Portal 2 is incredible, and it's really nothing less than I expected. You owe it to yourself to play this game.

This game really is free to win. Only items you can't buy with ingame money are cosmetics, which on my part would actually make game harder, since I use orbital defence cannon type robot which depends on inconspicuousness to stay in the sky. Then there are garage slots (you get 3 for free) which also cost real money, but by the time you start to lust after additional slots, you probably are quite willing to pay for them too.
Matches give decent amount of money and even more if you manage to survive without damage. Even when I didn't manage to do anything during the match I still got enough money to cover repairs. Another nice thing about matches is that you don't have to wait until it ends to get your robot back. Once you die, you collect what you have earned and move on(or continue spectating if you want to)
Robot building system is  quite interesting and easy to learn. There are enough parts in game to be able to build various kinds of robots, and once they add more it will be insane.
Control system is rather clever in my opinion. It adapts to what you add to your robot. For example, my robot uses thrusters to move around. There are 8 lift thrusters (space) and 4 navigation thrusters (arrow keys). I placed the navigational thrusters to point north-south,east-west -wise.  That way i can steer my platform a little like hotair balloon. I could also add another set of thrusters to point at the sky (shift) to make descending easier.
Another types of movement currently in game are wheels and hoverpads. Wheels are quite selfexplanatory and hoverpads do what it says in the tin, hover at certain altitude from the ground (you can control that with shift and space)
Currently you can put only one type of weapon to your robot. I use several plasma cannons(shoots exploding projectile that is affected by gravity) at the bottom of my robot. Another types of weapons currently in game are front/top smg and railgun . Only things that limit the amount of guns you can put to your robot are space, cpu (you get more by leveling up) and tier (higher tier means harder enemies. Works same way as in world of tanks or warthunder).
Shots collide with your robot (fortunately it doesn't do damage to yourself) so putting too many weapons might not be good idea. Weapons get also slower to use when you install more of them, so for example having just one plasma cannon is still viable vs having 5 of them.
There are some other things too, but you can find them yourself if this kind of game interests you. You can also watch some gameplay videos while waiting for game to get downloaded.
TLDR: It's a good game, you should try it.

In overall rating I would rate this game a 9/10.
1. The game offers fun building and customization of your choice. This causes the game to not only require strategy, but it requires creativity.
2.  You can take test runs with your newly made vehicles. This feature causes players to test their creations before they go into battle. This helps them fix mistakes that they may had made and not noticed.
3. Its early access. This game being early access just lets you know that there will be more stuff coming to the game.
4. "The Tech Shop." The tech shop is a feature in the game where you use "Tech Points" to unlock new things for you to buy. You get "Tech Points" from winning or losing battles.
5. The buying system. The buying system works in the way that you have to play the game to earn credits to buy things. The amount of credits you get from battle is determined by the amount of damage you dealt to enemies in the game. Also things are not underpriced in the way that newbies can get strong guns.
6. The weight limit. The weight limit is a feature that is used in the building phase of your ship. Your weight limit makes it so that you can only have a certain amount of blocks on your ship. Your weight limit (or CPU) can be increased by having your team win battles.
7. Kid friendly battle chat. The chat in the game does not have censores. Instead, if anybody uses innapropriate language, they either get suspended or banned from the Robocraft community.
8. The maps. The maps are designed so that you can either flank the enemy and capture their point, or you can go head on and fight the enemy. The maps have bridges, cliffs, and hills so that you have to restructure your vehicle to adapt.
9. Last but not least, the game matching. The system used to put you in battles will only provide you battles that are of your rank. If you get matched up with somebody not your level, it is probobly a glitch. This feature allows new players to get good stuff before that enter the big leagues.
Those are my 9 reasons why I would recommend this game. People may think that it won't be good because it is early access, but early access just means that it will get better and better.

Robocraft. A game where you build your own vehicle and test it against other players creations. As of now, I can solidly say that this game is very fun, and if you have not yet had the chance to play it: Do so. You will not be disappointed.
Here are some pro's and cons (and some opinions/thoughts on what I hope will happen)
- You can use and improve on the base three vehicles they start you with, or you can test your creativity and basically build whatever you think of (within the 33x33x33 area).
- The matches are quick. For most of the matches I have done, they tend to last about ~5 minutes.
- Once you are eliminated you don't have to stay and wait for the match to end. You can return to your garage at any point.
- Practice Mode. This mode lets you take your vehicle for a test run, allowing you to see what needs to be improved/fixed BEFORE entering a match and finding out you can't move, or are top heavy and flip as your hovercraft.
- The physics engine is actually pretty good.
- While yes you can spend real money on the game, all of the important blocks can be obtained via playing the game. The only things you would really pay for are optional cosmetic stuff such as vapor trails, a name plate that displays the name of your current vehicle, a bunch of different country badges, and premium.
- There isn't any tutorial or anything explaining how certain things (such as flying) work. It's kinda of a trial and error figure out as you go. Which is fine with me personally, but may bother some.

- There is only one gametype. The only gametype as of writing this is Capture the Base. There are however two ways to end it; By either eliminating one team, or capturing their base. I hope to eventually see at least a Team Deathmatch, where everyone respawns until the kill limit is reached. Or perhaps a Domination type where you capture and hold multiple points. One gametype that I personally would enjoy would be some kind of Aerial only deathmatch (Free for All or Team based).
- The Social system is a little buggy. Sometimes you have to relog multiple times for it to show you as online. Not that major of an issue, just an annoyance if you're tying to party up.
- You can't really interact with other players' builds. I see this as a downside because it negates the potential for certain builds. For example: I think it would be really fun to build some kind of transport (land or air based) that some of your team could load into and you drive them to your destination.
- There are currently only five maps. Hopefully they add a few more into rotation at some point.
- One of the biggest for me: Platoon size. You can only currently party up with two other friends (three if you have premium). This is a pretty low number, especially if you are like me and have a group of friends you normally play with. I hope they increase this at some point (without needing to pay for it). If you do need to pay for it, it should be a permanent purchase.
*EDIT* With the new damage model (which makes it so you take the entirety of the damage of the shot that hits you) One Tier 10 Rail Gun will do enough damage to destroy ~21 Tier 10 armor blocks. While yes they have a 15 second cooldown and you can only fire six of them per charge, that's still potentially 126 blocks destroyed - which can kill majority of players assuming they aim for center mass. One of the bigger issues however is how rapidly the railguns can fire and still keep high accuracy. When they line up a shot they can fire all 6 of thier shots within 2 seconds and easily hit with 5 of them. I feel like they need to be more bolt-action and require like a second or two delay between the shots. Also, I hope they change the way thier recharge works. Hopefully they make each railgun have their own recharge, instead of being required to fire all 6 of your shots before begining to recharge.
Feel free to comment your thoughts and opinions on these matters I covered.

I DO recommend this game, as it's free and lets you get really creative with your vehicles, but it has several problems that should be addressed. However, I forgive these problems, as the game is still in development.
Making your vehicles is currently the most fun part of the game. Though you need to buy almost all of your parts, called cubes, the shape and design of your vehicles is up to you. Do they fly? Are they wheeled? Do they hover over the ground? It's completely up to you, but make sure you don't block your guns. You can unlock new parts through the Tech Tree, though the Tech Points system is confusing and wasn't really explained to me.
Battles are where I start complaining HARD. I don't understand the Tier system; as with Tech Points, I may have missed the explanation when I put down my computer for a while, so I really don't understand it. Matching people of the same tier in battles is nice, though. You really get punished for death. You can't go back in once you're dead. You also have to repair your vehicles with your RoboPoints before you can use them again, and you can only get RoboPoints by either winning or participating in battles. There is literally no other way, which is annoying. Also, if you have a wheeled vehicle that flips over, sometimes you can't get up at all. You're completely screwed. Lastly, the map on the corner of the screen is in a hard spot to see.
So, I don't care if you get this game or not. It's free, so anyone can tell the developers what they screwed up on. Otherwise, building vehicles is fun, but there's little explanation of anything, and apparently, if you missed an explanation, you can't see it again. WTF? It has its issues, but Robocraft will be more fun later on. It's only a matter of time.
One last complaint: The self destruct thing is glitchy. Sometimes it won't let me leave the battle when I click it. This is really annoying, as instead of leaving with, like, 50% health left, you might get drained to 0% while you try to leave.

This is a fun game and mostly easy to start playing. It has 2 main parts: in the first part, you can build a 'robot' (well, it's more accurate to say 'vehicle') that drives, glides or flies, shoots guns and can be destroyed block by block. The other part is the part where you get to see this happening: in a PvP environment you either teamkill the other team or capture their base, while preventing them to do it to your team. Pretty standard.
You'll have three bots to start with. Each one is in its own garage. A garage is basically a save slot for the robots and if you want to, you can buy more. You can use the bot the game starts up with, or load any of the other two, or change their looks, or build one from scratch.
Of course, you build one from scratch. You have a number of different blocks to build with. Each block has a category. There's for instance 'chassis', containing basic building blocks, like light blocks and heavy blocks (good for balancing). They come in different shapes, allowing you to break away from the blocky visuals of constructions in a game like Minecraft.
The blocks you have in your inventory are limited in number. If you need more than for instance 150 heavy blocks, you'll have to go to the in-game market to buy additional blocks with in-game money.
Also, more blocks will become available (and visible) after you've unlocked the tech it needs. More on that in a bit. At this point i think it's more important to tell you that the in-game money you need to buy blocks with, is earned when playing online matches.
(However, there is another kind of in-game money that you can only get with real money. I think the Steam wallet can be used here, but i did not do this. There are some purely cosmetic items that you can only buy with this 2nd type of money, like a badge with your country's flag).
Once you have the blocks you need, you can start building. Some things are mandatory: you need a chair for the pilot, and all blocks must be connected. Any loose blocks will stay on their places as long as you are building,  but trying to take the robot out to fight will give you a warning that the loose parts will go back to your inventory.
For the most part, building is fun. It can be hard though to see exactly how a block is oriented - you can rotate them only before placing them. But, it costs nothing to delete it and try again: the block just goes back to your inventory.
Your design is stored in the cloud while you're working on it. It's not possible to build offline.
Once you have built something that moves, you can try it out in a practice map. There are no other players, but some vehicles drive around for you to try your guns at. Try, go back and adjust, and once you feel your robot can be trusted to not flip upside down when you steer, try out a battle.
I can't really say anything about the matchfinding system. I have played about 20 matches at tier 1 and some at tier 2 and got connected so fast that i hardly could see if there were any options available, such as the server to play on. It seems to me that there are no such options. Keep in mind that the game is still in alpha.
Once you're in the game, a countdown starts and there're nothing to do for about ten seconds. Then you and your comrades are released.
You're at your home base. From its center, a large beam of light shoots up in the sky. That's stupid! This way enemies can easily spot our base! (...yes, i know ;-)
You'll see some crazy vehicles around, but you're probably busy on figuring out what to do or where to go (that other shaft of light) and how to go faster. The maps feel pretty large at first glance. Nothing fancy,  no destructable environments or any stuff like that.
But then the vehicle before you suddenly explodes in a blue flash, and you wonder who's gonna safe you when you spot a small silhouette far up in the sky that aims a narrow red beam at you. You manage to hit it with a few bullets from your suddenly quite pathetic smg's, and then you explode in a blue flash. Game over.
You can now choose to spectate the rest of the match, or escape to the building screen. And then you'll find that you still got quite a reward for aiding and protecting and scouting, whatever way you did that, and after repairing your vehicle you still made a little profit. That was fun!
You try another match. This time you find yourself on an icy world and before you know it, your wheels loose their grip on the frozen lake. While you slide past a rocky intersection, one of your opponents accidently rams those rocks from the other side. You are just in the position to DESTROY HIM and so you open fire while sliding past him, you keep firing and firing and then - KABOOOM. Meanwhile you have found solid ground and just as you are happy that you killed and are still undamaged yourself, you explode in a blue flash. Game over.
Playing matches gives you rewards:
The money is to buy stuff with. The tech points are to unlock new technologies, and thus new blocks. The level experience increases your CPU load. Then there's  a "tier", and "weight", and "über tech points". Some of these things are clear, some are not. How does this complexity influence the game? Is it maybe a bit too complex to really get into?
It's true it feels a bit overwhelming because some things are poorly explained within the game. But it's really not so complicated.
and
should speak for themselves or are explained.
and
: each block you use to build with, adds a bit to CPU load. There's a counter for this in the interface. The higher level you are, the higher the load can be. You cannot place any blocks beyond this limit.
: each block you use to build with, adds to this. Some more than others. This is important for matchmaking: adding ten tier 5 smg's takes you out of matches where you would fight tier 1 armor. There's a counter for this in the interface.
: each block weights something, some more than others. Your movement type can only support so much weight. Also, heavy blocks on top might render your vehicle unstable: it's not hard to build a car that falls over at every bump. And there are bumps everywhere!
So: play matches. Try to damage other robots, capture their base, stay alive, help others by following them and attacking those they pick a fight with, protect your onw base, the usual stuff.
Use tech points to unlock blocks. Use money to buy them. Build them into a new robot. Play more matches and increase your level. Put new stuff on your robot. Go to tier 2. See your rewards become larger. Repeat.

Alright BIG REVIEW Coming up.
The Game: Welcome to World of tanks style fighting. Tier 1-10 Classes and capture the base or kill the team. Also, Welcome to Minecraft/Banjo Kazooie Nuts n Bolts.  If you can build it you can drive/fly it.
Pros: For an Early Development game this game is VERY well developed. You get infinte ways to customize your own vehicle (Literally, build piece by piece block by block ground up) Your design may work, it may not, Look at other players and learn from them to improve your own!
Extra Pros: Graphics are very balanced. I have a horrible pc and default ran fine, but a tweak to the Fastest setting makes me able to keep up with anyone and not lose much detail. Lightwieght games that have endless play time to them are so hard to come by. Also, ITS FREE.
Cons: Being early dev, yes it will have issues. Balanced weapons depending on class tend to have an effect. Plasmas for mortar/artillery can become a one hit wonder if you spam about 10 upon your vehicle, or snipe from the top of the map with some railguns. Once Balanced out a bit, this will be no issue.
Overall: Even for early dev, I already say 10/10 for me. It's free, its lightweight, endless ways to build.

A simple-to-learn, impossible-to-master type of game. Something as familiar on the video gamer's shelf as the artist's. A good deal of time is spent building a robot, but that's only where the fun begins. Then you squad up with 8-14 teammates, each piloting his or her own unique robot, and wage war on a equal number of custom bots. A player's robot can travel on land or in the air. Additionally, your robot can be designed any way you can dream up. It can be outfitted with an array of weapons and gadgets, placed strategically on the bot to optimize its killing potential. If you've any interest in robots, FPS's, or squad-baded combat, this easy, free game is for you.

While this game has a ways to go before I would consider it a game worth paying for, I can recommend it whole-heartedly as it's both free and in Early Access, meaning that new features should continue showing up in the game.
As-is, Robocraft feels like playing with Legos. And no one has to tell you that Legos are awesome. Unlike a lot of games, in Robocraft, you can really build a wide variety of robots from day 1 without needing to grind to get new parts or levels first. Later on, however, you start feeling the grind to try to buy bigger and better guns, or simply to upgrade the armor on your robot, or to attempt to build a second robot completely. All these things take RP, which only comes in through battles. When you make 200-600 RP per battle and need 900 for one new gun, outfitting your robot with 8 or 9 new turrets becomes quite tedious.
As the game expands, I expect that we will get new battle types which can change the pace and break up the monotony in the grind a bit. Ultimately, though, I haven't gotten bored of it yet. The matches go by fast and I really do enjoy the battles, even when loosing.

NEWEST REVIEW:
This is kinda weird, the game feels like a former shadow of itself. The cokpits that needed protection are gone, the blocks of differing strengths are gone, the non linear tech tree is gone, the tiers are gone.
I presume they switched to a linear tech tree to make players experiment more, but honestly i found the non linear tech tree fun. It was nice to be able to pick and choose what i did and did not want to research. It added another element to the game. Now it is entirely linear.
Building a craft to properly protect the cockpit was a fair bit of the fun, it also helped to ensure that vehicles were more than just platforms to carry guns. Add to the fact that all blocks are now of equal strength and nearly all the fun from building craft is gone. In the past you could consider the benefits of creating a vehicle with a stronger chassis over one with a weak chassis and stronger armour. All of that is now gone in favour of blocks of a single strength removing almost all depth and fun from building craft.
The tiers were also really nice, since trying to build a craft that got as close to the next tier as possible without moving into it was a fun challenge in and of itself. You had to try and optimise a craft to best suit its class of vehicle. Now because that has been removed it is no longer possible to try and create a best in class vehicle. This also means that there is no pre defined limit for each battle in terms of what you can be playing against. Some battles your craft will be weaker than average and in others it will be stronger.
All of this leads to a game which just isnt as fun as it once was. Often in games the developers will try to remove as much bloat as possible to leave all the good parts. Here it seems like they have removed over half the good parts leaving vehicle building feeling far more redundant.

This is sooo good. Most fun i have had in gaming in a while.

Would recomend it to anyone

Fun little team arena style battle game.
Build your bots with blocks, slap on some weapons and go to town!
The game functions a lot like World of Tanks / War Thunder with a Garage where you fit out your creation with its gear.
To progress you earn Tech Points(TP) by killing or capping, but there is a catch, you only earn TP for the tier you are in.
To start earning Tier 2(T2) points you need to increase your bots ranking to T2.
You do this buy unlocking Higher Level parts in the Tech Tree and fitting them to your bot, which in turn raises its Tier Rating and once you break into Tier 2 you are matched with other T2 players and can start earning T2 Tech Points.
Once you have created your battle bot you simple hit Battle and choose online and like WoT or WT you will be placed in a queue.
Alternatively the Testing mode is invaluable especially if you stand playing with flying or elaborate creations to not only see how they handle but how efficiently you places its guns.
Gameplay is WASD and mouse to aim for the most part with some additional controls for flying vehicles(have not played too much with them).
Kill as many as you can, try to cap the point, the more you help the more points you get at the end of the match.
If you die you are out for the rest of the round so you simply hit ESC to go back to your Garage and repair your bot then you are ready to jump into the next game.
This is one of those games you can jump in and just play, the rounds are short and sweet, you will spend more time building your bots in this game then playing(unless you are grinding for cash/TP).
On currency, there is essentially 3 types:
Tech Points split into 10 tiers (you need T3 TP to buy T3 tech tree stuff etc.)
RP which is a green currency, you earn this as you play and it is the currency used to buy blocks to build and also repair.
GC which is a blue currency, you earn this by spending real world monies, it can also be used to buy 'Premium Boost' but can be used to buy blocks and additional Bot Slots and so on.. standard micro-transaction stuff.
And finally you have Uber points which if I understand correctly are essentially tech points that can be used in any tier but you need to exchange Tech Points + GC (not 100% on this)
All in all a fun game that I stayed up way too late playing and can definitely seem myself playing more!

First of all: this is gummy ship building from Kingdom Hearts 1.
And it is awesome!
I will not pretend that this is one of the most realistic physics sandboxes out there, but it does indeed offer a lot of fun.
At the time of writing this review, and on a GMT+2 timezone, the online players fluctuate between 3000 and 6000 on daytime and nighttime respectively. I could safely state that the number of ready-to-play players at any time is ~1/20 of the total online players, but that happens because most people are building their robos at any time.
DISCLAIMER: Your first few hours of gameplay WILL consist of below average vehicles (or robos if you may).
DO NOT THINK FOR A SECOND THAT THE GAME IS BAD BECAUSE OF THAT.
It is after all, a physics sandbox. If you load your robo a lot, don't be surprised that it can't fly or run fast. If you front-load it, don't be surprised that it WILL topple over, rendering it useless.
This is not a game that concerns itself with looks, but with utility. Your robo doesn't have to look nice to be effective (in contrast with what the store page has to offer).(Effectiveness is measured in tiers between 1-10 [T1-T10])
Now onto the crafting part:
The game offers you 4 kinds of blocks: Building,Movement,Equipment and Utility Blocks
In oder to make a robo, you have to make it from bulding blocks with different attributes, make it somehow move, attack and see(having radar or any kind of enemy recognition)
The fighting part is pretty straightforward: You use your creation to overpower your enemy's creations and win the game.
If you die, there is no respawn, but you can leave the match then with no penalty, thus making an average match time (on T3 at least) ~5 mins, and the average waiting time 20 secs or so
Upon finishing a match, you gain in-game currency (Robo points or RP for short), which you can use to purchase EVERYTHING in the cube depot (or marketplace) except the cosmetics
The UI is intuitive and easy to learn, thus making your overall experience even more enjoyable
Other than some balance issues at the moment (and some people not knowing how to do stuff properly, but i always cut them some slack [heck, i look back at my learning curve]), i urge everyone that reads this review to at least try the game out and not drop out of it if their robos are ineffective(it took me 10 hours in-game to figure out a design i am fond of), so don't get dishearted
tl;dr; For a Free game on its 6th day of Early Access, the game shows a lot of potential if the engine is updated with more variables(like Moment and Inertia). Game is good, play it, and also, read last paragraph^
Fun-0-meter |------------||||-|
Gameplay Experience 8/10 (balance issues and some bad teamwork sometimes as i was saying)
Final Score: 8.5/10

After many discussions with the Robocraft community, Robocraft: Unleashed arrives to address some of the core concerns and unlock Maximum Freedom for robot building and fighting.  Completely overhauling the progression and match-making systems within the game. All previous restrictions have been removed, no more Tier CPU caps, no more Tier minimum armor requirements, no more overtier restrictions, in fact no more Tiers at all. Total freedom allows you to build whatever Robot you want and new match-making will ensure you play versus Robots of an equivalent power taking into consideration your Player Level too.
MAXIMUM FREEDOM
The Robocraft community spoke and Freejam went into action removing all the restrictions and limits from the game and adding in it’s place Maximum Freedom with a brand new match-making system.
Tier CPU caps lifted completely

Overtier restrictions lifted completely

Brand new Robot Ranking gauge, with pizazz!

Platoons now match-made based on (just above) the average Robot Ranking between the smallest and the largest

RP rewards are now based on your performance in battle and the Robot Ranking of your Robot

Like as advertised, it's like a combination of World of Tanks and Minecraft.  However, honestly if that is what you are hoping for you will be sadly mistaken, the core of the game is unique to both and any hopes you had that it would be similar will be shattered.  It does not possess the tactics and field designs of World of tanks where you can hide in the terrain, and the only think like minecraft is the block system to build your robot.
The game itself is a fast paced battle using only 3 styles of weapons on 3 styles of vehicles including plasma mortors, beam rifles, and beam machineguns used on planes, cars, or hovercrafts.
This review may sound critical but you need to remeber the game is still early and even at this stage it's great fun to build over and over to see if your creation is better than similar ones.  I recommend trying it now until you get bored and come back in a few monthes to see what's changed.

This game is definitely new. But do not let that discourage you. While I do not typically enjoy games that do not offer a single player, this one is a definite try. The very fact that it is free makes it worth checking out.
My time has been as follows:
Got on, checked out the starter vehicles. Didn't like any of them, so I sold all three. This gave me a TON of money to work with to build my own craft.
At first I went with a large flying vehicle, having never played before, I didn't realize my mistake. Being a large target is a bad idea. However, interestingly enough, physics apply. I had to test out where I was placing my hover things a couple times before I got a decent flat hover (Without flipping.)
Second I went with something medium-ish. And covered in guns. I found myself with two options in game due to the quality and nature of my craft: Either take time and snipe from afar, dealing little but accurate damage over time with little loss to myself, or fly right over someone and shoot them. The ladder I've found to be a quick way to get at least one kill (And you get XP per hit in this, not XP per kill because it is hard to get a kill), but leave myself quite damaged.
I haven't been playing long. But the fact that I built something capable of doing well in multiplayer without spending real money or spending a large amount of time playing shows that this game is largely skill based.
If you can build a good craft and are good at using it, you can win, no matter the money.
Have a good day!

Don't pay attention to hours, I played since early access and have a trophy in game for it. I'm gonna review this using the tag line as my outline.
Build
To start, well this game was super fun when there was a Tech Tree and Tier progression system of 1-10 where you were placed in a game close to your tier and now it's just based off on how much you can put on your bot.
Another problem is the part og the store where you can buy prebuilt bots, problem with this is that the point of the game is for you to make your own bot and then update it to make it better and what not. With the store, you can just buy a prebuilt bot almost taking the point of building out of the game. Although I am glad they threw away the colored blocks but now you don't even need any certain time into the game to get the good weapons, just to get lucky in a box for ingame currency and now you can buy the biggest baddest most OP weapon in the game. No time to wait.
Drive
In game controls are easy to use and theres really no complaint here.
Fight
This is the part that I dislike the most, LOCK ON WEAPONS KILL THE SKILL ASPECT OF THE GAME. These are the most annoying part imo. All you have to do is look at your enemy and click from halfway across the map with the missles. And the lock on SMGs are just point and click too, with less range of course.
There used to be classes in the game where you could not have every possible weapon on your bot. Having SMGs means you were CQB or a fighter. Having mortars meant you were a bomber. Railguns meant you were a sniper and Nano repair meant you were a medic. There also used to not be a healing feature and that healing was left to the medics making them vital to winning. With that aspect gone, people charge in and charge out and then charge back in.
Freejam had it on point a couple updates ago but now its just not as good as it once was. There are parts that I like and if the things I stated fit your needs, then go ahead and give this a go. I miss a battle playlist where a tier 10 bot played by 1 person with a huge amount of health got put against 10 or so tier 1-5. This game mode was probably my favorite.

After the first Portal came out, no one was REALLY expecting a sequel. Don't get me wrong, It was a great game. But, it was extremely short, and I mean EXTREMELY short, and the narrative kind of came full circle by the end. You test, you test, you find out Glados is evil, almost die, kill her, THE END. So really, when the sequel was announced, everyone was excited but still cautious, as no one really knew what it was going to be about. What came out however, is holding a place in my top ten video games of all time, Portal 2 is that good. The story should take over 10 hours, and below 15 hours to complete, smashing Portal 1's 3 hour journey. The length does depend, however, on how good you are at thinking with portals. But every second of this game is awesome. Glados makes a more than welcome return, a new character called Wheatley is introduced, who is hilarious. The voice acting is spectacular, the visuals are crisp and clean, the story is deep and envoking (yes, in a game where you go around shooting portals, the story is deep and envoking) and if that isn't enough, there is an awesome co-op side game you can play with friends, which is actually just as good as the main story. The level designs are awesome, and it is always fun with friends. The thing Portal 2 really succeeds at, however, is making it difficult enough but not making it seem unfair, and not making you want to stop playing. Portal 2 is a brilliant game, and.... Portal 3? Valve? Play Portal 2 if you haven't already.

I have played this game somewhat religeously for months before it hit steam. I have seen it go through ups and downs just like any indie game; however Robocraft has some key differences in gameplay and development.
For context on this review, here is a short description of the game:
Build tanks, hovercrafts, blimps, and planes from individual blocks and modules. Go into battle and watch as your bot and your enemies are destroyed block by block. Earn money for your battle performance and then pay for the repairs. (you will always make money in all but the latest of late-game stuff.)
Here are some things Robocraft does right.
1. The devs (devolopers) are quite vocal with the community, they interact on the forums with relative consistency. Most other games this far along don't have much interaction between players and devs.
2. The devs pay attention to gameplay problems and put serious effort into fixing them. Recently they introduced the concept of paying for repairs. For a while the system caused people to lose their in-game money. Now they have seriously nerfed repair costs such that it is impossible to lose money unless you are in the highest tiers of vehicles.
3. The meta-game is always evolving. With people always trying new vehicle designs, now and then something revolutionary happens. Various weapon balancing patches also effect this.
4. This game is seriously Free 2 Play. You never really feel cheated by the system, and paying money just helps you level faster, and make more money. The tech-point system is a little inconvinient when you are F2P, but that is fine, and easy to work around.
In summary. Try this game! It is free, and you wont be destroyed by a bunch of paying players! :D

I'm starting this humble review with the prerequisite that I am NOT a Portal fan. I have played the first game for, maybe an hour, but was not really impressed. Portal 2 though made me replay the first game and I had fell in love with this simple, yet unique franchise.
In Portal 2 you take control of Chell, your protagonist in the first game as well, when she tries to escape the Aparture Science facility or she will be doomed to get through tests forever along the psychotic robot, controlling the whole facility by the name of
[Genetic Lifeform and Disc Operating System] and a core with awkward behaviour by the name of Wheatley.
Talking about gameplay, the game is pretty much flawless - you posses a Portal gun you can create portals with (suprise!) to get through various objectives and test chambers. It's not only the portals that help you get through them though - there are also
[a small structure that shoots you in the air similar to a catapult],
[a blue liquid that can be used as a trampoline] and my personal favourite -
[an orange liquid that speeds you up... a LOT!]. There are also different cubes and paths to complete a test chamber - all you gotta do is improvise. Portal 2 has unique level design - you may have to repeat an action a few times, but you may never get into a same chamber.
Portal 2 isn't a game without its cons though, the main one is that if you are not fan of puzzle games, you will not like it. The game is one of the few that require brain and quick reflexes in order to be enjoyed completely. Also, I believe that the strongest part of the game is its co-op - the campaign got a bit lonely for me somewhere in the middle, so grab a friend and get through the missions together.
Overall, Portal 2 is a great addition to any game collection because of its unique game mechanics and the ingame humor. If you expect a bloody massacre or a hero that is total badass, this is not your game, but if you like a little brain tease - go get it. 10/10

It's been roughly two days since I downloaded this game, and I have not regretted it. Robocraft is a multiplayer game about building your robot, adding weapons, and using those weapons to smash other robots in combat. Plain and simple. Building a robot is a mixed bag, on the one hand, it can be incredibly fun to design your robot and test it. On the other hand, it can take some time to learn the controls, and breaking down and constructing a bot is sometimes tedious.
GAMEPLAY
Gameplay revolves around two central things: Combat, and construction. Combat is fun and fast, if simple. Drive (or fly) your robot and shoot other robots, and maybe capture their base. That's it. There's only one gametype at the moment, Capture the Base, which revolves around either eliminating all enemy bots, or, as said, capturing their base. At the moment, there are three or four maps and only one game type. Still, don't l;et it put you off. Though variety is very sparse, the gameplay makes up for it.
The gunplay is pretty good, I suppose, though the balance scheme is kinda off. As in, some weapons seem a lot better than others. What makes combat really fun, however, is the destructible parts. Spent an hour designing the perfect bot? Well, be prepared to watch all those carefully laid blocks get shot off one by one. Wanna cripple an enemy bot? Shoot off it's wheels. Want to blind it? Shoot off that radar dish. Want to disarm it? Well, shoot at the guns. Every problem is solved by shooting at them.
Construction is fun. Build your own bot, why not? Placing blocks can be a tedious affair, but for the most part, I enjoy it. (Though breaking down your bots is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Your construction is limited by two things: Materials, and your CPU stat.  Relatively soon, it'll be the latter that screws you up. In any case, it's fun.
Overrall, the gameplay is pretty good. In fact, it's the best (and maybe only) part of the game. Although it is hindered by slow progression. Or not, if you like that.
GRAPHICS
Honestly, they're not great. I don't care for these things, really, and the color scheme is unoffending. I don't care either way, not that I ever feel otherwise. In any case, it is Alpha, after all.
PERFORMANCE
I don't have a great rig, and this runs perfectly. No stutters, none that I noticed, anyhow, no lag, and the servers are excellent. The longest I've ever had to wait was 31 seconds to join a game. There's controller support too, but even though I'm a reformed console user, I've found the keyboard controls to be completely adequate.
OVERALL
Robocraft is a great game that seems relatively polished despite it's early state. Combine that with addicting combat, creative construction, and simple gameplay, and you have a really fun time-sink. Also, it's FREE. As in, no money wasted. You lose nothing if you buy this game. Except of course, for dozens of hours.
8.5/10

The sequel to 2007's Game of the Year, and this time there are whole new challenges to complete.
Once again it is set in Aperture laboratries, with the maniacal GLaDOS (Genetic Lifeform and Disk Operating System) trying to kill you as you complete test chambers.
Singleplayer campaign
Chell (the character you play as) wakes up in an Aperture relaxation vault, and a robotic voice asks you to do certain actions. This is by far one of the best tutorials I have ever seen, as it manages to add this stage somewhat into the story. You head back to bed and are woken up again after what the computer states as "9-9-9-9-9-9-9... years", to find someone knocking on the door. You open it and find a small robot sphere named Wheatley, and this is where the real journey begins.
Multiplayer (or co-operative) campaign
You play as one of two robots, Atlas or P-body; with your partner playing as the other. It is set after the singleplayer campaign, and challenges you to think in an entirely different way. It features the same testing elements, but completely new test chambers. Unfortunately, when playing co-op on Mac or PC, you require a friend who also has bought Portal 2 to play this mode (unless you have a controller, but split-screen on a computer monitor is awful).

- Hard-light bridges
- Excursion funnels
- Thermal discouragement beams
- Aerial faith plates
- Repulsion gel
- Propulsion gel
- and conversion gel
I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and it has plenty of things to make you come back, like hidden secrets and achievements, and a level editor that lets you create your own test chambers using many of the features available.

Trust me on this one. This game is something awful.
The general concept of creating and piloting your own custom built vehicles is fantastic but World of Tanks style gameplay along with "limitless" build possibilities give it a 90° nose dive to a stupid game.
If you get your one robot destroyed your match is at an end.
If you fall over, your match is at an end, there's no way to get up which gives air vehicles a great advantage over ground vehicles. Except for the clunky and overly sensitive aircraft controls.
Thanks to the "limitless" possibilities in crafting most of the time you will most likely encounter either a player with a crude and bad looking base construct which has 50 high damage weapons splattered onto it everywhere which basically 1 hit kills anything it comes across.
Or you'll come across a user that you won't really come across. They will just camp on the other side of the map usinng several high powered railguns to turn your vehicle into nothing with one or two shots.
And seeing as these problems are tied to the core gameplay possibilities that differ this game from stupid World of Tanks they can't take it away or limit you. Therfore these problems can't be fixed while the game is supposed to function as it is.
Also the ammount of grinding it takes to get pretty much anything is irritating. Join game, kill some robots or die instantly, repeat half a million times and MAYBE you'll get something remotely good for your robot which will get reduced to a pile of scrap by people who glue guns on every possible spot on their weapon rack type vehicle.
As I said, idea is fantastic but it's basically a ruined game. If there were a social area where you could play with your vehicles or try out other people's vehicles and such. Or a Co-op! Anything would be a nicer addition than the PvP in this game which you are forced to play and grind on to move on in the game.

First impressions:
(optional let's play footage)
I played Robocraft for just under half an hour until I started having trouble connecting to the server and was no longer able to play. I think it’s probably overloaded because of the popularity.
For an alpha the presentation is pretty good. Main menu area looks good. Sounds alright and has decent menu music.
You pilot pre-made or modified robot vehicles. Or build them from scratch piece by piece. You have a selection of different types of chassis blocks i.e. heavy armour or light, propulsion e.g. (hover or wheels, rear wheel drive or front wheel drive etc.), weapons and so on. You make your robot in any shape or configuration you want. You can make a heavy tank, a gunship with long range or short range weapons. Online matches appear to be a team deathmatch.
The typical players robot isn't very pretty but I think this game has a lot of potential for some really cool designs. And because of the apparently huge amount of customisation a large amount of variety to gameplay.
In the short time that I played I basically thought the game was awesome from the start. I've been avoiding Early Access titles but I would definitely recommend playing this game. What have you got to lose? It is free.

I'm sure at this point that anyone getting portal is someone who's just "getting around" to it like I was last year, but if you're one of those who for any reason has been hesitant to try it, you're missing out. The game is funny, challenging, unique, and, above all, genius. I have never seen anything like the Portal series and imagine it'll be a long time before any other such gem shall enter the world. The game appeals to the little rebel in us all. You can't help but love your four instructors. The pre-recorded messages provide more comic relief than emotional support or instruction. GLaDOS, although always insulting, clearly "cares" about you. Wheatley is always so eager, even after- wait! No spoilers! Cave Johnson, the founder of the company, has such a twisted view of the world but presents it in such a charismatic and matter-of-fact way that you almost don't notice. The game is really one of the best I've ever played.

Story is well-driven and easy to follow. Although the game features more/less 5 characters (including Cave Johnson and Caroline). They're so lively and have their own iconic personalities, Wheatley is awesome :D You'll never get bored of the dark humor continuously thrown at you xD I have to say that the story is a bit short compared to their flagship game, Half-Life.
The Source engine is by far my favorite. I'm playing this game at a consistent 100fps set to High/Very High.... no crashes in-game, and absolutely looks delightful (especially the lighting). It can also run very well on older systems, which is always a plus for me ^_^ Music is what you'd expect from Valve....... just pure awesomeness, nuff said xD

It's not a generic shoot-everything-that-moves FPS but a puzzle-solving FPS that involves Portals and require you to have a keen observation on your surroundings and lots of thinking. I honestly was stuck on a puzzle for a good 20-mins. until I went "Ohhhhh, now I get it" and proceed to finish the test chamber xD It stands out because of its one-of-a-kind gameplay and does it extremely well ;)

That feeling you get after solving a test chamber is quite awesome ^_^ and doing it again, but faster, feels even more rewarding. The highly anticipated sequel to 2007's Game of the Year, Portal 2 is a hilariously mind-bending adventure that challenges you to use wits over weaponry in a funhouse of diabolical science.

This game is utterly ground-breaking.   Portal 2 is a huge improvement over the first installment of the series, which should really say something since the original game brought some incredible mechanics and clever puzzles to the table.  The graphics are somewhat simple, but they are crisp and good-looking throughout.  The sound and music are really big highlights of the Portal experience here -- The music ALWAYS lends to the feel of the game.
One of the most notable differences between this and Portal is the story.  Portal's story was mostly non-existent if you didn't look into the backstory online, or if you didn't catch any of the large handfuls of references dropped in it.  Portal 2’s story, however, is constantly being fleshed out by (usually hilarious) dialogue between the characters.  If you liked GLaDOS’ dark sense of humor in the first game, then you’ll absolutely love her in this title.
If you were a fan of the first Portal, are a fan of puzzle games in general, and/or are a fan of unforgettable humor in video games, Portal 2 is a must buy.

Who'd have thought that such a simple concept could be so complex and intricate? Portal is like a modern day equivalent of chess, but with a portal gun, no board and no pieces. So, entirely nothing like chess then... There is the similarity of having to think several steps ahead though, so that malformed chess comparison might be of some merit after all. There's no story in chess either, unless you've made you're own narrative up, involving the queen running off with the bishop to a rook on the back of a knight. If so, then perhaps you should seek help.
"Taking a trip down the Funnel of Death."
So, the patented Aperture Science portal gun is back once again, and if you thought some of Portal's test chambers were convoluted, then you're in for a rude awakening with Portal 2, as there are some real brain-melting doozies awaiting in the numerous test chambers of Aperture Laboratories. Portal 1 feels like it was a dry run for this, the main event, which not only tells a killer story with more twists and turns than an Excursion Funnel (more on those later), but it takes the core portal concept and throws in a whole load of new mind-bending mechanics.
What follows is a blend of frustration, puzzlement, bewilderment and thankfully, a hefty dose of jubilation. You see, nothing beats the feeling of satisfaction upon solving one of Portal 2's expertly engineered tests, amid the taunts and barbs being dispensed by omnipotent AI, GLaDOS, who is back with a vengeance for the sequel. With the addition of Repulsion Gel, Propulsion Gel, Conversion Gel, Faith Plates, Hard Light Bridges and Excursion Funnels, Portal 2 kicks things up several notches, creating some of the most fiendish head-scratchers you're ever likely to come across.
At certain junctures, we'd become seemingly, insurmountably stuck and curse the game design, the level design and everything while trying to formulate a solution to a particular obstacle or what appears to be a total impasse. Moments like these are hugely frustrating, essentially because they make you feel stupid for not being able to get into the right mindset. And after that complete feeling of hopelessness at your own cognitive shortcomings, the reward of a 'eureka' moment, when the solution is suddenly right there in front of you, is entirely worth it.
"Atlas and P-body are proper endearing, innit?"
Of course, there is a lot to learn in Portal 2, but Valve pitches the learning curve perfectly, slowly easing you into the various mechanics, gently laying things out for you so it all makes sense, even if you missed playing the first Portal. Things start off nice and simple then, once returning protagonist Chell experiences her rude awakening, and before you know it, you're back in the clean-walled confines of the Aperture Laboratories ready to be taunted and cajoled through increasingly testing experiments. Soon, you'll come across blue Repulsion Gel that enables you to bounce off any surfaces painted in the stuff, orange Propulsion Gel that speeds up your running speed and white Conversion Gel that enables you to project portals on it. Then the game throws Excursion Funnels into the mix, which enable you to float through the air to otherwise inaccessible plateaus, and it's combining all of these elements that makes Portal 2 so immensely and gratifyingly challenging.
And for a while, you'll be prodded from test chamber to test chamber, bending to GlaDOS's every whim, until everything predictably goes horribly awry. To say any more would be a horrible spoiler, but suffice to say that Valve has crafted a narrative that really does have it all. It's funny, dark and tense in equal measure, as well as consistently entertaining from start to finish.
It's the gameplay that really makes Portal 2 such a joy though and everything else is just the icing on the... - we had to say it at some point – cake. That's before you even consider co-op, which is a whole separate campaign on its own, starring the most endearing droid duo since C3PO and R2D2. Playable in local split screen – vertical or horizontal: your call – or online with a friend or a random, Portal 2's co-op is pure genius, encouraging communication and actual, proper co-ordination. Playing without a headset really isn't an option, despite being able to project markers and start countdowns via the in-game HUD, and playing with someone you don't know proves remarkably difficult, if not nigh-on impossible. Even Valve knows this, as it even thought to include a warning disclaimer telling you that the game won't be as fun if you try and play with a person not on your friends list.
"We don't think BP is to blame for this one."
Get an actual friend to play with you though, and you'll find that tearing through all five Courses of test chambers is a blast, with Atlas and P-body high-fiving and dancing their way through even more slickly designed stages that deal with each specific game mechanic Course by Course. It's enormous fun to hit Portal 2 in co-op and being given four portals to play with rather than two puts a whole different spin on the game's basic mechanics. In fact, we can't remember the last time we played a co-op title like this, that required constant communication between the two-players in order to beat each puzzle. Be forewarned though, you may need a large TV screen to get the best out of playing co-op in split screen. Online however, it all works brilliantly.
Portal 2 continues a great tradition of clever and inventive achievement lists concocted by Valve, rewarding exploration with a few Easter eggs, including a few hidden surprises that shed light on certain aspects of the Aperture Science story. There's an excellent balance between single-player and co-op achievements too, making playing both modes even more essential. Most achievements are attained through natural progression, but there might be a few you miss along the way. Luckily, upon completing both the single-player and co-op facets of the Portal 2 story, you're able to jump back into any of the chapters. This is done via the hub in co-op, where you can also mess around gesturing and playing rock, paper, scissors to your heart's content. All in all, Portal 2's achievement list is excellent then.
A riveting journey from start to finish, Portal 2 is yet another unmitigated triumph for Valve, building upon an original concept that was incredible to begin with and making it even more incredible. At times it might have you tearing your hair out, but ultimately if you loved Portal 1 (and who didn't?), you're going to eat up Portal 2 like a big old piece of vanilla crazy cake.

Who'd have thought that such a simple concept could be so complex and intricate? Portal is like a modern day equivalent of chess, but with a portal gun, no board and no pieces. So, entirely nothing like chess then... There is the similarity of having to think several steps ahead though, so that malformed chess comparison might be of some merit after all. There's no story in chess either, unless you've made you're own narrative up, involving the queen running off with the bishop to a rook on the back of a knight. If so, then perhaps you should seek help.
"Taking a trip down the Funnel of Death."
So, the patented Aperture Science portal gun is back once again, and if you thought some of Portal's test chambers were convoluted, then you're in for a rude awakening with Portal 2, as there are some real brain-melting doozies awaiting in the numerous test chambers of Aperture Laboratories. Portal 1 feels like it was a dry run for this, the main event, which not only tells a killer story with more twists and turns than an Excursion Funnel (more on those later), but it takes the core portal concept and throws in a whole load of new mind-bending mechanics.
What follows is a blend of frustration, puzzlement, bewilderment and thankfully, a hefty dose of jubilation. You see, nothing beats the feeling of satisfaction upon solving one of Portal 2's expertly engineered tests, amid the taunts and barbs being dispensed by omnipotent AI, GLaDOS, who is back with a vengeance for the sequel. With the addition of Repulsion Gel, Propulsion Gel, Conversion Gel, Faith Plates, Hard Light Bridges and Excursion Funnels, Portal 2 kicks things up several notches, creating some of the most fiendish head-scratchers you're ever likely to come across.
At certain junctures, we'd become seemingly, insurmountably stuck and curse the game design, the level design and everything while trying to formulate a solution to a particular obstacle or what appears to be a total impasse. Moments like these are hugely frustrating, essentially because they make you feel stupid for not being able to get into the right mindset. And after that complete feeling of hopelessness at your own cognitive shortcomings, the reward of a 'eureka' moment, when the solution is suddenly right there in front of you, is entirely worth it.
"Atlas and P-body are proper endearing, innit?"
Of course, there is a lot to learn in Portal 2, but Valve pitches the learning curve perfectly, slowly easing you into the various mechanics, gently laying things out for you so it all makes sense, even if you missed playing the first Portal. Things start off nice and simple then, once returning protagonist Chell experiences her rude awakening, and before you know it, you're back in the clean-walled confines of the Aperture Laboratories ready to be taunted and cajoled through increasingly testing experiments. Soon, you'll come across blue Repulsion Gel that enables you to bounce off any surfaces painted in the stuff, orange Propulsion Gel that speeds up your running speed and white Conversion Gel that enables you to project portals on it. Then the game throws Excursion Funnels into the mix, which enable you to float through the air to otherwise inaccessible plateaus, and it's combining all of these elements that makes Portal 2 so immensely and gratifyingly challenging.
And for a while, you'll be prodded from test chamber to test chamber, bending to GlaDOS's every whim, until everything predictably goes horribly awry. To say any more would be a horrible spoiler, but suffice to say that Valve has crafted a narrative that really does have it all. It's funny, dark and tense in equal measure, as well as consistently entertaining from start to finish.
It's the gameplay that really makes Portal 2 such a joy though and everything else is just the icing on the... - we had to say it at some point – cake. That's before you even consider co-op, which is a whole separate campaign on its own, starring the most endearing droid duo since C3PO and R2D2. Playable in local split screen – vertical or horizontal: your call – or online with a friend or a random, Portal 2's co-op is pure genius, encouraging communication and actual, proper co-ordination. Playing without a headset really isn't an option, despite being able to project markers and start countdowns via the in-game HUD, and playing with someone you don't know proves remarkably difficult, if not nigh-on impossible. Even Valve knows this, as it even thought to include a warning disclaimer telling you that the game won't be as fun if you try and play with a person not on your friends list.
"We don't think BP is to blame for this one."
Get an actual friend to play with you though, and you'll find that tearing through all five Courses of test chambers is a blast, with Atlas and P-body high-fiving and dancing their way through even more slickly designed stages that deal with each specific game mechanic Course by Course. It's enormous fun to hit Portal 2 in co-op and being given four portals to play with rather than two puts a whole different spin on the game's basic mechanics. In fact, we can't remember the last time we played a co-op title like this, that required constant communication between the two-players in order to beat each puzzle. Be forewarned though, you may need a large TV screen to get the best out of playing co-op in split screen. Online however, it all works brilliantly.
Portal 2 continues a great tradition of clever and inventive achievement lists concocted by Valve, rewarding exploration with a few Easter eggs, including a few hidden surprises that shed light on certain aspects of the Aperture Science story. There's an excellent balance between single-player and co-op achievements too, making playing both modes even more essential. Most achievements are attained through natural progression, but there might be a few you miss along the way. Luckily, upon completing both the single-player and co-op facets of the Portal 2 story, you're able to jump back into any of the chapters. This is done via the hub in co-op, where you can also mess around gesturing and playing rock, paper, scissors to your heart's content. All in all, Portal 2's achievement list is excellent then.
A riveting journey from start to finish, Portal 2 is yet another unmitigated triumph for Valve, building upon an original concept that was incredible to begin with and making it even more incredible. At times it might have you tearing your hair out, but ultimately if you loved Portal 1 (and who didn't?), you're going to eat up Portal 2 like a big old piece of vanilla crazy cake.

Portal 2 takes elements of adventure, puzzle, platform and first-person action games and blends them into a unique genre mix. It builds on the foundation of its acclaimed predecessor, takes all the gameplay elements that made it great and vastly improves them in every aspect. With that said, I strongly recommend to play Portal first. If you don't you will still play through the sequel without any confusion, Portals plot was minimal (even though exceptionally well-written) and the basic puzzle design is picked up in Portal 2. But you would miss out on a great game and why would you want to do that?
Once again you take over Chell, Portals female protagonist, who finds herself rudely awakened from a cryogenic sleep and imprisoned in a small chamber inside the Aperture Science testing facility, an environment vaguely familiar from Portal - vaguely because a lot seems to have changed since your first time around. Some of the structures at the beginning of the game are indeed places you have already seen during your first escape but this time they are clearly aged, in a state of decay, overgrown with plants and seemingly abandoned. But soon you will have to make your way through unknown terrain and new test chambers that turn out to be anything but abandoned. Fans of Portal will be pleased to learn that GLaDOS makes its reappearance. Something else is different right from the start: You are now accompanied by a british-accented robot named Wheatley, who insists that an escape can only be accomplished together.
Portal 2 really shines in the writing department, the story is much more developed compared to the first installment. Many unanswered questions are revealed, such as bits and pieces of Aperture Sciences history and the origin of GLaDOS personality. Where GLaDOS was Portals only speaking character you now get to hear your goofy sidekick Wheatley and, through pre-recorded messages, Aperture Science founder Cave Johnson. All voice actors did an outstanding job and manage to really bring all three speaking characters to life.
If you played first-person shooters before you will be instantly familiar with the controls, mouse for camera movement, WASD to move, space to jump and left & right mouse buttons to shoot your portal gun. All game mechanics from Portal like pressure buttons, disintegration fields and of course the eponymous blue and orange portals, that are surprisingly simple in theory but make for surprisingly diverse and challenging puzzles, made it into the sequel and in addition many more are added: different sorts of gel that let you jump higher or run faster, catapults, light bridges, air tubes and lasers. Each element of its own already makes for complex puzzles but once the game starts to combine several of them you're in for a real challenge.
Compared to its predecessor, the game provides a lot more content. Not only is the single player campaign about twice as long, it even adds an extensive second co-op campaign. Two players open a lot more puzzle opportunities and the devs managed to use them to their fullest. But don't worry, you are given various means of communication. It's recommended to simply plugin your headset and make use of Steams voice chat feature but even if you don't you can still highlight spots by simply pressing a key, start countdowns to synchronize your actions, open a small screen that lets you look through the eyes of your co-op partner and perform small gestures to communicate non-verbally. Or you could just utilize the ingame chat to write.
But it doesn't end here. Thanks to user generated content the replayability is almost unlimited. When you mastered both campaigns, just tap into the huge library of player generated chambers, even whole campaigns are available to download, and keep playing with ever new challenges.
When you compare the visuals to Portal you cannot help but appreciate the excellent graphic design. While Portals test chambers looked bland and lifeless, they're now impoved with many small details. You have moving, transforming environments, plants growing through cracks in the walls and especially the vast, subterranean areas later in the game are a stunning sight.
Long story short: Portal 2 takes the premise of its predecessor and takes it to a whole new level. A game for the books.

I don't know which is better, Portal 1 or 2. If you haven't played either, then you need to start with part one. Otherwise, you aren't going to get much of the story or the humor in two. After I played Portal One, my mouth just hung open as I realized that I had just played one of the greatest video games in history, which was a pretty amazing experience. Seriously, if you haven't given the Portal series a chance, I highly recommend it. I know that not everyone is going to like a particular game or series of games, but I think this series is so good, it would be foolish of someone to not at least try the Portal One demo to see if they might enjoy it.
I think the only reason I didn't have that same reaction to Portal 2, is because I had played part one first, so I knew what to expect, and much of the groundbreaking and perfectly executed aspects of the game just didn't have the same effect on me at that point. Nevertheless, taking a step back from it, and keeping an open mind, I think that Portal 2 is equally as good if not better than part one.
J.K. Simmons and Stephen Merchant appear in Part Two and as I expected they were both spot on. Just brilliant voice over work that was a nice change from the first Portal. While there is no denvying that Glados was well writen and performed, she did become grating to me about 3/4 of the way through in the first game as I grew weary of her somewhat monotone delivery and at that point, predictability.
There is a nice mix of puzzles, world exploration, and advancement through the facility. It would have been a huge mistake on the part of the developers to force the player to solve testing chambers for the game's entirety, but thankfully they did not.
The character arcs are well written and keep you on the edge of your seat as you watch their demeanor and personalities change throught the course of the story. Again, this is accomlished largely in part to the perfect voice over work provided by Stephen Merchant. I can't praise his performance enough.
The graphics are very pretty and the game is well optimized to run on just about any desktop or laptop. I think you could even run this on the Intel HD series IGPs.
The puzzles are difficult, but not overly. It's a perfect chalenge level. So, anybody shold be able to complete the game to see the beautiful story in it's entirely.
MULTIPLAYER! Oh man, this was such a good move on Valve's part. Not only does it add a whole bunch of new challaneges and levels, but now you can work together with a friend to complete a whole slew of new specially designed co-op puzzles. Most importantly, playing co-op is a crapload of fun. From the satisfaction of completing a level together, to ragging on your teammate for not being able to complete a task necessary to finish the puzzle. The taunt/praise system is hilarious and my friend and I never grew tired of knocking each other upside the head or high fiving each other at the end of each level. The indcator system used to non-verbally communicate with your partner is brilliant and necessary if you can't use VOIP. The only negative comment I have for the co-op portion is that it was too short and there was not much of a story. Small things IMO.
So anyway, overall Portal 2 is one of the greatest games in the history of PC gaming and I highly suggest you give the series a try even if my review, trailers, or screen shots make it seem like it might not be your cup of tea, You won't know for sure, unless you dive in. So, what are you waiting for? The deep end of the pool is where the grown-ups play.

Portal 2 is a good game worth playing. Let me say that first and foremost. Yes, if you have the money and are considering getting it, you should.
However, if you haven't played Portal 1, play that instead. While Portal 2 has more puzzles and better graphics, I don't think it's a better game. The average puzzle in Portal 1 has 4-8 solutions, and the tutorial puzzles show enough that you learn how to use the mechanics, without making you feel like you're being told how to play. Portal 2 takes the subtle parts that made the first game a masterpiece and sort of hamhandles them. The average puzzle in Portal 2 has 1-3 solutions. The introduction of new mechanics, such as the goop, initially makes for more interesting puzzles, but ultimately creates a need to make the puzzles more restrictive and less intuitive. I didn't finish the game. I am an avid puzzle gamer, but one puzzle near the end of the game required such precision, timing, and execution that I couldn't manage it with the level of awareness I had.
Of course, being a very social gamer, a friend and I flew through the multiplayer maps with no difficulty. I think I will attribute that to the lack of goop.
TL:DR good game, the first one was better
